### UI Automation Commands (6)
docs.title: API-Reference#230

docs.body:
The interface as a command surface: list the visible windows, catalogue their controls, click
and type as the person would, capture a window, and switch reduced motion. Every control is
addressed by a stable identifier, never by its translated text: manifest-driven controls carry
their command id (`io.toggleConnection`, `app.preferences`), hand-built controls a lowercase
dotted literal (`console.send`, `setup.uart.baudRate`, `settings.general.language`), repeated
delegates fold in the identity of what they show (`dashboard.tile.3.close`,
`taskbar.window.7`), and windows are named after their file (`main`, `settings`,
`projectEditor`, `external.<widgetIndex>`). Roles follow the accessibility vocabulary:
`button`, `checkbox`, `radiobutton`, `switch`, `pagetab`, `menuitem`, `combobox`,
`editabletext`, `spinbox`, `slider`, `tile`, and `item` for a named control of no other kind.
Geometry is in window coordinates; multiply by the window's `scale` for pixels. A headless run
has no window: `listWindows` answers an empty list and the others an `EXECUTION_ERROR`.
docs.title: API-Reference#231

docs.body:
Through the AI Assistant, the two driving commands are device-gated and the screenshot is
Confirm-tier; see [The safety tiers](AI-Assistant.md#the-safety-tiers).

#### 🟢 `ui.automation.listWindows`
List the visible windows as `[{id, title, x, y, width, height, scale, active, modal, focusedId}]`.
`modal` is true while a modal popup is open in that window; `focusedId` names the control that
holds keyboard focus.

**Parameters:** None
docs.title: API-Reference#232

docs.body:
#### 🟢 `ui.automation.listElements`
List the interactive controls of a window as `[{id, role, label, text, x, y, width, height,
enabled, checked, focused, state}]`, in drawing order. `text` is present for editable fields, combos,
spin boxes and sliders; `checked` for controls that have the property. A masked field (a password
or key with a non-normal echo mode) reports no text and no label taken from its contents.
`state` is present for a control that publishes one: an output control's cell
(`dashboard.output.<groupId>.<widgetId>`) reports `outcome` (`none`, `waiting`, `acknowledged`,
`refused` or `unanswered`), `token`, `code`, `message`, `waiting`, `known`, `holding` and
`outOfRange`. Read `token` before and after driving the control to know the outcome is the
answer to your own command. A masked field never reports `state`.
docs.title: API-Reference#233

docs.body:
**Parameters:**
- `window` (string, optional): Window id, default `main`
- `id` (string, optional): Case-insensitive substring of the identifier
- `label` (string, optional): Case-insensitive substring of the label
docs.title: API-Reference#234

docs.body:
#### 🟢 `ui.automation.click`
Click a control by id, or a point in window coordinates, as the person would. A control that
is hidden, disabled or has no size is refused with `EXECUTION_ERROR`; a point outside the
window with `INVALID_PARAM`. The reply is `{hit, id, x, y, delivered}`: `hit` says a control
lies under the point after delivery, `id` names it, and `delivered` confirms the events were
dispatched. Needs the interface-driving consent from a remote client. A control that opens a
native file dialog blocks the application until a person dismisses the dialog, so drive the
path-taking commands instead of such buttons. The same holds for any control whose handler
opens a modal message box: the command is parked in that dialog's event loop until a person
answers, and commands served meanwhile run as nested dispatches, which take no pre-mutation
checkpoint. A command id can sit on more than one control
(the ribbon button, a menu item, a start-menu entry); the click goes to the first in drawing
order, the ribbon button unless a menu is open, and `listElements` with the `id` filter lists
every carrier.
docs.title: API-Reference#235

docs.body:
**Parameters:**
- `window` (string, optional): Window id, default `main`
- `id` (string, optional): Element id to click; alternatively give `x` and `y`
- `x` (number, optional): X in window coordinates
- `y` (number, optional): Y in window coordinates
- `button` (string, optional): `left` (default), `right` or `middle`
- `modifiers` (array of string, optional): Held modifiers among `ctrl`, `shift`, `alt`, `meta`
- `double` (boolean, optional): Double-click instead of a single click

#### 🟢 `ui.automation.key`
Type `text` one character at a time and press `keys`, a key sequence in `QKeySequence` notation
(`Ctrl+S`, `Down`, `Backspace`), after focusing the optional `target`. The reply is
`{delivered, focusedId}`. Needs the interface-driving consent from a remote client.
docs.title: API-Reference#236

docs.body:
**Parameters:**
- `window` (string, optional): Window id, default `main`
- `target` (string, optional): Element id to focus first
- `text` (string, optional): Text to type (up to 4096 characters)
- `keys` (string, optional): Key sequence to press

#### 🟢 `ui.automation.screenshot`
Capture a window, or one control of it, as a base64 PNG: `{png, width, height, scale}`. With
HDR output active the capture is converted back to standard dynamic range. The scale halves
until the reply fits 4 MiB, and the scale applied is returned.

**Parameters:**
- `window` (string, optional): Window id, default `main`
- `id` (string, optional): Element id to crop to
- `scale` (number, optional): Downscale factor from 0.1 to 1, default 1
docs.title: API-Reference#237

docs.body:
#### 🟢 `ui.automation.setReduceMotion`
Switch the reduced-motion preference, the same setting as the Preferences toggle, and return
`{enabled, previous}` so a client can restore it. With it on, popups and menus appear without
their entrance animation, which keeps a screenshot taken right after a click deterministic.

**Parameters:**
- `enabled` (boolean): Whether chrome motion is reduced

Convenience commands the in-app [AI Assistant](AI-Assistant.md) uses, each one a documented

mode, enable the matching dataset option, patch the ranges, and add the widget. Returns

docs.title: API-Reference#240

docs.body:
**Parameters:**

- `workspaceId` (int) or `workspace` (string): Target workspace

#### 🔵 `io.canbus.getConfig`
Get current CAN bus configuration.

**Parameters:** None

**Returns:** the selected plugin and interface, the bitrate pair, the `loopback`, `listenOnly` and
`tpReassembly` flags, `isOpen`, `configurationOk`, and `interfaceError` when the last open failed.
`reassembly` carries the pulled multi-frame counters, one sub-object per protocol:

```json
{
  "tpReassembly": true,
  "reassembly": {
    "enabled": true,
    "j1939": {"completed": 128, "timeouts": 0, "aborted": 1, "malformed": 0,
              "sizeOverruns": 0, "sequenceErrors": 2, "sessionOverruns": 0},
    "isotp": {"completed": 44, "timeouts": 3, "aborted": 0, "malformed": 0,
              "sizeOverruns": 0, "sequenceErrors": 0, "sessionOverruns": 0}
  }
}
```
docs.title: API-Reference#249

docs.body:
The counters are cumulative since the option was last toggled: unticking and re-ticking the
checkbox clears them and discards any half-collected session.
Multi-frame reassembly itself is enabled in the Setup panel; see
[CAN Bus Driver](Drivers-CAN-Bus.md#multi-frame-reassembly).

### MQTT Commands - Pro (6)
docs.title: API-Reference#266

docs.body:
**Note:** These commands require a Serial Studio Pro license.

MQTT is split into two independent surfaces, each configured with a single
patch-style `setConfig` command instead of one command per field. The
**publisher** forwards dashboard data to a broker and runs alongside any data
source. The **subscriber** is the MQTT data-source driver: configure it here,
then open it with `io.setBusType` + `io.connect` like any other driver.

Shared rules for both `setConfig` commands:
docs.title: API-Reference#267

docs.body:
- Pass only the keys you want to change; omitted keys keep their values.
- Setting `password` requires `username` in the same call. The pair is stored
  in the machine's credential vault, obfuscated in the machine's settings, never
  in the project file, and is never returned by `getConfig` (check `hasCredentials` instead). Pass empty strings
  for both to clear the stored pair.
- Enum-valued fields (`mqttVersion`, `sslProtocol`, `peerVerifyMode`) take
  integer indices; `getConfig` returns the canonical lookup tables
  (`mqttVersions`, `sslProtocols`, `peerVerifyModes`).

#### 🔵 `project.mqtt.publisher.getConfig`
Read the publisher configuration (broker, mode, TLS). Includes the enum lookup
tables and `hasCredentials`.
docs.title: API-Reference#268

docs.body:
**Parameters:** None

#### 🔵 `project.mqtt.publisher.setConfig`
Patch one or more publisher fields. Setting `enabled: true` starts publishing.

**Parameters (all optional):**
- `enabled` (bool): Start or stop publishing
- `hostname` (string), `port` (int): Broker endpoint
- `clientId` (string), `customClientId` (bool): Client identity; with
  `customClientId: false` the ID regenerates automatically
- `username`, `password` (string): Credential pair (vault rules above)
- `topicBase` (string): Publish topic root
- `mode` (int): 0=RawRxData, 1=ScriptDriven, 2=DashboardCsv, 3=DashboardJson
- `publishFrequency` (int): Publish rate in Hz (1-30)
- `publishNotifications` (bool), `notificationTopic` (string): Forward app
  notifications to MQTT
- `cleanSession` (bool), `keepAlive` (int): Session settings
- `mqttVersion`, `sslEnabled`, `sslProtocol`, `peerVerifyMode`,
  `peerVerifyDepth`: Protocol and TLS settings
docs.title: API-Reference#269

docs.body:
#### 🔵 `project.mqtt.publisher.getStatus`
Snapshot of publisher live state (`connected`, `messagesSent`, broker
endpoint). Does not trigger a connection attempt.

**Parameters:** None

#### 🔵 `project.mqtt.subscriber.getConfig`
Read the subscriber driver configuration, as used the next time `io.connect`
runs with the MQTT bus type. Password is never returned.

**Parameters:** None

#### 🔵 `project.mqtt.subscriber.setConfig`
Patch one or more subscriber driver fields. Changing fields while connected
schedules a reconnect.

**Parameters (all optional):**
- `hostname` (string), `port` (int): Broker endpoint
- `clientId` (string): Client identity
- `username`, `password` (string): Credential pair (vault rules above)
- `topicFilter` (string): Subscribe filter; `+` and `#` wildcards supported
- `cleanSession` (bool), `keepAlive` (int), `autoKeepAlive` (bool): Session
  settings
- `mqttVersion`, `sslEnabled`, `sslProtocol`, `peerVerifyMode`,
  `peerVerifyDepth`: Protocol and TLS settings
docs.title: API-Reference#270

docs.body:

## Calling the API from Frame Parsers, Transforms, and Canvas Widgets

Lua and JavaScript project scripts can call any command in this reference through `apiCall()`, with no TCP socket: the call is dispatched in process on the dashboard thread. A project's own scripts are first-party code, so the gateway has no allow-list, rate limit or payload cap for them. Consent prompts apply only to remote clients, except that starting a program asks once per project whoever causes it. See [Consent Prompts](#consent-prompts) and [Frame Parser Scripting](Frame-Parser.md).

```lua
local r = apiCall("project.dataset.list")
if r.ok then
  print("Got " .. #r.result.datasets .. " datasets")
end
```

### Custom Client (Python)

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import socket
import json
import time

class SerialStudioAPI:
    def __init__(self, host="127.0.0.1", port=7777):
        self.host = host
        self.port = port

def send_command(self, command, params=None):
        sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
        sock.connect((self.host, self.port))

msg = {
            "type": "command",
            "id": f"cmd-{time.time()}",
            "command": command
        }
        if params:
            msg["params"] = params

## Best Practices

### Reuse one connection

Open the socket once and send every command on it. Opening a socket per command works but costs a handshake each time. A monitoring loop that polls `io.getStatus` once a second belongs on one long-lived connection.

### Batch related commands

A batch sends several commands in one line and gets all the results back in one response, which saves round trips. Every command in a batch runs even after one fails, so read each entry of `results`.

```json
{
  "type": "batch",
  "commands": [
    {"command": "io.setBusType", "id": "1", "params": {"busType": 0}},
    {"command": "io.uart.setBaudRate", "id": "2", "params": {"baudRate": 115200}},
    {"command": "io.connect", "id": "3"}
  ]
}
```
docs.title: API-Reference#310

docs.body:
### Check every response

```python
response = api.send("io.connect")
if not response.get("success"):
    error = response.get("error", {})
    print(f"{error.get('code')}: {error.get('message')}")
```

`EXECUTION_ERROR` means the command was valid but could not run in the current state, for example a connect with no port selected. Ask for valid values with the list commands (`io.uart.listPorts`, `io.uart.listBaudRates`) instead of hard-coding them.

### Clean up in a finally block

```python
try:
    api.send("io.connect")
    api.send("csvExport.setEnabled", enabled=True)
    # ... do the work ...
finally:
    api.send("csvExport.close")
    api.send("io.disconnect")
```

## Troubleshooting

### Cannot Connect to API Server

1. Check that Serial Studio is running and that **Enable API Server** is on (Preferences, **General** tab, **API & Plugins**).
2. Check the port. The default is 7777; the **API Server Port** setting or `--api-port` may have changed it.
3. From another machine, check that **Allow External API Connections** is on, that the firewall lets the port through, and that your client sends the access token as its first line.
4. Test with `nc localhost 7777` (Linux and macOS) or the Python client from [Quick Start](#quick-start).
docs.title: API-Reference#312

docs.body:
### Commands Return Errors

`UNKNOWN_COMMAND` means the name is misspelled (names are case-sensitive) or the command belongs to a Pro driver and your build is GPL. `INVALID_PARAM` means a value is out of range or the wrong type. List the live commands with `api.getCommands`, and ask for valid values with `io.uart.listBaudRates`, `io.uart.listPorts` and the other list commands.

### CONSENT_REQUIRED

Serial Studio is showing a Yes/No prompt for the action, for example sending data to the device. Click Yes in the Serial Studio window and send the command again. See [Consent Prompts](#consent-prompts).
docs.title: API-Reference#313

docs.body:
### Batch Commands Fail

Check that the line is valid JSON, that `commands` is a non-empty array, and test each command alone first. The `id` of a command is optional.

### Connection Drops

The server never closes an idle connection. It closes yours when you send more than 200 messages in one second, fail authentication 3 times, send a line over 1 MiB, or when someone changes the **API Server Port** or turns the server off. See [Limits](#limits).

### Response IDs Don't Match

Lines with a `frames`, `data` or `event` key are push messages, not responses. Skip them and match `"type":"response"` by `id`. See [Server-Push Messages](#server-push-messages).
docs.title: API-Reference#314

docs.body:
### Pro Commands Not Available

Commands for Modbus, CAN Bus, MQTT, MDF4, Audio, USB, HID and Process I/O are not registered in a GPL build, which answers `UNKNOWN_COMMAND`. In the official binary, Pro features need an active license or the 14-day trial, which Serial Studio offers with a Yes/No prompt the first time you use a Pro feature (internet required). See [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md).

### Execution Error

`EXECUTION_ERROR` means the command failed in the current state. Check preconditions (you must be disconnected before changing the bus type), that the device configuration is valid, and that the hardware exists (the serial port is present).

docs.body:
### How It Works

The MCP handler wraps the Serial Studio TCP API (port 7777) in an MCP-compliant interface. Any MCP-capable client can discover and call more than 440 API commands as tools. The same socket serves both protocols: a JSON-RPC 2.0 message is answered as MCP, a `{"command": ...}` envelope as the TCP API.

Each tool carries a `title` and the MCP annotations that follow the in-app assistant's safety tiers: `readOnlyHint` on reads and queries, `destructiveHint` on the delete, clear, open-replace, credential and device-control families, and neither on reversible project or application settings. The licensing mutations and the process launcher are not listed. A hint describes a tool; it never authorizes a call, because every call passes the same remote gate and consent prompts as the TCP API. The server answers protocol revisions 2024-11-05, 2025-03-26 and 2025-06-18, echoing the revision the client offers in `initialize` and answering 2025-06-18 to any other.
docs.title: API-Reference#317

docs.body:
### Session Rules

The first JSON-RPC message makes a connection an MCP session. From then on it receives replies only: no frame broadcasts, raw device data or connection events arrive on it, so a client can read the stream line by line as JSON-RPC. Telemetry is read on request, with `resources/read` on `serialstudio://frame/current`, or by polling `dashboard.getData` or `dashboard.tailFrames`.

The five connection-scoped push commands (`mirror.subscribe`, `mirror.setRate`, `mirror.unsubscribe`, `stream.subscribe` and `stream.unsubscribe`) are refused on an MCP session. Called as a tool, they return an `isError` result that names the pull path. Sent as a `{"type":"command"}` line, they return an `EXECUTION_ERROR` with the same text. A plain TCP client that never sends JSON-RPC keeps receiving the broadcasts.
docs.title: API-Reference#318

docs.body:
### Errors

A tool call that fails, including one a gate refuses, returns a successful JSON-RPC response whose result has `isError: true`. The first text block holds the message. The second holds compact JSON with the `error` (`code`, `message` and `data` when present), the `tool`, the `providedArguments` and, when the cause is a bad argument, the `parameter`, `receivedValue`, `receivedType` and a `suggestion`. `receivedType` uses the JSON names `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `object`, `array` and `null`.

Only protocol faults are JSON-RPC errors: a parse error, an invalid request, a call before `initialize`, an unknown method, a missing tool name, an unknown tool, and `arguments` that is not an object (`-32602`).
docs.title: API-Reference#319

docs.body:
### Resources

`resources/list` and `resources/read` expose the current frame. Resource subscription is not supported: `initialize` advertises no `subscribe` capability, and `resources/subscribe` and `resources/unsubscribe` answer `-32601`.

### Use Cases

- Ask Claude to "connect to the serial port and start logging" without writing any code
- Have an AI assistant automate test sequences (connect → configure → export → disconnect)
- Use ChatGPT to analyze live sensor data and suggest configuration changes
- Script hardware-in-the-loop tests driven by an AI model

1. Enable the API Server in Serial Studio (Preferences → General → API & Plugins → Enable API Server).
2. **Claude Code or Cowork:** install the **Serial Studio** plugin (`serial-studio`) from the Claude directory. The plugin starts the bridge, lists the tools and bundles a skill that states the prerequisite, the read-first workflow and the consent prompts; no configuration file is edited. If your Arduino or ESP32 prints lines like `21.5,48,1013` with `Serial.println`, Serial Studio plots them in Quick Plot mode with no setup. To plot your first line, open [Getting Started](Getting-Started.md); [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md) lists what each edition includes. The rest of this page is project history and an overview of the 4.x feature set.

## Author

Serial Studio is built by **Alex Spataru**. The project started as a one-person tool for satellite and rover ground-station work, and is still primarily developed by Alex, with contributions from the open-source community on [GitHub](https://github.com/Serial-Studio/Serial-Studio). Anyone can read the source, file issues, and submit patches under GPL-3.0. The optional Pro edition funds development.
docs.title: About#0

docs.body:
## The problem that started it

Before Serial Studio, Alex worked on a [CanSat competition](https://cansatcompetition.com/) and later on the [NASA Human Exploration Rover Challenge](https://www.nasa.gov/learning-resources/nasa-human-exploration-rover-challenge/) during college. The CanSat work came with its own ground-station software, custom-written for that competition's telemetry format. Every protocol tweak meant another late night in the dashboard code instead of on the hardware. The pattern repeated across teams and semesters: a microcontroller printed sensor values over a serial cable, and somebody had to build a custom GUI around them.
docs.title: About#1

docs.body:
The first attempt at a generic answer was a personal project called **SigLAB**. It worked. The data model was already protocol-agnostic, and the dashboard was already data-driven. It was later renamed and moved to its own GitHub organization, with room for outside contributors.

On October 18, 2020 the SigLAB codebase was imported into a new repository under [github.com/Serial-Studio](https://github.com/Serial-Studio). The literal first commit message in this repo is *"Initial commit from SigLAB codebase"*, and the project took on its current name.

The launch blog post, [*Introducing Serial Studio*](https://www.aspatru.com/blog/introducing-serial-studio) (December 29, 2020), opens with the line that still describes the project:
docs.title: About#2

docs.body:
> *Did you ever have the need to display data from a microcontroller on a dashboard, and spent more time developing (and fixing) your dashboard software, than working on your MCU project?*

## Philosophy

Three ideas have stayed constant since 2020:
docs.title: About#3

docs.body:
1. **One tool, many devices.** You should not have to write a new dashboard every time you swap microcontrollers. Describe the data once in a project file (a `.ssproj` you build in the Project Editor), and each comma-separated value becomes a dataset: one named number that gets a plot, gauge or bar.
2. **The microcontroller stays simple.** The original blog post offered two modes: the device sent a self-describing JSON frame, or bare CSV with the dashboard layout living on the PC. Serial Studio kept the second idea (there is no Auto/Manual switch today). Project files configure frame parsing entirely on the PC. A frame parser is a small script that turns one line from your device into numbers, so firmware can keep printing comma-separated values.
3. **GPL core, optional Pro.** The source is GPL-3.0. A GPL build compiled from source contains the free feature set: Serial/UART, TCP, UDP, WebSocket, HTTP, Bluetooth LE, the standard widgets (see [Widget Reference](Widget-Reference.md)), Quick Plot, the full Project Editor, CSV export, the API Server, and Lua/JavaScript frame parsers. The official binary adds the Pro features, which unlock with a license or the trial. Without a license it runs the free features with no time limit for personal, educational, and open-source use; commercial use needs Pro. The first time you use a Pro feature, Serial Studio asks whether to start a 14-day trial (Yes/No; it needs an internet connection to register). After the trial ends, the prompt offers activation or purchase. See [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md).
docs.title: About#4

docs.body:
## How the project evolved

Serial Studio grew driver-by-driver as users brought new hardware to it. Most additions were not planned in advance. They came from a specific request and got generalized once they worked.

### Connectivity, in the order it landed

The Edition column marks each driver Free or Pro. The table is partial; [Communication Protocols](Communication-Protocols.md) covers the rest, including free WebSocket and HTTP and Pro OPC UA.
docs.title: About#5

docs.body:
| Driver | Landed | Edition | What prompted it |
|--------|--------|---------|------------------|
| Serial/UART | October 2020 | Free | The original transport, inherited from SigLAB. |
| TCP and UDP | early 2021 (UDP multicast October 2021) | Free | Running Serial Studio on a different machine from the device. This is when "Serial Studio" stopped being literally about serial. |
| MQTT | February-March 2021 | Pro | IoT users who wanted to bridge a fleet of devices through a broker. Publisher and subscriber. |
| Bluetooth Low Energy | February 2022 | Free | Wireless sensors and boards (ESP32, nRF52) without a USB cable. GATT services and characteristics. |
| Audio input | July 2025 | Pro | Microphones and line-in as a high-rate analog input. It added the FFT pipeline the rest of the dashboard reuses. |
| Modbus and CAN Bus | December 2025 | Pro | The first industrial drivers. Modbus TCP and RTU with a register-map importer; CAN Bus with a DBC importer. |
| Raw USB (libusb) | February 2026 | Pro | Devices with vendor-specific USB endpoints instead of a CDC serial profile, such as logic analyzers and custom acquisition boards. |
| HID and Process I/O | March 2026 | Pro | HID for game controllers and custom HID firmware; Process I/O for piping in output from `socat`, `nc`, or a Python script. |
docs.title: About#6

docs.body:
### Visualization and analysis

The widget set started with line plots, gauges, bar charts, and a GPS map in late 2020, and slowly grew into the current widget set. The bigger inflection points were:

- **XY plot** (November 2024, free) for arbitrary x/y mappings instead of time-on-x.
- **3D plot** (May 2025, Pro). It renders on the CPU, not Qt3D, so it needs no discrete GPU.
- **Image View** (Pro): live camera feed.
- **Canvas widget** (Pro, May 2026): a scriptable Canvas2D-style canvas driven by a JavaScript `paint(ctx, w, h)` callback, for visualizations that don't fit any standard widget.
- **FFT Plot** (free) and **Waterfall / spectrogram** (Pro), April 2026. They share the same per-dataset FFT settings.
docs.title: About#7

docs.body:
### The 1.0 to 2.0 rewrite

Serial Studio 1.x was a working dashboard, but the architecture had clear ceilings. Frame parsing was hard-coded around the JSON and CSV split from the original blog post, so any new frame layout meant patching C++ and shipping a new release. The UI was assembled out of the original SigLAB widgets and didn't scale cleanly as new visualizations were added.

The 2.0 release was effectively a new application sharing a name with the old one. The whole UI was rebuilt from scratch on Qt Quick. The biggest change was the **JavaScript frame parser**: every project carried a small `parse(frame)` function, so any framing convention (delimited, fixed-length, key/value, custom binary) could be handled without recompiling. It turned Serial Studio from a CSV/JSON viewer into a general-purpose telemetry tool.
docs.title: About#8

docs.body:
### The 2.0 to 3.0 rewrite

Version 3.0 rebuilt the data path for speed. The frame pipeline was redesigned so the dashboard handles 256 kHz+ frame rates, and the CI benchmark gates on that figure. The visible feature set barely changed.

The 3.x line that followed (v3.0.0 in October 2024 through v3.2.7 in March 2026) was additive: the connectivity and visualization growth in the sections above landed here. A taskbar and window manager arrived in mid-2025, so dashboard widgets float, snap, and tile like application windows, and the API Server (MCP over TCP, July 2025) opened the project and live data to external programs.
docs.title: About#9

docs.body:
### The 3.0 to 4.0 rewrite

Version 4.0 (the current release line) widened the scope from showing telemetry to running a station that an operator can use for a shift. It added:

- A shared data bus (Variables) and per-dataset transforms, so calibration and derived values live in the project instead of in firmware, plus a Lua engine (LuaJIT 2.1, 5.1 syntax) next to JavaScript for frame parsing and transforms.
- A Historian with replay and PDF reports.
- Output (control) widgets and a Control Loop scripting SDK, so Serial Studio can drive a device as well as read it.
- Operator deployments and a Project Lock, so an engineer can hand a fixed dashboard to an operator without exposing the editor.
- AI integration: external agents reach the same commands over MCP and gRPC, and an in-app assistant uses them too.
docs.title: About#10

docs.body:
3.x projects load as-is.

## Where the project is now

### Variables: a shared data bus (Pro)

Datasets are no longer islands. Every project carries an auto-generated **system table** with `raw:<id>` and `final:<id>` variables for every dataset, plus user-defined tables of `Constant` (project-time) and `Computed` (per-frame) variables. Frame parsers, value transforms, and output widgets all read and write the same variables, so a sensor calibration is written once. See [Variables](Variables.md).

### Per-dataset value transforms (Pro)

Each dataset can carry a small Lua or JavaScript snippet that defines a `transform(value)` function returning a number. It runs every frame. Transforms compile once when the project loads. They can also derive computed datasets (no frame index, computed entirely from other variables), which is how running averages, rate-of-change, and derived KPIs become datasets of their own. See [Dataset Value Transforms](Dataset-Transforms.md).
docs.title: About#11

docs.body:
### Output (control) widgets (Pro)

Buttons, toggles, sliders, knobs, text fields, and a freeform Output Panel send data *back* to the device. Each one runs a JavaScript template to convert UI state into bytes, whether the device speaks GCode, Modbus, CAN, or a custom binary format. A Transmit Test Dialog previews the wire output before you send the real command. See [Output Controls](Output-Controls.md).

### Control Loop and the scripting SDK (free)
docs.title: About#12

docs.body: The Control Loop is a `setup()` / `loop()` script, the same model as an Arduino sketch, that Serial Studio runs on a worker thread while a device is connected. Find it in the Project Editor under **Project Scripts > Control Loop**; a project carries one. Through the `io.*` scripting SDK the loop can send wake-up sequences, poll registers on a timer, or step a state machine, without touching firmware. A watchdog bounds each call, so a slow script can't stall parsing or the UI. The loop needs no license; some calls inside it (notifications, Variables tables) are Pro. See [Control Loop](Control-Loop.md).
docs.title: About#13

docs.body:
### Historian (Pro)

Serial Studio Pro can record sessions into a SQLite `.db` file. Parsed frames, raw bytes, table snapshots, and project metadata all live in one file. The Historian browses, tags, and exports sessions. The SQLite Player replays a stored session through the same path as live data so dashboards and reports work identically on recorded data. Session Reports turn the same database into a styled PDF with cover, test info, summary, and per-parameter chart sections. See [Historian](Historian.md) and [Session Reports](Session-Reports.md).

### File transmission (Pro)

XMODEM, YMODEM, and ZMODEM are built in for firmware uploads and log retrieval. ZMODEM resumes after an interrupted transfer. This is a Pro feature; builds compiled from source with GPL modules only do not include it. See [File Transmission](File-Transmission.md).
docs.title: About#14

docs.body:
### Operator deployments (Pro)

A deployment is a saved native launcher (`.lnk` / `.app` / `.desktop`) that opens a specific project with a fixed set of runtime flags (toolbar hidden, optional auto-connect and fullscreen). The operator gets a single icon instead of hunting for the right `.ssproj`. Generating a deployment requires a Pro license, and the target machine also needs a Pro build: a GPL build refuses the runtime flags and fails to launch. See [Operator Deployments](Operator-Deployments.md).

### Project Lock (all builds)

A Project Lock puts a password gate (salted PBKDF2-SHA256, stored in the project file) in front of the Project Editor, so an operator can run the dashboard but can't rewire parsers or move widgets mid-shift. It is not license-gated. Project Lock and deployments are not security boundaries; they separate operator from engineer. See [Project Lock](Project-Lock.md).
docs.title: About#15

docs.body:
### AI integration

- **API Server, MCP over TCP (GPL build and Pro).** The API Server is off by default. Enable it under **Preferences > General > API & Plugins** and it listens on TCP port 7777. It is a JSON-RPC API with a large command set (the GPL build has a subset), wrapped in the Model Context Protocol so any MCP host (Claude Desktop, custom agents, automation scripts) can read live values, edit projects, and manage sessions. The gRPC server (port 8888) starts only while the API Server is enabled. See [API Reference](API-Reference.md) and [gRPC Server](gRPC-Server.md).
- **In-app AI Assistant (Pro).** A bring-your-own-key chat panel that edits the project for you. Multiple providers are wired in: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini, DeepSeek, Groq, OpenRouter, and Mistral, plus any OpenAI-compatible local server (Ollama, llama.cpp, LM Studio, vLLM) for fully offline use. See [AI Assistant](AI-Assistant.md).
docs.title: About#16

docs.body:
The in-app AI Assistant (Pro) calls the same commands as the API Server. It runs read-only commands without asking. By default anything that changes the project shows an Approve/Deny card; the **Auto-approve edits** toggle in the Assistant panel's top bar settings menu lets reversible edits run without asking (off by default). Connection control (connect/disconnect, `io.*` device settings) stays blocked until you tick **Allow device control** in the same menu, and even then every such call asks for confirmation, so a wrong answer cannot knock you offline mid-shift.

## Where to learn more

Source and releases are on [GitHub](https://github.com/Serial-Studio/Serial-Studio), questions go in [Discussions](https://github.com/Serial-Studio/Serial-Studio/discussions), bugs in [Issues](https://github.com/Serial-Studio/Serial-Studio/issues), and [Getting Started](Getting-Started.md) walks you through a first project.

Actions#0

docs.body:
The **Reset Device** button sits in a strip above the dashboard widgets and becomes clickable once you connect. Clicking it sends the four bytes `52 53 54 0A` (the letters R, S, T, then a newline) and saves you typing `RST` and Enter on every reset. The steps are under [Creating an action](#creating-an-action).

Actions are available in the free edition. They belong to a project file, so open or create a project first (see [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md)). For continuous controls such as sliders and knobs, or for custom JavaScript transmit functions, see [Output Controls](Output-Controls.md): a Pro feature, and the first use offers a free trial (internet needed to register).
docs.title: Actions#1

docs.body:
## Creating an action

1. Open or create a project, then open the Project Editor (toolbar wrench icon).
2. Click **Action** in the Project Editor toolbar (in the Output section).
3. Select the new action in the project tree. Its properties open in the panel on the right. Rename it in **Action Title**.

## Action properties

### General information

**Action Title** is the label on the dashboard button (for example "Reset Device"), and **Action Icon** is picked from the built-in icon set; the icon also appears in the Project Editor flow diagram.

**Target Device** picks which connected device receives the command. The dropdown appears only when the project has more than one source. It lists the sources by title, and the default is the first source (shown as Device A unless you renamed it). The flow diagram draws an arrow from each action to its target.
docs.title: Actions#2

docs.body: ### Data payload
docs.title: Actions#3

docs.body:
- **Send as Binary.** When checked, the payload field becomes **Transmit Data (Hex)** and is read as hexadecimal bytes (for example `FF 01 A3`), with or without spaces. Anything else (a `0x` prefix, commas, an odd digit count) empties the payload.
- **Transmit Data.** The command to send, such as `RST` or `GET_TEMP`. In text mode these escapes are resolved before sending: `\n`, `\r`, `\t`, `\a`, `\b`, `\f`, `\v` and `\\`. Other escapes such as `\x41` are sent literally; use **Send as Binary** for arbitrary bytes.
- **Text Encoding.** The character encoding of the payload, default UTF-8. The list also offers UTF-16 LE/BE, Latin-1, System, GBK, GB18030, Big5, Shift-JIS, EUC-JP and EUC-KR. Hidden when **Send as Binary** is on.
- **End-of-Line Sequence.** Characters appended after the payload. If your sketch waits for a line, as with `readStringUntil('\n')`, choose New Line.
- **Checksum.** Default **No Checksum**. Any other choice appends the checksum bytes after the payload and the EOL, and the checksum covers both. It works in text and binary mode.
docs.title: Actions#4

docs.body:
The bytes go out in this order: payload, EOL, checksum.

| End-of-Line option      | Bytes sent         |
|-------------------------|--------------------|
| None                    | Nothing appended   |
| New Line (`\n`)         | `0x0A`             |
| Carriage Return (`\r`)  | `0x0D`             |
| CRLF (`\r\n`)           | `0x0D 0x0A`        |

In text mode the EOL is encoded with the action's Text Encoding, so the byte values above hold for single-byte encodings such as UTF-8 and Latin-1; a UTF-16 action sends two bytes per character.

The End-of-Line Sequence is greyed out while **Send as Binary** is on, but a sequence you chose earlier is still appended after the hex bytes. Set it to None before you switch to binary, or put the bytes in the hex payload.
docs.title: Actions#5

docs.body:
### Execution behavior

**Auto-Execute on Connect** sends the action once as soon as the device connects, which suits initialization commands such as a configuration string. On-connect sends go out in project-tree order.

The on-connect send is separate from the timer (see [Timer behavior](#timer-behavior)). If **Timer Mode** is not Off, Auto-Execute also starts the timer, so Start on Trigger and Toggle on Trigger begin repeating without a click, and Repeat N Times starts its series. Auto Start starts the timer without Auto-Execute. Either way the timer's first send comes one Interval after connect, so Repeat N Times with Auto-Execute sends Repeat Count + 1 messages in total.
docs.title: Actions#6

docs.body:
### Timer behavior

Actions can repeat on a timer, which suits periodic polling or keep-alive commands. In the Project Editor, select an action and set **Timer Mode** (free edition).
docs.title: Actions#7

docs.body:
| Timer Mode        | Behavior |
|-------------------|----------|
| Off               | Manual trigger only (default). Each click sends the command once. |
| Auto Start        | The timer starts when the device connects and repeats at the interval until the device disconnects. |
| Start on Trigger  | The timer starts on the first click and repeats until the device disconnects or the project's actions are rebuilt by an edit. Later clicks send the command once more without restarting the timer. To get a stop button, use Toggle on Trigger. |
| Toggle on Trigger | Each click starts or stops the repeating timer. Every click, including the one that stops it, also sends the command once. |
| Repeat N Times    | On a click, the first send is immediate, then one per interval until **Repeat Count** sends have gone out. Clicking again restarts the count. |
docs.title: Actions#8

docs.body:
- **Action Interval (ms).** Milliseconds between repeats. Default 100, which is 10 commands per second and can overflow a small UART buffer. It must be greater than 0, otherwise the action never repeats (the app log shows a warning). It is greyed out while Timer Mode is Off.
- **Repeat Count.** Editable only in Repeat N Times mode. Default 3, minimum 1.

Timers keep ticking while the connection is paused. A tick sends nothing, but a Repeat N Times series still counts it, so it can run out with nothing sent. Timers exist only while a device is connected, and editing any action stops every running timer. Auto Start timers come back on the next connect.
docs.title: Actions#9

docs.body:
## Dashboard appearance

The actions panel is a horizontal strip of buttons across the top of the dashboard, above the widgets. Each button shows the action icon and title. Buttons are greyed out until a device is connected, and while the connection is paused (nothing is sent then). In Toggle on Trigger mode the button shows as checked while its timer runs; no other mode changes the button.

The panel is hidden when the project has no actions or when **Show Actions Panel** is off in **Settings** -> **Layout**. Actions are also listed in the dashboard's start menu and in the Console's send library, so they stay reachable when the panel is hidden.
docs.title: Actions#10

docs.body:
## Examples

### Poll a sensor

Request a reading every 500 ms:

| Property             | Value             |
|----------------------|-------------------|
| Action Title         | Poll Temperature  |
| Transmit Data        | `GET_TEMP`        |
| End-of-Line Sequence | CRLF (`\r\n`)     |
| Timer Mode           | Auto Start        |
| Interval (ms)        | 500               |

### Send bytes on connect

Send a binary packet as soon as the device connects. The bytes come from your device's datasheet; `AA 01 FF 00 55` is a placeholder.

| Property                | Value               |
|-------------------------|---------------------|
| Action Title            | Initialize Sensor   |
| Transmit Data (Hex)     | `AA 01 FF 00 55`    |
| Send as Binary          | On                  |
| Auto-Execute on Connect | On                  |
docs.title: Actions#11

docs.body:
## Common mistakes

### Action button doesn't appear or is greyed out

**Symptom.** The action is configured in the Project Editor but no button shows up, or the button cannot be clicked.

**Fix:**

1. If the button is greyed out, connect the device and un-pause the connection. Buttons are clickable only while a connection is active and not paused.
2. If there is no panel at all, open **Settings**, go to the **Layout** tab and turn on **Show Actions Panel**. When it is off, the panel stays hidden even while connected.

### Command not received by the device

**Symptom.** The button appears and can be clicked, but the device doesn't respond.
docs.title: Actions#12

docs.body:
**Fix:**

1. Open the Console view and confirm the data is being sent.
2. Make sure the EOL setting matches what the firmware expects. Many embedded parsers need `\n` or `\r\n`.
3. In binary mode, make sure the hex is valid: pairs of hex digits, optionally separated by spaces. An odd digit count or any character other than 0-9, A-F and spaces (so no `0x` prefix, no commas) empties the payload. The EOL and checksum are still sent, and the only warning is in the app log.
4. In multi-source projects, check that **Target Device** is set correctly.
5. Check that the connection is not paused. Nothing is sent while it is.
docs.title: Actions#13

docs.body:
## Tips

- For a request/response protocol, pair a timed action with a [frame parser](Frame-Parser.md): the action sends the request, the parser decodes the reply.

## See also

- [Output Controls](Output-Controls.md): interactive dashboard controls (button, slider, toggle, text field, knob) with custom JavaScript transmit functions; a Pro feature, and the first use offers a free trial.
- [Control Loop (setup / loop)](Control-Loop.md): automates a connected device with `setup()`/`loop()` scripts; the automated counterpart to a manual Action.
- [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md): full guide to creating and configuring projects.
