docs.body:
# Aural Alerts

A temperature crosses 80 while you are looking at another window. With **Enable Sounds** on, Serial Studio plays a tone every 5 seconds until you press **Ctrl+Shift+A**.

To hear that alarm:

1. Turn on **Preferences > Sounds > Enable Sounds**. It is off by default, so nothing plays until you do.
2. In the Project Editor, select a temperature dataset, click **Alarm Bands** in the ribbon and add a Critical band above 80 (see [Alarm bands](Widget-Reference.md#alarm-bands)). Show the dataset in a Bar, Gauge or Meter widget. Other eligible widgets are listed in [If an alarm stays silent](#if-an-alarm-stays-silent).
3. Drive the value past 80. The Warning tone plays every 5 s until you acknowledge it.
docs.title: Aural-Alerts#0

docs.body:
To check the volume and output device first, press **Test** in **Preferences > Sounds**. Test creates no alarm point, so it does not prove a band works; only a value crossing the band does.

Sounds for alarm bands need no Pro license. Notifications posted from scripts or the API are a Pro feature, so their alarm points need Pro or an active trial (see [Notifications](Notifications.md) and [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md)).

## Priorities

A dataset that crosses into a Warning or Critical band, or a Warning or Critical notification, becomes an **alarm point**: one entry in the alarm list. Bands are named Info, OK, Warning and Critical. Sounds are named by priority, which is one step lower: a Critical band raises a Warning priority point, and a Warning band raises a Caution priority point.
docs.title: Aural-Alerts#1

docs.body:
| Priority | Fed by | Bundled sound | Repeats |
|----------|--------|---------------|---------|
| Warning  | Critical alarm band (severity 3), Critical notification (Pro) | One sustained 2.4 s tone | Default 5 s, adjustable 2.5 s to 15 s in Preferences > Sounds, until acknowledged, silenced or the condition clears |
| Caution  | Warning alarm band (severity 2), Warning notification (Pro) | Three-pulse burst | Default 10 s, adjustable 2.5 s to 30 s in Preferences > Sounds, until acknowledged, silenced or the condition clears |
| Advisory | Info notification (Pro) | Single pulse | Once, only while nothing else sounds |
docs.title: Aural-Alerts#2

docs.body:
### If an alarm stays silent

A band raises an alarm point only when all of these hold:

1. **Enable Sounds** is on and [Mute](#the-master-annunciator) is off.
2. The dataset has a Bar, Gauge or Meter widget with **Hide on Dashboard** off, or belongs to a Bar Panel or LED Panel group. Bands on any other dataset stay in the project file but raise no alarm point and post no notification.
3. **Suppress Alarms** (Project Editor, the dataset's Widget Settings) is off. With it on, the bands stay drawn but never raise a point, visible or not.
4. **Alarms only while visible** (also in the dataset's Widget Settings) is off, or a widget showing the dataset is on screen. Revealing the widget while the value sits in a band counts as entering the band.
docs.title: Aural-Alerts#3

docs.body:
See [Alarm bands](Widget-Reference.md#alarm-bands) for the dataset settings.

An **Alarm Deadband** on the dataset (default 0, in the dataset's units) holds the active band until the value has left it by that margin, so a reading hovering on a threshold raises one point rather than one per frame. A step into a more severe band is never held back.

Info and OK alarm bands never alert. The `Problems` and `System` notification channels never raise alarm points.

## Alarm points and sequences

The sequences are the ISA-18.1 annunciator sequences, and the priority names and tone patterns are modelled on IEC 60601-1-8. Serial Studio is not certified to either standard.
docs.title: Aural-Alerts#4

docs.body:
The default, **A-4**, suits most projects: a point appears when the value enters a band, sounds until you acknowledge it, and disappears when the value leaves. Read on only if you need alarms to wait for a manual Reset. The sequence is set in **Preferences > Sounds > Sequence (ISA-18.1)**, and a project may override it.

An alarm point is one dataset's alarm-band state, or one notification identified by its channel and title. Each point is in one of four states:

| State | Meaning | Bell | Sound |
|-------|---------|------|-------|
| **Normal** | No active condition. | Idle | Silent |
| **Alert** | Active, unacknowledged. | Flashes | The burst repeats |
| **Acknowledged** | Active, steady. | Steady | Silent |
| **Return-to-normal** | The condition cleared but the point waits for Reset. | Steady | Silent, or ringback in sequence R |
docs.title: Aural-Alerts#5

docs.body:
The point table holds at most 512 points; a new point raised past that limit is not added.

A sequence has a letter (A, M or R: what happens after Acknowledge) and an optional **-4** suffix (no lock-in: what happens if the condition clears before Acknowledge). The letter decides what happens when a condition returns to normal after Acknowledge:

| Sequence | Return to normal after Acknowledge |
|----------|------------------------------------|
| **A** (automatic reset) | The point disappears. |
| **M** (manual reset) | The point stays in Return-to-normal, steady and silent, until Reset. |
| **R** (ringback) | As M, and a distinct two-pulse ringback sounds at the Caution interval until Reset or Silence. |
docs.title: Aural-Alerts#6

docs.body:
The form decides what happens when the condition clears *before* anyone acknowledged:

| Form | Momentary alarm (clears before Acknowledge) |
|------|---------------------------------------------|
| **A-4**, **M-4**, **R-4** (ISA-18.1 option 4, no lock-in) | The audible stops the moment the value leaves the band, like an oil-pressure warning that goes quiet once the engine is running. |
| **A**, **M**, **R** (plain, lock-in) | The point keeps sounding and flashing until acknowledged, so a dip that lasted two seconds is never missed. The sequence's after-Acknowledge rule then applies. |

After a momentary alarm, A-4 drops the point; M-4 and R-4 park it in Return-to-normal until Reset.
docs.title: Aural-Alerts#7

docs.body:
A notification point clears when a `Resolved: <title>` Info event arrives on the same channel, which is what `notifyClear()` and `notifications.resolve` post.

A project overrides the app preference in **Project Editor > Project Summary > Settings > Alarm Sequence**. In the project file and the API it is the code string: `A-4`, `A`, `M-4`, `M`, `R-4` or `R`.

## The master annunciator

The bell at the right end of the dashboard taskbar tray is the master annunciator. Clicking the bell opens the alarm panel: the active points, newest first (click one to jump to its widget), and the Acknowledge, Silence, Reset, Clear, Test and Mute actions. Right-clicking the bell acknowledges.
docs.title: Aural-Alerts#8

docs.body: While any point is active the icon takes the colour of the highest active priority and shows the number of unacknowledged points. It flashes fast while anything is unacknowledged and slowly while a ringback is pending. With **Preferences > Startup > Reduce Motion** on, it holds a steady colour instead.
docs.title: Aural-Alerts#9

docs.body:
| Action | What it does | Shortcut |
|--------|--------------|----------|
| Acknowledge | Every alerting point becomes Acknowledged; the audible and the flash stop. | Ctrl+Shift+A |
| Silence | The audible stops; points stay unacknowledged and keep flashing. A new point, or a point rising in priority, re-sounds (reflash). | Ctrl+Shift+H |
| Reset | Return-to-normal points go Normal (sequences M and R). | Ctrl+Shift+R |
| Clear | Drops every point from the list, acknowledged and alerting ones included. A point still inside its band comes back on the next transition. | Panel only |
| Test | Plays Advisory, Caution, Warning and Ringback in turn and walks the annunciator through each priority. No point is created. | Ctrl+Shift+T |
| Mute | Silences every alarm and event sound without touching the point table. Persists across restarts and shows on the bell. Toggled from the alarm panel or with the shortcut; it is not in Preferences, and it is separate from **Enable Sounds**. | Ctrl+Shift+U |
docs.title: Aural-Alerts#10

docs.body:
At most one alarm sound plays at a time: the highest priority among unsilenced alerting points. When that priority is fully acknowledged or silenced, the next lower alerting priority takes over. Ringback plays only when nothing is in Alert.

Disconnecting on purpose returns every point to Normal without ringback, and the Disconnected event sound plays instead.

An **unrequested** link drop stops the audible for the outage but holds the point table. Acknowledged points stay acknowledged. When the link recovers, a dataset still in the same alarm band picks its point back up: an unacknowledged one resumes sounding, an acknowledged one stays quiet. Unacknowledged notification points are dropped at the loss, since the script that raised them cannot clear them across the outage.
docs.title: Aural-Alerts#11

docs.body:
Opening a project or starting the application never sounds.

## Preferences > Sounds

| Setting | Default | Notes |
|---------|---------|-------|
| **Enable Sounds** | Off | Nothing plays until it is on. |
| **Volume** | 80 | 0 to 100. |
| **Output Device** | System default | Any output the OS lists. |
| **Sequence (ISA-18.1)** | A-4 | A-4, A, M-4, M, R-4 or R. |
| Warning repeat interval | 5 s | 2.5 s to 15 s. |
| Caution repeat interval | 10 s | 2.5 s to 30 s. |
| Button Pressed, Toggle Changed | Off | UI feedback event sounds. |

### Missing output device

If the selected output device disappears, sounds continue on the system default, the Problem Center reports the lost device, and output returns to it when it comes back.
docs.title: Aural-Alerts#12

docs.body:
### Silent alarms hint

While sounds are disabled and the loaded project defines alarm sounds or alarm bands that can alert, the taskbar bell dims and the Problem Center says the alarms will be silent.

### Alarm sound files

Each alarm signal (Warning, Caution, Advisory, Ringback) has a row with its WAV file (empty means the bundled sound), a browse button, a play button and a clear button.

**Test** plays the same sequence as the alarm panel Test action.

**Reset to Bundled Sounds** discards every saved sound preference (files, intervals, volume, switches) and returns the output device to the system default.
docs.title: Aural-Alerts#13

docs.body:
Any PCM WAV file works: 8, 16, 24 or 32-bit integer or 32-bit float, mono or stereo, 8 kHz to 96 kHz, at most 10 s. A file that fails to decode is refused with the reason and the slot keeps its previous value. Every configured sound is decoded when it is picked or when the application starts.

### Event sounds

Each application event has a row with an enable switch: Connected, Disconnected, Link Lost, Reconnected, Export Finished, Recording Started, Recording Stopped, Error Dialog Shown, Button Pressed, Toggle Changed. Toggle Changed covers switches, checkboxes, combo boxes and spin boxes. Button Pressed covers buttons and tabs.
docs.title: Aural-Alerts#14

docs.body:
Event sounds play on their own lane, are lowered by 12 dB while an alarm sounds, and never delay an alarm burst. Changing a preference plays only the two off-by-default feedback events.

## Project overrides

Two overrides travel with the project file:

- **Per alarm band.** In the Project Editor, select the dataset and click **Alarm Bands**; the editor has a **Sound** column: pick a WAV to play instead of the priority default when the value enters that band. In the project file this is the band's `sound` key (see [Alarm bands](Widget-Reference.md#alarm-bands)).
- **Per notification channel.** **Project Summary > Settings > Channel Sounds** maps a channel name to up to three files, one per priority. Stored under the project's `sounds` object together with the sequence override:
docs.title: Aural-Alerts#15
Aural-Alerts#16

docs.body:
| Command | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| `alarms.state` | Sequence, mute, enable, highest priority, unacknowledged count, the sounding burst (`priority`, `file`, `burstStartedMs`, `burstCount`) and every active point (`kind`, `title`, `channel`, `priority`, `state`, `silenced`, `sinceMs`). |
| `alarms.acknowledge`, `alarms.silence`, `alarms.reset`, `alarms.clear`, `alarms.test` | The operator actions. |
| `alarms.setMuted` | Takes `muted` (boolean). |
| `alarms.getProjectSounds`, `alarms.setProjectSounds` | Read or replace the project's `sounds` object; the setter validates every path and returns the rejected ones. |
docs.title: Aural-Alerts#17

docs.body:
In a `--headless` session the alarm state machine still runs without an audio device.

## See also

- [Notifications](Notifications.md): the events that feed notification points.
- [Widget Reference](Widget-Reference.md#alarm-bands): alarm bands and the per-band `sound` key.
- [Problem Center](Problem-Center.md): where lost devices and unusable sound files are reported.
docs.title: Aural-Alerts#18

docs.body:
# Auto-Generating Projects

If your board prints comma-separated values with `Serial.println`, you do not need this page: Serial Studio plots those without a project file. This page is for devices that sit on a CAN bus, expose Modbus registers (the numbered memory slots a PLC or sensor publishes) or send Protocol Buffers, and that come with a vendor file describing them. A PLC with 80 holding registers is a long afternoon of typing. The CSV the vendor already sent is not.

Pick the file, check the preview, click **Create Project**, and Serial Studio writes a `.ssproj` with groups, datasets, dashboard widgets and a working frame parser. Modbus and Protobuf import need no hardware. DBC import needs a CAN interface to be listed, and a virtual backend counts.
docs.title: Auto-Generating-Projects#0

docs.body:
| Source file | Where | Edition |
|-------------|-------|---------|
| `.dbc` (CAN Bus) | Setup Panel > CAN Bus > **Import DBC File…** | Pro |
| `.csv` / `.xml` / `.json` (Modbus register map) | Setup Panel > Modbus > **Import Register Map…** | Pro |
| `.proto` (Protocol Buffers) | Project Editor toolbar > **Protobuf** | All builds |

The first time you use a Pro importer, Serial Studio asks whether to start the free trial (Yes/No). Registering the trial needs an internet connection. Protobuf import is free. Pro widgets in a generated project still need a license or the trial.

## What you get
docs.title: Auto-Generating-Projects#1

docs.body:
The DBC, Modbus and Protobuf importers each produce:

- A new project (`.ssproj`) with one or more **groups**. A group is a set of related values: a CAN message, a contiguous Modbus register block, a protobuf message.
- A **dataset** per signal, register or field. A dataset is one value. DBC and Modbus datasets carry a title, units, min/max and scale; Protobuf datasets carry the field name, protobuf type and tag. The DBC importer also picks a default widget (see [Widget inference](#widget-inference)).
- A **Lua frame parser** that decodes each frame into those datasets without user code.

Modbus only: the register groups are also pushed into the live Modbus driver, so it polls the right addresses as soon as you connect.
docs.title: Auto-Generating-Projects#2

docs.body:
Every importer shows a preview first; click **Create Project** and the `.ssproj` opens in the Project Editor. The OPC UA driver also generates projects, but it writes a Built-In (not Lua) parser; see [Generating from a live server](#generating-from-a-live-server).

## DBC import (CAN Bus)

DBC import is a Pro feature (the CAN Bus driver is Pro). Path: Setup Panel > CAN Bus > **Import DBC File…**. The button appears once the CAN backend lists an interface, so without an adapter you need a virtual one.

A DBC (CAN Database) file describes every message and signal on a CAN network: message IDs, signal bit positions, byte order, scaling, units and value tables. Most automotive and industrial CAN networks come with one. Serial Studio parses it and turns each message into a group.
docs.title: Auto-Generating-Projects#3

docs.body:
### How to run it

1. In the **Setup Panel**, select **CAN Bus** from the Connection dropdown.
2. Configure the CAN backend, interface and bitrate as usual (see [Protocol Setup Guides](Protocol-Setup-Guides.md)). No bus traffic is needed.
3. Click **Import DBC File…**.
4. Pick a `.dbc`. Serial Studio shows a preview listing every message: `1: EngineData @ 0x100 (5 signals)`, `2: VehicleSpeed @ 0x101 (2 signals)`, and so on.
5. Click **Create Project**, or **Add to Project** (see [Add to Project](#add-to-project)). You are asked where to save the `.ssproj`; any folder works.
6. Back in the Setup Panel, press Connect with your CAN interface.
docs.title: Auto-Generating-Projects#4

docs.body:
Messages are sorted by CAN ID so dataset positions stay stable across re-imports.

### What it generates

For each CAN message:

- One **group** named after the message (for example *EngineData*).
- One **dataset per signal** with the signal's name, units and a derived widget.
- An entry in the **MESSAGES** spec of the Lua frame parser that selects the message by CAN ID, extracts each signal at the correct bit offset and byte order, applies factor and offset, and publishes the value for its dataset.

### Widget inference

The DBC importer (Pro) gives most signals a sensible widget; change any of them in the Project Editor. The generated parser does not care which widget renders a value. The rules, from signal names, units and message shape:
docs.title: Auto-Generating-Projects#5

docs.body:
- **GPS Map**: the message has two or more signals, with names containing `lat` and `lon` (or `lng`).
- **Accelerometer** or **Gyroscope**: the message has exactly three signals, and all three match. Accelerometer: name contains `accel`, or unit contains `m/s` or `g`. Gyroscope: name contains `gyro`, `roll`, `pitch` or `yaw`, or unit contains `deg/s` or `rad/s`.
- Anything else gets a Data Grid group, with a widget chosen per signal: **Bar** for `%`, a 0-100 range, or temperature (unit °C/°F or name contains `temp`); **Meter** for rpm, speed and power units (`rpm`, `km/h`, `mph`, `m/s`, `kW`, `hp`) or names containing `speed`, `velocity`, `power` or `rpm`; **Gauge** for volts, amps, `psi`, `bar`, `kPa`, degrees and similar units, or any range up to 360.
- **Single-bit signals** become LEDs, regardless of name.
- Signals named `odometer`, `trip`, `counter`, `timestamp` or `status` get no default widget. Other signals whose unit and range match nothing above get none either.
docs.title: Auto-Generating-Projects#6

docs.body:
A multi-bit signal in a Data Grid group also gets its plot toggle, unless its name contains `odometer`, `trip`, `counter`, `timestamp`, `status` or `state`.

### Mux signals

A multiplexed signal is one whose meaning depends on a selector value in the same message. The DBC importer (Pro):

- Creates one dataset for the selector itself, titled `<name> (selector)`. A selector that is itself gated by a parent selector is titled `<name> (selector, mux N)`.
- Creates one dataset per gated signal, titled `<name> (mux N)` so payloads that share the same bits stay distinguishable.
- Writes a gate into the generated parser: the selector is extracted first, and a gated signal updates only when the selector's raw value matches. Otherwise the signal is left alone and its dataset keeps its last value instead of decoding noise from another payload.
docs.title: Auto-Generating-Projects#7

docs.body:
Extended multiplexing (`SG_MUL_VAL_`) is supported: a signal gated by a parent selector is decoded only when the parent's value falls in the declared range. Signals whose switch value is outside the integer range, or that sit in a circular `SG_MUL_VAL_` chain, are skipped, and the post-import dialog reports how many.

## Modbus map import

Modbus map import is a Pro feature (the Modbus driver is Pro). Path: Setup Panel > Modbus > **Import Register Map…**.

Register maps come in many ad-hoc layouts. Serial Studio accepts CSV, XML and JSON, picks the format from the file extension, and groups adjacent registers of the same type into one **register group** for efficient polling.
docs.title: Auto-Generating-Projects#8

docs.body:
### How to run it

1. In the **Setup Panel**, select **Modbus** from the Connection dropdown.
2. Click **Import Register Map…**.
3. Pick a `.csv`, `.xml` or `.json` file.
4. Review the preview: `1: Temperature @ 0 (Holding Registers, uint16) [°C]`, `2: Pressure @ 1 (Holding Registers, uint16) [PSI]`, ...
5. Click **Create Project** (you are asked where to save the `.ssproj`), or **Add to Project** (see [Add to Project](#add-to-project)).
6. Set the Modbus connection (host or serial port, unit ID) as usual and press Connect. The register groups are already in the driver, so polling starts immediately.
docs.title: Auto-Generating-Projects#9

docs.body:
A tiny map is enough to try it. Save this as `plc.csv`:

```csv
address,name,units
0,Temperature,°C
1,Pressure,PSI
```

With no `type` column, both rows import as Holding Registers, so the preview matches step 4 and **Create Project** gives one group with two datasets.

### What it generates

For each block of same-type registers (holding, input, coil, discrete input):

- One **group** named after the register type and start address (for example *Holding Registers @ 0*).
- One **dataset per register**, with its name, units, scale and offset baked in.
- An entry in the **BLOCKS** spec of the Lua frame parser that decodes each register from the Modbus response, handling word order for 32-bit and 64-bit values.
- A **register group** added to the Modbus driver, sized to cover the block.
docs.title: Auto-Generating-Projects#10

docs.body:
### Format details

The full format spec for CSV, XML and JSON register maps lives in [Protocol Setup Guides](Protocol-Setup-Guides.md). In short:

- **CSV** with a header row. Column order is flexible: `address`, `name`, `type`, `dataType`, `units`, `min`, `max`, `scale`, `offset`, and `slave` or `unit_id` for multi-device maps. Common aliases (`addr`, `register`, `data_type`) are recognized. `#` lines are comments.
- **XML** in either flat (`<register address="0" type="holding" .../>`) or nested (`<holding-registers><register address="0" .../></holding-registers>`) form.
- **JSON** as an object: a flat `{"registers": [...]}` array, or per-type arrays (`holdingRegisters`, `inputRegisters`, `coils`, `discreteInputs`).
docs.title: Auto-Generating-Projects#11

docs.body:
Only `address` and `name` are required; everything else has a default. The file extension picks the parser, and files over 10 MB are rejected.

Block grouping: a register joins the previous block only when its address is adjacent to or inside it and it has the same type and unit ID (column `slave` or `unit_id`). A gap starts a new group.

## Protobuf import

Protobuf import is available in all builds. Path: Project Editor toolbar > **Protobuf**.

[Protocol Buffers](https://protobuf.dev/) is Google's binary message format; a `.proto` file names each field and its type. Serial Studio parses the schema directly (no `protoc`, no generated code) and emits a frame parser that decodes the wire format at runtime.
docs.title: Auto-Generating-Projects#12

docs.body:
### How to run it

1. Open the **Project Editor**.
2. In the toolbar, click **Protobuf** (the command is *Import Protobuf Schema*; it moves into an overflow menu when the window is narrow).
3. Pick a `.proto` schema file.
4. Review the parsed messages in the preview. The picker lists every top-level message; selecting one shows its fields with their tag, type, name and `repeated` flag.
5. Click **Create Project**, or **Add to Project** (see [Add to Project](#add-to-project)).

The importer does not choose a connection. In the Setup Panel, pick the driver that delivers the serialized bytes (UART, TCP, MQTT, BLE) and make sure each frame holds one complete message.
docs.title: Auto-Generating-Projects#13

docs.body:
### What it generates

- One **group per message** in the schema. Nested messages become their own groups, added in declaration order, so the dashboard layout mirrors the schema's message tree.
- A **dataset per scalar field**, carrying the field name, its protobuf scalar type and its tag.
- A **Lua frame parser** with a self-contained varint and length-delimited decoder and per-message dispatch tables, so no generated stubs are needed. When the schema declares more than one root message, a score-based dispatcher inspects the incoming bytes and routes them to the matching decoder.

Strings and bytes decode to Lua strings; numeric scalars, including enums, decode to Lua numbers. Repeated fields keep only the last-seen occurrence per frame; the parser does not accumulate arrays.
docs.title: Auto-Generating-Projects#14

docs.body:
### Limitations

- Written for proto3. The importer does not check the `syntax` line; a file that fails to parse reports the line number and a proto3 hint.
- Supported: scalar fields, nested messages, enums, `repeated`, `oneof` (flattened to plain fields) and `map<K, V>` (decoded as a repeated bytes field). `service` and RPC blocks are skipped.
- `import` statements are ignored, so message types defined in other files, `Any` and the Well-Known Types are not expanded into datasets.
- Files over 10 MB are rejected.
- The generator emits a Lua parser, so the source must stay on Lua unless you rewrite the parser.
- One serialized message per Serial Studio frame. If the transport batches several, split them before the bytes reach Serial Studio.
docs.title: Auto-Generating-Projects#15

docs.body:
## Add to Project

**Create Project** starts a new `.ssproj`. **Add to Project**, in the DBC, Modbus and Protobuf preview dialogs, appends the imported source to the project that is already open: its groups, tables and workspaces, filed under a folder named after the imported file. New entities take fresh ids, and a table whose name is already used is renamed, with the generated parser updated to match.

The button is enabled when the preview holds at least one message and the open project has at least one group. Each importer keeps its own edition: DBC and Modbus are Pro, Protobuf is free.

## Generating from a live server
docs.title: Auto-Generating-Projects#16

docs.body:
Some drivers generate projects from the device itself rather than from a vendor file. The [OPC UA driver](Drivers-OPC-UA.md) (Pro) is the one that differs in output: **Browse Tags…** in the Setup Panel walks the server's address space, and **Generate Project** turns the ticked variables into one group per folder and one dataset per tag, typed after the server's data types, with a Built-In frame parser whose schema is written for you. Reopening the generated project reconnects and resubscribes without browsing again.

Other drivers carry similar buttons in their Setup Panel; see each driver page for edition and path: **Create Project from Variables** ([S7](Drivers-S7.md)), **Create Project from Tags** ([EtherNet/IP](Drivers-EtherNet-IP.md)), **Create Project from Births** ([MQTT](Drivers-MQTT.md)) and **Create Project from Points** ([IEC 104](Drivers-IEC-104.md)). The Modbus register-groups dialog has its own **Generate Project** button too.
docs.title: Auto-Generating-Projects#17

docs.body:
## When to build by hand

Build the project by hand when you only need a few signals out of a 200-signal DBC: importing all of them and deleting most is more work than adding three datasets. Do the same when the device packs several values into one register (bit-packed flags, packed structs), or when you want custom dispatch, conditional decoding or multi-frame state machines in the parser.

## Editing after import

The generated project is a project like any other: rename datasets, regroup them, swap widgets, attach datasets to workspaces. The importer produces a starting layout, not a fixed one. To change how frames are decoded, edit the Lua directly or switch the source's parser to JavaScript (see [Frame Parser Scripting](Frame-Parser.md)).
docs.title: Auto-Generating-Projects#18

docs.body:
If the vendor publishes a new DBC, the register map gains a register or the schema gains a field, import again as a new project and copy your dashboard customizations over rather than merging by hand. To bring a second device into an existing dashboard, use **Add to Project** instead.

## See also

- [Protocol Setup Guides](Protocol-Setup-Guides.md): full format reference for Modbus register maps, plus connection setup.
- [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md): where the generated project lands after import.
- [Frame Parser Scripting](Frame-Parser.md): editing the generated parser by hand.
- [Drivers — Modbus](Drivers-Modbus.md): the function-code and register-table model the importer maps onto.
- [Drivers — CAN Bus](Drivers-CAN-Bus.md): the DBC signal model.
docs.title: Auto-Generating-Projects#19

docs.body:
# Backups & Recovery

You deleted a dataset, saved, and only then noticed you needed it. Serial Studio has already written a snapshot of the project from before the change. Open the **Project Editor**, click the **Restore Backup** toolbar button, pick the row, and click **Restore** in the dialog. The steps are under [Restoring a backup](#restoring-a-backup).

A snapshot is a copy of your whole `.ssproj` (the file your project is saved in), written in the background while you work. Backups are on in every edition, GPL and Pro alike, and there is no setting to turn them off. The one exception is a [sealed session](Operator-Deployments.md#sealed-sessions) (a Pro session opened from a deployment package), which never writes snapshots so that its project never reaches disk in readable form.
docs.title: Backup-Recovery#0

docs.body:
> Backups protect the project *definition* (sources, groups, datasets, frame parsers, transforms, widgets, workspaces). They are not a recording of your telemetry. To archive incoming data, see [Historian](Historian.md) or [CSV Export & Playback](CSV-Export-Playback.md).

For step-by-step reversal of single edits, use **Undo** and **Redo** on the Project Editor toolbar. Backups restore a whole earlier version of the project.

## When a snapshot is taken

Serial Studio writes a snapshot:
docs.title: Backup-Recovery#1

docs.body:
- On load. Opening a project writes a baseline snapshot (`Project Loaded`) before you touch anything.
- After an edit. Each edit restarts a 5-second timer, so a snapshot is written 5 seconds after you stop editing and a burst of quick edits produces one snapshot. An edit made in the last 5 seconds before a crash is not captured.
- Before a destructive command. Deleting something by hand in the Project Editor takes no pre-delete snapshot; Undo and the 5-second automatic snapshot cover it. Scripts and the AI Assistant that go through the API Server's `project.*` commands or the AI Assistant's tools take a labelled snapshot first when they create, open or load a project, apply a template, delete or move datasets and groups, delete actions, output widgets or workspaces, clear or reorder workspaces, remove a widget, or run a batch. A dry run takes none. Labels such as `Before Delete Group` come only from these paths.
- On request. The AI Assistant can force a labelled checkpoint before a multi-step edit.
docs.title: Backup-Recovery#2

docs.body:
A snapshot whose content matches the newest one is skipped. An older matching snapshot does not count, so going from A to B and back to A writes a third file.

Snapshots cover edits made inside Serial Studio. For a program that changes the `.ssproj` on disk, see [Project Editor → If the project file changes on disk](Project-Editor.md#if-the-project-file-changes-on-disk).

## Where backups live

To find your backups, open the **Recover Backup** dialog and click **Open Folder**. It reveals the folder in your file manager.

For reference, the layout is:

```
<app data folder>/backups/<project-basename>-<hash>/<timestamp>[__label].ssproj
```
docs.title: Backup-Recovery#3

docs.body:
- The subfolder is the project's base name plus a short hash of its full path, so two projects with the same file name in different folders keep separate histories. A project you have not saved yet is filed under `untitled`.
- File names use a UTC timestamp, for example `2026-11-10T14-03-22-418__auto.ssproj`; the dialog shows local time. Labels keep letters, digits, `-` and `_` (spaces and dots become `-`, other characters are dropped) and are cut to 32 characters.
- Each file is your project, stored compactly, plus a small `_backupMeta` block that restore strips. A snapshot written by a newer Serial Studio is refused on restore.
- Serial Studio keeps the **50 most recent** snapshots per project and deletes the oldest beyond that. Automatic, load and before-a-command snapshots share that pool, so a long editing session can push out the `Project Loaded` baseline.
docs.title: Backup-Recovery#4

docs.body:
## Restoring a backup

1. Open the [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md).
2. Click the **Restore Backup** toolbar button, to the right of **Undo** and **Redo** (tooltip: "Restore a recent automatic snapshot of the current project"; also in the command palette). The **Recover Backup** dialog opens.
3. Select a snapshot. A one-line preview says what restoring would change: groups added or removed, a changed title, or a different frame parser.
4. Click **Restore** in the dialog, or double-click the row.

The list shows up to 50 recent snapshots, newest first, each with the time it was taken and a label saying why: `Project Loaded`, `Auto-save`, `Before Delete Group`, `Before Apply Template`, `Before Batch Operation`, `Before Restore`, or a checkpoint name. A label the app does not recognise is shown title-cased, so a checkpoint named `pre-flash-test` appears as `Pre Flash Test`.
docs.title: Backup-Recovery#5

docs.body:
Picked the wrong snapshot? Restore again. Before loading your pick, Serial Studio saves the current state as `Before Restore`. If that state already matches the newest snapshot, no extra file is written and the newest row is the one to go back to.

The dialog's **Restore** loads the snapshot into the project and marks it modified. Nothing is written to your `.ssproj` until you save.

If the dialog says "No backups for this project yet. Edit or save the project to start the rolling backup.", no snapshot exists for it: the project is new and has not been edited yet, or the session is sealed.

## Rolling back with the AI Assistant
docs.title: Backup-Recovery#6

docs.body:
The [AI Assistant](AI-Assistant.md) (Pro, see [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md)) restores from the same snapshots through the `assistant.checkpoint` and `assistant.restore` tools. Ask it to "undo that", "roll back the last change", or "revert to before you deleted that group" and it will:

1. List the recent checkpoints.
2. Show you the list; you pick one and approve the confirmation prompt, and it restores that snapshot.
3. Report the `Before Restore` snapshot it took, so the rollback is itself undoable.

If the project has been saved to a file, the assistant's restore writes it back to that file immediately. For an unsaved project it stays modified in memory. Every command that takes a snapshot first (see [When a snapshot is taken](#when-a-snapshot-is-taken)) returns the path of the snapshot taken beforehand, so a bad automated edit is one restore away.
docs.title: Backup-Recovery#7

docs.body:
# Benchmark Dialog

You do not need this dialog to use Serial Studio. It answers one question: how many frames per
second can this computer process? A frame is one line of your `Serial.println()` output. A board
printing at 115200 baud sends at most a few hundred to about a thousand lines per second. This
dialog checks a machine that can swallow hundreds of thousands, so a Pass leaves you plenty of
headroom.

The dialog matters for sources in the hundreds of thousands of frames per second, for comparing
machines, and after you change a parser or transform.

The Benchmark dialog is in the free and Pro builds. It pushes synthetic frames through the real
pipeline with no device attached, and reports frames per second for each phase. "256 kHz" in
Serial Studio means 256,000 frames per second.
docs.title: Benchmark#0

docs.body:
## Quick check

1. Disconnect your board. **Run Benchmark** is disabled while a device is connected or a
   recording is open.
2. Open the **About** window and click **Benchmark** (see [Opening the dialog](#opening-the-dialog)).
3. Choose **100 K frames** and **1 second**. Leave **Parsers** checked and uncheck **Mixed
   (numeric + text)**, so only **Numeric only** stays checked.
4. Click **Run Benchmark** and wait for the table.

The window stops responding while the run is going. That is the benchmark working, not the app
crashing.

| Pipeline | Throughput | Time | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Data pipeline | 3,100,000 frames/s | 1.00 s | Pass |
| Built-In parser (numeric) | 2,400,000 frames/s | 1.00 s | Pass |
| Lua parser (numeric) | 1,300,000 frames/s | 1.00 s | Pass |
| JavaScript parser (numeric) | 410,000 frames/s | 1.00 s | Pass |
docs.title: Benchmark#1

docs.body:
The numbers above are illustrative. Yours depend on the machine.

A parser is the code that turns one line of text into numbers. Built-In is the default; Lua and
JavaScript are scripts you write yourself (see [Frame Parser Scripting](Frame-Parser.md)).

## Opening the dialog

Open the **About** window (the **About** toolbar button), then click **Benchmark**. The button is
hidden in runtime (deployment) mode and appears only in authoring mode; see
[Operation Modes](Operation-Modes.md). The dialog runs entirely on the local machine; nothing is
uploaded.

## What it measures
docs.title: Benchmark#2

docs.body:
The benchmark feeds newline-delimited synthetic frames (sine-wave numeric channels, plus
rotating non-numeric status words for the mixed phases) through the same chain that live data
takes: `FrameReader` extraction, the `FrameBuilder` decode/parse/transform stage, and the
downstream consumers. Each phase reports a sustained **throughput** in frames per second and
the wall-clock **time** it took to reach the target frame count.
docs.title: Benchmark#3

docs.body:
| Control | Options | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Frames per phase** | 100 K / 250 K / 500 K / 1 M frames | 250 K frames | Frames pushed through each phase. More frames give a steadier average and a longer freeze. |
| **Minimum duration** | 1 / 2 / 5 / 10 seconds | 2 seconds | A wall-clock floor. A phase runs until it has both reached the frame count and run at least this long. |
| **Stages** | Parsers, Data export, Dashboard | Parsers only (Data export and Dashboard unchecked) | Which families of phases to schedule. The raw data pipeline always runs and is not a toggle. |
| **Data** | Numeric only, Mixed (numeric + text) | Both checked | Numeric channels, or numeric channels plus trailing text fields such as status words, or both. |
docs.title: Benchmark#4

docs.body:
**Run Benchmark** stays disabled until at least one stage and one data type are checked. It is
also disabled while a device is connected or a recording is open; the dialog says "Disconnect the
active device before running a benchmark." or "Close the open recording before running a
benchmark." Do that first.

## The phases

The data pipeline always runs first. Each selected stage then runs every parser engine
(Built-In, Lua, JavaScript) over each selected data type. A **gate** is the minimum speed a phase
must reach to show Pass. The data-pipeline and parser phases are gated; the data-export and
dashboard phases are informational and show `n/a` in the Result column.
docs.title: Benchmark#5

docs.body:
| Phase | What it exercises | Gate (frames/s) |
|---|---|---|
| **Data pipeline** | Raw `FrameReader` extraction only: delimiter scan and dequeue, no parse. | 1,024,000 |
| **Built-In parser (numeric)** | Native C++ template over numeric channels. | 1,024,000 |
| **Built-In parser (mixed)** | Built-In parser with trailing non-numeric string tokens. | 512,000 |
| **Lua parser (numeric)** | `parse()` in Lua over numeric channels. | 256,000 |
| **JavaScript parser (numeric)** | `parse()` in `QJSEngine` over the same channels. | 128,000 |
| **Lua parser (mixed)** | Lua `parse()` over the mixed workload. | 128,000 |
| **JavaScript parser (mixed)** | JavaScript `parse()` over the mixed workload. | 64,000 |
| **Built-In / Lua / JavaScript + data export** | Each engine with every export/output consumer enabled (CSV, API, plus MDF4 / Sessions / gRPC where built). | informational |
| **Built-In / Lua / JavaScript + dashboard** | Each engine feeding a full dashboard of widgets. | informational |
docs.title: Benchmark#6

docs.body:
The dialog uses fixed gates. They equal what `--benchmark-hotpath` uses at its default `--min-fps`
of 256000, scaled per phase. Built-In is fastest, then Lua, then JavaScript, and mixed data is
slower than numeric. The per-language ranking is also in
[Frame Parser Scripting: Performance Tips](Frame-Parser.md#performance-tips).

The dialog gates seven phases. The headless CI form gates two more, for nine: **Lua + data
export** and **Lua + dashboard**, each floored at 128,000 frames/s. Those two rows print `n/a` and
never fail in the dialog. In builds with allocation statistics enabled (`SS_ALLOC_STATS`), the CI
form also fails if the Built-In parser allocates per frame; other builds report `n/a`. See the
[CLI section](Command-Line-Interface.md#acquisition-pipeline-benchmark).
docs.title: Benchmark#7

docs.body:
## Why the interface freezes

The Benchmark dialog stops responding while it runs, and a warning in the dialog says so. For a
quick check, pick 100 K frames and a 1-second floor; the defaults (250 K frames, 2 seconds) take
longer. Every phase runs at least the minimum duration, so the default run (seven phases of 2
seconds or more) takes 14 seconds or longer. Wait for the table to appear.

Normally `FrameReader` and `FrameBuilder` live on a dedicated pipeline thread, away from the GUI.
To drive them with plain synchronous calls against your live session, the dialog relocates them
onto the GUI thread for the run and hands them back when it ends. The tight benchmark loop then
blocks that thread's event loop, so it cannot repaint until the loop returns. See
[Threading and Timing Guarantees](Threading-and-Timing.md#framereader-and-framebuilder-run-on-a-dedicated-pipeline-thread)
for where frame parsing normally lives and why.
docs.title: Benchmark#8

docs.body:
Each phase yields to the event loop about every 16 ms so the spinner and progress bar repaint.
The time spent on each of those pumps is discounted from the measurement, so a repaint never
deflates throughput.

## What it does to your session

Your project reloads automatically when the run ends, and exported files never touch your real
data folders. While the benchmark runs, the runner snapshots your session, switches to a built-in
test project, and loads the selected parser language. It redirects every exporter into a
throwaway temporary workspace, so CSV, MDF4, and Session files generated during the run are
deleted afterward. When the run ends, it restores your settings and reloads your original
project. If no project was open, it returns to the prior mode
with a clean dashboard.
docs.title: Benchmark#9

docs.body:
## Reading the results

In the Benchmark dialog (**About** > **Benchmark**), the results table has four columns:

- **Pipeline** names the phase.
- **Throughput** is the sustained frames per second for that phase. Higher is better.
- **Time** is the wall-clock seconds the phase ran.
- **Result** is **Pass** or **Fail** for the gated phases (up to seven), and `n/a` for the
  informational export and dashboard phases. A gated phase fails if its throughput is below its gate in
  [The phases](#the-phases).

Under the table, **Peak memory** shows the highest process memory observed during the run, in
MiB. It is included when you copy the results.
docs.title: Benchmark#10

docs.body:
A Fail means the machine is too slow for that phase, other heavy programs are competing for the
CPU, or the build is unoptimized (a debug build, or one without the shipped PGO profile). Close
other heavy programs and run again. If you built from source, use a Release build. A Fail on a
slow laptop does not affect normal Arduino-rate use. After you edit a parser, a Fail on its
phase means the change made it slower.

**Copy** places a Markdown report on the clipboard: a header with the version, OS, CPU, workload
and build, then the table with an extra **Target** column holding each gate (`n/a` for
informational rows), then **Peak memory**. **Clear** empties the
table. Both are enabled only when results exist and no run is active. **Close** dismisses the
dialog (also clearing the table) and is disabled during a run. For CI and deployment gating, use
the headless [CLI form](Command-Line-Interface.md#acquisition-pipeline-benchmark), which
defaults to 1 M frames and 10 seconds.
docs.title: Benchmark#11

docs.body:
## See also

- [The Acquisition Pipeline](Data-Hotpath.md): the pipeline being measured, stage by stage.
- [Threading and Timing Guarantees](Threading-and-Timing.md): where the pipeline normally runs,
  why it's single-threaded internally, and what that guarantees.
- [Frame Parser Scripting](Frame-Parser.md): the `parse()` API and the Lua-vs-JavaScript
  performance characteristics the benchmark quantifies.
- [Command-Line Interface](Command-Line-Interface.md#acquisition-pipeline-benchmark): the headless benchmark
  used for CI and deployment gating.
- [Operation Modes](Operation-Modes.md): the modes the benchmark runs under and why its button
  hides in runtime mode.
docs.title: Benchmark#12

docs.body:
# CSV export and playback

Your board prints values with `Serial.println` and you want them in a spreadsheet, or you logged a bench test last week and want it back on the dashboard. Serial Studio writes incoming frames to CSV and replays CSV files through the same pipeline as a live device. CSV export and playback are in both the free edition and Pro. For high-rate binary logging with per-channel sample rates and metadata, see [MDF4 Export & Playback](MDF4.md) (Pro).

## Quickstart

1. Pick Quick Plot as the operation mode ([Operation Modes](Operation-Modes.md)).
2. In the Setup panel, under **Data Export**, turn on **CSV Spreadsheet**.
3. Connect, and let a few lines arrive.
4. Open the folder shown in [File location](#file-location). To replay the file, follow [Opening a CSV file](#opening-a-csv-file).
docs.title: CSV-Export-Playback#0

docs.body:
## CSV export

### Turning export on

A frame is one line your board prints, for example `21.4,48`. CSV export is a switch in the Setup panel of the main window. Under **Data Export**, turn on **CSV Spreadsheet**, before or during a live connection. Serial Studio then writes every incoming frame to a CSV file on a background thread. The setting is remembered across launches.

The writer queues up to 8192 frames and flushes at 1024 rows or every second, so the display thread never blocks on disk.

The switch is greyed out in Console Only mode, which has no frame structure to export, and switching to Console Only turns export off. Pick Quick Plot or Project File first ([Operation Modes](Operation-Modes.md)).
docs.title: CSV-Export-Playback#1

docs.body:
In Quick Plot mode each channel is exported twice, because it feeds both the data grid and the plot. Three channels give six value columns.

### File location

Exported files land under your workspace folder (Documents/Serial Studio by default; configurable in Settings):

```text
<Workspace>/CSV/<Project Name>/<YYYY-MM-DD_HH-MM-SS>.csv
```

A session started at 3:30:05 PM on March 17, 2026 for a project named "Weather Station" writes:

```text
Documents/Serial Studio/CSV/Weather Station/2026-03-17_15-30-05.csv
```

A project with no title exports to a folder named `Untitled`.

### File format
docs.title: CSV-Export-Playback#2

docs.body:
A two-channel project produces a file like this:

```text
Elapsed (s),Weather Station/Temp/Celsius,Weather Station/Temp/Humidity
0.000000000,21.4,48
0.016384512,21.5,48
```

The header row is `Elapsed (s)` followed by `GroupName/DatasetName` for each dataset, in dataset order. `Elapsed (s)` is seconds since the session started, with nanosecond precision. A `SourceName/` prefix is added whenever the owning source has a non-empty title, including in a single-source project. In the sample, `Weather Station` is the source title, `Temp` the group and `Celsius` the dataset.

The file opens with a UTF-8 byte-order mark. Most tools handle it; pandas needs `encoding="utf-8-sig"` or the first header cell keeps a BOM character. Any cell starting with `=`, `+`, `-`, `@`, a tab or a carriage return gets an apostrophe prefix (unless it is purely numeric), so spreadsheets do not evaluate it as a formula.
docs.title: CSV-Export-Playback#3

docs.body:
For a single-source project, each row is one complete frame. If your project has several devices, rows are sparse: one row per distinct sample instant, with a source's columns left empty where that source produced no sample. Rows are merged inside a 250 ms reorder window, so a file you tail during recording lags the live data by up to 250 ms; closing the file flushes the rest.

### Row interval

**Row Interval (ms)** is in [Preferences](Preferences.md) (the **Preferences** button on the main toolbar), **Export** tab, under CSV Export. The field accepts any integer of 0 or more, with presets 0, 10, 100 and 1000. The value is remembered across launches.
docs.title: CSV-Export-Playback#4

docs.body:
- `0` (default): one row per received frame.
- `N` above 0: one row every N milliseconds, each a snapshot of the latest value of every dataset. It applies live, so a change takes effect on the next snapshot.

A 10 ms interval on a sensor that updates once a second writes 100 near-identical rows for every distinct value.

### File lifecycle

- Export opens the file on the first frame received after export is turned on.
- Disconnecting, turning export off, or pausing the dashboard closes the file.
- Reconnecting, resuming or re-enabling export opens a new file with a new timestamp.

Names have one-second resolution. If the name exists, Serial Studio appends `_2`, `_3` and so on, up to 64 tries, and never overwrites a file.
docs.title: CSV-Export-Playback#5

docs.body:
## CSV playback

### Opening a CSV file

1. Only a multi-source file needs its project loaded first (see [Multi-source CSV files](#multi-source-csv-files)). For a single-device file, skip to step 2.
2. Click **Open CSV** in the toolbar, or press Ctrl+O (Cmd+O on macOS). Both are disabled while a CSV file is already open or a device is connected. Dropping a file on the window works too.
3. Pick a `*.csv` file.

The CSV Player dialog opens and the dashboard shows the first row. Press Space to play.

Opening a file while a device is connected shows **Device Connection Active**; disconnect first. A file with no data row is rejected with **Insufficient Data in CSV File**. Playback indexes up to 2,000,000,000 rows, then shows **CSV Row Limit Reached**.
docs.title: CSV-Export-Playback#6

docs.body:
### Timestamp handling

Files exported by Serial Studio need no prompt. For any other CSV, Serial Studio reads the first column to work out the timestamp format, and a file from a spreadsheet or another tool usually lands in one of the prompt cases.
docs.title: CSV-Export-Playback#7

docs.body:
| First column | What happens |
|--------------|--------------|
| Numeric, unit in the header | A bracketed unit (`time(ms)`, `t [us]`) or a `_unit` suffix (`time_ms`) sets the scale: seconds, `ms`, `us` or `ns`, by name or common abbreviation. Serial Studio's own `Elapsed (s)` is this case. |
| Numeric, no recognizable unit | A **Timestamp Units** prompt offers Seconds (s), Milliseconds (ms) and Microseconds (us); seconds is preselected. It offers no nanoseconds, so put `ns` in the header instead. |
| Date/time strings, such as `2026/03/17 15:30:05` | Parsed into absolute timestamps, then converted to elapsed offsets. |
| Anything else | A **CSV Date/Time Selection** prompt offers **Select a date/time column** or **Set interval manually** (a fixed gap of 1 to 1,000,000 ms between rows, 1000 preselected), for tools that record no timestamps. The date/time option opens a **Select Date/Time Column** picker, and the chosen column is parsed as in the date/time row. |
docs.title: CSV-Export-Playback#8

docs.body:
### Player controls

| Control          | Action                           | Shortcut       |
|------------------|----------------------------------|----------------|
| Play / Pause     | Start or pause playback          | Space, media Play/Pause |
| Previous frame   | Step back one frame              | Left or Down Arrow, media Previous |
| Next frame       | Step forward one frame           | Right or Up Arrow, media Next |
| Progress slider  | Seek to any position in the file | Drag or click  |

The current timestamp shows next to the slider as `HH:MM:SS.mmm`.

### How playback works

The CSV Player feeds each row through the same Frame Builder and Dashboard path as a live connection, so widgets, plots and gauges render as they would with a device.
docs.title: CSV-Export-Playback#9

docs.body:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["CSV File"] --> B["CSV Player"]
    B --> C["Frame Builder"]
    C --> D["Dashboard"]
```

Playback runs in real time, using the gaps between timestamps. There is no speed multiplier; drag the progress slider to skip ahead.

### Multi-source CSV files

Load the project that produced the file before opening a multi-source CSV. The header carries labels, not machine-readable IDs, so the player maps columns positionally: it builds the export schema of the loaded project in unique-ID order and matches it against the file's data columns in that order. A project with an identical dataset and unique-ID layout works as well. Reconstructed per-source frames go back into the pipeline at the right routing.
docs.title: CSV-Export-Playback#10

docs.body:
## Analyzing exported data

CSV opens in every common analysis tool:

- Excel / LibreOffice Calc: open directly.
- Python: `df = pandas.read_csv('file.csv', encoding='utf-8-sig')`.
- MATLAB (`readtable`) and R (`read.csv`): check the first header cell for a BOM character.

## Automation

The [API](API-Reference.md) exposes `csvExport.getStatus`, `csvExport.setEnabled`, `csvExport.setInterval` and `csvExport.close` for export, and the `csvPlayer.*` family (`open`, `setPaused`, `setProgress`, `getStatus`, and `csvPlayer.step` for frame stepping) for playback. The API Server is off by default and listens on port 7777 once enabled.
docs.title: CSV-Export-Playback#11

docs.body:
The `--csv-export` flag in the [Command-Line Interface](Command-Line-Interface.md) turns export on at startup. The flag exists only in Pro builds; the Setup switch works in the free edition.

## See also

- [MDF4 Export & Playback](MDF4.md): binary logging with per-channel sample rates and channel metadata (Pro).
- [Historian](Historian.md): SQLite-backed project archive with built-in replay (Pro).
- [Operation Modes](Operation-Modes.md): Quick Plot vs Project File mode.
- [API Reference](API-Reference.md): the `csvExport.*` and `csvPlayer.*` commands.
docs.title: CSV-Export-Playback#12

docs.body:
# Canvas Widget (Pro)

A water-level sensor prints one number, and no built-in widget draws a tank. The Canvas widget is a blank rectangle on the dashboard that a few lines of JavaScript fill in from your live values: a tank, a custom dial, a radar. If a built-in widget already shows your data, use that instead. The built-in templates need no coding; a custom drawing needs a little JavaScript.

Canvas is a Pro widget (see [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md)); the first use offers the free 14-day trial with a Yes/No prompt, and registering it needs an internet connection. In the free edition, a Canvas group falls back to a data grid. (Formerly the Painter widget; the project-file key stays `"painter"`.)
docs.title: Canvas-Widget#0
Canvas-Widget#1

docs.body:
Fastest start: add the group, click **Template**, and pick **Dial gauge** or **Strip chart**. If the group has fewer datasets than the template expects, Serial Studio offers to add the missing ones with the template's defaults.

1. Open the **Project Editor** from the main toolbar.
2. In the Project Editor toolbar, click **Canvas**. A group titled "Canvas Widget" is added to the project.
3. Add datasets to the group. The script reads them through the `datasets` global.
4. Select the group in the tree and click **Edit Code**. The **Canvas Widget Code Editor** opens.
5. Click **Template** to load one of the [built-in templates](#built-in-templates). The **Add datasets for this template?** prompt appears when the group has too few datasets.
6. Edit the script. Changes compile and reload live. The **Canvas Live Preview** dialog shows the result without a device connected.
docs.title: Canvas-Widget#2

docs.body:
## Script structure

A Canvas script defines `paint()` (required), `onFrame()` (optional) and optional [pointer handlers](#pointer-handlers). `datasets[0]` is the first dataset in the group, for example the first comma-separated value your Arduino prints. `min` and `max` are the **Minimum Value** and **Maximum Value** set on that dataset in the Project Editor; when those are unset the script sees the fallback range described under [`datasets`](#datasets). The timing limits are in [Time limits](#time-limits).

## Pipeline

A dashboard tick is one screen refresh: 60 per second by default, set with **UI Refresh Rate (Hz)** on the **Plotting** tab of [Preferences](Preferences.md) (1 to 240). A data-bearing tick is a tick that carried new frames. Each Canvas widget is bound to one project group. On every tick:
docs.title: Canvas-Widget#3

docs.body:
1. Serial Studio updates the group's datasets with the latest parsed values.
2. If new data arrived since the last tick and the script defines `onFrame()`, it runs once. Use it for history buffers, peak-hold decay and accumulated angles.
3. `paint(ctx, w, h)` runs while the widget is visible. `ctx` is a Canvas2D-style context that uses the same drawing calls as the HTML canvas, `w` and `h` are the widget's pixel dimensions.

`onFrame()` runs when new data arrives; `paint()` runs on every refresh, so the widget repaints at the refresh rate regardless of the data rate. Put history and counters in `onFrame()`, drawing in `paint()`.
docs.title: Canvas-Widget#4

docs.body:
### `paint(ctx, w, h)`

Runs on every tick while the widget is visible. The bitmap is cleared to transparent before the call, and the path is empty. All other context state (`fillStyle`, `strokeStyle`, `font`, `globalAlpha`, transform, line styles) persists from the previous frame. Set every property on which the frame depends at the top of `paint()`, or wrap mid-frame changes in `save()` / `restore()` pairs. Bitmap pixels are wiped between frames; context state is not.

Aim for under 10 ms per call. The hard limits are in [Time limits](#time-limits).

### `onFrame()`
docs.title: Canvas-Widget#5

docs.body:
Called once per data-bearing tick, immediately before `paint()`. Optional. It is not invoked on refresh ticks that carry no new data, so state that must advance on every refresh, such as a sweep angle, cannot live there: advance it in `paint()` from `Date.now()`. `onFrame()` runs even when the widget is hidden (for example on another workspace tab), so history buffers keep filling and `deviceWrite()` / `actionFire()` calls still fire. `paint()` runs only while the widget is visible.

`onFrame()` is the place for time-domain bookkeeping: pushing samples into history buffers, decaying peak holds, integrating a phase angle. Keeping that logic out of `paint()` makes both functions easier to read and review.
docs.title: Canvas-Widget#6
Canvas-Widget#7

docs.body:
### Pointer handlers

A script can react to the mouse by defining any of these optional functions. Coordinates are widget pixels.

| Handler                  | Arguments            | Fires when |
|--------------------------|----------------------|------------|
| `onPress(x, y, button)`  | position, button number (1 left, 2 right, 4 middle) | A mouse button goes down. |
| `onDrag(x, y, dx, dy)`   | position, movement since the last event | The pointer moves while a button is held. |
| `onRelease(x, y)`        | position             | The button is released. |
| `onMove(x, y)`           | position             | The pointer hovers over the widget. |
| `onWheel(x, y, delta)`   | position, signed wheel notches (one notch is 1; trackpads give fractions) | The wheel turns. |
| `onDoubleClick(x, y)`    | position             | A double-click, for reset-style gestures. |
docs.title: Canvas-Widget#8

docs.body:
### Persistent state

Variables declared at the top of the script (`const`, `let`, `var`) live for the lifetime of the widget and retain their values between calls. State is reset when the script is recompiled (after an edit in the editor), when the user switches between light and dark themes, or when the widget is destroyed (project closed, group deleted). A theme switch clears history buffers; a disconnect and reconnect keeps them.

A widget has one set of variables, shared by all its datasets. A top-level `let trace = []` is one buffer for every dataset. Use an array indexed by dataset index instead:
docs.title: Canvas-Widget#9
Canvas-Widget#10

docs.body:
| Field        | Type    | Description |
|--------------|---------|-------------|
| `index`      | number  | Position of the dataset in the frame (not `frame.number`). |
| `uniqueId`   | number  | Stable unique ID across project edits. |
| `title`      | string  | Display name. |
| `units`      | string  | Measurement units (`"degC"`, `"rpm"`, ...). |
| `widget`     | string  | Dataset widget type, if any (`"bar"`, `"gauge"`, `"compass"`, `"meter"`). |
| `value`      | number  | Post-transform numeric value. `NaN` if the dataset is invalid. |
| `rawValue`   | number  | Pre-transform numeric value. |
| `text`       | string  | Post-transform string value. |
| `rawText`    | string  | Pre-transform string value. |
| `min`, `max` | number  | Effective range. Falls back through widget bounds, plot bounds, then FFT bounds. |
| `widgetMin`, `widgetMax`, `plotMin`, `plotMax`, `fftMin`, `fftMax` | number | The widget, plot and FFT bounds that `min` / `max` fall back through. |
| `alarmLow`, `alarmHigh`  | number | Alarm thresholds. Derived from `alarmBands`: the lower edge of the first, and the upper edge of the last, Warning-or-higher band. `NaN` when no such band exists. |
| `alarmBands`             | array of object | The dataset's alarm bands: `{min, max, severity, color, label, blink}`. `severity` is 0=Info, 1=OK, 2=Warning, 3=Critical. `alarmLow`/`alarmHigh` are a legacy view of this same data. |
| `ledHigh`, `hasPlot`, `hasFft` | number, boolean | LED activation threshold, and the plot and FFT visualization flags from the project. |
docs.title: Canvas-Widget#11

docs.body:
`datasets` is implemented as a Proxy. Out-of-range indices return `undefined`; entries cannot be added or removed.

### `group`

Metadata about the group bound to this Canvas.

| Field      | Type    | Description |
|------------|---------|-------------|
| `id`       | number  | Group ID. |
| `title`    | string  | Group title. |
| `columns`  | number  | Configured column count for the group. |
| `sourceId` | number  | Source feeding this group (for multi-source projects). |

### `frame`

Metadata about the last data-bearing tick.

| Field          | Type    | Description |
|----------------|---------|-------------|
| `number`       | number  | Monotonic frame counter, starting from 1. |
| `timestampMs`  | number  | Wall-clock timestamp in milliseconds since epoch. |
docs.title: Canvas-Widget#12

docs.body:
Both fields advance only when new data arrives; on a refresh-only tick `paint()` sees the previous values. Read `frame.timestampMs` in `onFrame()` for timestamps that match the data. For an animation that must advance on every refresh, read `Date.now()` in `paint()`, otherwise it freezes between frames.

### `theme`

The active color palette, refreshed automatically whenever the user switches themes. Every bundled template reads its colors from `theme` instead of hardcoding hex values.
docs.title: Canvas-Widget#13

docs.body:
| Field              | Type   | Description |
|--------------------|--------|-------------|
| `widget_base`      | string | Canvas / card background. |
| `widget_border`    | string | Grid lines, frames, and borders. |
| `alternate_base`   | string | Card body / recessed panel fill. |
| `widget_text`      | string | Primary value labels and titles. |
| `placeholder_text` | string | Muted secondary labels. |
| `widget_highlight` | string | Primary signal / value color. |
| `accent`           | string | Secondary accent color. |
| `alarm`            | string | Alarm color. |
| `widget_colors`    | array of string | Per-channel palette; index with `theme.widget_colors[i % theme.widget_colors.length]`. |
docs.title: Canvas-Widget#14

docs.body:
Other palette keys exist (`text`, `window`, `mid`, `groupbox_background`, `groupbox_border`, `highlighted_text`, `pane_section_label`, ...) mirroring the palette the QML dashboard widgets draw from, but the fields above cover what a Canvas script needs. `theme` is a plain object, not frozen — avoid mutating it. A theme switch replaces the global `theme` object and recompiles the script, which resets its state (see [Persistent state](#persistent-state)).

### `console`

`console.log`, `console.info`, `console.debug`, `console.warn`, and `console.error` route to the Canvas widget's console output, which is visible in the script editor. Each call has the same signature as the browser console. A `console.log` inside `paint()` emits one line per tick (60 lines per second at the default refresh rate): useful during development, remove it from shipped projects.

docs.body:
## Control APIs — `deviceWrite()` and `actionFire()`

Canvas scripts can write back to the device or fire any existing project [Action](Actions.md):

```javascript
deviceWrite(data, sourceId?)     // -> { ok: true } | { ok: false, error: "..." }
actionFire(actionId)             // -> { ok: true } | { ok: false, error: "..." }
```

Both are synchronous, fire-and-forget, and never throw. `deviceWrite` defaults `sourceId` to the canvas widget's group `sourceId`; pass an explicit one to target a different source.

**Important:** `paint()` runs at the refresh rate, 60 times a second by default. Calling `deviceWrite` or `actionFire` from `paint()` sends 60 writes a second to a device that wanted one. `onFrame()` runs at most once per data-bearing tick (frames batched at high rates), never on refresh ticks with no new data, so move the calls there and guard them on a state transition. `actionFire` takes the numeric ID of an existing action in the project (the `7` below):
docs.title: Canvas-Widget#16
Canvas-Widget#17

docs.body:
## Canvas code on a remote dashboard

On a dashboard mirrored from another instance (see [Remote Dashboard](Remote-Dashboard.md)), the publisher's Canvas widgets still draw on the viewer, but their code can only draw. The script runs on a draw-only surface: `apiCall()`, `deviceWrite()`, `actionFire()` and the dashboard helpers answer `{ ok: false, error: "dryRun" }`, `console` output is dropped, and nothing the script does reaches the viewer's devices, files, or processes. `datasets`, `group`, `frame`, `theme` and `ctx` work as usual, so `paint()` and `onFrame()` draw the same picture they draw on the publisher.
docs.title: Canvas-Widget#18

docs.body:
## Drawing API

The context exposes a Canvas2D-style API backed by Qt's QPainter, drawing into an off-screen bitmap. The sections below cover the commonly used methods and properties. Additional Canvas2D members are implemented (`roundRect`, `arcTo`, `ellipse`, `transform` / `setTransform` / `getTransform`, `setLineDash` / `getLineDash`, `isPointInPath`, `isPointInStroke`, `measureText`, `globalCompositeOperation`, `miterLimit`, `lineDashOffset`, the `shadow*` properties, and image-smoothing controls). Calling a member that does not exist throws.

### State

CSS `rgb()` and `rgba()` strings are not supported. For transparency, use the alpha-first hex form (`"#80ff0000"` is 50% red).

|----------------|-------|
| `fillStyle`    | Color string: hex (`"#22c55e"`, or `"#80ff0000"` with the alpha byte first) and named colors. |
| `strokeStyle`  | Same syntax as `fillStyle`. |
| `lineWidth`    | Pixels. |
| `lineCap`      | `"butt"`, `"round"`, `"square"`. |
| `lineJoin`     | `"miter"`, `"round"`, `"bevel"`. |
| `font`         | CSS font shorthand (`"bold 14px monospace"`, `"12px sans-serif"`). |
| `textAlign`    | `"left"` / `"start"`, `"center"`, `"right"` / `"end"`. |
| `textBaseline` | `"alphabetic"`, `"top"`, `"middle"`, `"bottom"`, `"hanging"`. |
| `globalAlpha`  | 0.0 to 1.0. |

docs.body:
`save()` and `restore()` push and pop the full state stack, including the current transform.

Gradient and pattern objects are supported. `createLinearGradient(x0, y0, x1, y1)`, `createRadialGradient(x0, y0, r0, x1, y1, r1)`, `createConicGradient(startRad, cx, cy)`, and `createPattern(src, repetition)` each return a handle that can be assigned to `fillStyle` or `strokeStyle`; gradient handles take stops via `addColorStop(offset, color)`. A gradient needs at least two `addColorStop()` entries to show visible color, and a pattern whose `src` falls outside the image sandbox resolves to an empty tile. The bundled templates favor stacks of solid-color rectangles or arcs for a flat look, but a gradient is available when a smooth ramp is wanted.
docs.title: Canvas-Widget#21

docs.body:
### Transforms

`translate(x, y)`, `rotate(radians)`, `scale(sx, sy)`, `resetTransform()`. Rotations are in radians. Convert from degrees with `* Math.PI / 180`.

### Paths

`beginPath()`, `closePath()`, `moveTo(x, y)`, `lineTo(x, y)`, `rect(x, y, w, h)`, `arc(x, y, r, startRad, endRad, counterClockwise=false)`, `quadraticCurveTo(cpx, cpy, x, y)`, `bezierCurveTo(c1x, c1y, c2x, c2y, x, y)`. Commit with `fill()`, `stroke()`, or `clip()`.

`arc()` requires a preceding `moveTo()` to the arc's start point. The implementation maps to `QPainterPath::arcTo`, which connects the path's current cursor to the arc's start with an implicit line. Without the `moveTo`, the cursor is at the origin (0, 0) and the chord becomes part of the path. A subsequent `stroke()` strokes the chord, `fill()` encloses it, and `clip()` removes a wedge from the clipping region.

docs.body:
## Performance

The Canvas pipeline targets the dashboard refresh rate (60 Hz by default) for moderately complex scenes: a few hundred line segments, a few hundred filled shapes, and about ten text labels per frame.

### Time limits

| Limit  | Applies to | What happens |
|--------|------------|--------------|
| 10 ms  | `paint()`  | A target, not enforced. |
| 30 ms  | `paint()`, two consecutive ticks | The message `warning: paint() took N ms (>30 ms budget)` appears next to the widget, once per script compile. |
| 250 ms | `paint()`, `onFrame()` and the initial compile, per call | The call is aborted, the widget stops updating and shows the error. See [Widget renders once and then freezes](#widget-renders-once-and-then-freezes). |
docs.title: Canvas-Widget#34

docs.body:
Common causes of slow paints:

- **Allocation in the paint path.** Iterating with `for (const ds of datasets)` is fine. `datasets.map(d => d.value)` allocates a new array each frame. So does `ds.title.toUpperCase()` inside a tight loop. Move the work into `onFrame()` and cache the result if the cost is non-trivial.
- **`measureTextWidth()` per label.** Each call is a real metrics call into Qt. Measure fixed labels once at compile time and cache the width.
- **One `stroke()` per point.** A single `beginPath()` followed by many `lineTo()` calls and one `stroke()` is one path-stroke call. A `beginPath()`, `lineTo()`, `stroke()` per point is N calls.
- **`drawImage` from disk every frame.** `drawImage` reloads the image from disk on every call with no internal caching, so per-frame disk reads are not free. Pre-resolve to `qrc:/` paths or read the image once at the top of the script and reuse it.
docs.title: Canvas-Widget#35

docs.body:
## Common errors

### Widget renders once and then freezes

`paint()` or `onFrame()` threw an exception. The widget stops updating and shows the error message next to it. Common causes: indexing `datasets[0]` when the group is empty; dividing by `(ds.max - ds.min)` when both are zero; calling `.toFixed()` on `undefined`. A call that runs past the 250 ms limit stops the widget the same way.

### A diagonal line crosses the arc

`arc()` without a preceding `moveTo()` draws a chord from (0, 0). Add the `moveTo()`; see [Paths](#paths).

### Gradient or pattern fill shows nothing

The handle must be assigned to `fillStyle` or `strokeStyle` before drawing, and a gradient needs two color stops. See [State](#state).
docs.title: Canvas-Widget#36

docs.body:
### Lines look fuzzy

A 1-pixel line at an integer coordinate renders as a 2-pixel band. Offset it by 0.5; see [Paths](#paths).

### Colors do not match what was set

Context state carries over between `paint()` calls. If a previous frame ended with `globalAlpha = 0.5`, the next frame starts with the same value. See [`paint(ctx, w, h)`](#paintctx-w-h).

### State leaks between channels

A top-level `let trace = []` is shared by every dataset. See [Persistent state](#persistent-state).

### `drawImage` shows nothing

A path outside `qrc:/` and the project file's directory is silently skipped. See [Images](#images).
docs.title: Canvas-Widget#37

docs.body:
# Command-Line Interface

You have an Arduino on `COM3` and want the dashboard up with one command. Open a terminal, run the
executable (by its full path, or as `serial-studio` if it is on your `PATH`), and pass the data
source:

```bash
serial-studio --uart COM3 --baud 115200 --quick-plot
serial-studio -p MyProject.ssproj --uart /dev/ttyUSB0
serial-studio --headless --api-server -p plant.ssproj --exit-after 60
```

The first plots whatever `Serial.println` prints. The second opens a project and points its
device at a serial port, replacing the port the project names. The third runs with no window,
with the [API Server](API-Reference.md) on (it lets other programs read and control the running
app over TCP), and quits after a minute. Pass `--help` to print the options your build accepts.
docs.title: Command-Line-Interface#0

docs.body:
`--quick-plot` expects lines of comma-separated numbers, such as `Serial.println("12,3.5,7")`.
`--baud` defaults to 9600 and must equal the value in your sketch's `Serial.begin()`. For a first
run you need only the [Devices](#devices) options and `-p` or `-q`.

Sections marked **(Pro)** or **(commercial builds)** exist only in commercial builds; a build
compiled from source rejects those options as unknown. Every other section works in every build.
Pro features need a license or the 14-day trial, which is offered the first time you use one and
never starts on its own. See [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md).
docs.title: Command-Line-Interface#1

docs.body:
## General

Options apply to the current run only and are not written to your saved settings. Two exceptions:
`--api-token` stores the API token on this machine, and `--reset` deletes the saved settings.
docs.title: Command-Line-Interface#2

docs.body:
| Option | Argument | Description |
|--------|----------|-------------|
| `-v`, `--version` | | Print the application version and exit. |
| `-r`, `--reset` | | Clear the saved application settings and exit. Project files are not touched, and the license is preserved. |
| `-f`, `--fullscreen` | | Launch the dashboard in fullscreen. |
| `--headless` | | Run without a window, for servers and CI. |
| `--dump-api-schema` | `file` | Write the API command registry (name, description, parameter schema per command) to a JSON file and exit. Input for SDK generators. |

## API Server

The API Server is off by default. `--api-server` turns it on at startup, and the gRPC server
(port 8888) starts with it; see [API Reference](API-Reference.md) and [gRPC Server](gRPC-Server.md).
Without `--api-external` it accepts connections from this machine only.

|--------|----------|-------------|
| `--api-server` | | Enable the API Server on startup (port 7777 unless `--api-port` is given). |
| `--api-port` | `port` | Listen on this port instead of 7777. A value outside 1-65535 logs a warning and keeps 7777. |
| `--api-external` | | Allow connections from other hosts, the non-interactive form of the "Allow External API Connections" confirmation. Clients still present the token, and the transport is not encrypted: use it on a trusted network or through a tunnel. |
| `--api-token` | `hex` | Set the token external clients must present (at least 32 hexadecimal characters). The token is stored on this machine and survives the run. The value is visible to every process on the machine; prefer `--api-token-file` or the `SS_API_TOKEN` environment variable. |
| `--api-token-file` | `path` | Read the token from a file. A file wins over `SS_API_TOKEN`, which wins over `--api-token`. |

## Acquisition Pipeline Benchmark

```bash
serial-studio --benchmark-hotpath --min-fps 256000 --benchmark-output report.txt
```

| Option | Argument | Description |
|--------|----------|-------------|
| `--benchmark-hotpath` | | Run the in-process frame-extraction throughput benchmark and exit. |
| `--min-fps` | `fps` | Minimum frames/sec the benchmark must sustain (default 256000). |
| `--benchmark-frames` | `count` | Frames to push through the benchmark (default 1000000). |
| `--benchmark-seconds` | `seconds` | Wall-clock seconds the benchmark must sustain (default 10). |

docs.title: Command-Line-Interface#8

docs.body:
- Any of `--min-fps`, `--benchmark-frames`, `--benchmark-seconds` or `--benchmark-channels` also
  starts the benchmark; `--benchmark-hotpath` alone uses the defaults in the table.
- At a width other than 8 channels, the throughput targets are printed for reference and cannot
  fail the run, because they were calibrated at 8.
- The process exits with a non-zero code when the run fails, so CI can gate on it.
- A non-numeric or out-of-range value falls back to the default without an error. A
  `--benchmark-channels` above 4096 is clamped to 4096.

The benchmark uses a synthetic project, so no device is needed. For the interactive version with a
per-phase results table, use **About > Benchmark**; see the [Benchmark Dialog](Benchmark.md).
