# Command palette

You have a device connected, the dashboard is showing, and you want a CSV log of it. Press **Ctrl+K** (**Cmd+K** on macOS), type `csv`, and press Enter on **CSV File**. Logging starts. No menu was opened. **CSV File** is a toggle, so pressing Enter on it again stops the log.

The command palette is one search box over your dashboard layouts (workspaces), the widgets on them, and every menu action in Serial Studio. It is in the free and Pro editions. Commands for Sessions, File Transmission, the AI Assistant and Notifications appear only in the Pro edition.

## Opening and closing
docs.title: Command-Palette#0

docs.body:
Press **Ctrl+K** (**Cmd+K** on macOS) to open the palette, and again to close it. **Esc**, **Ctrl+W** (**Cmd+W**) and a click outside the dialog close it too. The keys work in the main window, the Project Editor, and pop-out dashboard windows. In the Project Editor, **Ctrl+K** does nothing while the project is locked.

Two buttons open it as well: the workspace button in the dashboard taskbar, and the **Command Palette** button on the main toolbar. The palette is modal: the window behind it ignores input until you close it.

## What the palette lists
docs.title: Command-Palette#1

docs.body:
- **On the dashboard** it lists your [workspaces](Toolbar-Reference.md#a-note-on-workspaces) and the dashboard commands, such as **Pause** and the export toggles. A workspace is a saved layout of dashboard widgets. Typing also searches workspace folders, dataset groups, and open widgets.
- **In Console view, or while the dashboard is not showing,** it lists only the application commands: file actions, operation-mode switches, connection, preferences, and help. There are no workspace, group, or widget entries. Commands that need the dashboard, such as the View entries, are listed dimmed.
- **In the [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md)** it lists the project commands: new, open, save, and the add-item actions from the editor toolbar.
docs.title: Command-Palette#2

docs.body:
In runtime mode (an operator deployment) the authoring commands, such as the Project Editor and Open Project, are hidden.

## Browsing versus searching

The palette switches mode on its own, depending on whether the search box is empty.

### Browse (empty search box)

An empty box shows a grid of large cells. On the dashboard the first row is **Workspaces**, ending in an **Add Workspace** cell; commands follow in labeled sections, one per category. A cell marked **Folder** opens that workspace folder. Use **Back** or the breadcrumb bar at the top to go up a level. Inside a folder the grid shows only that folder's workspaces and an **Add Workspace** cell, which creates the workspace in that folder; the command sections appear only at the top level.
docs.title: Command-Palette#3

docs.body:
### Search (any text typed)

The grid becomes a dense list of results. Each row shows the item's icon, its name, a dimmed path or category, and its keyboard shortcut where one exists. Typing `csv` shows a row named **CSV File** under **Data Export**, with its shortcut at the right.

Search ignores case. Each space-separated word must appear somewhere in the item's name, in any order, so `export csv` and `csv export` find the same entries. Words match as substrings. The characters `-`, `_`, `.` and `/` count as spaces, and a word also matches the name with its spaces removed, so `csvfile` finds **CSV File**. Workspaces, folders and commands match on their own name only, not the dimmed category or path. Groups and widgets also match on the name of the group they belong to, so typing a group's name lists its widgets.
docs.title: Command-Palette#4

docs.body:
The same search reaches widgets: type part of a widget's name and Enter jumps to it. Typing `pause` finds **Pause**; while the dashboard is paused the same entry reads **Resume**.

On the dashboard, results fall into these sections, each hidden when empty:

| Section | Contains |
|---------|----------|
| **Folders** | Workspace folders whose name matches. |
| **Workspaces** | Workspaces whose name matches. |
| **Groups** | Dataset groups of the loaded project whose name matches. |
| **Widgets** | Open widgets whose name matches. |
| **File**, **Operation Mode**, **Connection**, **View**, **Data Export**, **Console**, **Project**, **License**, **Tools**, **Help** | Matching commands, one section per category, in that order. |
docs.title: Command-Palette#5

docs.body:
**Groups** and **Widgets** together show at most 30 results; add a word to narrow the query if the entry you want is missing.

## Keyboard and Enter

The search box keeps focus the whole time, so your hands never leave the keyboard. In search results, **Up** and **Down** (or **Left** and **Right**) move one result. In the browse grid, **Up** and **Down** move a row of cells, and **Left** and **Right** move one cell. Movement stops at the first and last entry instead of wrapping, and the first arrow press highlights the first entry.

**Enter** acts on the highlighted entry, or on the first one if nothing is highlighted:
docs.title: Command-Palette#6

docs.body:
- A workspace: the palette switches to it and closes.
- A widget: the palette shows it in the workspace that contains it. If no workspace contains it, the widget opens in its own window. The palette closes.
- A command: the palette runs it and closes. Dimmed commands are unavailable right now and ignore **Enter**.
- A **Folder** cell drills into the folder, and **Add Workspace** prompts for a new workspace. The palette stays open for both.

**Esc** always closes the palette; it never steps up a folder level.

## See also

- [Toolbar & Button Reference](Toolbar-Reference.md): the buttons these commands mirror.
- [Macros](Macros.md): the command terminal and script editor.
- [Problem Center](Problem-Center.md): the window behind the **Problem Center** and **Connection Diagnostics** entries.
- [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md): where the project commands live.
docs.title: Command-Palette#7

# Communication protocols

Your Arduino prints `Serial.println(temperature)` at 115200 baud. In the **Setup Panel**, pick **UART/COM** from the **Connection** dropdown, choose the port, set **Baud Rate** to the number in your `Serial.begin()` call and click **Connect**. The default is 9600, so a 115200 sketch shows garbage until you change it. The other protocols on this page are for devices that talk another way. Click-by-click steps are in [Protocol Setup Guides](Protocol-Setup-Guides.md); your first dashboard is in [Getting Started](Getting-Started.md).

## Which protocol fits
docs.title: Communication-Protocols#0

docs.body:
| Situation | Connection dropdown entry | Edition | Driver page |
|---|---|---|---|
| Microcontroller connected via USB cable | UART/COM | Free | [Drivers: UART](Drivers-UART.md) |
| Device on the same WiFi or Ethernet network (TCP, UDP, WebSocket, HTTP) | Network | Free | [Drivers: Network](Drivers-Network.md) |
| Battery-powered wireless sensor nearby | Bluetooth LE | Free | [Drivers: Bluetooth LE](Drivers-Bluetooth-LE.md) |
| Device publishing to an MQTT broker | MQTT Subscriber | Pro | [MQTT Subscriber](Drivers-MQTT.md) |
| Industrial equipment with Modbus registers (RTU or TCP) | Modbus | Pro | [Drivers: Modbus](Drivers-Modbus.md) |
| Vehicle CAN bus or OBD-II port | CAN Bus | Pro | [Drivers: CAN Bus](Drivers-CAN-Bus.md) |
| PLC or SCADA server with an OPC UA server | OPC UA | Pro | [Drivers: OPC UA](Drivers-OPC-UA.md) |
| Siemens S7 controller without OPC UA (S7comm) | Siemens S7 | Pro | [Drivers: S7](Drivers-S7.md) |
| Allen-Bradley or Omron controller | EtherNet/IP | Pro | [Drivers: EtherNet/IP](Drivers-EtherNet-IP.md) |
| Substation, RTU or utility SCADA gateway | IEC 60870-5-104 | Pro | [Drivers: IEC 104](Drivers-IEC-104.md) |
| Analyzing audio signals or vibrations (Audio input) | Audio | Pro | [Drivers: Audio](Drivers-Audio.md) |
| Custom USB device with bulk or isochronous endpoints (Raw USB) | USB Device | Pro | [Drivers: USB](Drivers-USB.md) |
| Gamepad, joystick or HID-class sensor | HID Device | Pro | [Drivers: HID](Drivers-HID.md) |
| Script or simulator writing to stdout or a pipe (Process I/O) | Process | Pro | [Drivers: Process I/O](Drivers-Process-IO.md) |
docs.title: Communication-Protocols#1

docs.body:
Serial Studio has 14 drivers in total. The Pro ones are built into the official binary and unlock with a license or the trial; a GPL build from source (without `BUILD_COMMERCIAL`) lists only UART/COM, Network and Bluetooth LE in the dropdown. You pick the protocol with the **Connection** dropdown in the **Setup Panel**, and the options for that protocol appear under it. See [Pro vs Free Features](Pro-vs-Free.md) for the edition split.

## Free protocols

### Serial/UART

An Arduino running `Serial.begin(115200); Serial.println(temperature);` already speaks UART. Choose **UART/COM** in the **Connection** dropdown, pick the port, set 115200 and connect. The same driver covers USB-to-serial adapters (CH340, FTDI, CP210x, PL2303), native hardware UARTs and RS-232/RS-485 transceivers. Full reference: [Drivers: UART](Drivers-UART.md). Only the baud rate usually needs changing; leave the rest at their defaults.
docs.title: Communication-Protocols#2

docs.body:
| Parameter      | Description |
|----------------|-------------|
| Baud Rate      | Must equal the value in your firmware's `Serial.begin()`. Default: 9600. Common values: 9600, 115200, 921600. |
| Data bits      | 5, 6, 7 or 8. Default: 8. |
| Parity         | None, Even, Odd, Space or Mark. Default: None. |
| Stop bits      | 1, 1.5 or 2. Default: 1. |
| Flow control   | None, RTS/CTS (hardware) or XON/XOFF (software). Use None unless your device needs it. |
| Send DTR Signal | On by default. Arduino boards such as the Uno restart when the DTR line goes high, so a board that reboots every time you connect is doing exactly that. Turn DTR off to connect without a reset. |
| Auto Reconnect | Off by default. When on, Serial Studio reconnects after the device is unplugged and replugged. |
docs.title: Communication-Protocols#3

docs.body:
- **Linux:** Reading `/dev/ttyUSBx` and `/dev/ttyACMx` without root depends on group membership; see [Serial port permissions](Linux-Installation.md#serial-port-permissions).
- **Windows and macOS:** If the port does not appear, install the adapter vendor's driver (CH340, PL2303, CP210x and FTDI each have one).

### Network (TCP, UDP, WebSocket, HTTP)

The Network driver connects to devices over TCP or UDP sockets, a WebSocket, or an HTTP endpoint that Serial Studio polls. All four are client connections; Serial Studio does not listen for incoming TCP connections. Choose **Network** in the **Connection** dropdown (free). If your ESP32 or ESP8266 sketch opens a `WiFiServer`, choose TCP. TCP delivers every byte in order; UDP is faster but can drop or reorder packets, so use it for multicast or low-latency datagrams. Full reference: [Drivers: Network](Drivers-Network.md).
docs.title: Communication-Protocols#4

docs.body:
| Parameter       | Description |
|-----------------|-------------|
| Socket type     | TCP, UDP, WebSocket or HTTP. |
| Remote address  | IP address or hostname of the device. |
| TCP port        | Remote port for TCP connections. Default: 23 (a placeholder; use your firmware's port). |
| UDP remote port | Port the device listens on or sends from. Default: 53 (a placeholder). |
| UDP local port  | Port Serial Studio binds to for receiving. Default: 0, which lets the OS pick a random port, so nothing reaches you; set it to the port the device sends to. |
| UDP multicast   | Join a multicast group given by the remote address. |
docs.title: Communication-Protocols#5

docs.body:
WebSocket and HTTP have their own URL fields, and HTTP has a polling interval (default 1000 ms); see [Drivers: Network](Drivers-Network.md).

If connections fail, check that your firewall allows Serial Studio through. On macOS, the first network connection can show a system permission dialog; allow it.

### Bluetooth Low Energy

A BLE module such as an HM-10, nRF52 or ESP32 BLE that advertises sensor data appears under the **Bluetooth LE** entry of the **Connection** dropdown (free): pick the device, then the characteristic that sends notifications. The driver discovers advertising devices, lists their GATT services and characteristics (GATT is the BLE data profile), and streams notification data into the pipeline. Full reference: [Drivers: Bluetooth LE](Drivers-Bluetooth-LE.md).
docs.title: Communication-Protocols#6

docs.body:
| Parameter      | Description |
|----------------|-------------|
| Device         | Picked from the discovered list. Scanning starts when you choose Bluetooth LE. The list is shared by every source that uses BLE. |
| Service        | The GATT service that carries your data, when the device exposes several. |
| Characteristic | The characteristic that sends notifications or indications with your telemetry. |

- **Windows:** Windows 10 version 1803 or later and a Bluetooth 4.0+ adapter.
- **macOS:** macOS 14 or later. The first scan shows a Bluetooth permission prompt; allow it.
- **Linux:** BlueZ 5.44 or later and a Bluetooth 4.0+ adapter. If the device does not appear, add yourself to the `bluetooth` group and check that `bluetoothd` is running.
- **All platforms:** The device must be advertising and not connected to another host.
docs.title: Communication-Protocols#7

docs.body:
## Pro protocols

These drivers are Pro features and exist only in the official binary. The first time you use one, Serial Studio asks whether to start a 14-day trial (a Yes/No prompt; registering the trial needs an internet connection). After the trial expires, the prompt offers activation or purchase instead. See [Pro vs Free Features](Pro-vs-Free.md).

### MQTT

The MQTT driver (Pro; dropdown entry **MQTT Subscriber**) subscribes to a broker and feeds the messages into the pipeline. The subscriber is a per-source bus type; the publisher, which forwards frames to a broker, is a project-level export configured separately.
docs.title: Communication-Protocols#8

docs.body:
| Parameter            | Description |
|----------------------|-------------|
| Hostname             | Broker address. Default: `127.0.0.1`. |
| Port                 | Broker port. Default: 1883. TLS brokers commonly use 8883; set it yourself. |
| Client ID            | Random 16-character lowercase string; the button generates a new one. |
| Username / password  | Broker authentication. |
| MQTT version         | 3.1, 3.1.1 or 5.0. Default: 5.0. |
| Topic filter         | Topic the subscriber listens on. Supports the wildcards `+` (one level) and `#` (all remaining levels). The publisher uses a separate per-project topic base; see [MQTT Publisher](MQTT-Publisher.md). |
| TLS/SSL              | Off by default. When on: protocol version, peer verification mode, verification depth and CA certificates. |
| Keep alive           | Seconds between PING packets. Default: 60. Automatic keep-alive is on by default. |
docs.title: Communication-Protocols#9

docs.body:
Subscriptions use QoS 0, and Last Will is not exposed. TLS connections need valid CA certificates, either the system store or a custom bundle.

See [MQTT Topics & Semantics](MQTT-Topics.md) for the vocabulary, [MQTT Subscriber](Drivers-MQTT.md) for the inbound side and [MQTT Publisher](MQTT-Publisher.md) for the outbound side.

### Modbus

The Modbus driver (Pro; dropdown entry **Modbus**) reads registers from PLCs, power meters and other industrial equipment over Modbus RTU (RS-485 serial) or Modbus TCP. It needs a device with a documented register map. Full reference: [Drivers: Modbus](Drivers-Modbus.md).
docs.title: Communication-Protocols#10

docs.body:
| Parameter       | Description |
|-----------------|-------------|
| Protocol        | Modbus RTU or Modbus TCP. |
| Slave address   | Device address on the bus, 1 to 247. Default: 1. |
| Register groups | One or more groups, each with a register type, start address and count. |
| Poll interval   | Milliseconds between queries. Default: 100. |
| RTU settings    | Serial port, baud rate, data bits, parity, stop bits. |
| TCP settings    | Host address and port. The default port is 5020, not the standard 502; set 502 for most real devices. |

| Register type     | Read function code | Access      | Size    |
|-------------------|--------------------|-------------|---------|
| Coil              | 01                 | Read/Write  | 1 bit   |
| Discrete input    | 02                 | Read-only   | 1 bit   |
| Holding register  | 03                 | Read/Write  | 16 bits |
| Input register    | 04                 | Read-only   | 16 bits |
docs.title: Communication-Protocols#11

docs.body:
Modbus RTU needs an RS-485-to-USB adapter, correct A/B polarity and a 120-ohm termination resistor at each end of the bus. Modbus TCP needs only network access. On Linux, make sure you can access `/dev/ttyUSBx`.

### CAN Bus

The CAN Bus driver (Pro; dropdown entry **CAN Bus**) reads and writes CAN frames through the host's CAN interface layer, including CAN FD. Full reference: [Drivers: CAN Bus](Drivers-CAN-Bus.md).

| Parameter | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| Plugin    | The CAN backend. Linux uses `socketcan`; Windows uses `peakcan`, `vectorcan` or `systeccan`; macOS needs third-party drivers. |
| Interface | The interface name, for example `can0` or `PCAN_USBBUS1`. |
| Bitrate   | Must match the network exactly. Common: 125, 250, 500 kbps, 1 Mbps. |
| CAN FD    | Enable for Flexible Data-rate frames (up to 64 data bytes per frame). |
docs.title: Communication-Protocols#12

docs.body:
Each received frame reaches your frame parser as a byte array, zero-padded to a fixed size. The DLC byte holds the real payload length, so read it rather than the array length.

| Frame type | Layout | Padded size |
|---|---|---|
| Standard (11-bit identifier) | `[ID_high, ID_low, DLC, data_0, data_1, ...]` | 11 bytes |
| Extended (29-bit identifier) | 4 identifier bytes (the first has its top bit set to mark an extended frame), then `DLC, data_0, ...` | 13 bytes |

FD frames longer than the padded size and the reassembly rules are in [Drivers: CAN Bus](Drivers-CAN-Bus.md).

- **Linux:** SocketCAN is built into the kernel. Bring an interface up with `ip link set can0 type can bitrate 500000 && ip link set up can0`.
- **Windows:** Install the vendor driver (PEAK, Vector, Systec) before connecting the adapter.
docs.title: Communication-Protocols#13

docs.body:
### OPC UA, S7comm, EtherNet/IP and IEC 60870-5-104

These four Pro drivers (dropdown entries **OPC UA**, **Siemens S7**, **EtherNet/IP** and **IEC 60870-5-104**) are clients that read from industrial controllers over Ethernet. None of them writes to the machine.
docs.title: Communication-Protocols#14

docs.body:
- **OPC UA** browses a server's tags and subscribes to the ones you pick, so any controller or gateway that ships an OPC UA server works. See [Drivers: OPC UA](Drivers-OPC-UA.md).
- **S7comm** polls absolute addresses on Siemens S7-300, S7-400, S7-1200 and S7-1500 controllers (port 102); use it when the controller has no OPC UA server. See [Drivers: S7](Drivers-S7.md).
- **EtherNet/IP** polls symbolic tag names on Allen-Bradley Logix, MicroLogix, Micro800 and SLC 500 controllers, and Omron NJ/NX. See [Drivers: EtherNet/IP](Drivers-EtherNet-IP.md).
- **IEC 60870-5-104** receives the monitor-direction data of a substation or RTU over TCP port 2404 after a general interrogation on connect. See [Drivers: IEC 104](Drivers-IEC-104.md).
docs.title: Communication-Protocols#15

docs.body:
### Audio input

The Audio input driver (Pro; dropdown entry **Audio**) captures raw PCM audio from a microphone, line-in or audio interface using the miniaudio library. Full reference: [Drivers: Audio](Drivers-Audio.md).

| Parameter             | Description |
|-----------------------|-------------|
| Input device          | Picked from the enumerated capture devices. |
| Sample rate           | Depends on the device. Common: 44100, 48000 Hz. |
| Sample format         | Bit depth, for example 16-bit integer or 32-bit float. |
| Channel configuration | Mono or stereo. |

- **macOS:** Allow Microphone access in System Settings > Privacy & Security > Microphone.
- **Windows:** To record what the computer plays, enable "Stereo Mix" or pick the right input in Sound Settings.
- **Linux:** Works with ALSA and PulseAudio. `arecord -l` lists capture devices.
- For sensor measurements, use line-in rather than the microphone input, which applies automatic gain control.
docs.title: Communication-Protocols#16

docs.body:
### Raw USB

The Raw USB driver (Pro; dropdown entry **USB Device**) reads USB device endpoints directly through libusb, bypassing the operating system's serial and HID drivers. It suits custom firmware with bulk endpoints (STM32, TinyUSB, PIC) and isochronous streaming devices. Full reference: [Drivers: USB](Drivers-USB.md).

| Parameter        | Description |
|------------------|-------------|
| Device           | Picked from the enumerated list (VID:PID and product string). |
| IN endpoint      | The endpoint to read from. |
| OUT endpoint     | The endpoint to write to. |
| Transfer mode    | Bulk/Interrupt Stream (default), Advanced (Bulk + Control) (bulk plus vendor control transfers; a Yes/No confirmation appears once, because a vendor control write can brick a device) or Isochronous. |
| ISO packet size  | Packet size for isochronous transfers. Only used in Isochronous mode. |
docs.title: Communication-Protocols#17

docs.body:
- **Linux:** Needs `udev` rules that grant your user access to the device, or root.
- **macOS:** If the system holds a kernel driver on the device, libusb tries to detach it.
- **Windows:** Needs a WinUSB or libusb-compatible driver for the device, for example installed with Zadig.

### HID

The HID driver (Pro; dropdown entry **HID Device**) reads interrupt reports from gamepads, joysticks, custom USB HID firmware and HID-class sensors using the hidapi library, with no custom OS driver. Full reference: [Drivers: HID](Drivers-HID.md).

Pick a device from the list, shown as `Product Name (VID:PID)`, or just `VID:PID` when the device has no product string. After you select it, Serial Studio shows its Usage Page and Usage. The list refreshes every 2 seconds, so plugged and unplugged devices appear on their own. Each report is 65 bytes (1 report ID byte plus 64 data bytes), and the driver forwards all of it.
docs.title: Communication-Protocols#18

docs.body:
- **Windows and macOS:** No extra drivers.
- **Linux:** Uses the `hidraw` interface. Add `udev` rules for `/dev/hidrawX` to avoid running as root.

### Process I/O

A Python script that prints CSV can pose as a sensor. The Process I/O driver (Pro; dropdown entry **Process**) reads data from a child process or a named pipe, which also suits simulators and synthetic data generators for testing dashboards. Full reference: [Drivers: Process I/O](Drivers-Process-IO.md).

| Mode       | Description |
|------------|-------------|
| Launch     | Serial Studio starts the process, reads its merged stdout and stderr, and can write to its stdin. |
| Named pipe | Serial Studio reads from a named pipe or FIFO. On Linux and macOS it creates the FIFO with `mkfifo` if it does not exist. On Windows it acts as the named-pipe server, using the `\\.\pipe\PipeName` convention. The external process writes to the pipe; set the pipe path in the setup pane. |
docs.title: Communication-Protocols#19

docs.body:
| Launch parameter  | Description |
|-------------------|-------------|
| Executable        | Path to the program, with a file dialog. |
| Arguments         | Command-line arguments. |
| Working directory | The directory the process runs in. |

Because stdout and stderr are merged, write only data frames to stdout if you want clean parsing. If the child process exits unexpectedly, Serial Studio shows a warning and disconnects.

## See also

- [Protocol Setup Guides](Protocol-Setup-Guides.md): step-by-step instructions for each protocol.
- [Getting Started](Getting-Started.md): first-time setup tutorial.
- [Troubleshooting](Troubleshooting.md): fixes for common connection problems.
- [Pro vs Free Features](Pro-vs-Free.md): protocol availability across editions.
docs.title: Communication-Protocols#20

docs.body:
# Concepts

## Overview

Your Arduino prints `Serial.println("21.5,48");` once a second. Serial Studio reads each line as a frame, the frame parser splits it into the values 21.5 and 48, and a dataset picks each value by position and shows it as a plot, a gauge, or whatever widget you choose.

If your device prints numbers separated by commas (name:value pairs and one-line JSON also work), set Operation Mode to **Quick Plot (Auto-Detected Format)** in the Device Setup panel and you are done. **Parse via Project File** lets you change each step below; see [Operation Modes](Operation-Modes.md).
docs.title: Concepts#0

docs.body:
## A worked example

The device sends this line, ending in a newline:

```text
21.5,48
```

- The frame is `21.5,48`. `println` ends the line with a newline, and the default frame detection, End Delimiter Only, ends a frame at the end delimiter, which defaults to `
` (a newline).
- The default decoder, Plain Text (UTF8), turns the bytes into text, and the frame parser splits it on commas and returns the list `[21.5, 48]`. In Quick Plot the splitter is fixed; in Project File mode you pick the Built-In, JavaScript or Lua parser.
- You create datasets in the Project Editor. The dataset Temperature reads frame index 1 and gets 21.5. The dataset Humidity reads frame index 2 and gets 48.
- A second dataset may read index 1 as well, so one value can appear as a Plot and as a Gauge.
docs.title: Concepts#1

docs.body:
To build this two-dataset project step by step, follow the [Project File tutorial](Project-File-Tutorial.md). Off-by-one trap: the frame index starts at 1, but the array a JavaScript `parse()` returns starts at 0, so index 1 is array element 0. Lua tables start at 1, so index N is table element N. The Built-In parser needs neither. The [Glossary](Glossary.md) lists every term alphabetically. ```mermaid flowchart LR D["Device"] --> F["Frame
(delimiters)"] F --> DE["Decoder"] DE --> P["Frame parser"] P --> A["Values
[1] [2] [3] ..."] A --> DS["Datasets
(frame index)"] DS --> G["Groups"] G --> W["Widgets"] W --> WS["Workspaces"] ```
docs.title: Concepts#2

docs.body:
## The chain, step by step

The **Operation Mode** selector in the Device Setup panel decides how much of this chain runs: **Console Only (No Parsing)** shows raw bytes, **Quick Plot (Auto-Detected Format)** plots lines of numbers, and **Parse via Project File** runs every row below. In Quick Plot the Frame, Decoder and Frame parser rows run with fixed settings; you edit them only in Project File mode.
docs.title: Concepts#3

docs.body:
| Step | What it is | Where you set it |
|------|------------|------------------|
| **Device** | Where the bytes come from: a serial port, a network socket, Bluetooth LE, or a Pro connection such as Modbus or CAN Bus. The **Connection** selector picks the kind; [Devices](Devices.md) lists which are free. | Device Setup panel |
| **Frame** | One complete message from the device. Frame detection decides where a frame ends. The default, End Delimiter Only, cuts at the newline, which matches `println`. In Quick Plot a frame is one line. Other modes are covered in [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md). | Project Editor, device page |
| **Decoder** | How the frame's bytes become text before parsing: Plain Text (UTF8), Hexadecimal, Base64, or Binary (Direct) for binary parsers. Plain Text (UTF8) is the default and what `println` sends. | Project Editor, device page |
| **Frame parser** | Turns a frame into an ordered list of values. It is the Built-In parser (configured, no code), a JavaScript `parse(frame)` function, or a Lua one. See [Frame Parser Reference](Frame-Parser.md). | Project Editor, frame parser page |
| **Values and frame index** | The parser's output is an ordered list of values. The frame index is a value's 1-based position in it: the first value is index 1, so in a JavaScript `parse()` index N reads array element N-1. A dataset reads exactly one index. Two datasets may read the same index. See [Dataset Identity Model](Identity-Model.md). | Project Editor, dataset page |
| **Dataset** | One named channel, such as a temperature: title, units, ranges, and the widgets that show it. | Project Editor |
| **Group** | A set of related datasets. A group can have a **Group Widget** that shows them together. | Project Editor |
| **Widget** | What appears on the dashboard. Datasets choose dataset widgets (such as Plot, Gauge or LED); groups choose a Group Widget (see the table under Rules). See [Widget Reference](Widget-Reference.md). | Project Editor |
| **Workspace** | A named page of the dashboard that shows a chosen set of widgets. Serial Studio generates workspaces from the groups until you customize them. | Project Editor, workspaces |
docs.title: Concepts#4

docs.body:
## Rules that follow from the chain

A value the parser does not return never arrives. If your Arduino prints three values and a dataset reads frame index 4, that dataset keeps its last value: the gauge looks fine and the number never moves. Nothing errors at once. Once the shortfall has lasted about three seconds, the [Problem Center](Problem-Center.md) (**Ctrl+K**, or Cmd+K on macOS, opens the [Command Palette](Command-Palette.md); type `Problem Center`) raises a warning titled "Frames deliver fewer values than the project expects" (id `short-frames`). See also [Troubleshooting](Troubleshooting.md).
docs.title: Concepts#5

docs.body:
Group Widgets bind datasets by tag, and each widget has its own count rule:

| Group Widget | Datasets it needs |
|--------------|-------------------|
| Accelerometer | Exactly three, tagged x, y and z |
| Gyroscope | Exactly three, tagged x, y, z or pitch, roll, yaw |
| Plot3D | Three or more, including x, y and z |
| GPS Map | Two or more, including lat and lon; alt is optional |
| Data Grid, Multi-Plot, Bar Panel, LED Panel | One or more |

See [Widget Reference](Widget-Reference.md).

A computed dataset (Pro) has no frame index. A transform that never reads `value` makes its dataset computed when the project loads, and the editor greys out the Frame Index field. See [Deriving values](Derived-Values.md), which also compares the ways to compute a value the device does not send.
docs.title: Concepts#6

docs.body:
## Optional layers

None of these is needed for a first dashboard. Two reshape values after parsing: [Value transforms](Dataset-Transforms.md) calibrate or convert one dataset (Pro), and [Variables](Variables.md) are named tables that parsers, transforms and scripts share (Pro). The rest talk to the device or run logic beside the project: [Actions](Actions.md) are free dashboard buttons that send commands, [Output widgets](Output-Controls.md) (sliders, knobs) are their Pro cousins for continuous values, and a [Control Loop](Control-Loop.md) is an optional `setup()` / `loop()` script.

# Console annotations

Your board prints lines, and one of them arrives garbled. Console annotations are a highlighter for the console: a small JavaScript decoder colors ranges of incoming bytes (a line, a newline, a checksum), and the Annotations panel shows them as lanes, lists them in a filterable table, and extracts the bytes of any one label class.

## Overview

The console shows bytes as text or hex. Annotations add a second layer on top of the same stream: the decoder marks byte ranges with a row and a class, and the panel draws them. It answers "where in the stream did this happen" for framing bytes, headers, checksums, and payloads. The frame parser, which turns frames into dataset values, is a separate thing; a decoder changes nothing in the data pipeline.
docs.title: Console-Annotations#0

docs.body:
Console annotations are available in the free and Pro editions and need no project: they work in Console Only and Quick Plot mode as well as with a project file.

Open the panel with the **Annotations** button in the console toolbar, next to Clear, Find, and Collapse. If the toolbar is narrow, the button sits under **Utilities**. The panel appears below the console output with four tabs: Track, Table, Payload, and Decoder.

Decoding runs only while the Annotations panel is open. Bytes that arrive while it is closed are neither decoded nor kept for the Payload tab, and reopening the panel starts with an empty carry-over.
docs.title: Console-Annotations#1

docs.body:
## Quick start

1. Connect a device so bytes arrive in the console, for example an Arduino printing with `Serial.println`. Console Only mode is enough.
2. Click **Annotations** in the console toolbar.
3. Open the **Decoder** tab. It is pre-filled with a working line decoder that labels every LF-terminated line. To try a protocol instead, pick its template from the dropdown (see [Decoder tab](#decoder-tab)).
4. Click **Apply**. The status dot turns green and reads `Decoding, N annotations`.
5. Switch to **Track** to see the labels as lanes, or **Table** to read them as a list.

With a sketch that prints one value per line, each line becomes a green bar labelled with its byte count, followed by a red `LF` mark.
docs.title: Console-Annotations#2
Console-Annotations#3

The inner loop looks for the next `0x0A` (newline). The first `annotate` colors the line, the second colors the newline. If the chunk ends before a newline arrives, the function returns `start`, so the unfinished line is presented again with the next chunk.

### `rows` and `classes`

`rows` is an array of names, one per lane in the Track tab. `classes` is an array of `{name, color}` objects, or plain name strings. A class without a valid color gets one from a built-in palette, and an unnamed class is labelled `class N`. Both arrays must be non-empty or the script fails to compile with `'decoder.rows' and 'decoder.classes' must be non-empty arrays`. Rows beyond 16 and classes beyond 64 are dropped silently.
docs.title: Console-Annotations#4

docs.body:
### `decode(bytes, offset, ctx, size)`

Called with each new chunk of console bytes:

| Argument | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| `bytes`  | The chunk to decode, as an ArrayBuffer. Wrap it in `new Uint8Array(bytes)` to index it. |
| `offset` | Absolute stream offset of `bytes[0]`, counted from the start of the session. |
| `ctx`    | The annotation store. Call `ctx.annotate(...)` on it. |
| `size`   | Number of bytes in `bytes`. Use this in loop conditions instead of `b.length`. |

Loop on `size`, not `b.length`: reading `.length` off a typed array is slower on a busy console. If you keep `.length`, copy it into a local before the loop.
docs.title: Console-Annotations#5

docs.body:
The return value is **how many bytes the function consumed**. Anything not consumed carries over and is presented again at the front of the next chunk, so a message split across two chunks decodes once, whole. If a chunk ends mid-line, return the offset where that line began, as the example does; the next chunk then starts there, with the rest of the line attached.

Carry-over is capped at 4096 bytes. A stuck decoder that never consumes gets 4,096 bytes of patience; after that its oldest carried bytes are dropped, so memory cannot grow without bound.

### `ctx.annotate(start, end, row, classIndex, texts)`
docs.title: Console-Annotations#6

docs.body:
Records one label. `start` and `end` are absolute stream offsets and both are inclusive. `row` and `classIndex` are positions in the `rows` and `classes` arrays, counted from 0. `texts` is an array of renderings, longest first: the Track tab draws the longest one that fits the bar, then falls back to the shorter one, then to none. An empty `texts` array is accepted and the bar shows `...`.

Records are silently ignored when `start` is negative, `end` is before `start`, or `row` or `classIndex` is not a declared index.

### Failure handling

Each `decode()` call runs under a 200 ms watchdog in its own JavaScript engine. A call that throws or exceeds the watchdog disables the decoder and stops decoding until you click **Apply** again. The message appears next to the red status dot in the Decoder tab; a compile error reads `Line N: message`. The console itself keeps running.
docs.title: Console-Annotations#7

docs.body:
## Track tab

In the Annotations panel (console toolbar > **Annotations** > **Track**), the Track tab draws one lane per declared row. Each bar is a labelled byte range, positioned by its offset inside the visible window: oldest at the left edge, newest at the right. The byte offsets of both window edges are printed under the lanes, and a legend maps each class color to its name.

**Window** sets how many bytes of the stream the lanes span, from 256 to 1,048,576. A narrow window separates individual records; a wide one shows density. At high data rates a few kilobytes is where individual bars stay legible.
docs.title: Console-Annotations#8

docs.body:
When more labels fall inside one pixel than can be drawn apart, neighbours of the same class merge into a single mark and the bar reads `N labels`. Hovering shows the merged count and the byte range; shrinking the window separates them again.

The caption above the lanes reads `Labelled bytes X to Y, oldest on the left.` Compare it with the ruler under the lanes to see where the decoder is working relative to the window. The store keeps 65,536 labels, so on a fast stream the labelled range covers only the most recent bytes, and the caption adds a note that the store is full.

## Table tab

In the Annotations panel, the Table tab lists every retained label as a row: Start, End, Length, Row, Class, and Text. Two dropdowns filter by row and by class, and **Export CSV** writes every retained label (ignoring the filters) with the header `start,end,length,row,class,text`.
docs.title: Console-Annotations#9

docs.body:
## Payload tab

In the Annotations panel, the Payload tab concatenates the bytes of one class, in stream order, up to 65,536 bytes. Pick the class, choose **Hexadecimal** for spaced upper-case hex or clear it for UTF-8 text, and click **Refresh**.

Only ranges still inside the retained bytes can be extracted; they are the most recent 1 MiB of the stream. When that span slides forward, labels that end before its start are dropped from the store and the table. A label straddling the edge stays, but its older bytes are gone.

## Decoder tab

In the Annotations panel, the Decoder tab is the script editor, with syntax highlighting and line numbers, a template dropdown, and three buttons.
docs.title: Console-Annotations#10

docs.body:
The dropdown loads a decoder for a known protocol into the editor, replacing what is there. Click Apply afterwards to arm it.

| Template | Framing it decodes |
|----------|--------------------|
| Line framing (LF) | Text lines terminated by `0x0A`. The default. |
| NMEA 0183 sentences | `$TALKER,fields*CS` with checksum verification; a bad checksum gets its own class. |
| SLIP framing (RFC 1055) | `0xC0` packet delimiter with `0xDB` escape pairs labelled separately. |
| COBS packets | Zero-delimited packets; the code-byte chain is walked and a chain that overruns the delimiter is flagged. |
| MAVLink v2 packets | `0xFD` header, payload, checksum, and the signature block when the incompatibility flag is set. |
| Modbus RTU frames | Frame length derived from the function code, since a byte stream no longer carries RTU's idle-gap framing. |
| Fixed-size records | Every N bytes is one record; edit `RECORD_SIZE` at the top of the script. |
docs.title: Console-Annotations#11

docs.body:
Every template is a normal script: load one, then edit it for your protocol.

| Button | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| **Apply** | Compiles the script, adopts its rows and classes, and starts decoding. Compiling always clears previously decoded labels, because the new script declares its own rows and classes. |
| **Clear** | Discards decoded labels and the retained bytes, and restarts offsets at zero. The script stays loaded. This is the Decoder tab's own button, separate from the console toolbar's Clear, which clears console output. |
| **Pause** / **Resume** | Stops and restarts decoding. Labels already captured stay on screen, which is how you freeze a capture to inspect it. |
docs.title: Console-Annotations#12

docs.body:
The status line shows one of `Decoding, N annotations`, `Paused, N annotations kept` (compiled but not decoding), `No decoder applied` (nothing compiled), or a red `Decoder error: ` followed by the message. While paused, the Track tab shows an amber `paused` badge.

## What is saved

The decoder script and its enabled state, the window size, the selected tab, and the Payload hex toggle are saved as application settings and restored on the next launch, in every operation mode.

With a project file loaded, the decoder script and its enabled state are also written into the project, so they travel with the `.ssproj`. Without a project, your decoder stays between launches. A project that carries a decoder replaces yours while it is open.
docs.title: Console-Annotations#13

docs.body:
## Limits

| Limit | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Retained labels | 65,536 (oldest dropped first) |
| Retained bytes for payload extraction | 1 MiB |
| Distinct label texts | 4,096 (further texts collapse to `...`) |
| Rows | 16 |
| Classes | 64 |
| Carry-over between chunks | 4,096 bytes |
| `decode()` watchdog | 200 ms per call |
| Payload extraction per refresh | 65,536 bytes |

Decoding runs on the interface thread at chunk rate, never on the frame pipeline, and only while the panel is open. Labels are published on the display tick, so counts and lanes advance in steps rather than per byte.
docs.title: Console-Annotations#14

# Control Loop (setup / loop)

Your Arduino prints a reading only after you send it `READ`. Without firmware changes, the Control Loop sends it for you:

```javascript
function loop() {
  io.writeData("READ\r\n", SerialStudio.Text);   // the host-side Serial.println("READ")
  delay(500);                                    // twice a second
}
```

`io.writeData` sends the bytes `READ` followed by CR LF to the open connection. The reply comes back through the [frame parser](Frame-Parser.md) like any other data. To try it, paste the script into **Project Scripts > Control Loop** in the Project Editor, then connect the device.
docs.title: Control-Loop#0

docs.body:
The Control Loop is a script of up to three functions that Serial Studio calls over the life of a connection: `setup()` once after the device connects, `loop()` repeatedly while it stays connected, and the optional `onConnect()` once just before the connection opens. It can send wake-up handshakes, send commands on a timer, issue keep-alives, or react to what the device prints.

The Control Loop is free; nothing in it checks a license. Three things a script can call need Pro: the `notify*()` functions, Variables tables, and `ensureDashboard()` creating a waterfall, 3D plot or image widget (see [Pro vs Free Features](Pro-vs-Free.md)).
docs.title: Control-Loop#1

docs.body:
It was previously called the Control Script, and the API keeps that name (`controlScript.*` commands).

It automates a device you have **already set up and connected**. It is not where you create or connect a device: choose the Connection, the device, and its settings in the Device Setup pane first.

A project has one Control Loop. With several devices, the calls that talk to a device take an optional `{ sourceId: n }`; the default is source 0.

Use it when:

- A device needs a command sequence to start streaming (many BLE probes and lab instruments only report data after a "begin measurement" handshake).
- You want to poll a device on a timer: request a Modbus register, send an `AT` query, ask for the next sample.
- A device needs a periodic keep-alive to stay awake.
- The dashboard should build itself from whatever the device sends ([self-building dashboard](#6-self-building-dashboard)).
docs.title: Control-Loop#2

docs.body:
## Where to configure it

Open the Project Editor and select **Project Scripts > Control Loop** in the left tree. It sits next to the two transform libraries and opens a code editor.

```
Project
├─ Project Scripts
│   ├─ Control Loop        <-- here
│   ├─ Lua Library
│   └─ JavaScript Library
├─ Actions
├─ Device 1 (Bluetooth LE)
├─ Groups
└─ ...
```

The editor toolbar mirrors the Frame Parser editor: **Reset** loads the starter template, **Open** imports a `.js` file, then the usual undo / redo / clipboard actions, **Help** opens this page, and **Validate** compiles the script and reports the first syntax error (or confirms it is clean) without running it. Errors appear in a banner below the editor.

Each call to `setup()` and `loop()` must return within 2000 ms, and `onConnect()` has its own 2000 ms limit. An overrun stops the script and shows `Control script loop() exceeded 2000 ms budget; stopped.` in the editor's status bar (for `setup()` the message reads `Control script setup() exceeded 2000 ms budget.`). A stopped script does not restart until the next connection. `delay()` does not count against the limit.

docs.body:
## Talking to the device: the SerialStudio SDK

Every script runs with the `SerialStudio` SDK loaded: namespaced functions over Serial Studio's I/O API. You call them directly, with positional arguments, and the editor offers them in autocomplete.

```javascript
io.writeData("READ\r\n", SerialStudio.Text);          // send text
io.ble.writeCharacteristic("fff1", "5600030C", SerialStudio.Hex);  // send hex bytes
var status = io.getStatus();                           // read connection state
```

Rules:
docs.title: Control-Loop#7

docs.body:
- Functions are dotted namespaces: `io.writeData`, `io.ble.writeCharacteristic`, `io.connect`, `controlScript.getStatus`.
- Required arguments are positional; any optional ones go in a trailing object.
- A byte-payload argument takes a trailing **encoding**: `SerialStudio.Hex`, `SerialStudio.Text`, or `SerialStudio.Base64`. The SDK does the base64 conversion, so you pass hex or text directly and never encode by hand.
- Every namespaced call (`io.*`, `project.*`, `system.*`) returns `{ ok, result, error, errorCode }`; `ok` is `false` on failure. Helpers such as `newFrame()`, `tableGet()` and `delay()` return plain values.
docs.title: Control-Loop#8

docs.body:
```javascript
var r = io.writeData("READ\r\n", SerialStudio.Text);
if (!r.ok)
  console.log("Write failed: " + r.error);
```

`console.log()` output goes to the Console pane (and to the terminal, if you started Serial Studio from one).

The most useful I/O calls for a control loop:

- `io.writeData(data, encoding)` -- write bytes to the active connection (any bus).
- `io.ble.selectServiceByUuid(uuid)` -- select a BLE service (e.g. `"fff0"`).
- `io.ble.setNotifyCharacteristic(uuid)` -- subscribe to incoming notifications (e.g. `"fff2"`).
- `io.ble.writeCharacteristic(uuid, data, encoding)` -- write to a specific BLE characteristic (e.g. `"fff1"`), independent of the notify one.
- `io.getStatus()` -- returns `{ isConnected, paused, ... }` plus the bus type, the link state and one entry per source.

The frame object carries these fields:

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `text` | The raw payload. |
| `values` | The numbers the parser extracted, in parser order. Empty when the parser has not yet produced channels for this frame, so check `values.length` before indexing. |

docs.body:
`newFrame()` returns the raw channels even if no dataset reads them yet, which is what you need to detect a new channel and create a widget for it. (`dashboard.getData()`, by contrast, returns only data already mapped to datasets.) The raw command underneath is `io.getLatestFrame`; it also accepts `{ encoding: "base64" }` for binary payloads. Pace any polling loop with `delay()`; 50-250 ms is plenty for channel detection.

The next three parts are advanced: Variables tables, the refresh and tick calls, and the watchdog matter for scripts that compute values themselves. If your device streams real data, skip to [ensureDashboard()](#ensuredashboardspec-declarative-widgets).
docs.title: Control-Loop#18

docs.body:
### Variables tables: tableGet() / tableSet()

Control loops can read and write the same table variables the frame parser and dataset transforms use (see [Variables](Variables.md); Variables are a Pro feature). `tableGet(table, variable)` returns the live runtime value (or `undefined` when the table or variable does not exist, so `tableGet(t, r) || fallback` works), and `tableSet(table, variable, value)` writes one. Both are marshalled to the GUI thread, so each call costs a thread round-trip: read what you need once per `loop()` pass, not in a tight inner loop.

### refreshDashboard() and dashboardTick()
docs.title: Control-Loop#19

docs.body:
Dataset transforms only re-run when a frame arrives. If your script writes table variables while the device is silent (a communication-loss watchdog marking sensors invalid, say), the dashboard keeps showing the last rendered values until the next frame. Two calls close that gap, and the difference between them is whether the result is exported:

- **`refreshDashboard()` is view only.** It re-runs every dataset transform from the last received values and republishes to the dashboard. Nothing is appended to CSV/MDF4/Historian/MQTT. Use it for a purely visual refresh.
- **`dashboardTick()` renders and exports.** It runs the same transform pass but publishes the synthesized frame through the export fan-out as well, so a script-owned (table-driven) simulation is recorded to CSV/MDF4/Historian/MQTT just like real device data. It also seeds the frame structure when no device frame has arrived yet, so it works from the very first `loop()`. Exports are still gated on a sink being enabled.
docs.title: Control-Loop#20

docs.body:
> **Choosing between them, and the parser's role.**
>
> | Who owns the values | Call from the script | `parse()` returns |
> |---------------------|----------------------|-------------------|
> | The script writes the tables; the device is silent or a dummy source | `dashboardTick()` | An empty list `[]` or `{}`, so the parser exports no frame |
> | `parse()` writes the tables; real frames arrive | No extra call | Its normal frame, for example `[23.5, 1013]` |
>
> Never do both. If `parse()` returns a non-empty frame and the script also calls `dashboardTick()`, every value is exported twice, and the two paths race in the export records. Keep `refreshDashboard()` for refreshes you explicitly do *not* want exported.
docs.title: Control-Loop#21
Control-Loop#22
Control-Loop#23

docs.body:
- Groups are matched by `title`; datasets are matched by their parser `index` within the group. `index` is the 1-based position of the value in the parser output, the same as a dataset's **Frame Index**. If you rename a generated group in the Project Editor, the script no longer finds it and recreates it under the original name; treat the spec as the source of truth for the generated parts of a project.
- Dataset flags map to widgets: `plot`, `fft`, `bar`, `gauge`, `compass`, `waterfall` (or pass a raw `options` bitfield instead, which is also how you request an LED). `waterfall` needs Pro.
- Group `widget` accepts `datagrid`, `accelerometer`, `gyroscope`, `gps`, `multiplot`, `none`, `plot3d`, `image`, `painter`, `webview`, `barpanel`, or `ledpanel`. `plot3d` and `image` need Pro; without a license, a `plot3d` group renders as a Multi-Plot titled "*(title)* (Fallback)". See [Pro vs Free Features](Pro-vs-Free.md).
- Created groups and datasets are real project edits: they are saved with the project exactly like changes made in the Project Editor, so the dashboard the script builds is still there the next time the project opens.

docs.body:
## Launching helper processes: the system.* API

A control loop can launch a helper program and let Serial Studio manage its lifetime. This is how the example projects start their Python data generators automatically: you click **Connect** and the generator is running, with nothing to type in a terminal. The example projects are downloaded from the **Examples** toolbar button the first time you open it, which needs an internet connection. The calls live under the `system.` namespace and are available to in-process scripts, including the control loop. For safety, `system.exec`, `system.kill`, and `system.runningProcesses` are rejected over the network API; `system.projectDir` is allowed everywhere.
docs.title: Control-Loop#25

docs.body:
- `system.projectDir()` -- returns `{ directory, filePath, fileName }` for the loaded project. Use `directory` to build a path to a script that sits next to the `.ssproj` file.
- `system.exec(program, { args, workingDir })` -- launch `program` with optional `args` (an array) and `workingDir` (defaults to the project directory). Returns `{ processId }`.
- `system.kill(processId)` -- stop one launched process.
- `system.runningProcesses()` -- list the processes Serial Studio is currently managing.

Serial Studio stops every process it launched when the device disconnects, when the project changes, and when the app quits, so a helper never lingers after you are done with it.
docs.title: Control-Loop#26

docs.body:
The first time a project's script asks to run a program, Serial Studio shows a prompt naming the program and its arguments and asks whether this project's scripts may launch programs. Until you answer, `system.exec` returns `ok: false` with `errorCode: "CONSENT_REQUIRED"`.

- **Yes**: the Control Loop restarts so `setup()` runs again with the permission in place, and the answer is remembered for that project file. A launch from `onConnect()` needs one more **Connect** after you allowed it.
- **No**: launches stay refused until you restart Serial Studio.
- **Unsaved project**: Serial Studio asks once per session instead of remembering the answer.
docs.title: Control-Loop#27

docs.body:
Open projects you do not trust with this in mind: a Control Loop runs with your user account's privileges. Headless runs cannot show the prompt; set the environment variable `SERIAL_STUDIO_API_AUTO_CONSENT=1` to grant it for that process.

The program name is resolved cross-platform: a bare `"python3"` or `"python"` is looked up on the system `PATH` plus the usual install locations a GUI app does not otherwise see (Homebrew, pyenv, and user-local directories), so the interpreter that has your installed packages is the one that runs. The launched program's standard output and standard error are captured and written to Serial Studio's console, tagged with the process id, so you can see what the helper prints.
docs.title: Control-Loop#28
Control-Loop#29

docs.body:
Put the launch in `setup()` when Serial Studio listens for the data it generates (a UDP source). Put it in `onConnect()` when Serial Studio connects to it as a client (a TCP socket or a Modbus master), because the server must already be listening before the connection opens and `setup()` only runs once the connection is open. `onConnect()` runs before any device is attached, so it cannot read frames or write to the device.

## Saving and lifecycle

The script is saved inside the project file, so it travels with the project. Editing it while connected restarts it immediately; otherwise it starts the next time the device connects and stops when the device disconnects. Use **Validate** before connecting to catch syntax errors early; runtime errors (an exception inside `setup()` or `loop()`) are shown in the editor's status bar and stop the script.
docs.title: Control-Loop#30

docs.body:
Every connection starts a fresh script engine: all top-level variables reset, exactly like an Arduino reset. Do not design around state surviving a connect/disconnect cycle. The latest-frame store also clears on each connection edge, so `io.getLatestFrame()` reports no data until the first frame of the current connection arrives; a watchdog built on `ageMs` can never trip from a previous connection's frame.

Tools and scripts can manage the control loop through the API: `controlScript.get`/`controlScript.getCode` read the source, `controlScript.dryRun` compile-checks source without installing or running it (syntax errors come back with line numbers), `controlScript.set`/`controlScript.setCode` install it, and `controlScript.getStatus` reports whether it is running. Each one is listed in the [API Reference](API-Reference.md#control-script-commands-6).

docs.body:
# Data flow in Serial Studio

## Overview

Your board prints `23.5,1013` followed by a newline. Serial Studio reads those bytes, finds the end of the line, splits it into two values and draws them. A frame is one complete message from your device, usually one line. If the dashboard stays empty, the bytes died at one of six stages, and the [troubleshooting table](#troubleshooting-data-flow) at the end maps symptoms to them.

## The pipeline

The diagram below shows the data flow from hardware to dashboard widgets, with the optional export path. Transforms and Variables run inside the frame builder (Stage 4).
docs.title: Data-Flow#0

docs.body:
```mermaid flowchart TD A["1 Device"] -->|bytes| B["1 Driver"] B --> C["2 Input Buffer"] C --> D["3 Frame Reader"] D --> E["4 Frame Builder"] E --> T["4 Transforms &
Variables"] T --> F["5 Dashboard"] T -->|export| G["6 CSV · MDF4 · Historian · InfluxDB"] ``` ## Stage 1: device and driver For an Arduino or ESP32 you pick UART (the serial port) in the Setup panel and set the baud rate to match `Serial.begin()`. UART, TCP, UDP, WebSocket, HTTP and Bluetooth LE are free. Audio input, Modbus RTU/TCP, CAN Bus, MQTT, USB, HID, Process I/O and the industrial clients (OPC UA, Siemens S7, EtherNet/IP, IEC 60870-5-104) need [Serial Studio Pro](Pro-vs-Free.md). See [Devices](Devices.md) for the full list.
docs.title: Data-Flow#1

docs.body:
The selected driver receives bytes from the operating system and hands them to the input buffer. It does no parsing; its only job is raw byte transport.

## Stage 2: input buffer

Each source has a 1 MB input buffer between its driver and the frame reader. It absorbs short bursts from a device that talks faster than the computer listens. If the buffer fills, Serial Studio discards the overflowing bytes, counts them and writes a warning to its log (at most once every 5 seconds), so the lost data shows up as missing frames. In Project File mode with No Delimiters, chunks bypass this buffer.

## Stage 3: frame reader
docs.title: Data-Flow#2

docs.body:
The frame reader scans the input buffer for frame boundaries and extracts complete frames. Quick Plot needs no setup and expects one newline-terminated line per frame. In Project File mode you choose the detection mode and delimiters in the [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md). Five detection modes are available:

| Mode | Finds frames by |
|------|-----------------|
| End Delimiter Only | The end marker; everything before it is the frame. |
| Start + End Delimiter | A start marker, then an end marker; the frame is what sits between them. |
| Start Delimiter Only | Consecutive start markers; a frame runs from one to the next. |
| No Delimiters | Nothing. All data passes through, for a frame parser script that handles length-prefixed or self-delimiting protocols. |
| Fixed Length | Counting N bytes. Optional Header and Body rules re-align the reader after a lost byte; see the [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md). |
docs.title: Data-Flow#3

docs.body:
The frame reader can also validate a checksum, chosen per source in the Project Editor. The default is none. Algorithms: `XOR-8`, `MOD-256`, `CRC-8`, `CRC-16`, `CRC-16-MODBUS`, `CRC-16-CCITT`, `Fletcher-16`, `CRC-32`, and `Adler-32`. Frames that pass move to the frame builder; frames that fail are dropped.

## Stage 4: frame builder

The frame builder turns each complete frame into a structured record of groups and datasets, based on the current operation mode.

### Quick Plot mode

Set **Operation Mode** to "Quick Plot (Auto-Detected Format)" in the **Device Setup** panel. No project file is needed. Start here with an Arduino printing comma-separated values: select this mode, connect, and the values appear as plots. The frame builder does this:
docs.title: Data-Flow#4

docs.body:
1. Split the line under the detected format (comma, semicolon, tab, space, name:value or JSON).
2. If the first row is all text and has the same number of fields as the data rows, use it as column titles.
3. Auto-generate a table of values (Data Grid group) and a plot of every channel (Multi-Plot group).
4. Assign values to auto-created datasets.

### Project File mode

Set **Operation Mode** to "Parse via Project File" in the **Device Setup** panel. A parser that splits a comma-separated line is one line of JavaScript, which you enter in the source's frame parser in the [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md):
docs.title: Data-Flow#5

docs.body:
```javascript
function parse(frame) { return frame.split(","); }
```

The frame builder then does this:
docs.title: Data-Flow#6

docs.body:
1. Apply the configured decoder (Plain Text (UTF-8), Hexadecimal, Base64, or Binary (Direct)) to turn raw bytes into a parse-ready form.
2. Call the `parse(frame)` function in the source's scripting engine (Lua or JavaScript; see [Frame Parser Scripting](Frame-Parser.md)). The Built-In parser templates skip the script.
3. The function returns a list of values (or a 2D list for multi-frame output).
4. Map returned values to datasets by their Frame Index.
5. Pro: for each dataset, apply its optional `transform(value)` function to convert the raw value into an engineering value. Free users skip this step. See [Dataset Value Transforms](Dataset-Transforms.md) for ordering rules and [Variables](Variables.md) for shared constants.
6. Build the final frame with the populated dataset values. Computed datasets (datasets with no Frame Index) are filled entirely by their transform at this point.
docs.title: Data-Flow#7

docs.body:
Frames reach the dashboard and the exports in small batches, flushed on every display tick or at 64 frames (4096 samples for continuous streams), whichever comes first. No frame is skipped; the batching only changes how delivery is grouped.

### Multi-source projects (Pro)

Serial Studio Pro supports multi-device projects: each device (source) is parsed independently, with its own frame reader and its own isolated script engine. Source frames are published to the dashboard independently. See [Threading and Timing Guarantees](Threading-and-Timing.md).

## Stage 5: dashboard

The dashboard updates all active widgets with the new values as they arrive. Time-series widgets (plots, FFT, GPS trajectory) append new samples to a fixed-size history and drop the oldest samples once the history is full.
docs.title: Data-Flow#8

docs.body:
Widgets redraw at most 60 times per second by default. Open **Preferences → Plotting** and set **UI Refresh Rate (Hz)** (1 to 240), or call `dashboard.setFps` through the API Server. Raise it for smoother motion, lower it to cut CPU and GPU load. Every incoming frame is still processed and exported; only the redraw is capped.

## Stage 6: export (optional parallel path)

When CSV export, MDF4 export, the Historian or InfluxDB export is on, every frame is also handed to an export worker. Each worker writes in the background, so disk and network I/O never block the dashboard.
docs.title: Data-Flow#9

docs.body:
| Target | Edition | Output |
|--------|---------|--------|
| CSV | Free and Pro | One file per session at `Documents/Serial Studio/CSV/<project title>/<yyyy-MM-dd_HH-mm-ss>.csv` (folder `Untitled` when the project has no title). Switch it on with **CSV Spreadsheet** under **Data Export** in the Setup panel. See [CSV Export & Playback](CSV-Export-Playback.md). |
| MDF4 | Pro | A binary measurement file suited to automotive and high-rate workflows. See [MDF4](MDF4.md). |
| Historian | Pro | Every frame, raw byte and table snapshot in a per-project SQLite file that you can browse, tag and replay. See [Historian](Historian.md). |
| InfluxDB 2.x | Pro | Live samples written to a bucket. See [InfluxDB](InfluxDB.md). |
docs.title: Data-Flow#10

docs.body:
The API Server is a separate path. It is off by default; enable it with **Enable API Server** in Preferences. It then serializes each frame to JSON on TCP port 7777 for connected clients. The gRPC server on port 8888 runs only while the API Server is enabled. See the [API Reference](API-Reference.md).

## Troubleshooting data flow
docs.title: Data-Flow#11

docs.body:
| Symptom | Likely cause and fix |
|---------|----------------------|
| No data in the console | Check the driver settings in the Setup panel: port, baud rate, IP address or BLE characteristic. |
| Garbled data | Wrong baud rate, wrong decoder (set in the Project Editor) or mismatched delimiters. Open the Console and compare the raw output with the format you expect. |
| Partial frames | Delimiter mismatch. If your device sends `\r\n` while only `\n` is configured, or the reverse, the frames come out cut or padded. Compare the raw console output with the configured delimiters. |
| Data in the console, dashboard empty or not updating | Check **Operation Mode** in the Device Setup panel and that the delimiters match what your device sends. In Project File mode, check that each dataset's Frame Index matches a position in the array `parse()` returns (index 1 is the first element) and that the parser returns a valid array. |
| A widget is frozen, not blank | A dataset keeps its last value when a frame returns fewer elements than its index needs. The parser is returning a shorter array on some frames. |
| High CPU with no dashboard | Short or noisy delimiters (for example a single `\n`) can match inside payload bytes and produce many tiny frames. Use a longer start/end marker or enable a checksum. |
| Choppy animation or high CPU from the dashboard | Set **UI Refresh Rate (Hz)** under **Preferences → Plotting**: raise it for smoother motion, lower it to cut redraw work. No incoming data is lost either way. |
| Export files empty | Export writes only while a device is connected, and the file is created on the first frame. Connect, then turn the export on, or turn it on before you connect. |
docs.title: Data-Flow#12

docs.body:
# The acquisition pipeline

Your board prints `23.5,41` and a newline. A moment later a number moves on a plot. In between,
Serial Studio splits the incoming bytes into frames, runs your parser and transforms, and hands
the values to the dashboard and to any export that is switched on. The chain that does this runs
once per received frame and is built to keep up with more than 256 kHz of frames.
[Benchmark](Benchmark.md) (About > Benchmark) measures the figure on your machine.

A parser for that line is two lines long:

```javascript
function parse(frame) {
  return frame.split(",");
}
```

Most projects never need to look at this page. If you use **Quick Plot (Auto-Detected Format)** in
the **Device Setup** panel, you write no parser at all: a built-in line tokenizer splits on
commas, spaces or tabs. See [Operation Modes](Operation-Modes.md).
docs.title: Data-Hotpath#0

docs.body:
A chunk is the bytes one read from the device returns, which can hold half a frame or many. A
frame is one complete message. The driver talks to the transport (UART, TCP/UDP, BLE and so on),
and a sink is any export or server that consumes frames besides the dashboard.

## Troubleshooting
docs.title: Data-Hotpath#1

docs.body:
| Symptom | What to do |
|---|---|
| `[FrameReader] Frame queue full -- frame dropped (total N)` in the log | A downstream stage is too slow. `N` is the running count of dropped frames. Run About > Benchmark to see which stage is slowest ([Benchmark](Benchmark.md)). Heavy string work or large loops in a parser or transform (a small per-dataset script, see [Dataset Value Transforms](Dataset-Transforms.md)) are the usual cause. |
| Several frames share one timestamp in a plot, CSV or the Historian | They arrived in one chunk, so they share its arrival time. Order is kept; the spacing between them is not measured. Only drivers that know their cadence, such as Audio, space frames. See [Timestamp ownership](#timestamp-ownership). |
| Parser appears to skip frames | Under **Operation Mode** in **Device Setup**, **Console Only (No Parsing)** skips the parser by design. Choose **Parse via Project File** or **Quick Plot (Auto-Detected Format)**, then check the delimiters in the Project Editor. In multi-source projects each source has its own parser engine; an error in one source does not affect the others. |
| Transform changes don't take effect | Transforms recompile when the project is applied to the pipeline: on project load, after a project edit, and when the Lua mode or the transform library changes. If a change still has no effect, reload the project. |
| High CPU but the dashboard is smooth | The bottleneck is upstream of the dashboard. Run About > Benchmark to find the slow stage. The UI refresh rate cap does not reduce parser load. |
docs.title: Data-Hotpath#2

docs.body:
## Stages ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Driver
(driver thread or GUI thread)"] -->|one chunk per read| B["Frame reader
finds frame boundaries"] B --> Q["Frame queue
65536 slots"] Q --> E["Frame builder
decode, parse, transforms"] E --> S["Data block
flushed on display tick or sample cap"] S --> F["Dashboard (GUI thread)"] S -->|if any sink is active| G["Exports and servers"] ``` Everything from the frame reader to the data block runs on one pipeline thread. Only two hops cross threads: the chunk from the driver, once per read rather than once per frame, and the display tick out to the dashboard. See [Threading and Timing Guarantees](Threading-and-Timing.md).
docs.title: Data-Hotpath#3

docs.body:
### Stage 1: driver

Each driver wraps one transport. Every chunk it publishes carries its bytes, its arrival time and,
when the driver knows them, the frame spacing and the frame count.

### Stage 2: frame reader

`IO::FrameReader` runs on the pipeline thread. It scans for frame boundaries (start delimiter, end delimiter, both, or none) and pulls out one frame at a time.

- Single-delimiter modes use a fast single-pattern search.
- Multi-delimiter modes use a single-pass scan of up to eight patterns that never touches the
  heap.
- Optional checksum validation runs right after extraction. The algorithms are `XOR-8`,
  `MOD-256`, `CRC-8`, `CRC-16`, `CRC-16-MODBUS`, `CRC-16-CCITT`, `Fletcher-16`, `CRC-32` and
  `Adler-32`. See [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md).
docs.title: Data-Hotpath#4

docs.body:
Each completed frame goes into a lock-free queue with 65536 slots. When the queue is full, the
frame is dropped and the log gets `[FrameReader] Frame queue full -- frame dropped (total N)`,
where `N` is the cumulative drop count. A full queue means a stage downstream is not keeping up.
Changing the delimiters, decoder or checksum creates a new reader.

### Stage 3: pipeline routing

`IO::PipelineHost::routeFrames` drains the reader's queue on the pipeline thread and hands each
frame to the frame builder, or, for multi-source projects, to the builder for that source.

### Stage 4: frame builder, parser, and transforms
docs.title: Data-Hotpath#5

docs.body:
`FrameBuilder` turns raw bytes into a populated `Frame` using the project's parsing rules. That
`Frame` is a reused per-source staging buffer; once it is populated, `FrameBuilder` copies its
values into the current `DataBlock` (see [Stage 5](#stage-5-fan-out)). It runs three things in
order:

1. The selected **decoder** (Plain Text (UTF8), Hexadecimal, Base64, or Binary (Direct))
   converts the raw bytes into the form `parse()` expects.
2. The **frame parser** (`parse(frame)` in Lua or JavaScript) returns an array of values. See
   [Frame Parser Scripting](Frame-Parser.md).
3. Per-dataset **transforms** (`transform(value)`) run in group, then dataset, order. See
   [Dataset Value Transforms](Dataset-Transforms.md).
docs.title: Data-Hotpath#6

docs.body:
A transform:

- reads raw values from any dataset, final values from datasets earlier in the order, and shared
  variables from [Variables](Variables.md). A later dataset's final value is the previous frame's.
- can return a string for label-style datasets.
- falls back to the raw value on `NaN`, `Infinity` or an error, silently.

In Quick Plot mode, steps 1 and 2 are replaced by the built-in line tokenizer, which detects the
separator and field names once per connection. In **Console Only (No Parsing)** mode this stage does nothing: bytes go straight to the terminal.

When one chunk holds several frames, they are timestamped as described in
[Timestamp ownership](#timestamp-ownership).
docs.title: Data-Hotpath#7

docs.body:
The parser and transforms are the only places where your code runs. A thrown error or a
non-finite return falls back to the raw value (transform) or an empty frame (parser), and the data
stream keeps going. A JavaScript transform that runs too long for one frame is stopped by a
watchdog and the raw values are used. The parser runs once per frame, and transforms run once per
frame for each dataset that defines one, so heavy work in a transform at 10 kHz across 50 datasets
adds up quickly. Transforms that don't declare an `info` parameter (`function transform(value)`)
pay no cost for it.

Computed variables hold their last written value indefinitely, so other transforms can read them
in the same frame or any later one. For state private to one dataset, transform-local upvalues
(top-level `local` in Lua, top-level `var` or `let` in JavaScript) are the lightest option.
docs.title: Data-Hotpath#8

docs.body:
#### Parser engine details

- One engine instance per source, never shared across sources.
- Lua runs on embedded LuaJIT 2.1 (Lua 5.1 syntax) with `base` (which includes the coroutine
  functions), `table`, `string`, `math` and `bit` loaded. There is no `utf8` module.
- JavaScript runs on Qt's `QJSEngine` with the Console and Garbage Collection extensions.
- Each parser compiles once, then is called many times.

Two datasets that copy the same template keep separate state in both languages.

### Stage 5: fan-out

`FrameBuilder` doesn't publish per frame. It appends each parsed frame's values as one row into
the current per-source `DataBlock`, a pooled, pre-sized slot. The block flushes when it reaches
its sample cap (64 for frame sources, 4096 for dense stream sources) or when the display tick
has moved since the last flush, whichever comes first:
docs.title: Data-Hotpath#9

docs.body:
- The dashboard drains the pooled block from an SPSC ring on `Dashboard::onDisplayTick`, with no
  copy.
- The asynchronous sinks share one detached, trimmed copy of the same block, made once per flush
  and only when at least one sink is active:
  - CSV export (free; **CSV Spreadsheet** under **Data Export** in **Device Setup**; unavailable in **Console Only (No Parsing)** mode).
  - MDF4 export (Pro; **MDF4 Recording** under **Data Export**).
  - The Historian (Pro; **Historian Database** under **Data Export**).
  - The MQTT publisher (Pro; **Enable Publishing** in the Project Editor's **MQTT Publisher** node,
    see [MQTT Publisher](MQTT-Publisher.md)).
  - The API Server (off by default; port 7777; see [API Reference](API-Reference.md)).
  - The gRPC server (port 8888; runs only while the API Server is enabled and only in builds with
    gRPC).
docs.title: Data-Hotpath#10

docs.body:
The pipeline thread is the single producer for every consumer. The trimmed copy exists so a slow
export backlog can't pin the pool slot the dashboard is reading. Export workers run on dedicated
threads and consume from lock-free queues, so writing to disk or the network never blocks the
dashboard or the pipeline.

## Timestamp ownership

Each chunk is stamped with the time it arrived, at the driver. Nothing downstream calls
`steady_clock::now()` to stamp a frame after the fact.

When one read returns several frames, as UART does at high rates, they all get nearly the same
timestamp. `frameStep` defaults to 1 ns and is clamped to at least 1 ns. Only drivers that know
their cadence set a real value. Audio does: it spaces the frames of a buffer by the sample rate
and backdates the chunk start so each sample lines up with when it was captured. On UART,
network, BLE, CAN, Modbus and MQTT, all frames from one chunk land within nanoseconds of the
arrival instant.
docs.title: Data-Hotpath#11

docs.body:
If timestamps look wrong in a chart or an export, check how the driver stamps the chunk first. The
parser and transforms never change time.

## Performance characteristics

Steady-state frames allocate nothing, and the dashboard reads the pooled block without copying it.

The cost per frame is dominated by your code: the parser call, plus one transform call per
dataset that defines one. The dashboard widget update path is rate-capped by the UI refresh rate
(**Preferences > Plotting > UI Refresh Rate (Hz)**, default 60, range 1 to 240). Every frame is
still parsed and exported; only the visual refresh is throttled.
docs.title: Data-Hotpath#12

docs.body:
The [Benchmark](Benchmark.md) (About > Benchmark) drives the real `FrameReader`,
`FrameBuilder` and consumer chain and reports sustained frames per second per stage and per
parser language. The same engine runs headless for CI; see
[Command-Line Interface](Command-Line-Interface.md#acquisition-pipeline-benchmark).

### SIMD instruction set

The vector kernels that scan the byte stream for frame delimiters, reduce plot minima and
maxima, and compute FFT magnitudes and waterfall rows are written once per instruction set and
picked at startup. They are available in every build. On x86-64 the candidates are Scalar, SSE4
and AVX2; on ARM64 they are Scalar and NEON. Serial Studio detects what the processor supports
and runs the widest one.
docs.title: Data-Hotpath#13

docs.body:
**Preferences > Startup > System > SIMD Instruction Set** overrides that choice. The list holds
`Auto`, labelled with the level it currently resolves to, plus every level this machine supports.
Selecting one applies it immediately and persists it, with no restart. A level the machine cannot
run is never offered, and a preference carried over from another machine falls back to `Auto`
without rewriting the setting.

`--simd <level>` pins the level for one run without touching the saved preference, which is the
way to compare lanes or to rule the kernels out while diagnosing a numeric difference. See
[Command-Line Interface](Command-Line-Interface.md#general).
docs.title: Data-Hotpath#14

docs.body:

  thread.
