docs.body:
# Dataset value transforms (Pro)

Your pressure sensor prints `2048`, and an ADC count of 2048 is not a pressure. A dataset transform turns it into PSI before it reaches the dashboard. In Lua, the whole transform is three lines:

```lua
function transform(value)
  return value * 100 / 4095
end
```

You paste it into the **Transform** dialog of a dataset in the Project Editor (see [Using the transform dialog](#using-the-transform-dialog)). You need a project first; see [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md#step-4-add-datasets) for adding datasets. The **dataset** is one channel of your data, such as `pressure`. The **raw value** is the number the [frame parser](Frame-Parser.md) extracted for it; by default a comma-separated line like `2048,3.3` becomes one raw value per comma. Whatever the transform returns replaces the raw value in every plot, widget, export, and alarm.
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#0

docs.body:
A dataset transform can be written in **Lua**, **JavaScript**, or **Expression**, a single arithmetic formula such as `v * 0.01 + 273.15` with no function around it. If you are unsure, pick Expression for scaling and clamping and Lua for anything with memory (filters, counters). Lua and JavaScript transforms use a `transform(value)` function; Expression transforms are covered in [Expression transforms](#expression-transforms).

Dataset transforms of all three languages are a **Pro feature**. Opening the transform editor needs a license or an active trial, and so does connecting with a project that contains a transform. The first time you use one without either, Serial Studio asks in a Yes/No box whether to start the free 14-day trial. Nothing starts automatically, and registering the trial needs an internet connection. See [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md).
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#1

docs.body:
To run a project without a license, right-click the dataset in the Project Editor and choose **Remove Transform**. Removing is always free and can be undone.

## Overview

The frame parser (`parse(frame)`) produces an array of raw values, and each value is mapped to a dataset by its Frame Index (the position of the value in the parsed array). An optional transform sits between the parser and the dashboard:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["parse(frame)"] --> B["Raw Value"]
    B --> C["transform(value)"]
    C --> D["Dashboard"]
```

Calibration, unit conversion, filtering, and derived values (rate of change, running total, decibels) belong here; protocol decoding stays in the parser. A dataset without a transform shows the raw parsed value unchanged. You can reuse one parser across projects with different calibrations by changing only the per-dataset transforms.
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#2

docs.body:
### When a format is enough

A linear scale and offset need no script: set them under **Value Format** on the dataset page (see [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md#step-4-add-datasets)). The same page holds fixed-point and bit-field decoding, hexadecimal and binary display (**Label Format**), and value-to-text **Labels**. Formats and labels are not Pro content, so a project that uses them without a transform connects with no license.

A dataset can combine a format, a transform, and labels. The format decodes the parsed value first, and the transform receives the decoded number. On a computed dataset, whose transform is its only source, the format decodes the transform's result instead. Labels and the hexadecimal or binary notation apply last, to the text on screen only; every plot, alarm, and export reads the number the format and transform produced.
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#3

docs.body:
A transform can also read and write [Variables](Variables.md) tables: constants defined at project time, and computed variables that hold their value across frames. Use them to pass one calibration value into several channels, to have one transform feed another, or to keep state for an integrator, filter, or latch.

## The `transform()` function

Lua and JavaScript transforms use this function. An Expression transform has no function.

### Transform function signature

**Lua:**

```lua
function transform(value)
  return value * 0.01 + 273.15
end
```

**JavaScript:**

```javascript
function transform(value) {
    return value * 0.01 + 273.15;
}
```
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#4

docs.body:
### Transform function input

The `value` parameter is the value already parsed from the frame and mapped to this dataset by its Frame Index. When the parsed value is numeric it arrives as a floating-point number (Lua `number` / JS `number`); when it isn't, it arrives as a string (Lua `string` / JS `string`).

Non-numeric dataset values are still passed to the transform as a string. If the transform returns a number, the dataset becomes numeric; if it returns a string, the string value is kept.

### Transform function output

In Lua and JavaScript, the function returns a number, or a string for a text dataset. The returned value replaces the raw value everywhere: dashboard widgets, plots, CSV export, MDF4 export, and the API.
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#5

docs.body:
| Condition | Result |
|-----------|--------|
| Returns a number | The dataset value is that number. |
| Returns a string | The string is kept as the dataset value. |
| Returns `nil` (Lua) or `undefined` (JavaScript), or a `NaN` or infinite number in either language | The raw value is kept. |
| Throws or errors, or runs longer than 100 ms | The raw value is kept and a warning with the error message and dataset ID goes to the application log. |

## Using the transform dialog
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#6

docs.body:
1. Open the Project Editor and select a dataset in the tree (see [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md#step-4-add-datasets) for adding datasets).
2. Click the **Transform** button in the dataset toolbar.
3. A dialog titled "Dataset Value Transform" opens, with:
   - **Language selector.** Lua, JavaScript, or Expression. Defaults to the source's frame parser language, but each dataset can pick its own.
   - **Template dropdown.** 34 ready-made transforms for common operations. Disabled for Expression.
   - **Code editor.** Syntax-highlighted, with auto-completion.
   - **Clear** button. Resets the editor to the placeholder.
   - **Parameters table.** Named values the transform reads as `params.<name>`; see [Dataset parameters](#dataset-parameters).
   - **Test area.** Enter a raw value, click Test, see the transformed output. The test loads the shared library and the parameter table first, so a transform that calls a library function tests like it runs.
4. Write or pick a `transform(value)` function.
5. Click **Apply** to save the transform to the dataset.
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#7

docs.body:
On a dataset with no transform yet, the editor is pre-filled with a comment that explains `transform(value)`. The comment is a placeholder, not a transform. What **Apply** does depends on the editor content:

| Editor content | Apply result |
|----------------|--------------|
| Placeholder only, or empty | Nothing is saved, the dataset keeps showing raw values, and the dialog closes. |
| Text or comments with no `transform()` function | Refused with "The value transform must define a transform(value) function."; the dialog stays open until you define `transform()` or click **Clear**. |
| A valid transform | Saved to the dataset. |
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#8

docs.body:
### Switching languages

When you switch the language dropdown, the editor loads the equivalent template in the new language automatically (if the current code matches a known template). Custom code is left unchanged and not translated, so rewrite it for the new language yourself.

## Practical examples

The pressure example at the top is the simplest case. Three more:

### Example 1: noisy temperature sensor

An RTD sensor fluctuates ±0.5°C around the true value. Smooth it with EMA:

```lua
local alpha = 0.15
local ema

function transform(value)
  if ema == nil then
    ema = value
  end

ema = alpha * value + (1 - alpha) * ema
  return ema
end
```
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#9

docs.body:
The state rules are in [Persistent state](#persistent-state).

### Example 2: compass heading normalization

A magnetometer reports heading in radians. Convert to degrees and wrap into 0 to 360:

```lua
function transform(value)
  local degrees = value * 180 / math.pi
  return degrees % 360
end
```

### Example 3: battery voltage with dead zone

A battery monitor fluctuates around 0 V when disconnected. Suppress noise below 0.5 V:

```lua
function transform(value)
  if value < 0.5 then
    return 0
  end

return value
end
```

## Expression transforms

**Expression** is the third language in the transform dialog's language dropdown, beside Lua and JavaScript, and is Pro like the other two. It has no function, no statements, and no script engine. The editor holds one arithmetic expression, and its value is the dataset's new reading:
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#10

docs.body:
```text
v * 0.01 + 273.15
```

Expressions compile to a flat program that runs without allocating, which makes them the cheapest option for the common case of scaling, clamping, and combining channels. Use Lua or JavaScript when the transform needs state, branching over several lines, table access, or `deviceWrite`.

Lines starting with `#` are comments and run to the end of the line.

### Expression inputs

| Name | Value |
|------|-------|
| `v`  | This sample's raw value |
| `t`  | The frame's timestamp in seconds, on the app's monotonic clock (same clock as the JS transform's `info.timestampMs`). Not zero-based at stream start: use `dt`, or subtract the first sample's `t`, for an elapsed-time value. |
| `dt` | Seconds since the previous sample; 0 on the first sample after a connect or recompile |
| `n`  | Sample index, starting at 0 |
| `pi`, `e`, `nan`, `inf` | Constants |
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#11

docs.body:
Other datasets of the same source are read by their **Script Alias**, the same identifier `datasetGetRaw` and the API accept. Set the alias in the dataset's Script Alias field in the Project Editor. Dataset titles do not resolve: titles are display text and change freely, while the alias is stable.

```text
v * shunt_current
```

A dataset with no alias is addressed by its **dataset ID**, wrapped in braces because a bare number is a numeric constant:

```text
v * {12}
```

Braces also carry an alias containing spaces.

A sibling holds the latest value published for it, so a dataset processed later in the tree contributes its previous sample. Order datasets in the Project Editor accordingly.
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#12

docs.body:
`sample(name, k)` reads a dataset's value `k` samples back, up to 256:

```text
v - sample(shunt_current, 1)
```

The name is bare or braced, never quoted.

### Expression: reading Variables tables

Expressions read table variables with `table(name, variable)`, the same constants and computed variables `tableGet` reaches from Lua and JavaScript:

```text
v * table(calibration, voltage_scale)
```

Both names are bare, or braced when they contain spaces. The variable is resolved to a handle when the expression compiles, so the read costs an array lookup per sample; an unknown variable is a compile error naming the pair.
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#13

docs.body:
Access is **read-only**. Writing a variable from an expression would give it an execution-order dependency, which is where a Lua or JavaScript transform with `tableSet` belongs. Computed variables carry the same processing-order caveat as sibling datasets: an expression sees the last value written, which for a variable written later in the same frame is the previous frame's.

`table()` fails to compile on an audio source or any source running the stream lane, since the variable store belongs to another thread.

### Expression operators and functions

Operators, loosest binding first: `||`, `&&`, `==` `!=`, `<` `<=` `>` `>=`, `+` `-`, `*` `/` `%`, `^` (right-associative), unary `-` and `!`, and the conditional `condition ? a : b`.
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#14

docs.body:
| Arity | Functions |
|-------|-----------|
| One   | `abs` `floor` `ceil` `round` `sqrt` `cbrt` `exp` `log` `log10` `log2` `sin` `cos` `tan` `asin` `acos` `atan` `sinh` `cosh` `tanh` `deg` `rad` |
| Two   | `min` `max` `pow` `atan2` `hypot` |
| Three | `clamp` `lerp` |

`log` is the natural logarithm. `deg` and `rad` convert between radians and degrees.

### Expression examples

```text
# Scale and offset an ADC reading
v * 0.01 + 273.15
```

```text
# Limit to a range
clamp(v, 0, 100)
```

```text
# Ratio of two channels, guarding the divide
bus_voltage == 0 ? 0 : v / bus_voltage
```

```text
# Difference from one sample ago
v - sample(flow, 1)
```
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#15

docs.body:
```text
# Rate per second, guarding the first sample where dt is 0
dt == 0 ? 0 : (v - sample(flow, 1)) / dt
```

### Expression limits

An Expression transform (Pro) compiles to at most 512 nodes (each operator, function call, number, or name counts as one); a longer one is rejected with `expression too long`. `sample(name, k)` accepts `k` up to 256. A compile error is reported once and the dataset publishes its raw value.

The Template dropdown is disabled for Expression: the built-in templates are Lua and JavaScript code and have no expression equivalent.

## Persistent state
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#16

docs.body:
In a Lua or JavaScript dataset transform (Pro), variables declared at the top level of the transform code, outside the `transform()` function, keep their value between frames. That is how a filter remembers its last output or a counter remembers its count. Each dataset gets its own copy, so two EMAs on two channels never share a variable. A filter that remembers the last reading is a transform with a short memory; it forgets everything when you disconnect.

Declare stateful variables with `local` (Lua) or `var` (JavaScript) at the top of the file. Someone scanning the top of the transform then sees which variables carry state. The two languages differ on bare globals:
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#17

docs.body:
| Language | Top-level `local` / `var` | Bare global (no declaration) |
|----------|--------------------------|------------------------------|
| Lua | Private to the dataset | Also private; still use `local` |
| JavaScript | Private to the dataset | Written to the shared engine and leaks across datasets |

**Lua: declare `local` at the top of the file:**

```lua
local alpha = 0.1
local ema

function transform(value)
  if ema == nil then
    ema = value
  end

ema = alpha * value + (1 - alpha) * ema
  return ema
end
```

`alpha` and `ema` survive between calls and are private to this dataset. Another dataset on the same source with its own `local ema` neither sees nor overwrites them.
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#18
Dataset-Transforms#19

docs.body:
Declare `var ema;` at the top instead. Lua has no such problem; see the table above.

### Helper functions

In JavaScript, helpers defined at the top of the file (for example `function clamp(x, lo, hi) { ... }`) are also private per dataset. Safe to use.

In Lua, write helpers as `local function`:

```lua
local function clamp(x, lo, hi)
  if x < lo then return lo end
  if x > hi then return hi end
  return x
end

function transform(value)
  return clamp(value, 0, 100)
end
```

A plain `function foo() end` at the top level also stays private to the dataset in Lua; `local function` is just clearer.
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#20

docs.body:
### When state resets

Persistent state (top-level Lua and JavaScript variables and computed table variables) is cleared when:

- The device is disconnected (transform engines are destroyed).
- The user clicks **Apply** in the transform editor (engines are recompiled with fresh state).
- The project is reloaded or saved with changes.

Filters and accumulators start from scratch on each connection; nothing wipes them between frames within one connection.

## Computed datasets

In the Project Editor, if a Lua or JavaScript transform never reads `value`, Serial Studio marks its dataset **computed** when the project loads, and the Frame Index field greys out. The check looks for the free identifier `value`, not `something.value` or `obj:value`. A transform that ignores `value` but expects a frame-driven column loses its Frame Index this way; read `value` at least once to keep the dataset driven by the incoming frame.
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#21

docs.body:
A computed dataset has no Frame Index, so nothing in the incoming frame feeds it. You can also tick the computed checkbox yourself in the Project Editor. The transform computes the value entirely, usually by reading other datasets or table variables, and the `value` argument is always `0`.

```lua
function transform(value)
  local a = datasetGetFinal(10)   -- final value of the dataset with ID 10
  local b = datasetGetFinal(11)
  return (a + b) / 2              -- average of two channels
end
```

Use computed datasets for derived metrics (averages, ratios, sums, percentage-of-total) that should appear on the dashboard and in exports but are not in the wire format. A computed dataset still runs every frame in tree order, so place it after the datasets it reads.
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#22

docs.body:
## Shared library and parameters

A large project repeats the same formula in many datasets: forty RTD channels that each carry a copy of the same conversion, differing only in three constants. Two project-level features remove the copies.

### The shared libraries

The project can hold one Lua chunk that every Lua transform of the project can call, and one JavaScript chunk that every JavaScript transform can call. Both live under **Project Scripts** at the top of the Project Editor tree, next to the Control Loop, as **Lua Library** and **JavaScript Library**; a transform editor also has an **Open Lua Library** / **Open JavaScript Library** button that jumps to the one its language uses. The API exposes them as well (`project.transformLibrary.get`, `project.transformLibrary.set`, `project.transformLibrary.dryRun`, each with an optional `language` of `lua` or `js`).
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#23

docs.body:
```lua
-- Shared library
function rtd(raw, p)
  return (raw * p.scale + p.offset) / p.r0
end
```

The chunk runs once, into the global table of each source's transform state, before the dataset transforms compile. Its top-level functions are visible from every Lua transform through the normal global lookup; a transform's own `local` values still stay private to that transform. Because the library is evaluated at compile time, calling one of its functions costs the same as calling a local helper.

The JavaScript library works the same way: it is evaluated once into the global object of each source's transform engine, so its top-level functions are visible from every JavaScript transform closure of that source. Each library is seen only by transforms of its own language; Expression transforms have no functions to call.
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#24

docs.body:
If the library fails to compile or run, the transforms still compile without it: a dataset that calls a missing function falls back to its raw value and the failure appears in the Problem Center under "the shared Lua library" or "the shared JavaScript library". Fix the library and the engines recompile on Apply, without reconnecting.

### Dataset parameters

Each dataset can carry named parameters that its transform reads as `params`. Add them in the **Parameters** table of the transform dialog, one name and value per row, or through the API (`project.dataset.update {transformParams: {...}}`). Values are typed: numeric text becomes a number, `true` and `false` become booleans, anything else stays a string.
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#25

docs.body:
```lua
-- Dataset transform: the same three lines on every RTD channel
function transform(value)
  return rtd(value, params)
end
```

With `transformParams` set to `{"scale": 0.1, "offset": -40, "r0": 100}` on one dataset and `{"scale": 0.1, "offset": -40, "r0": 1000}` on the next, both channels share one formula and differ only in their table rows.

`params` is available in Lua and JavaScript. In Lua it is a table in the transform's environment (`params.r0`); in JavaScript it is the object passed to the transform's closure (`params.r0`). Both are fixed at compile time: editing a parameter recompiles the transform. Expression transforms do not read `params`; use a table variable there instead.
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#26

docs.body:
## Table API

Lua and JavaScript dataset transforms (Pro) have four built-in functions for reading and writing the project's Variables tables. An Expression transform reads variables with `table(name, variable)` instead, and cannot write. Tables are covered in full in [Variables](Variables.md). This section documents the API surface from the transform's point of view.
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#27

docs.body:
| Function                       | Returns                        | Purpose |
|--------------------------------|--------------------------------|---------|
| `tableGet(table, reg)`         | number, string, or nil/undefined | Read a user-defined variable |
| `tableSet(table, reg, value)`  | nothing                        | Write a **computed** variable (constants are read-only) |
| `datasetGetRaw(id_or_alias)`   | number, string, or nil/undefined | Raw (pre-transform) value of any dataset in the current frame |
| `datasetGetFinal(id_or_alias)` | number, string, or nil/undefined | Final (post-transform) value of any dataset already processed in the current frame |
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#28

docs.body:
The API is identical in Lua and JavaScript. `table` and `reg` are strings. The dataset lookup takes either the integer dataset ID (`uniqueId` in the API) shown next to each dataset in the Project Editor, or the dataset's alias string (the **Script Alias** field). A number argument is always a dataset ID and a string is always an alias, so `datasetGetRaw(128)` and `datasetGetRaw("128")` are different lookups. An unknown alias returns `nil`/`undefined` with a one-time console warning, the same as an unknown dataset ID.

For a transform that touches the same variables on every value, resolving a name once to a **handle** and using `tableGetH` / `tableSetH` avoids the per-call name lookup. See [Fast table access with handles](SerialStudio-SDK.md#handles-the-fast-path-for-table-heavy-parsers).
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#29
Dataset-Transforms#30

docs.body:
```lua
-- Dataset 20 (processed later): compute power from current × voltage
function transform(value)
  local i = tableGet("runtime", "total_current") or 0
  return value * i
end
```

### Processing order

Transforms are applied in order: groups in frame order, datasets in group order. Inside a single frame:
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#31

docs.body:
- `datasetGetRaw(uid)` returns the current frame's raw value only for the current dataset and the ones already processed before it. Later datasets still hold the previous frame's raw value, because raw and final values are written incrementally per dataset, not in a pre-pass.
- `datasetGetFinal(uid)` only works for datasets that have already been transformed (earlier datasets in the same group, or any dataset in an earlier group).
- Computed variables hold their last written value, so a value written in one frame is still visible in the next, which suits integrators, derivatives, and latched flags. To start a variable fresh each frame, write the reset value yourself at the top of an early transform.
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#32

docs.body:
If you need dataset B to consume dataset A's final value, make sure A comes before B in the Project Editor tree.

## Change-driven transforms (opt-in)

The **Change-Driven Transforms** option is a project setting for dataset transforms (Pro). By default every dataset's transform runs on every frame. For a large table-driven project, where the frame parser writes table variables and many computed datasets each read one variable, that means a frame for one device re-runs the transforms of *every* dataset, even the ones whose data did not change.
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#33

docs.body:
The toggle turns on a faster mode for computed datasets only; non-computed datasets still run every frame. A computed dataset's transform runs only when one of the variables (or datasets) it reads has changed since it last ran; otherwise it keeps its previous output for that frame. Serial Studio detects reads of table variables and datasets automatically, so you change nothing in your scripts. The dashboard shows the same values either way; the option skips recomputing values that did not change.

To turn it on in the Project Editor:

1. Select the project root.
2. Click the **Settings** button (wrench icon) next to the Project Title.
3. Toggle **Change-Driven Transforms** in the popup, alongside Time Range and Point Count.
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#34

docs.body:
It is **off by default** and saved per project. Turn it on for heavy table-driven dashboards that are dropping frames. Two things to know:

- A per-sample filter (an EMA, a deadband) then steps once per *real* new sample of its input rather than once per global frame.
- Serial Studio cannot detect clock reads. A computed dataset that reads the clock (`Date.now()`, `os.time()`) re-runs only when one of its inputs changes; leave the option off for that project, or keep such datasets non-computed.

## Frame metadata: the second `frameInfo` argument

Every transform may declare a second argument with metadata about the frame the value belongs to. One-arg transforms (`function transform(value)`) keep working and pay no extra cost: the engine inspects each transform's parameter count at compile time and skips building the info table or object entirely when it isn't used.
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#35
Dataset-Transforms#36

docs.body:
`info.frameNumber` is per-source and restarts at 1 after a disconnect or project reload.

### Example: rate-limit a control update

A transform that nudges the device's setpoint, but no more than ten times per second regardless of frame rate:

```lua
local lastTs = 0
function transform(temperature, info)
  if info.timestampMs - lastTs >= 100 then
    lastTs = info.timestampMs
    local sp = tableGet("Control", "setpoint") or 25.0
    deviceWrite(string.format("SP=%.2f\n", sp))
  end
  return temperature
end
```

### Example: request a status push every 50th frame

```javascript
function transform(value, info) {
  if (info.frameNumber % 50 === 0) deviceWrite("STATUS?\n");
  return value;
}
```
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#37

docs.body:
## Writing back to the device: `deviceWrite()`

Lua and JavaScript dataset transforms (Pro) can send bytes back to the connected device with `deviceWrite(data, sourceId?)`. `deviceWrite` is for **closed-loop control**: read a sensor value, compute a setpoint or correction, and push it back to the device in one step.

Lua and JavaScript only; Expression transforms cannot call `deviceWrite`.

### deviceWrite signature

```text
deviceWrite(data, sourceId?)
  data:     string (Lua) or string / array of bytes (JavaScript)
  sourceId: optional number; defaults to the source the transform's dataset belongs to
  returns:  { ok = true }                  on success
            { ok = false, error = "..." }  on failure
```
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#38

docs.body:
`deviceWrite` is **synchronous and fire-and-forget**: it pushes the bytes to the driver immediately. It does not block waiting for a reply, and it does not throw. Every failure becomes `{ ok = false, error = "..." }`.

Every call is logged to the application log as `[deviceWrite] source=<id> bytes=<n> written=<n>` so you can verify control commands fired the way you expected.

### Lua example: PWM controller

```lua
local kp = 4.0
local setpoint = 25.0

function transform(sensor_temp)
  local error = setpoint - sensor_temp
  local pwm = math.max(0, math.min(255, kp * error + 128))
  deviceWrite(string.format("PWM=%d\n", math.floor(pwm + 0.5)))
  return sensor_temp
end
```
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#39
Dataset-Transforms#40

docs.body:
```lua
function transform(value)
  if value < 5 then
    deviceWrite("REQ_FULL_REPORT\n", 0)  -- ask source 0 for a full status frame
  end
  return value
end
```

### deviceWrite failure modes

`deviceWrite` never throws. Possible `error` values:

- `"device not connected or write failed"`: the target source has no live driver, or the driver's `write()` returned 0/negative.
- `"deviceWrite: data is empty"`: the payload was zero bytes.
- `"deviceWrite: data must be a string"` (Lua) / `"... string or byte array"` (JS).
- `"deviceWrite: sourceId must be a number"`.

### When not to use deviceWrite
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#41

docs.body:
- For a button or slider the user clicks, use an **Output Widget**. Transforms run on every frame; an Output Widget runs when the user acts.
- A computed dataset can call `deviceWrite`, but it runs in tree order like any other dataset, not last, and fires every frame unless Change-Driven Transforms is on, in which case it runs only when an input changes. Put it after the datasets it reads.
- Keep payloads short. `deviceWrite` runs inside the transform, and a transform that runs longer than 100 ms is stopped and its dataset keeps the raw value.

## Firing actions: `actionFire()`

Lua and JavaScript dataset transforms (Pro) can also trigger any **Action** already defined in the project (see [Actions](Actions.md)). Reuse an existing action (with its prebuilt payload, encoding, and timer mode) instead of hardcoding bytes in a `deviceWrite`.
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#42

docs.body:
```text
actionFire(actionId)
  actionId: integer (the action's stable identifier)
  returns:  { ok = true } | { ok = false, error = "..." }
```

`actionId` is the action's `actionId` field: the same persistent integer the project file stores and the API returns. It is **not** the position in the action list. Find it with `project.action.list` (MCP) or read it off the Actions panel in the Project Editor.

```lua
local triggered = false
function transform(value, info)
  if not triggered and value > 100 then
    local r = actionFire(7)
    if r.ok then triggered = true end
  end
  return value
end
```
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#43

docs.body:
Behaves like the user pressing the action's button, including running the action's timer (`AutoStart`, `RepeatNTimes`, ...). Calls are logged as `[actionFire] id=N index=M ok`.

`actionFire` is also available in frame parsers and canvas scripts.

## Controlling the dashboard

Transforms can also drive a small set of dashboard helpers: `clearPlots()`, `setPlotPoints(n)`, `setTerminalVisible(bool)`, `setNotificationLogVisible(bool)`, `setClockVisible(bool)`, `setStopwatchVisible(bool)`, and `setActiveWorkspace(idOrName)`. They behave the same way they do in parsers and return the same `{ ok, error }` shape. The typical pattern from a transform is "fire once on a state transition", for example:
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#44

docs.body:
```lua
function transform(value)
  if value >= 9999 then    -- device reboot sentinel
    clearPlots()
    return 0
  end
  return value
end
```

Full reference, including argument types and longer examples (GPS fix reset, mode-driven workspace switching, focus mode): see [Controlling the dashboard](Frame-Parser.md#controlling-the-dashboard-clearplots-and-friends) in the Frame Parser Scripting Reference.

## Built-in templates

The Transform Editor includes 34 ready-to-use templates for Lua and JavaScript. Pick one from the Template dropdown and it loads into the editor ready to tune.

### Calibration and conversion
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#45

docs.body:
| Template                | Description |
|-------------------------|-------------|
| Linear Calibration      | `y = slope × value + offset`. Sensor calibration. |
| Polynomial (2nd order)  | `y = a×x² + b×x + c`. Non-linear response curves. |
| Map Range               | Rescale from `[inMin, inMax]` to `[outMin, outMax]`. |
| ADC to Voltage          | `value * v_ref / resolution` with `v_ref = 3.3` and `resolution = 1024`, both constants in the code. Edit them for your ADC; a 10-bit full scale is 1023 counts. |
| Calibration from a Variables table | Read slope/offset from a table variable and apply it. |
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#46

docs.body:
### Smoothing filters

| Template                         | Description |
|----------------------------------|-------------|
| Moving Average                   | Averages the last N samples via a circular buffer. |
| Exponential Moving Average (EMA) | Weighted average, tunable responsiveness (alpha). |
| Low-Pass Filter                  | First-order IIR, adjustable cutoff via alpha. |
| High-Pass Filter                 | First-order IIR. Removes DC drift and slow offsets. |
| Median Filter                    | Rolling-window median. Robust to outlier spikes. |
| Kalman Filter (1D)               | Scalar Kalman filter with tunable Q (process) and R (measurement) noise. |
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#47

docs.body:
### Statistical

| Template              | Description |
|-----------------------|-------------|
| Rolling RMS           | Root-mean-square over the last N samples. Useful for AC signals, vibration, audio. |
| Running Minimum       | Smallest value observed since the transform started. |
| Running Maximum       | Largest value observed since the transform started. |
| Running Accumulator   | Discrete integral (running sum). |
| Rate of Change        | Discrete derivative (`value - previous`). |

### Signal shaping
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#48

docs.body:
| Template             | Description |
|----------------------|-------------|
| Clamp                | Restrict output to `[min, max]`. |
| Dead Zone            | Suppress small values near zero. |
| Slew-Rate Limiter    | Cap how much the value can change between consecutive samples. |
| Auto-Zero / Tare     | Average the first N samples, then subtract that bias from every later value. |
| Schmitt Trigger      | Hysteresis comparator. Outputs 0/1 with separate rising and falling thresholds. |

### Angle math

| Template                  | Description |
|---------------------------|-------------|
| Unwrap Angle              | Remove ±360° jumps so the output is continuous across the boundary. |
| Integrate Rate to Angle   | Integrate an angular rate (deg/s) into an absolute angle at a fixed sample rate. |
| Radians to Degrees        | deg = rad × 180/π. |
| Degrees to Radians        | rad = deg × π/180. |

docs.body:
### Unit conversions

| Template                  | Description |
|---------------------------|-------------|
| Celsius to Fahrenheit     | °F = °C × 9/5 + 32. |
| Fahrenheit to Celsius     | °C = (°F - 32) × 5/9. |
| Kelvin to Celsius         | °C = K - 273.15. |
| Logarithmic (dB)          | Convert linear amplitude to decibels. |

### Logic and bit operations

| Template             | Description |
|----------------------|-------------|
| Bit Extract          | Return a single bit from a packed status word (0 or 1). |
| Absolute Value       | Unsigned magnitude. |
| Invert Sign          | Negate the value. |

### Sensors

|-----------------------------|-------------|
| Steinhart-Hart Thermistor   | NTC resistance to temperature (°C). |

## Rules and limitations
docs.title: Dataset-Transforms#51

docs.body:
1. The function has to be named `transform` (case-sensitive).
2. It takes one required parameter (`value`), plus an optional second parameter (`info`) with frame metadata (`frameNumber`, `sourceId`, `timestampMs`).
3. It has to return a number, or a string for text datasets (a returned string is kept as the dataset value).
4. Each dataset picks its own transform language (Lua, JavaScript, or Expression); datasets on the same source can mix them. The source's frame parser language is only the default when none is picked. Rules 1 to 3 describe the `transform()` function and apply to Lua and JavaScript; an Expression dataset has no function and publishes the value of its single expression.
5. The engine is sandboxed: no file I/O, no network, no OS commands.
6. Transforms run on every incoming frame, so keep them fast. Avoid unbounded loops or heavy computation. A per-call watchdog kills a transform after 100 ms (Lua: a deadline armed before the call; JavaScript: an interrupt armed once per frame); a timed-out transform logs a warning and falls back to the raw value. Expression transforms are limited to 512 nodes instead (see [Expression limits](#expression-limits)).

docs.body:
# Deriving values

Your sensor sends hundredths of a degree Celsius, such as `2531` for 25.31 C, and the dashboard should show kelvin. A dataset is one channel of the device's output, such as one comma-separated value on a `Serial.println` line. Select the dataset in the Project Editor, open its transform, pick **Expression** in the language dropdown, and type:

```text
v * 0.01 + 273.15
```

`v` is the dataset's value. When one line is not enough, the table below picks the next mechanism.
docs.title: Derived-Values#0

docs.body:
| Mechanism | Use it for | Runs | Edition |
|-----------|-----------|------|---------|
| [Value transform](#value-transform) | Calibrating, converting, or filtering one dataset's own value | Once per frame, per dataset | Pro |
| [Computed dataset](#computed-dataset) | A new channel built from other datasets, such as an average or a ratio | Once per frame | Pro |
| [Variables](#variables) | Constants and state shared between datasets: calibration tables, integrators, flags | Read and written by transforms and scripts | Pro |
| [Control Loop](#control-loop) | Driving the device and reacting to data over time, outside the frame cycle | On its own thread, paced by `delay()`; JavaScript | Free; reading or writing Variables from it needs Pro |
| [`dashboardTick()`](#dashboardtick) | Values a script owns, with no device frame, that must also be recorded | When the Control Loop or a JavaScript macro calls it | Free; the Variables it reads need Pro |
docs.title: Derived-Values#1

docs.body:
If the value comes from one dataset, use a transform. If it comes from several, use a computed dataset. If it must be remembered between frames or shared, use Variables. If it depends on time, or the device has to be asked first, use the Control Loop.

A project that contains a transform or a Variables table needs a license or an active trial to connect. The first use of a Pro feature shows a Yes/No prompt that offers the trial (it needs an internet connection to register); answer No to keep working in the free edition. See [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md).

## Value transform

Value transforms are a Pro feature. In the Project Editor, select a dataset and use the transform editor's language dropdown: **Lua**, **JavaScript** or **Expression**. A transform rewrites that dataset's value after parsing and before display and export. An Expression is one arithmetic line with no script engine, and `v` is the dataset's value, as in the example at the top of this page.
docs.title: Derived-Values#2

docs.body:
Lua and JavaScript transforms define `transform(value)` instead, and can keep state between frames:

```lua
local avg = nil
function transform(value)
  avg = (avg == nil) and value or (0.9 * avg + 0.1 * value)
  return avg
end
```

See [Dataset Value Transforms](Dataset-Transforms.md).

## Computed dataset

A computed dataset is a Pro feature: a dataset with no Frame Index (the position of its value in the parsed frame), whose transform produces the whole value, typically from other datasets' final values. Serial Studio marks a dataset computed automatically, or you can tick the computed checkbox in the Project Editor. The final value is what a dataset holds after its own transform. `datasetGetFinal()` takes the integer unique ID shown next to a dataset in the Project Editor, or its **Script Alias**; replace 10 and 11 below with those of your two channels, or pass an alias string such as `datasetGetFinal("temp1")`:
docs.title: Derived-Values#3

docs.body:
```lua
function transform(value)
  return (datasetGetFinal(10) + datasetGetFinal(11)) / 2
end
```

A Lua or JavaScript transform that never reads `value` makes its dataset computed when the project loads, and the Frame Index field greys out. Inside a computed dataset `value` is always `0`. Transforms run in project-tree order, so place a computed dataset after the datasets it reads. See [Computed datasets](Dataset-Transforms.md#computed-datasets).

## Variables

Variables are a Pro feature. A Variables table holds named numbers that stay between frames, such as a running total or a calibration constant, and that parsers, transforms and scripts share. **Read-Only** (constant) variables are set in the Project Editor and fixed for the session; **Read/Write** (computed) variables are written with `tableSet()` and keep their last value. A computed variable stores a value; a computed dataset is a channel shown on the dashboard.
docs.title: Derived-Values#4

docs.body:
Define the table first. This example needs a table named `energy` with a Read/Write variable `total`, because `tableSet()` on a variable that does not exist is ignored:

```lua
function transform(value)
  local total = (tableGet("energy", "total") or 0) + value * 0.1
  tableSet("energy", "total", total)
  return total
end
```

Use them for calibration constants that change per deployment, and for state that more than one dataset reads. See [Variables](Variables.md).

## Control Loop
docs.title: Derived-Values#5
Derived-Values#6

docs.body:
Transforms only re-run when a frame arrives. `refreshDashboard()` re-runs them from the last received values and repaints the dashboard only, so it does nothing until the device has sent at least one frame, and nothing reaches CSV, MDF4, Historian or MQTT. For a device that has never sent a frame, use `dashboardTick()`. `delay(100)` waits 100 ms. `refreshDashboard()` and `dashboardTick()` have no Lua equivalent. See [Control Loop](Control-Loop.md).

## dashboardTick()

When a script owns the values, for example a simulation that writes Variables while the device sends nothing useful, call `dashboardTick()` from the Control Loop instead of `refreshDashboard()`:
docs.title: Derived-Values#7
Derived-Values#8

docs.body:
In this setup, make the frame parser (the Frame Parser script in the Project Editor) return an empty list `[]` or `{}`, or the device's frames and the ticks are both exported. See [Reading data: See, Decide, Act](Control-Loop.md#reading-data-see-decide-act) and [Frame Parser Reference](Frame-Parser.md).

## See also

- [Concepts](Concepts.md): where these mechanisms sit in the chain from device to dashboard.
- [Frame Parser Reference](Frame-Parser.md): when the right fix is to change what the parser returns.

Device-Declarations#1

docs.body:
A GPS Map widget appears. `graph(false)` leaves out the per-channel plots, so only the map shows.

Declarations are free and work in Quick Plot mode. Project File mode offers them without applying them (see [Adopting a Declaration](#adopting-a-declaration)). Declared controls need Pro, because the Output Panel they generate is a [Pro feature](Output-Controls.md). Serial Studio offers the 14-day Pro trial in a Yes/No prompt the first time you use a Pro feature; registering it needs an internet connection. See [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md).

The library is MIT licensed, so it can be embedded in closed firmware, and lives in the `firmware/` directory of the Serial Studio repository. Releases up to 4.2.1 do not understand declarations: they rebuild the dashboard on any text line. Use a later release. A device that declares nothing is a plain Quick Plot stream, exactly as before.
docs.title: Device-Declarations#2

docs.body:
## How it works

1. The device sends the declaration at power-up, and again whenever Serial Studio asks.
2. In Quick Plot mode, Serial Studio skips its guess at your data format and builds the dashboard from the declaration.
3. Every later line is a frame whose values follow the declared channel order.

**Ask Devices for Their Dashboard** in **Preferences → Plotting** is off by default. When it is on, Serial Studio sends one request line, `#ss?`, as a Quick Plot connection opens, and the library answers with the declaration. That finds a device that declared at boot before Serial Studio was listening, including after a reset. Console Only and Project File modes never send the request. If the dashboard does not appear, turn the setting on and reconnect; with it off, a declaration is read only when the device sends it, for example at power-up.
docs.title: Device-Declarations#3

docs.body:
Sending the same declaration again changes nothing. A changed declaration rebuilds the dashboard. Each declaration, accepted or refused, is reported in the Console pane.

A declaration never changes the operation mode, never writes a file and never changes a connection setting. The generated dashboard is an ordinary Quick Plot session: use **Save as Project** in the dashboard's start menu to keep it as a project file.

## Wire format

This section is for firmware that does not use the library. A declaration is a single line ending in a newline:

```
#ss1{"title":"TinyGPS","groups":[{"title":"GPS Map","widget":"gps","datasets":[{"title":"Latitude","units":"°","widget":"lat"},{"title":"Longitude","units":"°","widget":"lon"},{"title":"Altitude","units":"m","widget":"alt"}]}]}
```
docs.title: Device-Declarations#4

docs.body:
- `#ss` is the reserved prefix. The digit after it is the wire version, currently `1`. An unknown version is ignored with a console message.
- The rest of the line is a JSON object with a non-empty `title` and a `groups` array of 1 to 64 groups. The declaration needs at least one dataset, so a controls-only declaration is refused.
- A group has a `title`, an optional `widget` (`datagrid`, `multiplot`, `accelerometer`, `gyro`, `gps`, `plot3d`, `barpanel` or `ledpanel`) and a `datasets` array. A group whose datasets do not fit its widget is shown as a data grid, with a console note.
- A dataset takes the same properties the Project Editor shows for a dataset: `title`, `units`, `widget`, `plotMin`, `plotMax`, `widgetMin`, `widgetMax`, `fft`, `alarmBands` and `labels`, among others. Keys that are not dataset properties are dropped and listed in the console.
- The libraries call a dataset a channel.
- Dataset order is frame order. A dataset takes the next frame position, unless it names an `index`, which reuses that position so two groups can show the same channel.
- Frames after a declaration are plain values in declared order, `1.5,2.5,3.5`, or named values, `Latitude:48.8584`, which map by name.
docs.title: Device-Declarations#5

docs.body:
A declaration is data. It never carries a script, a transform, a file path or a connection setting. A malformed, oversized or over-cap declaration is ignored with a console message; the caps are listed under [Limits](#limits).

### Declared controls

Declared controls generate an Output Panel, a [Pro feature](Pro-vs-Free.md); the declaration itself is free. A group with `"groupType":1` holds `outputWidgets` instead of datasets. Each control has a `title` and an `outputType`: `0` button, `1` slider, `2` toggle, `3` text field (numeric input only), `4` knob. Sliders and knobs take `outputMin`, `outputMax` and `outputStep`.
docs.title: Device-Declarations#6
Device-Declarations#7

docs.body:
## Limits

| Limit | Value | Counts |
|-------|-------|--------|
| Title or label | 64 bytes | each string |
| Declaration line | 16384 bytes | whole line |
| Groups | 64 | per declaration, control groups included |
| Datasets | 512 | per group, and 512 in total across all groups |
| Controls | 64 | per control group |
| Alarm bands | 16 | per dataset |
| FFT markers | 16 | per dataset |
| Labels | 256 | per dataset |
| Control title | 32 bytes | each control |

Past a cap, Serial Studio ignores the declaration and reports it in the Console pane. The Python library raises `ValueError`; the C and Arduino libraries stop declaring.
docs.title: Device-Declarations#8

docs.body:
## The library

All three variants share one wire format, and each calls a dataset a channel. Call `poll()` once per loop. On the first loop after power-up, and after every `#ss?` request, the library writes the declaration instead of a frame and drops that loop's values. On every other loop it sends a frame.

### Arduino

Install **SerialStudio** from the Arduino Library Manager, or copy `firmware/arduino` to `Arduino/libraries/SerialStudio`. The header allocates nothing at run time and keeps its declaration text in flash.

The GPS sketch in the [introduction](#device-declarations) is a complete example.
docs.title: Device-Declarations#9

docs.body:
| Call | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `group(title, widget)` | Opens a dataset group. The widget is optional. |
| `channel(name, value, places)` | Declares and sends one channel; `places` is the number of decimal places sent. Without a value, the channel is declared only. |
| `units`, `widget`, `range`, `plotMin`, `plotMax`, `widgetMin`, `widgetMax`, `fft`, `index` | Dataset properties, chained after `channel()`. |
| `alarm(min, max, severity, label)` | Adds an alarm band. |
| `label(value, text)`, `labelsDefault(text)` | Names the values of a state channel. |
| `graph(false)` | Plots are on by default. This turns them off. |
| `controlGroup(title)`, `control(title, kind)` | Declares an Output Panel and its button, slider, toggle or knob. |
| `named(true)`, `separator(c)` | Sends `name:value` frames, or another separator. |
| `onControl(fn)`, `onLine(fn)` | Receives `#ss!` commands, and every other input line. |
| `poll()` | Reads input. Call once per loop. |
docs.title: Device-Declarations#10
Device-Declarations#11

docs.body:
`ss_group`, `ss_channel_int`, `ss_channel_double`, `ss_channel_str`, `ss_control_group` and `ss_control` open groups and declare channels. Property macros such as `ss_units`, `ss_widget`, `ss_plot_min`, `ss_range` and `ss_alarm` apply to the channel just opened. `ss_set_handlers()` registers the control and line callbacks.

### Python

Install with `pip install serialstudio`. The module uses the standard library only and writes bytes through a callable, so it works over a serial port, a socket or a pipe. The example below talks to a serial port, so it also needs `pip install pyserial`. The first `send()` writes the declaration; each later one writes a frame.
docs.title: Device-Declarations#12

docs.body:
```python
import time
import serial
import serialstudio

port = serial.Serial("COM3", 115200)
device = serialstudio.Device("TinyGPS", write=port.write)

while True:
    device.poll()
    device.group("GPS Map", "gps")
    device.channel("Latitude", 48.8584, places=4, units="deg", widget="lat", graph=False)
    device.channel("Longitude", 2.2945, places=4, units="deg", widget="lon", graph=False)
    device.channel("Altitude", 35.0, places=1, units="m", widget="alt", graph=False)
    device.send()
    time.sleep(0.1)
```

Dataset properties are keyword arguments in snake case (`plot_max=5`, `fft_sampling_rate=200`). Pass `range=(0, 100)` to set both the widget and plot range. `Device(title, write, separator=",", named=False, on_control=None, on_line=None)` takes the callbacks; `feed(data)` buffers received bytes and `poll()` dispatches them. `serialstudio.tcp_server(device)` serves a device over TCP on localhost, for testing against a [Network](Drivers-Network.md) source.
docs.title: Device-Declarations#13

docs.body:
## Adopting a declaration

If you opened a `.ssproj` in Project File mode and the connected device also sends a declaration, the declaration never rebuilds the loaded project. Serial Studio only compares it with the loaded project. When it differs, one notification reports that the device declares a different dashboard, and two buttons appear in the Setup panel under the project file: **Use Device Dashboard** and **Keep Project**.

**Use Device Dashboard** (Project File mode) disconnects, offers to save unsaved edits, and opens the declared project as a new, unsaved project with the loaded project's connection. The loaded file stays untouched on disk: reopening it reverses the choice.
docs.title: Device-Declarations#14

docs.body:
**Keep Project** (Project File mode) dismisses the offer for this project and this declaration. It comes back only when the device declares something different or another project file is loaded. Disconnecting forgets the declaration, because the next connection may be another device.

Adopting is the only way a declaration reaches Project File mode. To keep a Quick Plot dashboard instead, use **Save as Project**.

## Binary frames

Skip this if your device prints text. Binary declarations work in Quick Plot mode only. A device that sends packed binary frames declares their layout in the same line. The declaration itself is always text; only the frames after it are binary. The libraries write the numeric codes (`frameDetection`, `decoderMethod`), so you never type them. The line gains a `sources` array with one entry that names the framing and the `packed_struct` frame parser template:
docs.title: Device-Declarations#15

docs.body:
```
#ss1{"title":"MPU6050","sources":[{"frameStart":"AA55","hexadecimalDelimiters":true,"frameDetection":3,"checksumAlgorithm":"CRC-16","decoderMethod":3,"frameParserTemplate":"packed_struct","frameParserParams":{"fields":"f32,f32,f32,f32,f32,f32,f32","endianness":"little"}}],"groups":[...]}
```

Each frame is the start delimiter, the fields in declared order and a checksum. `fields` lists `i8`, `u8`, `i16`, `u16`, `i32`, `u32`, `i64`, `u64`, `f32` or `f64` per channel, and `endianness` is `little` or `big`. A frame whose length does not match the layout is dropped. The `connection` of a source is never read from a declaration.
docs.title: Device-Declarations#16

docs.body:
The one-call `binary()` route is the recommended one; the libraries send the frames for you:

```python
device = serialstudio.Device("MPU6050", write=port.write)
device.binary("f32,f32,f32,f32,f32,f32,f32", "little", b"\xaa\x55", "CRC-16")
```

The C library offers `ss_set_binary()` and the Arduino header `binary()`. The libraries write the `CRC-16` checksum only. On an AVR board `double` has 32 bits, so `f64` fields carry single-precision values.

When Serial Studio switches to the declared framing, the first frames after a declaration can be dropped. A device that declares again sends the declaration as a text line inside the binary stream. Serial Studio finds it in the raw bytes of the connection, and a changed declaration clears the binary framing and rebuilds the dashboard from the new one.
docs.title: Device-Declarations#17

# Devices

## Choosing a connection (drivers)

A driver is the piece that talks to the hardware and hands raw bytes to the rest of Serial Studio. You pick one in the **Connection** dropdown of the **Device Setup** panel (called the Setup panel in the sections below).

Say a board runs `Serial.begin(9600)` and prints `Serial.println(String(temp) + "," + String(hum));` once a second. In **Device Setup**, set **Operation Mode** to "Quick Plot (Auto-Detected Format)", choose **UART/COM** in **Connection**, pick the port, set the baud rate to 9600 and click **Connect**. Each comma-separated value becomes a plot. [Operation Modes](Operation-Modes.md) covers the other modes and the frame delimiters that decide where one frame ends.
docs.title: Devices#0

docs.body: There are fourteen driver types: three free (UART, Network, Bluetooth LE) and eleven that need a Pro license. A GPL build lists only the three free ones. The official binary lists all fourteen, but a Pro driver connects only with a Pro license or the 14-day trial (see [Pro vs Free Features](Pro-vs-Free.md)).
docs.title: Devices#1

docs.body:
| Connection entry | Edition | Use it for | Section |
|------------------|---------|------------|---------|
| UART/COM | Free | Arduino, ESP32, STM32, USB-to-serial adapters, RS-232, RS-485 | [Serial port (UART)](#serial-port-uart) |
| Network | Free | TCP and UDP sockets, WebSocket and HTTP feeds | [Network socket (TCP/UDP)](#network-socket-tcpudp) |
| Bluetooth LE | Free | BLE sensors and custom BLE firmware | [Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE)](#bluetooth-low-energy-ble) |
| Audio | Pro | Microphones, line-in, piezo and other audio-band signals | [Audio input](#audio-input) |
| Modbus | Pro | PLCs and industrial sensors over RTU or TCP | [Modbus (RTU and TCP)](#modbus-rtu-and-tcp) |
| CAN Bus | Pro | Vehicle and industrial CAN networks | [CAN Bus](#can-bus) |

docs.body:
Each driver has a primer with the protocol background: [UART](Drivers-UART.md), [Network](Drivers-Network.md), [Bluetooth LE](Drivers-Bluetooth-LE.md), [Modbus](Drivers-Modbus.md), [CAN Bus](Drivers-CAN-Bus.md), [Audio](Drivers-Audio.md), [Raw USB](Drivers-USB.md), [HID](Drivers-HID.md), [Process I/O](Drivers-Process-IO.md) and [MQTT Subscriber](Drivers-MQTT.md). The topics, wildcards and QoS levels the MQTT driver assumes are in [MQTT Topics & Semantics](MQTT-Topics.md); the outbound side is the per-project [MQTT Publisher](MQTT-Publisher.md).

A project with several devices picks each device's driver in the Project Editor instead; see [Multi-device mode](#multi-device-mode).

docs.body:
## Free drivers

### Serial port (UART)

UART (free) talks to physical or virtual serial ports: Arduino, ESP32, STM32, USB-to-serial adapters, RS-232, and RS-485 links. RS-485 needs an adapter that handles the transmit direction for you.

**Configuration** (Setup panel > Connection > UART/COM):
docs.title: Devices#4

docs.body:
| Parameter        | Options / range                                    | Default   |
|------------------|----------------------------------------------------|-----------|
| Serial Port | Auto-detected list of available ports (labelled COM Port on Windows) | None selected |
| Baud rate        | 110 to 921,600 in the list; custom values accepted | 9600      |
| Data bits        | 5, 6, 7, 8                                         | 8         |
| Parity           | None, Even, Odd, Space, Mark                       | None      |
| Stop bits        | 1, 1.5, 2                                          | 1         |
| Flow control     | None, RTS/CTS (hardware), XON/XOFF (software)      | None      |
| Send DTR Signal  | On / Off. Raises the Data Terminal Ready line when the port opens | On |
| Auto Reconnect   | On / Off. Reconnects automatically on disconnect   | Off       |
docs.title: Devices#5

docs.body:
Port names depend on the platform: `COM3` on Windows, `/dev/ttyUSB0` or `/dev/ttyACM0` on Linux, `/dev/cu.usbserial-*` on macOS. On Linux and macOS the port box is editable: type a device path and press Enter to add it to the list.

**Quick start:**

1. Select your port from the **Serial Port** dropdown (**COM Port** on Windows).
2. Set the baud rate to the number in your firmware's `Serial.begin(9600)` call. A mismatch shows up as garbage characters.
3. Leave data bits, parity, stop bits and flow control at their defaults (8, None, 1, None), which Arduino sketches use.
4. Leave **Send DTR Signal** on unless your board restarts every time you connect. Many Arduino boards reset when DTR changes; turn it off to connect without a reset.
5. Click **Connect**. Values appear in the Console and, in Quick Plot mode, as plots within a second.
docs.title: Devices#6

docs.body:
### Network socket (TCP/UDP)

Network (free) talks over TCP or UDP sockets: ESP32 boards on WiFi, a Raspberry Pi, remote telemetry servers, network-attached instruments. The driver also speaks WebSocket and HTTP polling; those are covered in [Network](Drivers-Network.md).

**Configuration** (Setup panel > Connection > Network). Choose TCP or UDP in the **Socket Type** dropdown first; the columns show the fields each type then exposes. Ports marked "default" are pre-filled in the field.
docs.title: Devices#7

docs.body:
| Parameter       | TCP                     | UDP                              |
|-----------------|-------------------------|----------------------------------|
| Remote Address  | IP or hostname          | IP or hostname (the group address when Multicast is on) |
| Remote Port     | TCP port (default: 23)  | Port to send to (default: 53); hidden while Multicast is on |
| Local Port      | —                       | Listening port (default: 0, auto-assign) |
| Multicast       | —                       | On / Off                         |

Port 23 is the telnet default, which almost nobody's firmware uses; 53 is DNS. Set the port your device uses.
docs.title: Devices#8

docs.body:
Serial Studio is always the client for TCP and never listens. If your ESP32 runs a WiFi server sketch, use TCP with its IP address (the Arduino serial monitor prints it) and the port from the sketch. If it sends UDP packets to your computer, use UDP and set **Local Port** to the destination port in the sketch.

**TCP** keeps a persistent, reliable connection: data arrives in order and lost packets are retransmitted. Hostname resolution runs asynchronously before the connection opens. **UDP** is connectionless, with lower latency and no delivery guarantee, and it can receive from a multicast group.
docs.title: Devices#9

docs.body:
**Quick start (TCP):**

1. Select TCP as the **Socket Type**.
2. Enter the **Remote Address** and **Remote Port**.
3. Click **Connect**.

**Quick start (UDP):**

1. Select UDP as the **Socket Type**.
2. Enter the **Remote Address** and **Remote Port** of the device.
3. Set **Local Port** to the port the device sends to, or leave it at 0 for auto-assignment.
4. Turn on **Multicast** to receive from a multicast group, and put the group address in **Remote Address**. The **Remote Port** field is hidden while Multicast is on.
5. Click **Connect**.

### Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE)

Bluetooth LE (free) subscribes to a GATT characteristic on a BLE peripheral. The peripheral must send its data as notifications on that characteristic. GATT is the BLE layout of services, each holding characteristics; [Bluetooth LE](Drivers-Bluetooth-LE.md) explains it.
docs.title: Devices#10

docs.body:
**Configuration** (Setup panel > Connection > Bluetooth LE):

| Parameter       | Description                                                |
|-----------------|------------------------------------------------------------|
| Device          | Discovered BLE peripherals (scanning starts automatically) |
| Service         | GATT service to subscribe to                               |
| Characteristic  | Specific characteristic for data notifications             |

Supported on macOS (CoreBluetooth), Windows 10+ (WinRT), and Linux (BlueZ 5+). An empty device list means the adapter is off, the device is out of range or not advertising, or the OS denied Bluetooth permission to Serial Studio.
docs.title: Devices#11

docs.body:
**Quick start:**

1. Select Bluetooth LE in **Connection**. Scanning starts automatically.
2. Pick a peripheral from the **Device** dropdown.
3. Wait for service discovery to finish, then pick a **Service**.
4. Pick the **Characteristic** your firmware uses for notifications, for example the one defined in your ESP32 BLE sketch.
5. Click **Connect**.

## Pro drivers

The drivers in this section, and the industrial protocol clients after them, need a Serial Studio Pro license. Each one is picked in the same place as the free ones: Setup panel > **Connection**.

### Audio input

Audio (Pro) captures samples from system input devices through the miniaudio library: microphones, acoustic sensors, piezo vibration pickups, and any analog signal inside the audio frequency range.
docs.title: Devices#12

docs.body:
**Configuration** (Setup panel > Connection > Audio):

| Parameter           | Options                                                     |
|---------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|
| Input device        | System audio inputs (microphone, line-in, and so on)        |
| Sample rate         | Device-dependent, 8 kHz up to 384 kHz (common: 44.1, 48, 96, 192) |
| Sample format       | PCM unsigned 8-bit, signed 16/24/32-bit, float 32-bit       |
| Channel config      | Mono, stereo, or any layout the device supports             |
| Output device       | Optional playback device; data written to it plays back as audio |
docs.title: Devices#13

docs.body:
Pick the device, sample rate, format and channels, then click **Connect**. Audio samples reach the frame pipeline as CSV rows, or as a raw sample stream when the stream lane is active.

Use line-in instead of mic-in to avoid automatic gain control, and turn off OS-level noise cancellation and effects for a clean signal. Grant microphone permission if your OS asks.

### Modbus (RTU and TCP)

Modbus (Pro) polls registers from PLCs, sensors, and industrial controllers. A *slave* (or unit) is the device being polled, and a *register* is a numbered memory cell on it. Use Modbus RTU for serial links (RS-485 or RS-232) and Modbus TCP for devices on Ethernet. [Modbus](Drivers-Modbus.md) has the protocol background.
docs.title: Devices#14

docs.body:
**Common configuration** (Setup panel > Connection > Modbus):

| Parameter        | Range / options                                 | Default |
|------------------|-------------------------------------------------|---------|
| Protocol         | Modbus RTU, Modbus TCP                          | Modbus TCP |
| Slave address    | 1 to 247                                        | 1       |
| Poll interval    | 50 to 60,000 ms                                 | 100     |
| Register groups  | Type + start address + count (multiple groups)  | —       |

**Register types:** coil (read/write bit), discrete input (read-only bit), holding register (read/write 16-bit), input register (read-only 16-bit).
docs.title: Devices#15

docs.body:
**RTU parameters.** Serial port, baud rate, data bits, parity and stop bits, set the same way as in UART. The baud rate defaults to 9600.

**TCP parameters.** Host address and TCP port. The port defaults to 5020, not the standard Modbus port 502, so most PLCs need it changed.

**Quick start (RTU):**

1. Connect an RS-485 adapter to the Modbus device and your computer.
2. Select Modbus RTU and configure the serial port and line parameters.
3. Set the slave address and the poll interval, then click **Configure Register Groups…** and use **Add Group** to add one or more groups. A group is a register type, a start address and a count, for example holding register, address 0, count 4.
4. Click **Connect**. Register values are polled on a timer and delivered as frames.
docs.title: Devices#16

docs.body:
**Quick start (TCP):** Select Modbus TCP, enter the device IP address and port, set the slave address (unit ID) and register groups, and click **Connect**.

### CAN Bus

CAN Bus (Pro) receives and transmits CAN frames through CAN interface plugins. CAN is the two-wire bus in vehicles and industrial machines; frames carry an identifier plus up to 8 data bytes (64 with CAN FD). [CAN Bus](Drivers-CAN-Bus.md) has the protocol background.

**Configuration** (Setup panel > Connection > CAN Bus):
docs.title: Devices#17

docs.body:
| Parameter       | Options                                                                  |
|-----------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Plugin          | SocketCAN, PEAK PCAN, Vector CAN, Systec, others                         |
| Interface       | can0, can1, PCAN_USBBUS1, and so on (plugin-dependent)                   |
| Bitrate         | 10K to 1M (common: 125K, 250K, 500K, 1M)                                 |
| CAN FD          | On / Off. Enables flexible data-rate frames (up to 64 bytes)             |

**Platform support:**
docs.title: Devices#18

docs.body:
- **Linux:** SocketCAN is built into the kernel. Bring the interface up with `ip link set can0 type can bitrate 500000 && ip link set can0 up`.
- **Windows:** Needs a CAN adapter with a Qt CAN Bus plugin (PEAK, Vector, Systec), or one of the adapters below.
- **macOS and Windows:** CANable (gs_usb), slcan serial and Seeed/Waveshare USB-CAN adapters work through Serial Studio's own backends, with no vendor SDK.

**Frame format.** Identifiers up to 0x7FF are standard 11-bit; larger ones are sent as 29-bit extended frames. On receive, the frame's own extended flag decides, not the ID value. The driver delivers each frame as a byte array, zero-padded to a minimum of 11 bytes (standard) or 13 (extended):
docs.title: Devices#19

docs.body:
- Standard: `[ID_high, ID_low, DLC, data...]`
- Extended: `[0x80|ID_28..24, ID_23..16, ID_15..8, ID_7..0, DLC, data...]`, where bit 7 of the first byte marks the extended form.

DLC is the data length code, the number of payload bytes.

**Quick start:**

1. Connect your CAN adapter and install its drivers.
2. Select CAN Bus as the Connection, pick the plugin that matches your hardware, and select the interface.
3. Set the bitrate to match your CAN network exactly. A mismatch causes bus errors.
4. Turn on CAN FD if your network uses it.
5. Click **Connect**.

### Raw USB

Raw USB (Pro) opens a USB device directly through libusb, bypassing the OS serial and HID layers. It suits custom USB firmware and high-bandwidth sensors. The entry in the Connection dropdown is **USB Device**.
docs.title: Devices#20

docs.body:
**Configuration** (Setup panel > Connection > USB Device):

| Parameter       | Options                                               |
|-----------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| Device          | Enumerated USB devices (VID:PID, product name)        |
| Transfer mode   | Bulk/Interrupt Stream (default), Advanced (Bulk + Control), Isochronous |
| IN endpoint     | USB endpoint to read from                             |
| OUT endpoint    | USB endpoint to write to                              |
| Max packet size | Packet size in bytes (isochronous mode only)          |
docs.title: Devices#21

docs.body:
VID:PID is the vendor and product ID pair that identifies the device. In **Bulk/Interrupt Stream** mode, standard bulk IN/OUT transfers cover most custom firmware. **Advanced (Bulk + Control)** adds control transfers for devices that need vendor-specific commands. **Isochronous** is fixed-rate streaming for real-time audio, video and similar devices. [Raw USB](Drivers-USB.md) covers enumeration (hotplug versus a 2-second polling fallback) and endpoints.

**Quick start:**

1. Plug in your USB device and select USB Device as the Connection.
2. Pick your device from the enumerated list.
3. Leave the transfer mode on Bulk/Interrupt Stream unless your device needs something else.
4. Select the IN and OUT endpoints that match your firmware, then click **Connect**.
docs.title: Devices#22

docs.body:
**Platform notes:**

- **Linux:** You need a `udev` rule (for example `SUBSYSTEM=="usb", ATTR{idVendor}=="1234", MODE="0666"`) or root access.
- **macOS:** The kernel HID or serial driver may have to be detached before libusb can claim the device.
- **Windows:** A WinUSB or libusb-compatible driver must be installed (for example with Zadig).

### HID device

HID Device (Pro) connects to Human Interface Devices (gamepads, joysticks, custom HID sensors) through hidapi. Most devices need no extra driver on Windows, macOS or Linux.

**Configuration** (Setup panel > Connection > HID Device):

| Parameter   | Description                                              |
|-------------|----------------------------------------------------------|
| Device      | Enumerated HID devices (VID:PID, product name)           |
| Usage page  | Read-only. HID Usage Page reported by the device         |
| Usage       | Read-only. HID Usage reported by the device              |
docs.title: Devices#23

docs.body:
To connect, pick your device and click **Connect**. On a device with several interfaces, check Usage Page and Usage to find the right one.

The device list refreshes every 2 seconds. Each read returns one report: the report-ID byte plus up to 64 bytes of data (a 65-byte read buffer). If the device is unplugged or a read fails, Serial Studio disconnects and shows a message.

On Linux, add a `udev` rule for `hidraw` access (for example `SUBSYSTEM=="hidraw", GROUP="plugdev", MODE="0664"`). macOS and Windows need no configuration for most devices.

### Process I/O

Process (Pro) reads a child process's output or a named pipe. If a Python script can print it, Serial Studio can plot it. The entry in the Connection dropdown is **Process**.
docs.title: Devices#24

docs.body:
**Modes** (Setup panel > Connection > Process):

| Mode       | Description                                                     |
|------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------|
| Launch     | Spawns a child process and reads its combined stdout and stderr |
| Named pipe | Reads from a named pipe or FIFO. On POSIX the driver creates the FIFO if it doesn't exist; on Windows the external process must create the named pipe first. |

| Launch parameter | Description                              |
|------------------|------------------------------------------|
| Executable       | Path to the program to launch            |
| Arguments        | Command-line arguments                   |
| Working dir      | Working directory for the child process  |
docs.title: Devices#25

docs.body:
Named pipe mode takes one parameter, **Pipe path**, such as `/tmp/mydata` or `\\.\pipe\mydata`. Use it to attach to a long-running process whose lifecycle Serial Studio shouldn't manage.

**Quick start (Launch mode):** Pick Launch mode, enter the path to your script or executable and any arguments, then click **Connect**. Serial Studio spawns the process and reads its output.

**Quick start (Named pipe mode):** Pick Named pipe mode, enter the pipe path, and click **Connect**.

The child process must print data Serial Studio can parse, such as CSV lines or delimited frames. Python buffers stdout when it isn't a terminal, so a script that looks silent is usually just waiting: run it with `-u` or call `flush()` after each `print()`. If the child process crashes, Serial Studio prints a warning and disconnects.
docs.title: Devices#26

docs.body:
### MQTT subscriber

MQTT Subscriber (Pro) subscribes to a broker topic filter and feeds each received payload into the frame pipeline as if the bytes had arrived over UART or TCP. Use it when the telemetry is already on a broker, or when several Serial Studio instances need the same data without each talking to the device.

**Configuration** (Setup panel > Connection > MQTT Subscriber):
docs.title: Devices#27

docs.body:
| Parameter         | Description                                                              |
|-------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Hostname          | Broker address (IP or hostname). Default `127.0.0.1`.                    |
| Port              | Broker port. Default `1883`; use `8883` for TLS.                         |
| Client ID         | Identifier sent on CONNECT. Auto-generated; **Regenerate** picks a new one.|
| Username/Password | Optional broker authentication.                                          |
| Topic filter      | Topic to subscribe to. Supports `+` (one level) and `#` (rest) wildcards. |
| MQTT version      | 3.1, 3.1.1, or 5.0.                                                      |
| Clean session     | Discard persistent session state on CONNECT. Default on.                 |
| Keep alive        | Seconds between PING packets when idle. Default 60.                      |
| SSL / TLS         | Master toggle, protocol family, peer-verify mode, peer-verify depth.     |
| CA certificates   | Load extra PEM certificates for self-signed brokers.                     |
docs.title: Devices#28

docs.body:
**Quick start:**

1. Select MQTT Subscriber as the Connection (or as a device's bus type in the Project Editor).
2. Enter broker hostname, port, and credentials.
3. Set the topic filter to the topic the device publishes on, or a wildcard pattern that covers it.
4. Click **Connect**. Incoming messages go to the project's frame parser.

One MQTT message is one chunk of bytes, because the broker preserves payload boundaries. With **No Delimiters** selected, each publish becomes one frame. A wildcard filter such as `sensors/+/temp` merges many publishers into one source; to tell them apart, put the publisher's identity in the payload or use one source per publisher. [MQTT Subscriber](Drivers-MQTT.md) has the full primer and [MQTT Topics & Semantics](MQTT-Topics.md) the topic, wildcard and QoS reference.
docs.title: Devices#29

docs.body:
### Industrial protocol clients

Each of these Pro drivers is listed in the Connection dropdown under the name shown here, and each has its own page.

| Connection entry | What it connects to | Page |

| OPC UA | Servers that publish a browsable address space of named tags: PLCs, SCADA servers, gateways | [OPC UA](Drivers-OPC-UA.md) |
