docs.body:
## Multi-device mode

Multi-device mode (Pro) runs several devices at once. It starts when a project file defines more than one device (the Project Editor calls each one a source and lists them under Devices). Each device sets its own bus type, connection settings, frame delimiters, and optionally a frame parser in Lua or JavaScript.

All configured devices connect together when you click **Connect**, and each device's data goes to its own groups and datasets in the dashboard. Add devices, each with its own connection, in the Project Editor. In this mode the Setup panel shows a "Multi-Device Project" notice with an **Open Project Editor** button instead of a single driver's settings, because each source carries its own.
docs.title: Devices#31

docs.body: ## Troubleshooting
docs.title: Devices#32

docs.body:
| Driver        | Symptom and fix                                                                |
|---------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| UART          | Port busy: close the Arduino IDE serial monitor or any other program holding it. Garbage characters mean the wrong baud rate. On Linux, your user needs permission to open the device (the `dialout` group on Debian-family systems). |
| Network       | No data: a firewall may be blocking the port. Check that the IP address and port are reachable, and that you replaced the pre-filled default port (23 for TCP, 53 for UDP). |
| BLE           | Device not listed: it is out of range or not advertising. Check that the Bluetooth adapter is enabled. |
| Audio         | Silence: the input device is muted or permission is denied. Check OS audio and privacy settings. |
| Modbus        | No values: slave address or register address mismatch. For RTU, check wiring and termination. For TCP, check the port (default 5020). |
| CAN Bus       | Bus errors: bitrate mismatch. Check CAN-H/CAN-L wiring and termination.        |
| USB Device    | Device won't open: missing `udev` rule (Linux) or a kernel driver holds it (macOS). Check the endpoints. |
| HID Device    | Device won't open: another application has claimed it, or the Linux `udev` rule is missing. |
| Process       | Nothing arrives: executable not found, or stdout is buffered. Use `-u` for Python and check the path. |
| MQTT          | No messages: broker unreachable, wrong topic filter, or client-ID collision. To rule out the broker itself, the [MQTT Publisher](MQTT-Publisher.md) page has a **Test Connection** button that probes a broker with the settings entered there. |
| OPC UA, Siemens S7, EtherNet/IP, IEC 60870-5-104 | Start from the driver's own page, linked in [Industrial protocol clients](#industrial-protocol-clients). [OPC UA](Drivers-OPC-UA.md) has a Common pitfalls section. |
docs.title: Devices#33

docs.body:
# Audio Driver (Pro)

A vibration sensor behind a microphone preamp, or a current shunt wired to a line-in jack, looks like a microphone to your computer. The Audio driver reads any OS audio input device (microphones, line-in, audio interfaces, USB DACs, virtual loopback devices) and turns it into an analog input for the dashboard. A $3 microphone module on a laptop logs AC signals up to about 20 kHz; DC does not pass.

A board that prints text with `Serial.println` is not an audio device; connect it with the [UART driver](Drivers-UART.md). The Audio driver is for signals that arrive through a sound input.
docs.title: Drivers-Audio#0

docs.body:
Audio is a Serial Studio Pro feature, and the free edition does not list it. The first time you use a Pro feature, Serial Studio offers a trial through a Yes/No prompt; registering the trial needs an internet connection. See [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md).

## Quick example: a live waveform and spectrum

1. In the **Setup Panel**, choose **Audio** from the Connection dropdown.
2. Pick your microphone or interface under **Input Device**. Leave the other settings at their defaults, or pick 48000 under **Sample Rate** (Windows defaults to 22050).
3. Click **Connect** in the toolbar.
4. With **Operation Mode** set to "Quick Plot (Auto-Detected Format)", the default (see [Operation Modes](Operation-Modes.md)), the dashboard builds itself: one dataset per channel, in an *Audio Input* group, each with an FFT spectrum. With two or more channels the group is a MultiPlot, and each channel keeps its own FFT.
docs.title: Drivers-Audio#1

docs.body:
The samples arrive as floats from -1.0 to 1.0. Tap the microphone and the waveform moves.

Three numbers describe any digital audio stream: the **sample rate** (measurements per second), the **bit depth** (bits per measurement) and the **channels** (independent waveforms interleaved together, `L,R,L,R,...` for stereo). Sample at least twice the highest frequency you care about; 44100 or 48000 Hz covers everything up to about 20 kHz. Sampling slower than that causes aliasing, where high frequencies fold back as ghost signals at the wrong pitch. Audio hardware filters them out before sampling; custom hardware on a line input needs the same filter.
docs.title: Drivers-Audio#2

docs.body:
## Audio driver settings

Open the **Setup Panel**, choose **Audio** as the connection, and these settings appear. None of them can change while the device is open; disconnect first.
docs.title: Drivers-Audio#3

docs.body:
| Setting | What it does | Default |
|---------|--------------|---------|
| **Input Device** | Which OS audio device to capture from. | Device dependent |
| **Sample Rate** | Capture rate in Hz. Only rates the device reports are offered, from 8000 up to 384000 Hz. | 44100 Hz (22050 Hz on Windows). If the device lacks it, the first listed rate. |
| **Normalization** | Publishes samples as floats in the -1.0 to 1.0 range and lets the driver choose the PCM format. Hides the two **Sample Format** selectors while on. | On |
| **Sample Format** | Unsigned 8-bit, Signed 16-bit, Signed 24-bit, Signed 32-bit, or Float 32-bit, filtered to what the device supports. Shown only when **Normalization** is off. | Chosen by the driver |
| **Channels** | Mono, Stereo, or a multichannel layout (3.0 up to 7.1), as the device reports. | Device dependent |
| **Output Device** | Optional playback device that plays audio out through the speakers or headphones while capturing, with its own **Sample Format** and **Channels** selectors. | None |
docs.title: Drivers-Audio#4

docs.body:
Selections persist across sessions and are saved with the project by stable identifiers (device name, rate in Hz, format name, channel count), so they survive index changes when devices are plugged or unplugged.

When an **Output Device** is configured, the driver opens in duplex mode and data written to it plays back as audio. Each outgoing frame is a comma-separated list with one value per playback channel: `-1.0` to `1.0` under normalization, otherwise integer sample values for the integer formats and `-1.0` to `1.0` for Float 32-bit. A value captured and written straight back reproduces the same amplitude.
docs.title: Drivers-Audio#5

docs.body:
For a walk-through, see the [Protocol Setup Guides, Audio Input section](Protocol-Setup-Guides.md).

### Scripting the settings

Every setting is also available through the `io.audio.*` commands of the [JSON-RPC API](API-Reference.md). Enable the API Server first; it is off by default and listens on port 7777. Indexes are zero-based, in Setup Panel order.
docs.title: Drivers-Audio#6

docs.body:
| Command | Parameter | Notes |
|---------|-----------|-------|
| `setInputDevice`, `setOutputDevice` | `deviceIndex` | |
| `setSampleRate` | `rateIndex` | |
| `setNormalization` | `enabled` | The only setter that takes a boolean. |
| `setInputSampleFormat`, `setOutputSampleFormat` | `formatIndex` | No lasting effect while normalization is on, since the driver re-picks the format. |
| `setInputChannelConfig`, `setOutputChannelConfig` | `channelIndex` | |
| `listInputDevices`, `listOutputDevices`, `listSampleRates`, `listInputFormats`, `listOutputFormats`, `getConfig` | none | Read-only. `getConfig` reports the normalization state and the selected indices. |
docs.title: Drivers-Audio#7

docs.body:
When the in-app AI issues one of the eight setters, it sits behind the **Allow device control** toggle. The read-only commands run unconditionally.

## Audio backends and timestamps

The Audio driver is built on [miniaudio](https://miniaud.io/), which talks directly to the OS audio API:

- **WASAPI** on Windows
- **Core Audio** on macOS
- **PulseAudio** on Linux, which is also how PipeWire systems are reached (through `pipewire-pulse`); **ALSA** is the fallback when no sound server is running

Each sample carries the time it was captured, not the time the OS delivered the buffer, so audio lines up with other sources in CSV exports and session reports. A 10 ms worker forwards captured buffers, and the first sample of each buffer is stamped `now - (N-1) / sample_rate`. Consecutive buffers extend one continuous sample clock, which snaps back to wall time only when it drifts more than 50 ms. See [Threading and Timing Guarantees](Threading-and-Timing.md) for the timestamp-ownership rules.
docs.title: Drivers-Audio#8

docs.body:
## Audio data format

The driver converts each captured buffer to CSV text: one line per sample period, channels separated by commas. A stereo capture hands the [frame parser](Frame-Parser.md) lines like this:

```
0.0123,-0.0098
0.0141,-0.0102
0.0159,-0.0107
```

Under line-delimited framing (the Quick Plot default), Serial Studio treats each line as one frame, with its own sample-clock timestamp. A 48000 Hz capture therefore produces 48000 frames per second, which is what drives CPU use and the frame counter. In a project, set the frame delimiter to newline and use a one-argument `parse(frame)` that splits on commas.
docs.title: Drivers-Audio#9

docs.body:
From there the values can be plotted as time-domain waveforms, fed into an FFT widget for the spectrum, fed into a Waterfall (spectrogram) widget, or reshaped by [per-dataset transforms](Dataset-Transforms.md) for filtering, scaling or unit conversion. The FFT and Waterfall widgets share the same per-dataset settings, so one channel can drive both views.

In [Quick Plot mode](Operation-Modes.md) the dashboard configures these for you:

- Each channel becomes a dataset in an *Audio Input* group with FFT enabled. With more than one channel, the group is a MultiPlot and the per-dataset plot is off.
- **FFT Sampling Rate** is set to the device sample rate, and **FFT Samples** to the power of two (256 to 8192) covering roughly 50 ms of signal.
- Plot and FFT ranges are -1 / 1 under normalization, or the sample format's limits without it.
docs.title: Drivers-Audio#10

docs.body:
In a project, set **FFT Sampling Rate**, **FFT Samples** and the plot and FFT ranges yourself in the Project Editor's dataset settings, or start from **Save as Project** in the dashboard's start menu, which carries the Quick Plot values over.

### Audio normalization

**Normalization is on by default.** With it enabled, every sample reaches the dashboard as a float in the **-1.0 to 1.0** range, whatever PCM format the hardware delivers:

| Capture format | Normalized as |
|----------------|---------------|
| Unsigned 8-bit | `(v - 128) / 128` |
| Signed 16-bit  | `v / 32768` |
| Signed 24-bit  | `v / 8388608` |
| Signed 32-bit  | `v / 2147483648` |
| Float 32-bit   | unchanged |
docs.title: Drivers-Audio#11

docs.body:
Because amplitude no longer depends on bit depth, the driver picks the best native format itself (Float 32-bit first when the device offers it, so there is no backend conversion), and the **Sample Format** selectors disappear from the Setup Panel. Changing the device or its channel count re-picks the format.

Dataset transforms get simpler too. In a [value transform](Dataset-Transforms.md), `value * 2.5` means 2.5 volts full-scale whether the interface is 16-bit or 24-bit, so a project keeps working when you swap the hardware.

Turning **Normalization** off brings the **Sample Format** selectors back, and samples arrive as raw per-format integers (`-32768` to `32767` for Signed 16-bit, and so on).
docs.title: Drivers-Audio#12

docs.body:
> **Upgrading from an older version.** Projects built before normalization existed expect raw integer magnitudes, so their plot and FFT ranges look flat with normalization on. Widen those per-dataset ranges to `-1` / `1`, or turn **Normalization** off for that project. Quick Plot mode adjusts on its own.

## Common pitfalls
docs.title: Drivers-Audio#13

docs.body:
- **No audio detected.** Verify the input device in the OS audio settings first. On macOS, grant Serial Studio Microphone permission in **System Settings → Privacy & Security → Microphone**. On Linux, run `pactl list sources short` (PulseAudio or PipeWire) or `arecord -l` (ALSA) to confirm the device exists and is not muted. Raw `hw:` devices bypass the system's processing chain, so prefer the sound server's source when both are listed.
- **Distorted signal at high amplitude.** The input is clipping. A clipped sine wave looks like a sine wave that hit a ceiling. Reduce the input gain in the OS or on the hardware preamp.
- **FFT or waterfall frequency axis is wrong.** In a project, **FFT Sampling Rate** (`fftSamplingRate`) defaults to 100 Hz. Set it to the audio sample rate on each dataset; otherwise the frequency axis is off by the ratio of your sample rate to 100. Quick Plot sets it automatically.
- **Required sample rate is not listed.** The hardware reports its supported rates and Serial Studio offers only those. The driver cannot fake one; use a different audio interface.
- **Noisy signal.** Microphone inputs expect a millivolt-range source and amplify noise from anything else. Use a line input for line-level signals.
- **Latency feels high.** The OS audio backend sets the capture buffer size, and Serial Studio does not expose it. That is fine for visualisation but not for closed-loop control.
- **High CPU at 192 kHz.** FFT plus waterfall at a high sample rate is expensive. Reduce **FFT Samples** or disable the waterfall in the per-dataset settings.
docs.title: Drivers-Audio#14

docs.body:
# Bluetooth Low Energy Driver

Your ESP32 or nRF52 board sends sensor values over Bluetooth Low Energy instead of USB. Serial Studio connects to it as the BLE central, subscribes to one characteristic, and treats every notification as incoming bytes, exactly as if they had arrived over UART. Bluetooth LE is available in both the free and Pro editions. The terms central, service, characteristic and notification are explained in [BLE terms you need](#ble-terms-you-need).

"Classic" Bluetooth devices (the older Serial Port Profile) show up as a virtual COM port; use the [UART driver](Drivers-UART.md) for those.
docs.title: Drivers-Bluetooth-LE#0
Drivers-Bluetooth-LE#1
Drivers-Bluetooth-LE#2

docs.body:
1. In the **Device Setup** panel, set **Operation Mode** to "Quick Plot (Auto-Detected Format)" (see [Operation Modes](Operation-Modes.md)) and the interface to **Bluetooth LE**. The **Device** dropdown appears once a scan finds a named peripheral; the circular-arrow icon beside it rescans.
2. Pick `SensorNode` in **Device**, then click **Connect** in the main toolbar. Connect opens the link and starts service discovery, so the **Service** dropdown stays hidden until discovery finishes.
3. Pick `FFE0` in **Service**. The **Characteristic** dropdown appears once the service lists characteristics.
4. Pick `FFE1` in **Characteristic**, the one with the Notify property. No data arrives before this step, because Serial Studio enables notifications when you select the characteristic.
docs.title: Drivers-Bluetooth-LE#3

docs.body:
Two plots (23.4 and 51.0) start drawing, one point per second. Quick Plot splits the stream on line endings, so each `\n` ends one frame.

## What Serial Studio does

On selecting a characteristic, Serial Studio turns notifications on for it by writing the CCCD (the descriptor that switches notifications on) with the Notify value `0x0001`. You do not enable anything by hand. Indicate-only characteristics are not supported, because the driver never requests indications, and a characteristic without a CCCD delivers nothing. If the characteristic already holds a value when you select it, that value arrives as the first chunk.
docs.title: Drivers-Bluetooth-LE#4

docs.body:
Every notification's payload enters the incoming stream unchanged, and the configured frame detection splits it into frames. In a project, set the source's frame detection to **No Delimiters** to map one notification to one frame, and decode packed binary payloads in a [frame parser](Frame-Parser.md).

Each dropdown starts on its own placeholder, **Select Device**, **Select Service** or **Select Characteristic**; choosing it clears the selection. The Service and Characteristic dropdowns appear only when they list at least one entry. Until the first named peripheral is found, the pane shows **Scanning…**; once one is listed, the **Device** dropdown replaces it. With no radio present it shows **No Bluetooth Adapter Detected**, and on operating systems without Qt Bluetooth support it shows **This OS is not Supported Yet.**
docs.title: Drivers-Bluetooth-LE#5

docs.body:
### BLE terms you need

- A **peripheral** advertises its name and exposes data. A **central** scans and connects. Serial Studio is the central.
- A **service** groups related data, and a **characteristic** is one value inside it. Standard ones use 16-bit UUIDs (`0x180F` is Battery Service); custom ones use 128-bit UUIDs.
- **Notify** means the peripheral pushes each new value without being asked. This is the telemetry pattern Serial Studio uses.

### Writing to the device

Data sent through the console or an [action](Actions.md) is written to the selected characteristic. Serial Studio uses Write Without Response when the characteristic supports it and Write With Response otherwise. Devices that split RX and TX across two characteristics (the Nordic UART Service pattern) take writes through `io.ble.writeCharacteristic`, which resolves any characteristic in the selected service by UUID.
docs.title: Drivers-Bluetooth-LE#6

docs.body:
### Reconnecting and saved settings

A project saves the device (by name or address) and the service and characteristic (by UUID, so a firmware update that reorders the GATT table does not break it). On the next connection Serial Studio reselects them after discovery and reports the source as connected only afterwards. Anything that runs on connect, such as a [Control Loop](Control-Loop.md) or an auto-execute action runs only after the characteristic is selected, so it can write to the characteristic as soon as the source reports connected.

Projects saved by older versions may hold a notify characteristic but no service UUID. Serial Studio then probes the discovered services one by one to find it.
docs.title: Drivers-Bluetooth-LE#7

docs.body:
### MTU and throughput

The default MTU (maximum packet size) is 23 bytes, of which 20 are payload. BLE 4.2+ devices can negotiate up to 247 bytes of payload. Serial Studio does not set the MTU or the connection interval; the operating system and the peripheral negotiate both. On paper the ceiling is roughly 260 kbps (one 247-byte packet per 7.5 ms interval); real links are lower.

A 20-byte frame at 100 Hz is 2 kB/s, comfortable for BLE. Several channels at 1 kHz are not; use [TCP or UDP](Drivers-Network.md) for those.

## Scripting and API control

The same flow is scriptable through the `io.ble.*` commands of the [JSON-RPC API](API-Reference.md). The API Server is off by default; when enabled it listens on port 7777.
docs.title: Drivers-Bluetooth-LE#8

docs.body:
| Command | Parameter | Selects by |
|---------|-----------|------------|
| `io.ble.selectDevice` | `deviceIndex` | index into `io.ble.listDevices` |
| `io.ble.selectService` | `serviceIndex` | index into `io.ble.listServices` |
| `io.ble.selectServiceByUuid` | `serviceUuid` | UUID |
| `io.ble.setCharacteristicIndex` | `characteristicIndex` | index into `io.ble.listCharacteristics` |
| `io.ble.setNotifyCharacteristic` | `characteristicUuid` | UUID |
| `io.ble.writeCharacteristic` | `characteristicUuid`, base64 `data` | UUID, any characteristic in the selected service |
| `io.ble.startDiscovery` | none | n/a |
| `io.ble.listDevices`, `io.ble.listServices`, `io.ble.listCharacteristics`, `io.ble.getConfig`, `io.ble.getStatus` | none | n/a |
docs.title: Drivers-Bluetooth-LE#9

docs.body:
UUID parameters accept the 16-bit short form (`fff1`, `0xFFF1`) or the full 128-bit form, with or without braces. Index selection depends on list order; UUID selection survives GATT-table reordering.

When the in-app AI assistant sends these commands, every one except the list and get commands needs **Allow device control** switched on, and each call still asks for your confirmation. The toggle is in the AI Assistant panel, under the wrench (**Settings**) button in its top bar.

## Common pitfalls
docs.title: Drivers-Bluetooth-LE#10

docs.body:
| Symptom | Cause and fix |
|---------|---------------|
| Device does not appear in the scan | Serial Studio lists only peripherals that advertise a name; set one in the firmware. Otherwise power-cycle the peripheral and click the rescan icon. On macOS, grant Serial Studio Bluetooth permission in **System Settings > Privacy & Security > Bluetooth**. |
| Connected, but no characteristic appears | The **Characteristic** dropdown stays hidden until you pick a service and its characteristics are discovered; pick the service first. Some peripherals expose their services only after pairing in the OS Bluetooth settings (Windows Bluetooth settings, macOS System Settings, or `bluetoothctl` on Linux). |
| Connected, but no data arrives | The characteristic must have the Notify property (`PROPERTY_NOTIFY` in the sketch) and a CCCD (`BLE2902` descriptor); Notify-less and Indicate-only characteristics deliver nothing. Serial Studio does not show characteristic properties, so check them in the firmware. |
| Throughput is lower than expected | The connection interval, set by the peripheral and the OS, caps the packet rate. See [MTU and throughput](#mtu-and-throughput); ask the firmware for a shorter interval. |
| Connection drops after a few seconds | Some peripherals that require encryption drop the link until you pair them in the OS Bluetooth settings. Pair first, then reconnect. |
| A second window cannot connect | Most peripherals accept one central at a time. Your phone, still paired to it from yesterday, counts. |
| Linux shows no adapter | Run `bluetoothctl list`; if it prints no controller, BlueZ does not see the adapter. |

# CAN Bus Driver (Pro)

You have a CAN adapter plugged into a car, a motor controller or a pair of boards, and you want the values on a dashboard. The CAN Bus driver reads frames from the bus and hands them to Serial Studio. If you have a DBC file that names the signals, you can skip the parser entirely.

This driver needs a CAN adapter (or a CAN-capable board with a transceiver) and a live bus. An Arduino or ESP32 that only calls `Serial.println` is a UART device, not a CAN one: use the [UART driver](Drivers-UART.md) for that.

The CAN Bus driver is a Pro feature. On the free edition, the first Pro feature you use shows a Yes/No prompt offering a trial (needs an internet connection); see [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md).
docs.title: Drivers-CAN-Bus#0

docs.body:
## Quick start

1. Open the Setup panel (the sidebar on the left) and pick **CAN Bus** in the Connection dropdown at the top.
2. Pick the **CAN Driver** that matches your adapter (see the table below).
3. Pick the **Interface**, then set **Bitrate** to the rate the bus already runs at. If no Interface appears, Serial Studio does not see the adapter: see [Common pitfalls](#common-pitfalls). On Linux SocketCAN, bring the interface up first (see [Setup settings](#setup-settings-pro)).
4. In the CAN Bus Setup panel, click **Import DBC File…** and choose your `.dbc` file. A DBC file is a text file from the vehicle or device maker that names each signal in a CAN message (see [DBC: the signal database](#dbc-the-signal-database)). Serial Studio generates a project from it (see [Auto-Generating Projects](Auto-Generating-Projects.md)).
5. Connect.
docs.title: Drivers-CAN-Bus#1

docs.body:
No DBC file? Skip step 4 and write a parser by hand, see [Frame parsing](#frame-parsing). No hardware yet? Pick `virtualcan` as the CAN Driver and tick **Loopback** to try the driver without an adapter.

| Your adapter | CAN Driver |
|--------------|------------|
| Linux, built-in or USB adapter | `socketcan` |
| CANable and other gs_usb devices | `canable_gsusb` |
| Serial (slcan) adapters | `slcan` |
| Seeed / Waveshare USB-CAN Analyzer | `seeed_usbcan` |
| PEAK PCAN | `peakcan` |
| No hardware, just testing | `virtualcan` |

Qt's own plugins also provide `vectorcan`, `systeccan` and `tinycan`. The three Serial Studio backends (`canable_gsusb`, `slcan`, `seeed_usbcan`) talk to the adapter directly and need no vendor SDK; the PCAN, Vector, SysTec and Tiny-CAN plugins need the vendor's driver installed.
docs.title: Drivers-CAN-Bus#2

docs.body:
## CAN basics

Three ideas are enough to use this driver.

- **Arbitration ID.** Identifies the message, not a destination. 11 bits is "standard", 29 bits is "extended". When two nodes talk at once the lower ID wins, so a lower ID means higher priority. Your parser compares the ID to pick out the message you want.
- **Data.** 0 to 8 bytes in classic CAN, up to 64 in CAN FD. The bytes are vendor-defined: what byte 3 of message `0x7E8` means is written in the DBC file or the OEM's spec. The frame carries the byte count in its DLC (data length code) field.
- **Bit rate.** Every node on the bus must run the same one, such as 125 kbps, 250 kbps, 500 kbps or 1 Mbps. CAN FD adds a second, faster rate for the data phase of each frame, and up to 64 bytes of payload, while the arbitration phase stays at the slower rate.
docs.title: Drivers-CAN-Bus#3

docs.body:
### DBC: the signal database

**DBC** (CAN Database) files describe what the bytes inside a message mean. A typical entry:

```
BO_ 256 EngineData: 8 ECU
 SG_ EngineRPM : 0|16@1+ (0.25,0) [0|16383] "rpm" Dashboard
 SG_ ThrottlePosition : 16|8@1+ (0.392,0) [0|100] "%" Dashboard
 SG_ EngineTemp : 24|8@1+ (1,-40) [-40|215] "°C" Dashboard
```

That declares message ID 256 (`0x100`), 8 bytes long, sent by `ECU` (the sending device) and received by `Dashboard`. It contains three signals:

- **EngineRPM** at bit 0, 16 bits wide, little-endian, unsigned, factor 0.25, offset 0, range 0-16383, units rpm.
- **ThrottlePosition** at bit 16, 8 bits wide, factor 0.392, offset 0, units %.
- **EngineTemp** at bit 24, 8 bits wide, factor 1, offset -40, units °C.
docs.title: Drivers-CAN-Bus#4

docs.body:
Serial Studio's importer reads the file and generates a project (see [Auto-Generating Projects](Auto-Generating-Projects.md)). A signal with a `VAL_` value table and plain scaling (factor 1, offset 0) imports with those descriptions as its [Labels](Project-Editor.md), so a gear signal reads as a name while its plot keeps the number.

## Setup settings (Pro)

Select **CAN Bus** in the Setup panel's Connection dropdown and these fields appear. Everything except **CAN Driver** stays hidden until an interface is detected.
docs.title: Drivers-CAN-Bus#5

docs.body:
| Setting | Controls | Default |
|---------|----------|---------|
| **CAN Driver** | Which CAN backend to use (see the table in [Quick start](#quick-start)). | first available |
| **Interface** | Which physical interface inside that backend, for example `can0` or `PCAN_USBBUS1`. | first available |
| **Bitrate** | Must match the bus exactly. Pick a preset (10, 20, 50, 100, 125, 250, 500, 800 kbps or 1 Mbps) or type a custom value in bit/s. | 500000 bit/s |
| **Flexible Data-Rate** | Whether to use the CAN FD frame format. Greyed out, with the tooltip "The selected adapter does not support CAN FD", when the interface cannot do FD. | off |
| **Data Bitrate** | The CAN FD data-phase rate. Shown only while **Flexible Data-Rate** is on. Presets are 1, 2, 4, 5 and 8 Mbps. | 2000000 bit/s |
| **Loopback** | Echo transmitted frames back to the application (self-reception). | off |
| **Listen-Only** | Silent monitoring: receive frames without acknowledging or transmitting. | off |
| **Multi-Frame Reassembly** | Joins J1939 transport-protocol and ISO-TP multi-frame messages into one long frame before parsing. See [Multi-frame reassembly](#multi-frame-reassembly). | off |
| **DBC Database** | **Import DBC File…** generates a project from a signal database (see [Auto-Generating Projects](Auto-Generating-Projects.md)). | none |
docs.title: Drivers-CAN-Bus#6

docs.body:
The driver runs on the main thread, with Qt's async I/O delivering frames by signal; see [Threading and Timing Guarantees](Threading-and-Timing.md).

For Linux SocketCAN, the interface must be brought up from a terminal *before* Serial Studio connects:

```sh
sudo ip link set can0 type can bitrate 500000
sudo ip link set up can0
```

For CAN FD, the `dbitrate` here matches the **Data Bitrate** default:

```sh
sudo ip link set can0 type can bitrate 500000 dbitrate 2000000 fd on
sudo ip link set up can0
```

### Frame parsing

Serial Studio publishes every received CAN frame to the frame parser as a binary byte array.
docs.title: Drivers-CAN-Bus#7

docs.body:
| Frame | Layout | Padded to |
|-------|--------|-----------|
| Standard (11-bit) | `[ID_hi, ID_lo, DLC, payload...]` | 11 bytes |
| Extended (29-bit) | `[0x80 \| (ID >> 24 & 0x1F), ID23..16, ID15..8, ID7..0, DLC, payload...]` | 13 bytes |

Bit 7 of the first byte marks an extended frame; only the low 5 bits of that byte carry ID bits, so the 29-bit ID is split 5 + 8 + 8 + 8. Transmitting uses the same layout: write the header and payload bytes and the driver assembles the CAN frame.

To receive those raw bytes in `parse(frame)`, open the Project Editor and set the source's **Frame Detection** to **No Delimiters** and its **Data Conversion** to **Binary (Direct)** (`decoder: 3` in the project file). A standard frame `01 00 08 11 22 ...` is ID `0x100`, 8 data bytes, first byte `0x11`:
docs.title: Drivers-CAN-Bus#8
Drivers-CAN-Bus#9

docs.body:
### Multi-frame reassembly

Advanced: skip this unless your messages exceed 8 bytes. A diagnostic reply is longer than 8 bytes and arrives in pieces. A classic CAN frame carries at most 8 data bytes, 64 with CAN FD, so the protocols that move longer messages split them across frames. J1939-21 announces a transfer with a TP.CM packet (PGN `0xEC00`) and streams the body as TP.DT packets (PGN `0xEB00`). ISO-TP (ISO 15765-2, the transport under UDS and OBD-II) sends a FirstFrame followed by ConsecutiveFrames. Decoding either one in a frame parser means carrying session state between frames.

Tick **Multi-Frame Reassembly** in the Setup panel (Pro, CAN Bus driver) and the driver does it instead. It is off by default, because reading the J1939 transport parameter groups on a bus that does not speak J1939 would turn ordinary traffic into synthesized long frames. It claims only two kinds of traffic:
docs.title: Drivers-CAN-Bus#10

docs.body:
- **J1939**: extended (29-bit) frames whose parameter group is TP.CM or TP.DT.
- **ISO-TP**: the ISO 15765-4 diagnostic identifiers (11-bit `0x7E0` to `0x7EF`, 29-bit
  `0x18DAxxyy` and `0x18DBxxyy`), and only when the payload's first nibble is a multi-frame PCI. A
  SingleFrame reaches the parser unchanged.

Everything else on the bus is published exactly as it was with the option off.
docs.title: Drivers-CAN-Bus#11

docs.body: A completed message arrives as one extended-format frame whose DLC byte is `0xFF`, the marker for a reassembled payload: `[0x80|ID28..24, ID23..16, ID15..8, ID7..0, 0xFF, payload...]`. The payload is appended whole, so a reassembled frame is longer than the 13 bytes of a raw extended frame (see [Frame parsing](#frame-parsing)) and is not capped at 64 data bytes. For J1939 the identifier is rebuilt from the transfer's priority, PGN and source address; for ISO-TP it is the identifier the session arrived on. The timestamp is the capture time of the message's **first** packet, not of the fragment that completed it. A long transfer is dated when it began.
docs.title: Drivers-CAN-Bus#12

docs.body:
Reassembly is listen-only. FlowControl frames are consumed and never sent, and a J1939 session opens on the announcement without waiting for a CTS that Serial Studio will not transmit, so the feature works while tapping a bus between two other nodes.

The limits are fixed, and a session that exceeds one is dropped whole and counted rather than truncated into a half-decoded message:

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Concurrent sessions, per protocol | 16 |
| J1939 transfer size | 1785 bytes, 255 packets |
| ISO-TP message size | 4095 bytes |
| Session timeout since the last fragment | 750 ms |

`io.canbus.getConfig` reports the current state and the per-protocol counters (`completed`, `timeouts`, `aborted`, `malformed`, `sizeOverruns`, `sequenceErrors`, `sessionOverruns`). Unticking and re-ticking the **Multi-Frame Reassembly** checkbox clears both the counters and any half-collected session. See [API Reference](API-Reference.md).
docs.title: Drivers-CAN-Bus#13

docs.body:
### API control

The `io.canbus.*` commands work only while the API Server is enabled (off by default, port 7777). The [Socket API](API-Reference.md) and the in-app [AI Assistant](AI-Assistant.md) configure this driver through them.

| Command | Parameter | Notes |
|---------|-----------|-------|
| `setPluginIndex` | `pluginIndex` | Index into `listPlugins`. |
| `setInterfaceIndex` | `interfaceIndex` | Index into `listInterfaces`. |
| `setBitrate` | `bitrate` | Bit/s. A value below 10000 is read as an index into `listBitrates`, not as a rate. |
| `setCanFd` | `enabled` | Flexible Data-Rate on or off. |
| `setDataBitrate` | `dataBitrate` | CAN FD data-phase rate. |
| `setLoopback` | `enabled` | Loopback on or off. |
| `setListenOnly` | `enabled` | Listen-Only on or off. |
docs.title: Drivers-CAN-Bus#14

docs.body:
Read-only: `getConfig`, `listPlugins`, `listInterfaces`, `listBitrates`, `getInterfaceError`. Multi-frame reassembly has no setter in the API: tick it in the Setup panel, then read `tpReassembly` and its counters back from `getConfig`. For the AI Assistant the setters are device-gated: blocked until the user ticks **Allow device control**, and each call still requires confirmation.

For step-by-step setup, see the [Protocol Setup Guides, CAN Bus section](Protocol-Setup-Guides.md).

## Common pitfalls
docs.title: Drivers-CAN-Bus#15

docs.body:
| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---------|-------|-----|
| No frames received | Bit-rate mismatch. The rate must match on every node; a wrong step such as 500 kbps against 250 kbps gives silence or error frames. | Check the rate with the bus owner or the device documentation, and confirm traffic exists with a CAN analyser (PCAN-View, `candump`, BusMaster). |
| Error frames only | Termination is missing or wrong. | A CAN bus needs two 120 Ω terminators, one at each physical end of the trunk, and no more: a third one is not extra safety. Measured between CAN-H and CAN-L with the bus powered off, the resistance should be about 60 Ω. Anything else points to a wiring problem. |
| Interface not listed (Linux) | The kernel module is not loaded. | Run `ip link show can0`; if it is missing, run `sudo modprobe can_dev`, and `sudo modprobe vcan` for virtual-CAN testing. |
| Interface will not come up (Linux) | `ip link set` requires root or `CAP_NET_ADMIN`. Opening an already configured SocketCAN interface needs no privileges. | Bring the interface up once with `sudo`, then connect as a normal user. For `slcan` and other serial adapters, the user must be able to open the serial device (the `dialout` group on Debian-family distributions). |
| DBC import produces wrong values | Wrong byte order on a signal. DBC supports both little-endian (Intel) and big-endian (Motorola) inside the same message; a manually edited DBC with the wrong order gives values that look scaled or shifted by a constant. | Correct the byte order in the DBC and import again. |
| Multiplexed (MUX) signals do not decode | Extended multiplexing (`SG_MUL_VAL_`, `SwitchAndSignal` intermediates, value ranges) is not supported; those signals are skipped and the post-import dialog reports how many. Simple multiplexing works: the importer gates each muxed signal on the `MultiplexorSwitch` value and titles datasets `Foo (mux 3)`. | Switch the source to a Lua or JavaScript frame parser and decode them by hand. |
| A long message arrives as fragments | Diagnostic responses and J1939 transfers longer than one frame reach the parser as separate TP.DT or ConsecutiveFrame payloads. | Tick **Multi-Frame Reassembly**. The joined message then arrives as one frame carrying the `0xFF` DLC marker, and a parser written for raw frames must branch on that byte. |
| CAN FD frames are dropped | The bus, the adapter and Serial Studio must all be in CAN FD mode, and a classic-only node raises an error on an FD frame. | Turn **Flexible Data-Rate** on only when every node is FD-capable; otherwise leave it off and set the adapter to classic mode. |
| PCAN/Vector/SysTec driver not found (Windows) | The vendor driver and runtime are separate installs; Qt's CAN plugin is only a wrapper. | Install the vendor driver. The CANable, slcan and Seeed/Waveshare backends are the exception: Serial Studio talks to those adapters directly. |

# EtherNet/IP Driver (Pro)

A CompactLogix runs a conveyor, and its program has a tag called `MotorSpeed`. Give Serial Studio Pro that name and the value plots. EtherNet/IP carries CIP (Common Industrial Protocol) over ordinary Ethernet; the driver is a client that polls a list of tag names and streams their values into the dashboard.

The driver is for Rockwell/Allen-Bradley and Omron controllers on a network, not for boards that print over USB serial; for those use the [UART driver](Drivers-UART.md). It is read-only: it cannot change the machine, so connecting to a running line is safe.

The EtherNet/IP driver is a Pro feature. The first time you use a Pro feature without a licence, Serial Studio offers the free [trial](Pro-vs-Free.md) in a Yes/No prompt (registering the trial needs an internet connection); after it ends the prompt offers activation or purchase. GPL builds, and builds configured with `SS_ENABLE_EIP=OFF`, contain no EtherNet/IP client.
docs.title: Drivers-EtherNet-IP#0

docs.body:
## Quick start

1. In the Setup panel, open the **Connection** drop-down, choose **EtherNet/IP** and enter the **Gateway**: the IP address or host name of the controller.
2. Keep **CIP Path** `1,0` for ControlLogix and CompactLogix; MicroLogix and PLC-5 need it cleared (see [Settings](#connection-settings)). Pick the **Controller** that matches the line printed on the controller's label ([Controller families](#controller-families)).
3. Open **Configure Tags…**, fill in the channel name, the tag name and the type (for `MotorSpeed`, `f32`), press **Add Tag**, and close the dialog. The pane reads **No tags configured** until a row exists.
4. Press **Connect**. Press **Create Project from Tags** to get a dashboard for the list; `MotorSpeed` appears as a plot titled `MotorSpeed`.
docs.title: Drivers-EtherNet-IP#1

docs.body:
The same setup from a terminal (the slug after `--ethernetip-plc` comes from [Controller families](#controller-families)):

```bash
SerialStudio --ethernetip 192.168.0.10 --ethernetip-plc controllogix --ethernetip-tag "MotorSpeed:f32"
```

## Addressing

You tell Serial Studio each tag's type, because the driver does not read it from the controller. Pick it to match the controller: a `DINT` is `i32`, a `REAL` is `f32`, a `BOOL` is `bool`, a `STRING` is `str`. A wrong type gives a wrong number, not an error, so check each one against the data type column of the controller's tag list in its programming software.
docs.title: Drivers-EtherNet-IP#2

docs.body:
A tag is named exactly as the controller names it:

| Example | Reads |
|---------|-------|
| `MotorSpeed` | A controller-scoped tag |
| `Program:MainProgram.Counter` | A program-scoped tag |
| `Tank.Level` | A member of a tag whose type is a UDT (user-defined structure) |
| `Temperatures`, element `3` | One element of an array tag; leave **Element** empty for a scalar |

The declarable types are `bool`, `i8`, `u8`, `i16`, `u16`, `i32`, `u32`, `i64`, `u64`, `f32`, `f64` and `str`. A tag name is limited to 256 characters and cannot contain `&`, `=` or whitespace; Serial Studio refuses such a name before connecting. A `str` value is truncated to 255 bytes. Gateway and CIP Path cannot contain `&` or `=` either; **Connect** then fails with "The connection is not configured: check the host and the tag list".
docs.title: Drivers-EtherNet-IP#3

docs.body: ## Connection settings
docs.title: Drivers-EtherNet-IP#4

docs.body:
1. **Gateway.** The IP address or host name of the device that answers EtherNet/IP: the controller itself on a CompactLogix, or the Ethernet bridge module on a ControlLogix rack.
2. **CIP Path.** The route from the gateway to the CPU, as a comma-separated CIP path. Default `1,0`: backplane port 1, slot 0. Clear the field to address the gateway itself, which is what MicroLogix and PLC-5 controllers need.
3. **Controller.** The controller family the client speaks, picked from [Controller families](#controller-families). Default ControlLogix. A wrong family makes every tag fail at connect.
4. **Poll Interval (ms).** How often the whole tag list is read, and the frame rate of the source. Default 250 ms; the UI and API clamp it to 50-60000 ms.
5. **Tags.** The **Configure Tags…** dialog holds the list: a channel name, the controller's tag name, the declared type and an optional **Element** index per row. The channel name is what the dashboard shows; leaving it empty uses the tag name. Up to 2048 tags can be configured. The list is locked while connected, because the frame layout is sized when the session starts; disconnect to edit it.
6. **Create Project from Tags.** Builds a project from the list ([Generated project](#generated-project)).
docs.title: Drivers-EtherNet-IP#5

docs.body:
### Controller families

Pick the line printed on the controller's label. The **Controller** picker names each family the way its vendor does. The command line and the API take the slug beside it:

| Picker | `--ethernetip-plc` and `plcType` |
|--------|----------------------------------|
| ControlLogix | `controllogix` |
| CompactLogix | `compactlogix` |
| MicroLogix | `micrologix` |
| Micro800 | `micrologix800` |
| PLC-5 | `plc5` |
| SLC 500 | `slc500` |
| Logix PCCC | `logixpccc` |
| Omron NJ/NX | `omron-njnx` |

### Polling and delta frames

Reads run on a thread the driver owns, never on the UI thread, so a controller that stops answering slows the poll rate instead of freezing the window.
docs.title: Drivers-EtherNet-IP#6

docs.body:
Opening the session creates one libplctag handle per configured tag. A tag the controller does not recognise fails the connection attempt with the name it refused, so a typo is reported at connect time rather than as a channel that never updates.

Every tick reads each tag in list order and compares it with the value the previous tick stored. Only what changed is encoded into one binary frame; unchanged tags are not resent and the dashboard keeps showing their last value.

Reads that time out are counted and the channels keep their last value, because libplctag reconnects on its own. After three consecutive ticks in which no tag answered, the link is declared lost and Serial Studio disconnects.
docs.title: Drivers-EtherNet-IP#7

docs.body:
Every frame is stamped on the poll thread when the tick starts, so recordings and CSV exports carry the poll's own time, and a stamp never goes backwards.

### Generated project

**Create Project from Tags** writes a project with:

- One source of type EtherNet/IP carrying the gateway, CIP path, controller family, interval and the tag list, so reopening the project reconnects without retyping the tags.
- One group per program scope (`Program:MainProgram`), plus one **Controller Tags** group for controller-scoped tags.
- One dataset per tag: the channel name as the title, booleans become lights in a separate LED Panel group, numeric types are plotted, and strings go to the data grid.
- A Built-In frame parser using the **EtherNet/IP tags** template. Its schema parameter is regenerated with the project; edit the tag list and generate again rather than editing the schema by hand.
docs.title: Drivers-EtherNet-IP#8

docs.body:
The project opens in the Project Editor for customization. The headless API command `io.eip.generateProject` performs the same generation without a save dialog.

### Connection lifecycle

Pressing **Connect** starts the session on the poll thread, and the verdict is reported once when the controller answers. A failed attempt names the tag that was refused and the reason. A session that drops after it was established ends as a normal disconnect; press **Connect** again to poll the same tags.

## Command line

`--ethernetip-path` defaults to `1,0` and `--ethernetip-plc` to `controllogix`. The CLI rejects an `--ethernetip-interval` outside 50-60000 and keeps 250.
docs.title: Drivers-EtherNet-IP#9

docs.body:
```bash
SerialStudio --ethernetip 192.168.0.10 --ethernetip-path 1,0 \
  --ethernetip-plc controllogix \
  --ethernetip-tag "MotorSpeed:f32" \
  --ethernetip-tag "Temperatures:f32:3" \
  --ethernetip-interval 250
```

`--ethernetip-tag` takes `tag[:type[:element]]` and repeats; the type code defaults to `f32` and the element index is omitted for scalar tags. Without `--project`, Serial Studio generates a project from the tag list so the frames decode.

## API
docs.title: Drivers-EtherNet-IP#10

docs.body: The API Server is off by default; once you enable it, it listens on port 7777, and the Socket API exposes the driver under `io.eip.*`: `getConfig`, `getStatus`, `setProperty`, `addTag`, `removeTag`, `clearTags` and `generateProject`. `setProperty` takes a `key` and a `value` and accepts `host`, `cipPath`, `plcType` and `pollInterval`. `plcType` takes either a slug from [Controller families](#controller-families) or that family's row number in the order of the Controller families table (zero-based, `controllogix` is 0); `getConfig` and `getStatus` always report the slug, because the API is machine-facing. `getStatus` returns the session state and the pulled counters: successful reads, failed reads, frames published and link drops. Each command, with its parameters, is listed under [EtherNet/IP Driver Commands](API-Reference.md#ethernetip-driver-commands---pro-7).
docs.title: Drivers-EtherNet-IP#11

docs.body:
# HID Driver (Pro)

Your board shows up as a gamepad, a custom HID device or a USB sensor, not as a COM port? Use this driver. A board that prints with `Serial.println` shows up as a COM port (or `/dev/ttyACM0`): use the [UART driver](Drivers-UART.md) instead.

HID is a Pro feature. The first time you use a Pro feature, Serial Studio offers the 14-day trial in a Yes/No prompt (it needs an internet connection). After the trial ends, the prompt offers activation or purchase instead. See [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md).

## Connect a HID device
docs.title: Drivers-HID#0

docs.body:
1. In the **Setup Panel**, choose **HID Device** from the Connection dropdown.
2. Pick your device in the **HID Device** dropdown. Entry 0, **Select Device**, is a placeholder and cannot be opened. While disconnected, Serial Studio rescans every 2 seconds, so a device you plug in appears within a moment. The selection is remembered; if the selected device disappears, it resets to **Select Device**.
3. Click **Connect**.
4. Set the project's frame detection to **Binary (Direct)**, which treats each input report as one frame, and write a frame parser for the report bytes in the Project Editor (see [Frame parsing](#frame-parsing)).
docs.title: Drivers-HID#1

docs.body:
The read-only **Usage Page** and **Usage** fields show the selected device's usage as hex values as soon as you pick it (a joystick shows `0x0001` and `0x0004`). They go empty after Disconnect, and stay empty when the device reports no usage page.

Each entry is listed as `Product Name (VID:PID)` with VID and PID in uppercase hex. If the device reports no product string, the entry shows the manufacturer string, or just `VID:PID`. Interfaces of a composite device that share VID, PID and serial number are merged into one entry.

Input reports: each report arrives as one chunk of raw bytes, so set frame detection to **Binary (Direct)**.
docs.title: Drivers-HID#2
Drivers-HID#3

docs.body:
Move the stick and the X and Y datasets change. Leave it centred and the console stays quiet, because the device sends nothing.

Devices with numbered reports prepend the report ID byte to every read; the example assumes unnumbered reports. Skip that byte, or branch on it when the device has several report formats. Byte order and field sizes are whatever the firmware sends. See [Frame Parser Scripting](Frame-Parser.md).

### Threading

The HID driver runs a dedicated read thread that calls `hid_read_timeout` (100 ms timeout, 65-byte buffer: one report ID byte plus 64 data bytes), so each read returns at most one input report and anything longer is truncated. The thread stamps each report with `SteadyClock::now()` as it arrives. See [Threading and Timing Guarantees](Threading-and-Timing.md).
docs.title: Drivers-HID#4

docs.body:
## Common pitfalls

- **Device not listed, or listed but will not open.** On Linux the user needs `hidraw` access. Create `/etc/udev/rules.d/99-hidraw.rules` with a rule scoped to your device, putting your own VID and PID in place of the placeholders:

```text
  SUBSYSTEM=="hidraw", ATTRS{idVendor}=="1234", ATTRS{idProduct}=="5678", MODE="0666"
  ```
docs.title: Drivers-HID#5

docs.body:
Then run `sudo udevadm control --reload-rules` and replug the device. The open-failure dialog on Linux also suggests checking that your user is in the `plugdev` group. Windows and macOS expose HID without extra setup.
- **Composite device opens the wrong interface.** Serial Studio lists one entry per VID, PID and serial number and opens the first interface hidapi reports for it. The Usage Page and Usage fields come from the first interface with a nonzero usage page, so they can differ from the interface that opened. If the wrong one opened, expose the data interface with a distinct serial number or its own VID:PID in firmware.
- Connected but no data arrives? Some HID devices only send reports on state change. An untouched gamepad is a very quiet device; move it to confirm.
- **Writes fail on macOS.** Serial Studio sends output only through `hid_write`. A device that accepts output only as feature reports cannot be written to.
- Device unplugged while connected: Serial Studio disconnects and shows a **HID Device Error** dialog. The device list does not rescan while a session is open; it refreshes once on disconnect.
docs.title: Drivers-HID#6

docs.body:
## Remote API commands

The TCP API and the in-app AI assistant configure this driver through the `io.hid.*` scope. They need the API Server, which is off by default (port 7777).

| Command | Parameters | Returns |
|---------|------------|---------|
| `io.hid.listDevices` | none | `devices` array and `selectedIndex` (index 0 is the "Select Device" placeholder) |
| `io.hid.setDeviceIndex` | `deviceIndex` (integer) | `deviceIndex` and `deviceName`; an out-of-range index returns `Invalid deviceIndex: N. Valid range: 0-M` |
| `io.hid.getConfig` | none | `deviceIndex`, `usagePage`, `usage` (`0xNNNN` strings, empty when the device reports none) |
docs.title: Drivers-HID#7

docs.body:
Transport details are in the [API Reference](API-Reference.md); command safety tiers are in [AI Assistant](AI-Assistant.md#the-safety-tiers).

## USB HID basics

A HID device is a USB device that declares itself as HID class, describes its data in a **report descriptor**, and exchanges **reports** over interrupt endpoints (see the [USB driver page](Drivers-USB.md)). The OS's generic HID driver reads the descriptor, so the device works without a per-vendor driver.

A **report** is a unit of data exchanged between host and device. There are three types:

- **Input report**: device to host. Carries button state, axis position or sensor readings.
- **Output report**: host to device, such as an LED on/off or a vibration motor strength.
- **Feature report**: bidirectional configuration and calibration values.
docs.title: Drivers-HID#8

docs.body:
Reports are *numbered* (each starts with a 1-byte report ID, used when the device has several formats) or *unnumbered* (one format, no ID byte).

The descriptor declares each field's **usage page** and **usage** (its meaning), size in bits, count and value range. A trivial gamepad might declare two signed 8-bit axes (X and Y, -127 to +127) and 8 single-bit buttons:

```
Usage Page (Generic Desktop)
Usage (Joystick)
Collection (Application)
  Usage (X)
  Usage (Y)
  Logical Minimum (-127)
  Logical Maximum (127)
  Report Size (8)
  Report Count (2)
  Input (Data, Var, Abs)

Usage Page (Button)
  Usage Minimum (Button 1)
  Usage Maximum (Button 8)
  Logical Minimum (0)
  Logical Maximum (1)
  Report Size (1)
  Report Count (8)
  Input (Data, Var, Abs)
End Collection
```
docs.title: Drivers-HID#9

docs.body:
A report from that device is 3 bytes: X, Y and a packed byte of button states.

The driver is built on [hidapi](https://github.com/libusb/hidapi), a small cross-platform C library over the OS HID stacks (HIDClass on Windows, IOHIDManager on macOS). The OS keeps its own HID driver bound to the device, so no driver unbinding is needed.

## Further reading

- [Human Interface Devices (HID) Specifications and Tools (USB-IF)](https://www.usb.org/hid)
- [Introduction to HID report descriptors (Linux Kernel Documentation)](https://docs.kernel.org/hid/hidintro.html)
- [HID Report Descriptors (Adafruit Learning System)](https://learn.adafruit.com/custom-hid-devices-in-circuitpython/report-descriptors)
- [hidapi on GitHub](https://github.com/libusb/hidapi)
docs.title: Drivers-HID#10

docs.body:
