docs.body:
# IEC 60870-5-104 Driver (Pro)

If your Arduino or ESP32 prints lines over USB, you want the UART driver instead. IEC 60870-5-104 is the TCP protocol power utilities use to report substation measurements, and this page is for the day you have a protection relay, an RTU (a field controller that reads sensors) or a substation gateway that speaks it. Select **IEC 60870-5-104** as the bus type in the Setup panel, connect to TCP port 2404, and Serial Studio asks the station for everything it has, then builds a project from the points it finds.

The driver is a **client** in the monitor direction only. It cannot send a command, set a setpoint or select-before-operate, so connecting Serial Studio to a live substation cannot change its state. IEC 60870-5-104 is a Pro feature; see [Availability](#availability).
docs.title: Drivers-IEC-104#0

docs.body:
## Connect to a station

1. In the Setup panel, choose **IEC 60870-5-104** as the bus type.
2. Enter the station's address in **Host**. Leave **Port** at 2404 and **Common Address** at 1 unless the station's documentation says otherwise. The common address is the station number, so ask whoever configured the device.
3. Press **Connect**. The driver asks the station for its whole database and then streams the changes it reports ([Session lifecycle](#session-lifecycle)).
4. Watch the label under the **Create Project from Points** button. It changes from "Connect to discover the station's points" to "N point(s) discovered", usually within seconds. If it stays at the first text, the connection failed: read `lastError` in `io.iec104.getStatus`.
5. Press **Create Project from Points** to generate a project from those points ([Generated project](#generated-project)). A station with 12 single points and 6 float measurements gives 18 datasets: twelve LEDs and six plotted measurements.
docs.title: Drivers-IEC-104#1

docs.body:
No station to test against? Any IEC 60870-5-104 server simulator listening on port 2404 works.

## Point discovery

You do not type point addresses. The interrogation answers with every information object in the station's database, and each object arrives with its address (the information object address, IOA), value and quality. The timed types (30 to 37) also carry a CP56Time2a timestamp, the protocol's 7-byte date and time.

The point list is a result of connecting, not a prerequisite for it. Connect first, let the interrogation finish, and then generate a project from what arrived.

## Configuration model
docs.title: Drivers-IEC-104#2

docs.body: These are the fields of the IEC 60870-5-104 Setup panel. Every field except **Host** is checked against its range, and the timing fields are clamped, not rejected.
docs.title: Drivers-IEC-104#3

docs.body:
| Field | Default | Range | Meaning |
|-------|---------|-------|---------|
| Host | 127.0.0.1 | | The station's IP address or host name. |
| Port | 2404 | 1-65535 | The port the specification assigns. |
| Common Address | 1 | 0-65535 | The station number (common address of ASDU, the protocol's message unit) this client accepts. Messages carrying any other station number are ignored, so one gateway can front several stations without their data mixing. |
| Send Window (k) | 12 | 1-32767 | At most `k` sent frames may wait for the station's acknowledgement. |
| Ack Window (w) | 8 | 1-32767, at most k | This client acknowledges after `w` received frames. |
| Timeout t1 (ms) | 15000 | 1000-255000 | How long the station has to confirm a sent frame before the link is dropped. |
| Timeout t2 (ms) | 10000 | 1000-255000, at most t1 | How long this client may wait before acknowledging received frames. |
| Timeout t3 (ms) | 20000 | 1000-255000 | How long the link may sit idle before the client sends a test frame. |
docs.title: Drivers-IEC-104#4

docs.body:
Host, Port and Common Address are the fields you set. Leave k, w and t1 to t3 at their defaults unless the station's documentation says otherwise. A `w` above `k` or a `t2` above `t1` is clamped down to `k` or `t1`, so no configuration can ask for an acknowledgement later than the timeout that would kill the link first.

## Generated project

Press **Create Project from Points** again whenever the station adds points. Press it in the IEC 60870-5-104 Setup panel after the interrogation has finished. The button stays disabled while no points are known. The headless API command `io.iec104.generateProject` does the same without a save dialog.
docs.title: Drivers-IEC-104#5

docs.body:
The generated project contains:

- One source of type IEC 60870-5-104 carrying the host, port, common address, protocol parameters and the discovered point table, so reopening the project reconnects with the same point layout.
- Up to three data grid groups by type class: **Status Points** (single and double points), **Measurements** (normalized, scaled and float measurands) and **Counters** (integrated totals). A group appears only when the station reported something for it.
- One dataset per point, titled `IOA <n>` after its information object address. Single points also appear as LEDs in a group titled `<group> LEDs` (an LED Panel). Measurands and counters are plotted. Double points are logged only, as a value from 0 to 3.
- A Built-In frame parser using the **IEC 60870-5-104 points** template. Its schema is regenerated with the project, so connect again to discover new points and generate again rather than editing the schema by hand.
docs.title: Drivers-IEC-104#6

docs.body:
The project opens in the Project Editor for customization.

## Point slots

The table holds at most 2048 points. A point beyond that is dropped without a counter or message; compare `pointCount` in `io.iec104.getStatus` with the size of the station's database.

To start over, clear the table with the API command `io.iec104.clearPoints`, connect again and generate a new project.

Each pair of information object address and type identification gets a position the first time the station reports it, and positions are only ever appended. A generated project reads its datasets by position, so renumbering would silently repoint every dataset at a different object. For the same reason the discovered table is remembered between sessions.
docs.title: Drivers-IEC-104#7

docs.body:
An address reported under two types gets two points, and both datasets carry the same `IOA <n>` title.

## Type identifications

The driver decodes six monitor-direction types that carry process data, each also in a CP56Time2a-stamped form, twelve in all. Each message is an ASDU (application service data unit):

| Type ID | Name | Carries | Timestamped type ID | Timestamped name |
|---------|------|---------|---------------------|------------------|
| 1 | M_SP_NA_1 | Single point (on/off) | 30 | M_SP_TB_1 |
| 3 | M_DP_NA_1 | Double point (off/on/intermediate) | 31 | M_DP_TB_1 |
| 9 | M_ME_NA_1 | Normalized measurand (fraction of full scale) | 34 | M_ME_TD_1 |
| 11 | M_ME_NB_1 | Scaled measurand (signed engineering integer) | 35 | M_ME_TE_1 |
| 13 | M_ME_NC_1 | Short float measurand (IEEE 754) | 36 | M_ME_TF_1 |
| 15 | M_IT_NA_1 | Integrated total (counter) | 37 | M_IT_TB_1 |
docs.title: Drivers-IEC-104#8

docs.body:
Both addressing modes of the variable structure qualifier are honoured: each object carries its own address (`SQ = 0`), or one base address is sent and the following objects take consecutive addresses (`SQ = 1`).

A type identification outside this table is **skipped and counted**, never guessed at. An unknown type has an unknown element width, so walking its object list would publish values assembled out of the wrong bytes. The end-of-initialization report and the interrogation's own confirmations are understood and carry no measurand, so they are not counted as skips.

### Quality

Every point carries a quality descriptor, kept per point rather than collapsed into one link-level health flag. The five conditions the specification defines are preserved: **IV** (invalid), **NT** (not topical), **SB** (substituted), **BL** (blocked) and **OV** (overflow, on measurands only). A counter carry-over is stored as overflow, and a counter adjustment as substituted.
docs.title: Drivers-IEC-104#9

docs.body:
A point flagged **invalid** does not overwrite the channel. The station is saying its own reading is untrustworthy, so the last good value stands and the point is counted instead. A bad reading never looks like data. A point with any other quality flag still updates the channel and is also counted. Both counts appear as `badQualityPoints` in `io.iec104.getStatus`; the quality flags themselves are not shown on the dashboard.

### Timestamps
docs.title: Drivers-IEC-104#10

docs.body:
Points that changed in the same 100 ms tick are published as one frame, plotted at the earliest station time among them. The station time is shifted so the first stamp lines up with your computer's clock, so a wrong station clock shows as a fixed offset, not a drift. A frame whose stamp is missing, has the time-invalid bit set, or sits more than 24 hours from the projected local time is plotted at receive time and counted in `unstampedPoints`. A frame is never plotted earlier than the previous one: the driver moves its time forward to 1 ns past the last.

## Session lifecycle

Many stations accept only one master. If another client, such as your SCADA system, is already connected, **Connect** fails with an error instead of connecting and then going silent. Disconnect the other client first. The dial gives up after 5 s.
docs.title: Drivers-IEC-104#11

docs.body:
Pressing **Connect** dials once and the result of that dial is the outcome. A station that accepts one master treats your SCADA system and Serial Studio as rivals for the same chair. On the established link it sends **STARTDT act**. When the station confirms with **STARTDT con**, it issues a **C_IC_NA_1** station interrogation with qualifier 20 and the station answers with its database.

After the interrogation completes, points keep arriving as spontaneous reports, and interrogation replies and spontaneous reports update the same channels. An idle link is kept alive with **TESTFR act** at `t3`, and the driver answers the station's own test frames. A frame the link cannot decode, a sequence number that does not follow, or an activation the station never confirms within `t1` all end the session through the normal disconnect path. Pressing **Connect** again starts a fresh one.
docs.title: Drivers-IEC-104#12

docs.body:
## Command line

```bash
SerialStudio --iec104 192.168.0.20 --iec104-ca 1 --iec104-port 2404
```

`--iec104-k`, `--iec104-w`, `--iec104-t1`, `--iec104-t2` and `--iec104-t3` set the protocol parameters. `--iec104 <host>` selects the driver and sets Host; the other flags take the ranges of the Setup panel. Without `--project`, the CLI generates a project from the remembered point table. With an empty table it logs a warning and connects with no datasets, so on the first run against a new station connect once from the GUI, press **Create Project from Points**, save the project, then run headless with `--project <file>`.
docs.title: Drivers-IEC-104#13

docs.body:
## API

The Socket API exposes the driver under `io.iec104.*`. Each command, with its parameters, is listed under [IEC 60870-5-104 Driver Commands](API-Reference.md#iec-60870-5-104-driver-commands---pro-6).

| Command | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| `getConfig` | The driver configuration. |
| `getStatus` | The link state and the pulled counters. |
| `getPoints` | The discovered table in wire order, which is the order the datasets read it in. |
| `setProperty` | Takes a `key` and a `value`: `host`, `port`, `commonAddress`, `windowK`, `windowW`, `timeoutT1`, `timeoutT2` or `timeoutT3`. |
| `clearPoints` | Empties the discovered table. |
| `generateProject` | Generates and loads the project without a save dialog. |
docs.title: Drivers-IEC-104#14

docs.body:
`getStatus` returns `connected`, `started`, `pointCount`, `badQualityPoints`, `skippedAsdus`, `testTimeouts`, `sequenceErrors`, `malformedFrames`, `framesPublished`, `unstampedPoints`, `linkDrops`, `lastError` and `statusText`, plus `host`, `port` and `commonAddress`.

## Availability

IEC 60870-5-104 is a Pro feature. The first time you use a Pro feature, Serial Studio offers a free trial with a Yes/No prompt; an internet connection is needed to register it. After the trial expires, the prompt offers activation or purchase instead, and a Pro license unlocks the driver. See [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md). Builds compiled from source without the commercial modules do not include this driver, so the bus is unavailable.
docs.title: Drivers-IEC-104#15

docs.body:
# MQTT Subscriber Driver (Pro)

Your ESP32 publishes a reading to an MQTT broker and you want it on a dashboard. Add a source with **Bus Type** set to **MQTT Subscriber**, enter the broker address and a topic filter, and Serial Studio treats each message like a line arriving on a serial port.

MQTT Subscriber is a Pro feature. Serial Studio offers the 14-day trial with a Yes/No prompt the first time you use a Pro feature; registering the trial needs an internet connection. See [Pro vs Free Features](Pro-vs-Free.md). Without an active license or trial, Connect fails with the dialog "MQTT Feature Requires a Commercial License" and the source does not open. If the license lapses while connected, received messages are dropped and logged.
docs.title: Drivers-MQTT#0

docs.body:
New to MQTT? [MQTT Topics & Semantics](MQTT-Topics.md) explains brokers, topics and wildcards in five minutes.

## Quick start

1. In the main window's **Device Setup** pane, set the bus type to **MQTT Subscriber**.
2. Set **Hostname** to `test.mosquitto.org`, **Port** to `1883` and **Topic Filter** to `yourname/sensor`. Replace `yourname` with something unique: the broker is public and shared, and anyone using the same topic sees your data.
3. Under **Operation Mode** in the same pane, pick **Quick Plot (Auto-Detected Format)** and connect. Quick Plot needs no frame-detection setting.
4. Publish a line from any machine with the Mosquitto command-line tools installed (`mosquitto_pub` is included with the Mosquitto package):
docs.title: Drivers-MQTT#1
Drivers-MQTT#2

docs.body:
```mermaid flowchart LR Dev1["Device A
publishes to factory/A"] --> Broker Dev2["Device B
publishes to factory/B"] --> Broker Broker -- "filter: factory/+" --> SS["Serial Studio
MQTT source"] SS --> Dash["Dashboard"] ``` The broker keeps message boundaries: a 200-byte publish arrives as one 200-byte read. In Project File mode, set **Frame Detection Method** to **No Delimiters** on the source (Project Editor, source settings) and each message is one frame, which suits most MQTT payloads. If the payload carries start or end delimiters, set them there instead. A filter like `sensors/+/temp` accepts many publishers on one source, and Serial Studio cannot tell them apart from the bytes alone. If the dashboard has to distinguish them, put the publisher's identity in the payload (an ID column in CSV, a `device` field in JSON) or use one source per publisher.
docs.title: Drivers-MQTT#3

docs.body:
### Payload expectations

The driver does not decode the payload. It hands the bytes to the frame parser of the source's [operation mode](Operation-Modes.md):

- **Quick Plot (Auto-Detected Format)** plots comma-separated numbers: publish `23.5,48.2,1013.25` and each value becomes a plot.
- **Parse via Project File** uses whatever the project's parser accepts: JSON (with a parser that calls `JSON.parse(frame)`), CSV, fixed-byte structs, binary.
- **Console Only (No Parsing)** shows the payload as-is in the terminal.

## Fields

The same settings appear in two places: the Project Editor (the source's **Connection Settings**) and the main window's **Setup** pane. The tables use the Project Editor labels. Port and Topic Filter are enough for a first connection.
docs.title: Drivers-MQTT#4

docs.body:
| Field | Controls |
|-------|----------|
| **Hostname** | Broker address (IP or hostname). Default `127.0.0.1`. |
| **Port** | Broker TCP port. Default `1883`. For TLS brokers set `8883` yourself; toggling TLS does not change the port. |
| **Topic Filter** | Topic to subscribe to. Supports `+` (one level) and `#` (rest) wildcards. Required; the source will not open without one. Ignored while Sparkplug is on. |
| **Client ID** | Identifier sent on CONNECT. Auto-generated (random 16 characters) when empty. |
| **Username / Password** | Optional broker authentication. |
| **MQTT Version** | MQTT 3.1, 3.1.1, or 5.0. Default MQTT 5.0. |
| **Clean Session** | Ask the broker to forget this client's previous subscriptions and queued messages on every connect. Default on. |
| **Keep Alive (s)** | Keep-alive interval sent to the broker on connect, in seconds. Default 60. |
| **Auto Keep Alive** | Sends those keep-alive pings for you; leave on. Default on. |
docs.title: Drivers-MQTT#5

docs.body: The TLS fields:
docs.title: Drivers-MQTT#6

docs.body:
| Field | Controls |
|-------|----------|
| **SSL/TLS Enabled** | Master TLS toggle. Off by default; when on, the fields below appear. |
| **SSL Protocol** | TLS protocol family. One of Any Protocol, DTLS 1.2 or Later, Secure Protocols Only, TLS 1.2, TLS 1.3, or TLS 1.3 or Later. Default Secure Protocols Only. |
| **Peer Verify Mode** | One of Auto Verify Peer, None, Query Peer, or Verify Peer. Default Auto Verify Peer. |
| **Peer Verify Depth** | Maximum certificate chain length accepted. Default `10`. |
| **Client Certificate** | Path to a PEM client certificate, for mutual TLS. Optional; leave empty for ordinary CA-only (server-authentication) TLS. |
| **Private Key** | Path to the client certificate's private key. Defaults to the certificate file itself when left empty. |
| **Key Passphrase** | Passphrase for an encrypted private key, if the key requires one. |
| **ALPN (MQTT over port 443)** | Offer an ALPN protocol during the TLS handshake, which is how a broker multiplexes MQTT onto port 443. Off by default. |
| **ALPN Protocol** | The protocol name to offer, shown only while ALPN is on. Default `x-amzn-mqtt-ca`, the name AWS IoT Core expects on port 443; other brokers document their own. |
docs.title: Drivers-MQTT#7

docs.body:
ALPN applies to the handshake only. Offering the wrong protocol name is refused during the handshake, so a failure here reads as a TLS error, not an MQTT one.

The Setup pane adds a **Regenerate** button beside **Client ID**, a **CA Certificates** row whose **Load From Folder…** button imports PEM certificates for self-signed brokers, and **Browse…** buttons beside **Client Certificate** and **Private Key** (both hidden unless **Use SSL/TLS** is on). It omits **Auto Keep Alive** and shortens four labels: **Version**, **Use SSL/TLS**, **Peer Verify** and **Verify Depth**.

Connect is refused, with a log warning and no dialog, when **Hostname** is empty, **Port** is `0` or **Topic Filter** is empty.
docs.title: Drivers-MQTT#8

docs.body:
Broker username and password are stored obfuscated in the application settings, not in the OS keychain.

The fields are also available through the API Server (off by default, port 7777): `project.mqtt.subscriber.getConfig`, `setConfig` and `getStatus`. See the [API Reference](API-Reference.md). For another walk-through, see the [Protocol Setup Guides, MQTT section](Protocol-Setup-Guides.md#mqtt-setup-pro).

## Multiple MQTT subscribers in one project

Each MQTT source has its own broker session, TLS settings and subscription, so a project with two ESP32 fleets, one on a local broker and one in the cloud, is an ordinary multi-source project:
docs.title: Drivers-MQTT#9

docs.body:
1. In the Project Editor, add a source and set its **Bus Type** to **MQTT Subscriber**.
2. Set **Hostname**, **Port**, **Topic Filter** and any credentials for the first fleet.
3. Add a second source the same way for the second broker, or for a different topic on the same broker.

Each source has its own frame parser, and its datasets stay tied to their source.

Two sources on one broker work as they are: each gets its own random **Client ID**, so there is no clash unless you copy an ID from one source to another. Two clients sharing an ID is a hallway with one name tag: the broker keeps the newer connection and throws out the older, and with auto-reconnect they can keep kicking each other. In the Project Editor, type a different **Client ID** by hand; the Setup pane also has a **Regenerate** button beside it.
docs.title: Drivers-MQTT#10

docs.body:
## TLS

For a broker reachable from outside your local network, use TLS:

1. Set **Port** to `8883`, the standard MQTT-over-TLS port.
2. Turn on **SSL/TLS Enabled** (**Use SSL/TLS** in the Setup pane).
3. Leave **Peer Verify Mode** (**Peer Verify** in the Setup pane) on Auto Verify Peer. Set it to None only to test against a self-signed broker, and never against a public one.
4. If the broker uses a private CA, click **Load From Folder…** under **CA Certificates** in the Setup pane and pick the directory with the PEM chain.

For mutual TLS, fill in **Client Certificate**, **Private Key** and **Key Passphrase**. For a broker that serves MQTT on port 443, turn on **ALPN**. The [field table](#fields) lists the defaults.
docs.title: Drivers-MQTT#11

docs.body:
TLS settings belong to the source, so two subscribers in one project can use different brokers with different trust roots.

## Common pitfalls
docs.title: Drivers-MQTT#12

docs.body:
- **Subscribed but no data.** Topics are case-sensitive: `Sensors/Temp` is not `sensors/temp`. A filter with the wrong number of levels misses everything silently. Without a license or trial the source never connects, so check for the license dialog too. To see what the broker receives, run `mosquitto_sub -h <broker> -t '#' -v` on your own broker; on a public one, narrow the filter instead.
- **An old value appears first.** The broker replays a topic's retained message the moment you subscribe, so you see the last stored value before any live one.
- **TLS handshake fails.** The broker's certificate chain is not trusted. Import the CA with **Load From Folder…** as described in [TLS](#tls).
- **Mixed payloads on one filter.** A `sensors/+/temp` filter that catches `room1` (CSV) and `room2` (JSON) cannot be parsed cleanly by one frame parser. Standardize the format or use one source per format.
- **High publish rates.** Public brokers add jitter, and a high-rate publisher queues up at the broker. Batch several readings into one message and split them in the frame parser.
docs.title: Drivers-MQTT#13

docs.body:
## Sparkplug

Skip this section unless your devices already speak Sparkplug.

Sparkplug is a convention layered on MQTT: a fixed topic namespace rooted at `spBv1.0` (for example `spBv1.0/Plant/NDATA/Line1`), protobuf payloads, birth certificates that declare what a node publishes, and a death certificate the broker delivers when that node drops off. As a subscriber, the MQTT driver acts as a host application and turns the namespace into datasets. As a producer, the [MQTT Publisher](MQTT-Publisher.md) acts as an edge node, and the edge-node fields are documented there. Payloads follow the Sparkplug B v1.0 specification, in the Eclipse Tahu schema.
docs.title: Drivers-MQTT#14

docs.body:
### Subscribing

Tick **Sparkplug** in the Setup pane's MQTT section; the Project Editor does not expose it for the subscriber. The driver then subscribes to the `spBv1.0` namespace itself, so **Topic Filter** does not apply. Two more rows appear:

| Field | Controls |
|-------|----------|
| **Group ID** | Restricts the subscription to one group. Empty means every group on the broker. Wildcards and `/` are refused, because a group id is a single topic element. |
| **Create Project from Births** | A button in the **Sparkplug Project** row. Generates a project from the metrics discovered so far. Enabled once the source is connected. |
docs.title: Drivers-MQTT#15

docs.body:
Decoding is driven by birth certificates. A node's birth certificate names its metrics and hands out the numeric aliases its later data messages carry. A data message with no birth yet, or with an alias the birth never declared, is held until the birth arrives and counted if it cannot be resolved. Every edge node also gets a synthetic `Online` metric carrying its birth and death state, so a node that dies reads as offline instead of merely going stale. Sequence numbers are checked per node, and a gap is counted rather than interpolated over.

Traffic past these ceilings is refused and counted.
docs.title: Drivers-MQTT#16

docs.body:
| Limit | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Metrics | 2048 |
| Nodes | 256 |
| Devices per node | 64 |
| Messages held ahead of a birth | 256 |

`project.mqtt.subscriber.getStatus` returns a `sparkplug` block beside the connection state with the group id, the number of discovered metrics and the counters (sequence gaps, cap drops, decode errors, and others). See the [API Reference](API-Reference.md).

### Create Project from Births
docs.title: Drivers-MQTT#17

docs.body: Connect first, let the birth certificates arrive, then click **Create Project from Births**. The button builds a project with one MQTT Subscriber source carrying the broker settings and the group id, one group per publishing scope (an edge node, or a device when the node publishes devices), one dataset per discovered metric, and a Built-In frame parser using the **Sparkplug** template. The template's schema parameter is machine-managed: connect again to discover more metrics and generate again rather than editing it by hand. Generating before any birth has arrived reports that nothing was discovered instead of writing an empty project.
docs.title: Drivers-MQTT#18

docs.body:
The project opens in the Project Editor for customization.

### Publishing as an edge node

To publish your datasets as a Sparkplug edge node instead, open the Project Editor, go to the MQTT publisher's **Sparkplug** section and turn on **Publish as Edge Node**. The fields (**Group ID**, **Edge Node ID**, **Device ID**) and the birth, data and rebirth behavior are documented in [MQTT Publisher](MQTT-Publisher.md).

- [Protocol Setup Guides](Protocol-Setup-Guides.md): step-by-step MQTT setup in the Project Editor.
- [Drivers: Network](Drivers-Network.md): raw TCP/UDP, when you do not need a broker.
- [Troubleshooting](Troubleshooting.md)
- [Eclipse Mosquitto](https://mosquitto.org/): lightweight broker for self-hosting and testing.

docs.body:
# Modbus Driver (Pro)

Your PLC, power meter or simulator answers on port 502 and you want its registers on a dashboard. Serial Studio polls the device as a Modbus master over **Modbus TCP** (Ethernet) or **Modbus RTU** (serial) and turns each reply into a binary frame for the frame parser. A [register-map importer](Auto-Generating-Projects.md) builds the whole project from a vendor CSV/XML/JSON file. Modbus is how PLCs and meters expose numbered registers; if your board just prints text lines, use [Drivers: UART](Drivers-UART.md) instead.

Modbus is a Serial Studio Pro feature. Without a license, the first use of a Pro feature offers a trial through a Yes/No prompt (it needs an internet connection). See [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md).
docs.title: Drivers-Modbus#0

docs.body:
## Quick start

This reads four holding registers from a Modbus TCP server. With no device yet, run any Modbus TCP simulator on your machine (most bind port 5020).

1. In the **Setup** panel, open the **Connection** dropdown and choose **Modbus**.
2. Leave **Protocol** on Modbus TCP, **Host** on `127.0.0.1` and **Port** on `5020`. A real device usually listens on 502.
3. Click **Configure Register Groups…** and add one group: Holding Registers (see [the four register tables](#the-four-register-tables)), start address `0`, **Register Count** `4`.
4. Click **Connect**.
docs.title: Drivers-Modbus#1
Drivers-Modbus#2

docs.body:
To skip the hand-written parser, use **Generate Project** in the register-groups dialog or **Import Register Map…** (see [Auto-generation](#auto-generation)). Parser details are in [Frame Parser Scripting](Frame-Parser.md).

## How Serial Studio uses it

Serial Studio acts as the master (Modbus client). Each connection has a slave address (called Unit ID on TCP) that its register groups follow by default, and any group may name a slave of its own, so one connection can read several devices sharing a bus.

Writes from [Output Controls](Output-Controls.md) target holding registers on the connection's own slave. A write payload is a big-endian start address followed by one 16-bit value per register, so it covers anything from a single register up to the 123 a Write Multiple Registers request can carry. The `modbusWriteRegister` and `modbusWriteRegisters` helpers (see the [SDK](SerialStudio-SDK.md)) build it for you.
docs.title: Drivers-Modbus#3

docs.body:
### Configuration model

Setup is a hierarchy, all under **Connection: Modbus** in the **Setup** panel:
docs.title: Drivers-Modbus#4

docs.body:
1. **Protocol.** Modbus RTU or Modbus TCP (default: TCP).
   - RTU: **Serial Port**, **Baud Rate** (default 9600), **Parity** (default None), **Data Bits** (default 8), **Stop Bits** (default 1). They must match the device.
   - TCP: **Host** (default `127.0.0.1`) and **Port** (default 5020, the unprivileged port most local simulators bind). Real devices listen on 502, so change it. The `--modbus-tcp` CLI flag falls back to 502 when you give no port.
2. **Slave Address** (called Unit ID on TCP). 1 to 247 on both protocols. Default 1. This is the address a register group uses unless it names its own.
3. **Register groups** (the **Configure Register Groups…** button). One group per contiguous block of same-type registers to read. Each group has:
   - Register type (Holding Registers, Input Registers, Coils, Discrete Inputs).
   - Starting address (0-based, protocol numbering, 0-65535).
   - **Register Count**, the entries to read in one request. The dialog accepts 1 to 125 for every type. Groups added through the API accept 1 to 125 for holding and input registers and 1 to 2000 for coils and discrete inputs.
   - **Slave Address**, optional. Leave it empty and the group is read from the connection's own slave; set 1 to 247 to read that block from another device on the same bus. This is how one RS-485 pair carrying, say, a PLC on address 1 and a power meter on address 2 becomes a single connection. Every reply names the device that sent it in the first byte of the frame, so a frame parser tells them apart by that byte rather than by counting frames.
4. **Poll Interval (ms).** How often Serial Studio restarts the read cycle. Default 100 ms, clamped to 50-60000 ms. `io.modbus.setPollInterval` accepts 10 and up, but the driver raises anything under 50 to 50. Serial lines are slower: a 60-register read takes about 140 ms of wire time alone at 9600 baud (a ~133-byte round trip), plus device processing time.
docs.title: Drivers-Modbus#5

docs.body: On each poll tick, Serial Studio reads the groups sequentially: it sends the request for the first group, waits for the reply, then moves to the next. Each reply is published to the frame parser as its own binary frame in RTU layout, `[slave address, function code, byte count, data...]`, with no CRC appended; the same layout is used on TCP connections. Register data arrives big-endian (high byte first); coil and discrete-input data arrives as packed bits, least-significant bit first. A reply that reports an error produces no frame. If a reply is still outstanding when the timer fires again, that cycle is skipped, so a slow slave lowers the effective poll rate instead of queueing requests. Requests time out after 1000 ms with 3 retries. Polling and reply handling are event-driven; [Threading and Timing Guarantees](Threading-and-Timing.md) says which thread processes replies.
docs.title: Drivers-Modbus#6

docs.body:
Use the **Binary (Direct)** decoder with no frame delimiters. Because the groups arrive as separate frames, a hand-written parser must tell them apart by the first byte (slave address) and the function code; the auto-generated parser routes each reply by the unit, function code and byte count it carries. See [Frame Parser Scripting](Frame-Parser.md).

### Auto-generation

For devices with documented register maps, the [Modbus map importer](Auto-Generating-Projects.md) reads vendor CSV/XML/JSON files and generates the register groups, datasets, and a complete Lua frame parser. It is the recommended starting point:
docs.title: Drivers-Modbus#7

docs.body:
1. With **Connection: Modbus** selected in the **Setup** panel, click **Import Register Map…**.
2. Choose the CSV, XML or JSON file.
3. Review the registers in the preview dialog and confirm. The groups load into the driver.

Without a vendor file, the **Generate Project** button in the register-groups dialog builds an equivalent project from the groups configured by hand.

A map can describe a whole bus: a `slave` column puts each register on its unit, so one connection polls several devices and the generated parser routes every reply by the unit, function code and byte count the reply carries rather than by polling order (a dropped reply no longer shifts the ones after it). `bit` rows expose one bit of a register as a light in an LED Panel group, `rw` rows become output controls, and `order` fixes a device's word order. The full column reference is in [Protocol Setup Guides](Protocol-Setup-Guides.md#modbus-register-map-import-pro).
docs.title: Drivers-Modbus#8

docs.body:
**Writing to another unit.** A write payload normally targets the connection's unit. Prefix it with `0xFF 0x83 <unit>` (`[0xFF, 0x83, unit, addr_hi, addr_lo, value_hi, value_lo]`) to write to another device on the same bus; the SDK helpers take that unit as an optional last argument, for example `modbusWriteRegister(0x0010, value, 2)`. Any other odd-length payload is refused.

**Known limitation.** The importer groups contiguous same-type registers into one block per group and does not split a block once it exceeds 125 registers, the driver's per-request read limit for register tables. A generated group larger than 125 registers is silently dropped and never polled: the group is missing from **Configure Register Groups…** and its datasets stay empty. If a vendor register map has a contiguous run that long, split it into groups of 125 registers or fewer, either in the map file before import (list the run as separate rows) or in **Configure Register Groups…** after.
docs.title: Drivers-Modbus#9

docs.body:
### API control

The [Socket API](API-Reference.md) and the in-app [AI Assistant](AI-Assistant.md) configure this driver through the `io.modbus.*` command scope.
docs.title: Drivers-Modbus#10

docs.body:
| Command | Parameter | Values |
|---------|-----------|--------|
| `setProtocolIndex` | `protocolIndex` | 0 = RTU, 1 = TCP |
| `setSlaveAddress` | `address` | 1-247 |
| `setPollInterval` | `intervalMs` | 10 and up; the driver raises anything under 50 to 50 |
| `setHost`, `setPort` | `host`, `port` | TCP target |
| `setSerialPortIndex`, `setBaudRate`, `setParityIndex`, `setDataBitsIndex`, `setStopBitsIndex` | `portIndex`, `baudRate`, `parityIndex`, `dataBitsIndex`, `stopBitsIndex` | RTU line settings |
| `addRegisterGroup` | `type`, `startAddress`, `count`, `slaveAddress` | `type`: 0 = Holding Registers, 1 = Input Registers, 2 = Coils, 3 = Discrete Inputs; `startAddress`: 0-65535; `count`: 1-125 (1-2000 for coils and discrete inputs); `slaveAddress`: optional, 1-247, or 0 or omitted to follow the connection's own |
| `removeRegisterGroup` | `groupIndex` | Index in the group list |
| `clearRegisterGroups` | none | Removes every group |
docs.title: Drivers-Modbus#11

docs.body:
Read-only: `getConfig`, `listProtocols`, `listSerialPorts`, `listParities`, `listDataBits`, `listStopBits`, `listBaudRates`, `listRegisterTypes`, `listRegisterGroups`. For the AI Assistant the setters are device-gated: blocked until the user ticks **Allow device control**, and each call still requires confirmation.

For step-by-step setup, see the [Protocol Setup Guides, Modbus section](Protocol-Setup-Guides.md).

## Common pitfalls

Modbus driver symptoms in Serial Studio Pro:
docs.title: Drivers-Modbus#12

docs.body:
| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---------|-------|-----|
| No response from the slave | Wrong slave address (vendors differ; 1 is common, not universal), or RS-485 wiring. | Check **Slave Address** in **Setup**. Wire A-to-A and B-to-B, with a common ground when the bus spans power domains. |
| Values off by one register | PLC numbering versus protocol numbering. "Holding register 40101" is protocol address 100. | Enter the 0-based protocol address. |
| CRC errors on RTU | Wiring or termination. | Terminate both ends of the trunk with 120 Ω and keep stubs short. See [Drivers: UART](Drivers-UART.md) and [Troubleshooting](Troubleshooting.md). |
| 32-bit values look wrong | Word or byte order differs from the decoder's. A float reading `1.234e-23` is the classic sign. | Compare the raw bytes to the vendor documentation and set the map's `order` column. |
| Low or irregular frame rate | The slave cannot answer at the poll rate, so cycles are skipped while a reply is pending. | Raise **Poll Interval (ms)**; see [Configuration model](#configuration-model). |
| TCP works but RTU does not | Long cables, missing ground, termination, or an adapter without bias resistors on the idle bus. | Fix the electrical side first; a scope on the line is the fastest check. |
| "Illegal data address" and no frames | The slave's memory map lacks that register. Serial Studio discards error replies, so the group produces nothing. | Check the group's start address and **Register Count** against the vendor documentation. Some PLCs answer only for addresses their program configures. |
docs.title: Drivers-Modbus#13

docs.body:
## Modbus overview

Modbus is a request/response, master/slave protocol for reading and writing memory locations on a remote device. The master polls; the slave answers. There is no streaming and no push, so continuous data needs continuous polling.

### The four register tables

Every device exposes a flat memory map divided into four tables:

| Table              | Width    | Access | Typical use                           |
|--------------------|----------|--------|---------------------------------------|
| **Coils**          | 1 bit    | R/W    | Digital outputs (relays, valves)      |
| **Discrete inputs**| 1 bit    | R only | Digital inputs (switches, sensors)    |
| **Input registers**| 16 bits  | R only | Analog inputs (sensor readings)       |
| **Holding registers**| 16 bits | R/W   | General-purpose storage (setpoints, configuration, scratch values) |
docs.title: Drivers-Modbus#14

docs.body:
Vendors put the same quantity in either table, so check the device manual for which one to pick.

Addresses inside each table go from 0 to 65535. Vendors document them in two ways:

- **PLC numbering** (1-based, table-prefixed): `40001`-`49999` for holding registers, `30001`-`39999` for input registers, and so on.
- **Protocol numbering** (0-based, no prefix): `0`-`65535` per table.

Modbus on the wire uses protocol numbering, and so does Serial Studio. Holding register `40100` in PLC numbering is *address 99* in protocol numbering. Off-by-one is the most common Modbus debugging story.

### Function codes
docs.title: Drivers-Modbus#15

docs.body:
Every request carries a one-byte function code:

| Code | Function | Tables it touches |
|------|----------|-------------------|
| 1    | Read Coils | Coils |
| 2    | Read Discrete Inputs | Discrete inputs |
| 3    | Read Holding Registers | Holding registers |
| 4    | Read Input Registers | Input registers |
| 5    | Write Single Coil | Coils |
| 6    | Write Single Register | Holding registers |
| 15   | Write Multiple Coils | Coils |
| 16   | Write Multiple Registers | Holding registers |

More codes exist (read/write combined, file records, diagnostics). Register groups issue codes 1 to 4.
docs.title: Drivers-Modbus#16

docs.body:
### Multi-register data types

A Modbus register is 16 bits. Anything wider spans consecutive registers:

- `uint32`, `int32`, `float32`: 2 registers (4 bytes).
- `uint64`, `int64`, `float64`: 4 registers (8 bytes).

Byte and word order are device-specific:

| Name | `order` value | Register A | Register B |
|------|---------------|------------|------------|
| Big-endian (default) | `abcd` | `0x1234` | `0x5678` |
| Word swap | `cdab` | `0x5678` | `0x1234` |
| Byte swap inside each register | `badc` | `0x3412` | `0x7856` |
| Fully reversed | `dcba` | `0x7856` | `0x3412` |

The table shows how `0x12345678` lands in two registers. Vendor documentation specifies the order. The register-map importer assumes big-endian (an empty `order` cell); a register map can state another order per entry with an `order` column, and the generated parser undoes it before decoding.
docs.title: Drivers-Modbus#17

docs.body:
### RTU vs TCP

Modbus RTU runs over RS-232 or RS-485, adds a CRC-16, and addresses slaves 1 to 247 (0 is broadcast). Modbus TCP runs over Ethernet and needs no CRC; its **Unit ID** equals the slave address and picks the target behind a TCP-to-RTU gateway. Serial Studio emits the same RTU-layout frame for both.

docs.title: Drivers-Modbus#18
Drivers-Network#0

docs.body:
In Serial Studio:

1. In the **Setup Panel**, select **Network** from the Connection dropdown.
2. Leave **Socket Type** on **TCP**, set **Remote Address** to the board's IP and **Remote Port** to 23.
3. Click **Connect**.

Serial Studio splits the incoming bytes into frames using the frame detection setting (newline-terminated lines by default), then hands each frame to the [frame parser](Frame-Parser.md). In Quick Plot mode, which needs no project, the three values `1,2,3` appear as plots as soon as the link is up; see [Getting Started](Getting-Started.md#your-first-connection-quick-plot-mode). For the full walkthrough, see [Protocol Setup Guides](Protocol-Setup-Guides.md).
docs.title: Drivers-Network#1

docs.body:
The driver speaks four protocols, all of them clients, all available in the Free and Pro editions. Pick by what the other end offers:

| Socket Type | Use it for |
|-------------|------------|
| **TCP** | An Arduino or ESP32 on Wi-Fi, or any device with a plain text stream. |
| **UDP** | Low-overhead packets, including multicast. |
| **WebSocket** | A gateway, a broker, or a cloud service that pushes messages. |
| **HTTP** | A REST endpoint that returns a reading per request. |

Whichever one you select, the frame parser, dashboard, recording and export behave identically.

## Network settings
docs.title: Drivers-Network#2

docs.body:
**Edition:** Free and Pro. **UI path:** Setup Panel > Connection dropdown > **Network**. The fields shown depend on the **Socket Type**.

> **Serial Studio is always the client.** It dials out; it never listens. There is no server mode for any of the four transports, and no setting that adds one. If the device expects to push data to a listener, run a small server in front of Serial Studio (see [Common pitfalls](#common-pitfalls)).

**Socket Type** selects TCP, UDP, WebSocket or HTTP. The default is TCP.

### TCP settings

| Field | Controls | Default |
|-------|----------|---------|
| **Remote Address** | Server IP or hostname | `127.0.0.1` |
| **Remote Port** | Port to connect to; 1-65535, and TCP refuses 0 ("Enter a TCP port first") | 23 |
docs.title: Drivers-Network#3

docs.body:
Clicking **Connect** dials in the background, so a refused or unreachable endpoint shows up as an error in the console rather than a frozen window.

- **Retry:** a refused connection is retried every 250 ms, so a helper process that binds its listening socket late is still caught.
- **Deadline:** the attempt gives up after 5 seconds.
- **Hostname:** Serial Studio resolves it itself; a bad one fails with "Host not found" after you click **Connect**, rather than a disabled **Connect** button.
- **Queue:** data written while the dial is pending is held, up to 1 MiB.

### UDP settings
docs.title: Drivers-Network#4

docs.body:
| Field | Controls | Default |
|-------|----------|---------|
| **Remote Address** | Peer address for sending, or the multicast group when **Multicast** is checked | `127.0.0.1` |
| **Remote Port** | Port that outbound data is sent to; hidden while **Multicast** is checked | 53 |
| **Local Port** | Port to bind for receiving. Set it to the port the device sends to; with `0` the OS picks a random port and nothing reaches you | 0 |
| **Multicast** | Treats **Remote Address** as a multicast group (for example `239.1.1.1`) and joins it on connect | off |

UDP opens immediately because there is no remote endpoint to dial. UDP uses a single socket; there is no separate Receiver / Sender / Multicast mode. Incoming datagrams are read one at a time, so on the receive side UDP preserves the message boundaries that TCP discards. Outbound data (actions, output controls, the console send line) is sent as datagrams to **Remote Address** / **Remote Port**.
docs.title: Drivers-Network#5

docs.body:
For multicast, Serial Studio binds **Local Port** and then joins the group, so set **Local Port** to the group's port. An invalid group address fails the connect. The steps are in [Multicast](#multicast).

### WebSocket settings

| Field | Controls | Default |
|-------|----------|---------|
| **URL** | Endpoint to dial; must be `ws://` or `wss://` | `ws://127.0.0.1:8080` |
| **Send Format** | How written payloads are framed: **Automatic** (text when the bytes are valid UTF-8, binary otherwise), **Text**, or **Binary** | Automatic |
| **Ignore TLS Errors** | Accepts a self-signed or hostname-mismatched certificate | off |
docs.title: Drivers-Network#6

docs.body:
### HTTP settings

| Field | Controls | Default |
|-------|----------|---------|
| **URL** | Endpoint to request; must be `http://` or `https://` | `http://127.0.0.1:8080/` |
| **Method** | `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, or `DELETE` | GET |
| **Poll Interval (ms)** | Milliseconds between requests: `0`, or 10 to 3600000 (1-9 become 10). `0` sends only when you write | 1000 |
| **Request Body** | Body sent with every request | empty |
| **Request Headers** | One `Name: Value` pair per line | empty |
| **Ignore TLS Errors** | Accepts a self-signed or hostname-mismatched certificate | off |

HTTP limits: a response body is capped at 8 MiB, each request times out after 30 seconds, and at most 3 redirects are followed (`GET` only).
docs.title: Drivers-Network#7

docs.body:
A **URL** whose scheme does not match the selected transport is refused with a message saying so.

## TCP basics

TCP provides a reliable, ordered stream of bytes between two endpoints, hides packet loss and retransmits what is missing ([RFC 9293](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293)).

### Stream, not message

TCP is a stream of bytes, not a stream of messages. If a device writes 100 bytes followed by 100 bytes, the receiver may see one read of 200 bytes, or two of 100, or 200 of 1. The boundaries are not preserved.

Frame detection works on the stream, so "one TCP packet = one frame" never holds. With a delimiter (newline, custom byte sequence) Serial Studio finds frames regardless of how the OS chunked the stream; with fixed-length frames it counts bytes. Each extracted frame reaches the project's [frame parser](Frame-Parser.md) as a single `parse(frame)` call.
docs.title: Drivers-Network#8

docs.body:
## UDP basics

UDP sends one packet with no acknowledgement, retransmission or ordering ([RFC 768](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc768)). A lost packet stays lost.

UDP fits real-time data where freshness beats reliability, since a dropped reading is replaced by the next and a retransmitted stale one is worse than none. It also suits devices with little RAM (no per-connection state), discovery beacons, and one-to-many distribution, which TCP cannot do.

### Multicast

One sender publishes to a multicast group address and any number of receivers subscribe, so several dashboards on a LAN get the same telemetry without each opening a TCP connection. Use an address in `239.0.0.0/8`, the range meant for application traffic. The operating system handles the group membership when Serial Studio joins.
docs.title: Drivers-Network#9

docs.body:
To receive a group such as `239.1.1.1` on port 5000:

1. In **Socket Type**, select **UDP**.
2. Tick **Multicast** and set **Remote Address** to `239.1.1.1`.
3. Set **Local Port** to `5000` and click **Connect**.

## WebSocket basics

WebSocket ([RFC 6455](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455)) starts as an ordinary HTTP request that asks the server to switch protocols. Once the server agrees, the same TCP connection becomes a two-way channel that either side can write to at any time.

### WebSocket messages, not a byte stream
docs.title: Drivers-Network#10

docs.body:
In the **WebSocket** socket type, message boundaries are preserved. If the server sends 100 bytes and then 100 bytes, you receive exactly two messages. Serial Studio publishes each one separately, so with **No Delimiters** frame detection you get exactly one frame per message, the same way one UDP datagram becomes one frame. If your project uses a delimiter instead, that still works: the delimiter is applied to the message contents just as it would be to a TCP stream.

Messages come in two flavours, text (UTF-8) and binary. Serial Studio receives both and passes the raw bytes to the parser either way; a text message reaches it as its UTF-8 encoding.
docs.title: Drivers-Network#11

docs.body:
### When to choose WebSocket

Choose it when the device or service already exposes one, as gateways, cloud brokers and anything with a browser dashboard do. You get message framing without inventing a delimiter, the server pushes data as it happens so nothing is polled, and the link passes proxies and firewalls that only permit HTTP ports.

`wss://` is WebSocket over TLS, and is the right default over any network you do not control. WebSocket connects in the background; the connect settles on the handshake.

## HTTP basics

Serial Studio requests a URL and the response body is the data. Because HTTP is request/response rather than a push protocol, Serial Studio **polls**: it repeats the request on a fixed interval and treats each response body as one chunk of incoming data.
docs.title: Drivers-Network#12

docs.body:
### When to choose HTTP

- The only interface the device or service offers is a REST API.
- The data changes slowly enough that polling once a second, or once a minute, is enough: weather stations, building sensors, cloud telemetry, lab instruments behind a web front end.
- You need to *interact* with an API rather than only read from it, sending a command and charting the response.

Each reading costs a full request/response round trip, so HTTP is comfortable at a few readings per second, not thousands. For high-rate data, use TCP, UDP, or WebSocket.

### HTTP polling and Poll Interval

In the **HTTP** socket type, **Poll Interval (ms)** decides the cadence:
docs.title: Drivers-Network#13

docs.body:
- A value in milliseconds repeats the request forever at that rate. Be considerate with public APIs, which frequently rate-limit.
- **Zero** turns polling off entirely. Serial Studio connects, sends one request, and then stays quiet until *you* send something. This is the mode for a command/response API driven from the console, an [action widget](Actions.md), or an output widget: each send issues one request and its response comes back as a frame.

Only one request is ever in flight. If a response has not arrived by the time the next interval elapses, that tick is skipped rather than queued, because a backlog of requests behind a slow endpoint reports data older than the dashboard already displayed. A request that takes longer than 30 seconds is aborted. Skipped ticks are counted and readable through the API.
docs.title: Drivers-Network#14

docs.body:
### HTTP failed polls

In the **HTTP** socket type, a failed poll does **not** disconnect. A transport error, a TLS failure, or any non-2xx status leaves the link up and the timer running; the first failure of a run is written to the console, the rest are counted silently, and a recovery is announced once. A 503 during a deploy should not end a recording that has been running for an hour.

The connect attempt is stricter. Clicking **Connect** issues the configured request once and that request *is* the verdict, so an unreachable host or a 404 is caught immediately instead of surfacing quietly at the first poll. Its response body is published like any other, giving you an initial reading straight away.
docs.title: Drivers-Network#15

docs.body:
### Authentication and headers

There are no dedicated username, password, or token fields. Anything an API needs goes into **Request Headers**, one pair per line:

```
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...
X-Api-Key: 4f9a2c...
Accept: application/json
```

Serial Studio sends `Content-Type: application/octet-stream` unless you supply a `Content-Type` header yourself, in which case yours wins. Redirects are followed for `GET` only: replaying a request body against a redirect target would be a second side effect you did not ask for.

## TLS

In the WebSocket and HTTP socket types, `wss://` and `https://` verify the server's certificate chain by default, and a failure aborts the connection before any data is exchanged. **Ignore TLS Errors** exists for lab endpoints with self-signed certificates; when it is on, every connection that uses the bypass says so in the console, so it cannot be inherited silently from a shared project file.
docs.title: Drivers-Network#16

docs.body: ## Common pitfalls
docs.title: Drivers-Network#17

docs.body:
- **Serial Studio cannot connect over TCP.** Confirm that the device or remote service is listening. From a terminal, `telnet host port` (or `nc host port`) tries the same connection; if that fails, the problem is in the network or the remote endpoint, not in Serial Studio.
- **The dashboard shows nothing, or one giant frame.** Check frame detection. A TCP stream needs a delimiter (newline) or a fixed length; if a device sends `frame1frame2frame3` with no delimiter and no length prefix, parsing is impossible. For an HTTP endpoint, set frame detection to **No Delimiters** so each response becomes one frame, then parse the JSON in the frame parser.
- **Firewall blocks the port.** For UDP receive, allow inbound UDP on the **Local Port**; on Windows the firewall prompt may have been dismissed without granting access. On Linux, `ufw status` shows whether the port is blocked.
- **The device wants to push to a listener.** Serial Studio is a client on every transport and cannot accept inbound connections. Run a relay, a small server that accepts the device's connection and re-serves the data to Serial Studio (`ncat -lk --broker <port>` does this), or send the data over UDP, since Serial Studio binds a local port for that.
- **An `https://` endpoint refuses to connect.** If the console reports a certificate error, the endpoint uses a certificate your machine does not trust, such as a self-signed one. Install the certificate in the OS trust store, or tick **Ignore TLS Errors** if it is a device on your own bench.
- **The WebSocket connects and then immediately drops.** The server probably expects a subprotocol or an authentication token in the handshake. Serial Studio sends no subprotocol; if the server needs a token, put it in the URL query string (`ws://host/feed?token=...`). The console reports the close reason the server gave.
- **HTTP charts update far slower than the poll interval.** Check `pollsSkipped` through `io.network.getStatus`. A skipped tick means the endpoint had not answered the previous request yet, so the effective rate is bounded by the server's response time, not by your interval.
- **UDP shows no data.** **Local Port** must be the port the device sends to; the default `0` receives nothing useful. Also check the firewall (previous item).
- **UDP bind failed.** The connect fails and the console logs "UDP bind failed". Serial Studio binds with `ShareAddress` and `ReuseAddressHint`, so a second receiver on the same port usually does not block the bind, and which program receives the datagrams then depends on the operating system. To see what holds a port, run `netstat -an | findstr :5000` (Windows) or `lsof -i :5000` (Linux/macOS).
- **UDP packets arrive out of order or get lost.** That is UDP working as designed. If the application cannot tolerate it, switch to TCP or layer sequence numbers on top.
- **Multicast traffic does not cross subnets.** Most home routers do not forward multicast across VLANs without IGMP-snooping configuration. Multicast works on a single LAN segment; cross-subnet routing is a network-admin problem.
- **TCP shows added latency on small writes.** Nagle's algorithm holds small writes until the previous one is acknowledged; with delayed ACK on the receiving side that adds up to about 200 ms. Serial Studio leaves the socket at Qt's defaults, so disable Nagle (`TCP_NODELAY`) on the device or remote service if latency matters.
docs.title: Drivers-Network#18

docs.body:
## Scripting the driver

The `io.network.*` commands of the [JSON-RPC API](API-Reference.md) drive the same settings. The API Server must be enabled first (off by default, port 7777).

- **Setters:** `setSocketType` (`socketTypeIndex` 0 = TCP, 1 = UDP, 2 = WebSocket, 3 = HTTP), `setRemoteAddress`, `setIgnoreTlsErrors`, and the port, URL and HTTP setters. Port commands take a `port` from 1 to 65535 (`setUdpLocalPort` also accepts 0).
- **Read-only, no confirmation:** `lookup`, `getConfig`, `listSocketTypes` and `getStatus`. `getStatus` reports the link state and the HTTP poll counters (`pollsOk`, `pollsFailed`, `pollsSkipped`, `consecutiveFailures`), which is how you check on a source that is quietly failing.
docs.title: Drivers-Network#19

docs.body:
When the in-app AI calls a setter, it sits behind the **Allow device control** toggle.

## Further reading

- [RFC 9293: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293)
- [RFC 768: User Datagram Protocol (UDP)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc768)
- [RFC 6455: The WebSocket Protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455)
- [RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110)

## See also

- [Protocol Setup Guides](Protocol-Setup-Guides.md): step-by-step Network setup in the Setup Panel.
- [Frame Parser](Frame-Parser.md): turning each received frame into values.
- [Troubleshooting](Troubleshooting.md): firewall, port-conflict, and connectivity diagnostics.
- [MQTT Subscriber](Drivers-MQTT.md): when you need pub/sub semantics on top of TCP.
- [API Reference](API-Reference.md): Serial Studio's own JSON-RPC TCP API on port 7777, including the `io.network.*` commands that script this driver (the API Server is off by default).
docs.title: Drivers-Network#20

docs.body:
# OPC UA Driver (Pro)

A PLC on the bench at 192.168.1.10 publishes `Plant.Line1.Filler.Level_pct`, and you want it on a plot. OPC UA is how PLCs, SCADA servers and gateways publish named, typed values over Ethernet, and this driver is the Serial Studio client for it. If your device prints text over a serial port (an Arduino with `Serial.println`), you want the UART driver instead.

The driver connects to an OPC UA server, so you need one: a PLC, a gateway such as KEPServerEX or Ignition, or the [bundled simulator](#try-it-with-the-simulator). You do not write a parser or script: Serial Studio generates the project for you.
docs.title: Drivers-OPC-UA#0

docs.body:
OPC UA is a Pro feature. A Free install is offered the 14-day Pro trial the first time you use a Pro feature (a Yes/No prompt; registering the trial needs an internet connection, and after the trial ends the prompt offers activation or purchase instead). See [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md).

## Try it with the simulator

The `OPC UA PLC Simulator` is a Python 3 server that models a bottling line. Its script, `opcua_plc_simulator.py`, lives in the Serial Studio GitHub repository under `examples/OPC UA PLC Simulator/`. Download that folder, or clone the repository. The **Examples** toolbar button fetches example projects, not this script.
docs.title: Drivers-OPC-UA#1

docs.body:
1. Install the server library and start the simulator: `pip install asyncua`, then `python "examples/OPC UA PLC Simulator/opcua_plc_simulator.py"`.
2. In the **Device Setup** panel, set the **Connection** selector to **OPC UA**. On a Free install this shows the Pro trial prompt (Yes/No). Keep the endpoint `opc.tcp://127.0.0.1:4840` and press **Discover**.
3. Press **Browse Tags...**. In the dialog that opens, tick the `Plant` folder and press **OK**. Back in the panel, press **Generate Project**.
4. Press **Connect** in the toolbar. The generated dashboard has one group per folder the ticked tags live in. `FaultySensor` is a tag the simulator makes fail on purpose: it holds its last good value while the simulator reports the fault.
docs.title: Drivers-OPC-UA#2

docs.body:
The address space mixes string and numeric node ids, engineering units and ranges, a six-element float array, string status tags and a struct-shaped Variable with child Variables.

| Simulator flag | Effect |
|----------------|--------|
| `--user NAME --password PW` | Require username/password login. |
| `--no-subscriptions` | Refuse subscriptions, which forces the polling fallback. |
| `--drop-after N` | Stop publishing after N seconds without closing the socket (the watchdog case). |
| `--secure-only` | Advertise only a secured endpoint. |

The simulator README lists the rest.

## OPC UA overview
docs.title: Drivers-OPC-UA#3

docs.body:
An OPC UA server is a tree, a file explorer for variables. Under the **Objects** folder, vendors arrange folders (a plant, a line, a machine) and inside them **variable nodes**: the tags. Every node has a **node id** (`ns=2;s=Plant.Line1.Filler.Level_pct` or `ns=3;i=1017`), a display name, a data type and an access level. The client asks for values by node id and receives typed values with a **status code** (Good, or a Bad reason) and a **source timestamp** from the device's own clock.

The efficient way to get values is a **subscription**: the client tells the server which tags it wants and the server pushes every change. The alternative is a timed **read** of all tags, which Serial Studio uses as a fallback.
docs.title: Drivers-OPC-UA#4

docs.body:
### Endpoints and security

A server advertises one **endpoint** per security configuration. Each endpoint pairs a **security policy** (`None`, `Basic256Sha256`, ...) with a **message security mode** (None, Sign, Sign and Encrypt). A client picks one endpoint and opens a secure channel with it.

On a local test server leave the policy at `None`. On a real plant network use `Basic256Sha256` or newer.

Serial Studio bundles its own OPC UA stack, so it needs no system crypto library. Six security policies are supported: `None`, `Basic128Rsa15`, `Basic256`, `Basic256Sha256`, `Aes128_Sha256_RsaOaep` and `Aes256_Sha256_RsaPss`. Each secure policy can be used in **Sign** (messages are authenticated) or **Sign and Encrypt** (authenticated and confidential). `Basic128Rsa15` and `Basic256` are deprecated by the OPC Foundation (SHA-1, RSA-1.5); they are labelled as deprecated wherever they appear and never chosen automatically.
docs.title: Drivers-OPC-UA#5

docs.body:
Login is **Anonymous**, **Username / Password**, or an **X.509 certificate** (a digital identity file issued to you). A password is protected only under Sign and Encrypt: the Setup panel warns when it would travel unencrypted (Policy `None` or Mode Sign) and clears the warning under Sign and Encrypt.

Secure policies need a one-time certificate trust step: see [Secure connections](#secure-connections).

## Setup panel settings

The OPC UA driver (Serial Studio Pro) is configured in the **Device Setup** panel: set the **Connection** selector to **OPC UA**. One source is one session with one server; the session subscribes to every selected tag.
docs.title: Drivers-OPC-UA#6

docs.body:
| Setting | Default | What it does |
|---------|---------|--------------|
| Endpoint | `opc.tcp://127.0.0.1:4840` | The server address, `opc.tcp://host:port/path`. The **Discover** button next to it fetches the server's endpoint list. |
| Poll Interval (ms) | 100 | The OPC UA publishing interval requested from the server, also the read timer and the frame rate of the source. Clamped to 10-60000 ms. |
| Security | - | Shown only after Discover returns endpoints. One row per endpoint, as `policy / mode / url`. A row is disabled when the server offers no user identity token the selected Authentication can present. |
| Policy | `None` | The policy you prefer. With no row selected, an endpoint matching this Policy and Mode wins; otherwise the most secure non-deprecated endpoint is picked. |
| Mode | `None` (becomes Sign and Encrypt when you pick a Policy) | **Sign** or **Sign and Encrypt**. Hidden while Policy is `None`. |
| Authentication | Anonymous | **Anonymous**, **Username / Password** or **X.509 Certificate**. |
docs.title: Drivers-OPC-UA#7

docs.body:
The API command `setPublishingInterval` and the CLI flag `--opcua-interval` set the same value as Poll Interval.

**Endpoint.** Press **Discover** to fetch the server's endpoint list. The most secure endpoint whose user tokens match the selected authentication is picked automatically (never a deprecated policy on its own), and an explicit choice survives the next discovery. Connecting without a selected endpoint runs the same discovery first. Serial Studio always dials the **host and port you typed**, keeping the rest of the discovered description: servers routinely advertise their own hostname (`opc.tcp://PLC-01:4840`), which may be a name your laptop's DNS does not know.
docs.title: Drivers-OPC-UA#8

docs.body:
**Poll Interval.** Servers revise the interval upward when it is below their minimum (PLC-embedded servers commonly floor it at 50-100 ms). The status line under the pane reports the rate in force, not the one requested.

**Authentication.** The password is stored in the same per-machine credential vault the MQTT driver uses, obfuscated in the machine's settings and keyed by host and port; it is never written to a project file. For certificate login, pick the certificate and its private key: only their **paths** are saved, never the key itself.

### Selecting tags
docs.title: Drivers-OPC-UA#9

docs.body:
**Browse Tags...** opens a browse-only session and fetches exactly one level per expansion: one Browse plus one batched Read for the whole level. Nothing below a node is read until you expand it, so a gateway with a hundred thousand nodes stays responsive. Variables expand too, because PLC structs (UDTs) expose their members, and their `EngineeringUnits` and `EURange` (the min/max range the PLC declares) properties, as child Variables.

Ticking a folder marks it: every readable supported variable under it is selected, including ones fetched later when you expand it. **Select All Readable** ticks everything fetched so far. **OK** commits the selection; **Cancel** and the window's close button discard it. Tags in branches you never expanded keep their place. An edit made while a session is connected is applied when the link closes.
docs.title: Drivers-OPC-UA#10

docs.body:
Up to 2048 channels can be selected; the dialog warns above 512 because a very wide frame slows the dashboard. A frame is capped at 64 KiB, so many String channels can reach the limit before 2048.

Supported tag types: Boolean, SByte, Byte, Int16, UInt16, Int32, UInt32, Int64, UInt64, Float, Double, String, and one-dimensional arrays of those. The common namespace-0 subtypes resolve too (`Duration`, `UtcTime`, `Enumeration`, `IntegerId`, `DateTime`, `Guid`, `ByteString`, `LocalizedText`); when a vendor declares a type the table does not know, the value's own type decides, and anything printable becomes a string channel. Strings are capped at 256 bytes of UTF-8, truncated on a character boundary. Variables of any other type show in the browser but cannot be ticked.
docs.title: Drivers-OPC-UA#11

docs.body:
Press **Generate Project** to build a project from the selection ([Generated project](#generated-project)).

### Subscription and polling

On connect the driver asks the server for one monitored item (a server-side watch on one tag) per tag and reports progress as **Subscribing, n of N tags**. The status line then settles on one of three texts:

| Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `Subscribed, N tags, X Hz` | Every tag is subscribed. X is the rate in force. |
| `Subscribed N tags, polling M refused, X Hz` | The server refused M individual tags (an item cap, per-user access, a node id gone stale after a PLC download). Each is logged with its node id and moves to timed reads; the rest stay subscribed. |
| `Polling (server refused subscriptions), N tags, X Hz` | The server refused every item (no subscription support, or its quota is exhausted), so the driver reads all tags on a timer. |
docs.title: Drivers-OPC-UA#12

docs.body:
Timed reads are batched to the server's `MaxNodesPerRead`, one read at a time. A tick that arrives while the previous read is still open is skipped and counted.

A subscription can go silent without any error when a server reloads its project but leaves the session up. After silence longer than six revised publishing intervals (3 s at minimum), the driver falls back to polling instead of freezing the dashboard.

Each publishing tick, the driver publishes the tags whose value changed since the previous tick as one frame, and the generated frame parser keeps the last value of the rest. An array tag fans out into one channel per element.
docs.title: Drivers-OPC-UA#13

docs.body:
Value quality follows the OPC UA severity bits: Good and Uncertain values (a gateway serving its last usable value, a device in warm-up) are published, Bad values are dropped. A tag whose newest value is Bad keeps its last good value on the dashboard, increments the bad-status counter and appears in the API status `badTags` list.

### Timestamps

Values keep the PLC's own timestamp, so recordings and CSV exports follow the device clock, even a PLC without NTP. A stamp more than 5 s away from the offset sampled at connect, or a missing one, falls back to the receipt time and counts as unstamped. A frame stamp never goes backwards.
docs.title: Drivers-OPC-UA#14

docs.body:
### Generated project

**Generate Project** writes a project with:

- One source of type OPC UA carrying the endpoint, authentication mode, username, interval and the tag list, so reopening the project reconnects without browsing again.
- One group per folder the selected tags live in, titled after the folder.
- One dataset per channel: the tag's display name as the title (`name[i]` for array elements), booleans become lights in an LED Panel group placed after the group, plotting enabled for numeric types, string tags routed to the data grid. `EngineeringUnits` becomes the dataset unit and `EURange` its widget and plot range, read from the ticked tags' properties.
- A Built-In frame parser using the **OPC UA tag frames** template. The template's schema parameter lists each channel's wire type and is regenerated with the project; edit the tag selection and generate again rather than editing the schema by hand.
docs.title: Drivers-OPC-UA#15

docs.body:
The project opens in the Project Editor for customization, like any other generated project. The headless API command `io.opcua.generateProject` performs the same generation without a save dialog.

### Connection lifecycle

Connecting is asynchronous. The driver reports exactly one outcome per attempt: the session becomes connected, or the attempt fails with a reason (unreachable, access denied, unsupported authentication, rejected endpoint), at the latest after a 15 s deadline. A session that drops after it was established is reported through the normal disconnect path; pressing connect again resubscribes to the same tags.
docs.title: Drivers-OPC-UA#16

docs.body:
## Command line

The command-line flags need Serial Studio Pro, like the Setup panel. A minimal run:

```bash
SerialStudio --opcua opc.tcp://192.168.1.10:4840/ \
  --opcua-tag "ns=2;s=Plant.Line1.Filler.Level_pct:f64:Level" \
  --opcua-tag "ns=2;s=Plant.Line1.Filler.Running:bool:Running" \
  --opcua-interval 100
```

| Flag | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `--opcua URL` | The endpoint to connect to. |
| `--opcua-tag SPEC` | One tag; repeat for more. |
| `--opcua-interval MS` | Publishing interval, 10-60000 ms. An invalid value is rejected with a warning. |
| `--opcua-user NAME`, `--opcua-pass PW` | Username/password login. Without `--opcua-user` the login is Anonymous; certificate login is Setup panel and API only. |
| `--project FILE` | Use this project. Without it, Serial Studio generates a project from the tag list so the frames decode. |
docs.title: Drivers-OPC-UA#17

docs.body:
`--opcua-tag` takes `nodeId[:type[:name]][:n=N][:unit=U]`. The node id may itself contain colons: the suffixes are parsed from the right. `n` gives an array length and `unit` a dataset unit. The type code is one of `bool`, `i8`, `u8`, `i16`, `u16`, `i32`, `u32`, `i64`, `u64`, `f32`, `f64` (the default) or `str`.

## API

The Socket API exposes the driver under `io.opcua.*`.

- **Connection:** `getConfig`, `setEndpointUrl`, `discoverEndpoints`, `listEndpoints`, `setEndpointIndex`, `setPublishingInterval`, `getStatus`.
- **Security and login:** `setSecurityPolicy`, `setSecurityMode`, `setAuthMode`, `setIdentityType` (an alias of `setAuthMode`), `setUsername`, `setPassword`, `setUserCertificate`.
- **Client certificate:** `getCertificate`, `regenerateCertificate`, `exportCertificate`.
- **Trust:** `listTrusted`, `trustServer`, `revokeTrust`.
- **Tags:** `startBrowse`, `browse`, `stopBrowse`, `listTags`, `setTags`, `addTag`, `removeTag`, `clearTags`, `generateProject`.
docs.title: Drivers-OPC-UA#18

docs.body:
Discovery and browsing are asynchronous: the command starts the request and the matching list command is polled for the result. `getStatus` returns the session state and the pulled counters: values received, bad-status count and the node ids currently bad, unstamped values, frames published, link drops, refused tags, skipped polls and the revised publishing interval. Each command, with its parameters, is listed under [OPC UA Driver Commands](API-Reference.md#opc-ua-driver-commands---pro-29).

## Secure connections

In the OPC UA driver (Serial Studio Pro), a secure policy needs the server to be trusted once, and the server to trust Serial Studio once.
docs.title: Drivers-OPC-UA#19

docs.body:
### Connecting for the first time

1. Choose a **Policy** other than `None` and leave **Mode** on Sign and Encrypt (picking a policy sets it).
2. Press **Connect** in the toolbar. The first attempt stops and a trust prompt appears, because Serial Studio has never seen this server's certificate. The prompt shows the certificate's subject, issuer, validity window and **SHA-256 fingerprint**. Compare the fingerprint with the one the server operator gave you, then press **Trust This Server**.
3. Press **Connect** again. Accepting a certificate records the decision but does not reconnect for you.
docs.title: Drivers-OPC-UA#20

docs.body:
The decision is stored per installation, keyed by fingerprint. A server that is re-keyed presents a different fingerprint and asks again, which is the point: a silent inheritance would defeat the check.

### Letting the server trust you

A secure channel is mutual. On the first secure connection Serial Studio generates its own client certificate and keeps it, so a server operator has to trust this installation once rather than on every launch. With a Policy other than `None`, an **Identity** row appears in the OPC UA section of the Device Setup panel:

- **Export…** is enabled once the first secure connection has generated the certificate. It writes the certificate where the server expects trusted clients (`pki/trusted/certs` on many servers). The private key is never exported.
- **Replace** generates a new certificate and key. Every server that trusted the old one has to trust the new one, so use it only when the key may have been exposed.
docs.title: Drivers-OPC-UA#21

docs.body:
### Why a secure connection was refused

The four causes are reported separately, because they have four different fixes:

| Reason | What to do |
|--------|------------|
| The server certificate is not trusted | Compare the fingerprint and accept it in the prompt. |
| The server certificate has expired | Renew it on the server. Serial Studio will not accept an expired certificate. |
| The server certificate is not valid yet | Check the clock on the server and on this machine. |
| The server certificate was not issued for this host | You are dialing a name the certificate does not cover. Use the name it was issued for, or reissue it with the right SubjectAltName. |
docs.title: Drivers-OPC-UA#22

docs.body: ## Common pitfalls
docs.title: Drivers-OPC-UA#23

docs.body:
| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---------|-------|-----|
| Discover fails or hangs | Wrong URL or port, or the server is not running. | Check the URL the server prints on start, and test the port from this machine. |
| The **Security** rows are greyed out | None of the server's endpoints advertises a user identity token the selected Authentication can present (a server offering Anonymous only rejects a username session). | Switch the authentication mode, or enable a matching endpoint on the server. |
| "Access denied" | Anonymous login is disabled on the server, or the username/password is wrong. | Switch the authentication mode and check the account. If browsing fails after login, grant the account read access to the folders. |
| Discovery works, connect times out | A firewall blocks the port, or the server binds an interface this machine cannot reach. Serial Studio dials the host you typed, so the hostname the server advertises does not matter. | Check the firewall for the port in the Endpoint field (4840 by default) and the server's bind address. Connect fails after 15 s at the latest. |
| Everything polls instead of subscribing | The server hit its subscription limit. A previous session that was not closed cleanly holds its subscriptions until the server times it out. | Wait for the timeout, or raise the limit on the server. |
| A tag is visible but cannot be ticked | Its data type is not supported (a structure as a whole, a multi-dimensional array), or the account has no read access. | Expand a struct and tick its members. |
| Values update slower than the interval | The server revised the publishing interval upward; asking politely does not change its floor. | Read the rate in the status line, then ask the server for a faster minimum or accept its floor. |
docs.title: Drivers-OPC-UA#24
