docs.body:
# Process I/O Driver (Pro)

You have a Python script, a command-line tool or another program that prints your readings, and no built-in driver fits it. Process I/O runs that program and reads what it prints, as if the bytes had arrived from a serial port. If your Arduino or ESP32 sits on a USB serial port, use the [UART driver](Drivers-UART.md) instead.

Process I/O is a Pro feature. Without an active license or trial the driver is unavailable. The first time you use a Pro feature, Serial Studio asks Yes or No whether to start a trial; registering the trial needs an internet connection. See [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md).
docs.title: Drivers-Process-IO#0

docs.body:
In the Setup pane, choose the Process I/O driver, then set **Mode**:

- **Launch Process** (Launch mode). Serial Studio starts a program and reads what it prints to standard output (stdout), the same stream `Serial.println` feeds on an Arduino. A shell script or a Python program works.
- **Named Pipe** (Named pipe mode). A named pipe is a file-like channel that one program writes into and another reads from. Serial Studio reads from it and creates it when it does not exist. The producer is whatever process opens the same path for writing.

## Example: piping a Python data generator

Save this as `sine.py`. It prints two CSV values about 100 times a second:
docs.title: Drivers-Process-IO#1

docs.body:
```python
import time, math
t = 0
while True:
    t += 0.01
    print(f"{math.sin(t):.3f},{math.cos(t):.3f}", flush=True)
    time.sleep(0.01)
```

1. In the Setup pane, choose the **Process I/O** driver and set **Mode** to **Launch Process**.
2. Set **Executable** to `python3` (use `python` or `py` on Windows if `python3` is not on PATH) and **Arguments** to the full path of `sine.py`.
3. Set **Operation Mode** to Quick Plot, which plots comma-separated values with no project file (see [Operation Modes](Operation-Modes.md)).
4. Click Connect. Serial Studio asks **Allow this project to launch programs?**; answer Yes (see [launch consent](#launch-consent)).
docs.title: Drivers-Process-IO#2

docs.body:
Two lines, a sine and a cosine, start plotting. If the plot stays flat, the script is still holding its output back; the `flush=True` is what prevents that (see [Common pitfalls](#common-pitfalls)). For step-by-step setup, see the [Protocol Setup Guides, Process I/O section](Protocol-Setup-Guides.md).

## How Process I/O works

Serial Studio treats whatever the program writes to stdout as incoming bytes. Data you send from the console goes to the program's standard input (stdin). In Launch mode, stderr is shown in the console only and is never parsed as frames, so a program that logs diagnostics to stderr does not corrupt your data.
docs.title: Drivers-Process-IO#3

docs.body:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Launch[Launch mode]
        SS1[Serial Studio] -->|spawns| Child[Child process]
        Child -->|stdout| SS1
    end

subgraph Pipe[Named pipe mode]
        Producer[Some process] -->|writes to| FIFO["/tmp/mypipe"]
        FIFO -->|reads from| SS2[Serial Studio]
    end
```

Use Launch mode when a fresh process should start with each connection. Use Named pipe mode when the producer is already running. Serial Studio timestamps each chunk when it reads it, so a slow producer does not distort the time axis; see [Threading and Timing Guarantees](Threading-and-Timing.md).
docs.title: Drivers-Process-IO#4

docs.body:
### Launch mode configuration

In the Setup pane, with the Process I/O driver selected, set **Mode** to **Launch Process**.

| Setting | Controls |
|---------|----------|
| **Executable** | Path to the program to run, or a bare name resolved against PATH plus common install directories that GUI apps often miss (Homebrew, `/usr/local/bin`, `~/.local/bin`, snap and Flatpak exports on Linux; `WindowsApps` and Scoop shims on Windows) |
| **Arguments** | Command-line arguments (whitespace-separated; wrap an argument that contains spaces in double quotes) |
| **Working Dir** | The directory the child should be spawned in (cwd); optional |
docs.title: Drivers-Process-IO#5

docs.body:
The extra search directories are also appended to the child's PATH, so a script that spawns `python3` or similar finds it even when Serial Studio was launched from a desktop shortcut.

### Launch consent

Process I/O Launch mode runs a program with your account's privileges, so it asks before it starts one. The first time a project starts its program, Serial Studio asks **Allow this project to launch programs?** and names the program. Click Yes; the answer is remembered for that project file, so later connects of that project do not ask again. The prompt appears whatever triggered the start: the Connect button, an API connect, a reconnect, a project load, or a program set through the API. A Control Loop's `system.exec` needs the same per-project consent.
docs.title: Drivers-Process-IO#6

docs.body:
- **Yes** starts the Process I/O program, and the connect that was refused while the prompt was open is retried once.
- **No** blocks the Process I/O launch until you reopen the project or restart Serial Studio.
- After a remote API client changes the project's scripts or program, or loads a project, the project's remembered answer is cleared once per session, so the next start asks again. Once you answer yes again, later remote changes in the same session leave it granted.
- In a headless run, a project named on the command line (`--headless`) may launch its programs for that run without a prompt. Any other headless start is denied unless `SERIAL_STUDIO_API_AUTO_CONSENT=1` is set.
docs.title: Drivers-Process-IO#7

docs.body:
Named pipe mode starts no program and never asks.

### Named pipe mode configuration

In the Setup pane, with the Process I/O driver selected, set **Mode** to **Named Pipe**.

| Setting | Controls |
|---------|----------|
| **Pipe Path** | Filesystem path (Linux/macOS) or pipe name (Windows) |

Named pipe mode is read-only; the write path (console send) only exists in Launch mode.

For Linux/macOS, if the path does not already exist Serial Studio creates the FIFO for you (with `0600` permissions) when you connect. If the path exists but is not a FIFO, the connection fails with a **Pipe Error** dialog. You can also create the FIFO yourself beforehand:
docs.title: Drivers-Process-IO#8

docs.body:
```sh
mkfifo /tmp/serialstudio_in
```

For Windows, name the pipe with the standard prefix: `\\.\pipe\serialstudio_in`. A Unix-style path makes pipe creation fail with a **Pipe Error** dialog. On Windows the pipe accepts one writer, and on Linux/macOS several writers can share one FIFO, but only Serial Studio should read it because a second reader steals bytes. On Windows Serial Studio acts as the pipe server and always creates the named pipe (byte mode, inbound only), then waits for a writer to connect. The connection stays in the connecting state until a writer opens the pipe. On Linux/macOS it reports connected as soon as the FIFO is open for reading.
docs.title: Drivers-Process-IO#9

docs.body:
In Named Pipe mode, **Pick Running Process…** lists running processes and fills **Pipe Path** with `/tmp/ss-<name>.fifo` (Windows: `\\.\pipe\ss-<name>`), where `<name>` is the process name lowercased with characters other than letters, digits, `_` and `-` replaced by `_`. The producer still has to open that path itself.

### Remote API commands

With the API Server enabled (off by default, TCP port 7777), the TCP API and the in-app AI assistant configure this driver through the `io.process.*` scope. Paths are checked against the API path policy described in the [API Reference](API-Reference.md).
docs.title: Drivers-Process-IO#10

docs.body:
| Command | Parameters | Notes |
|---------|------------|-------|
| `io.process.setMode` | `mode` (0 = Launch, 1 = NamedPipe) | |
| `io.process.setExecutable` | `executable` (string) | Path is validated against the API path policy |
| `io.process.setArguments` | `arguments` (string) | Shell-style argument string; double-quoted substrings stay one argument |
| `io.process.setWorkingDir` | `workingDir` (string) | Path is validated against the API path policy |
| `io.process.setPipePath` | `pipePath` (string) | Path is validated against the API path policy |
| `io.process.listRunning` | none | Refreshes and returns running processes as `name [pid]` |
| `io.process.getConfig` | none | Returns mode, executable, arguments, workingDir, pipePath |
docs.title: Drivers-Process-IO#11

docs.body:
These commands configure the driver; none of them starts a program. Starting it asks the [launch consent](#launch-consent), whoever set the program, so a remote client that points a source at a program still cannot run it without your answer.

Transport details are in the [API Reference](API-Reference.md); command safety tiers are in [AI Assistant](AI-Assistant.md#the-safety-tiers).

## Common pitfalls
docs.title: Drivers-Process-IO#12

docs.body:
- **Nothing plots and the child is running.** The child is buffering its own output. Most runtimes (C stdio, Python `print`) block-buffer stdout when it is a pipe instead of a terminal, so nothing arrives until the buffer fills. Force a flush after each line: in Python use `print(..., flush=True)`; in C use `fflush(stdout)`; for programs you cannot modify, `stdbuf -oL my_program` (Linux coreutils) forces line-buffered output.
- **"Waiting for permission to launch" or "was denied for this project".** The [launch consent](#launch-consent) prompt is open, or it was answered no. Answer the prompt (a yes retries the connect), or reopen the project to be asked again after a no.
- **"Failed to start process" or `Executable "X" not found in PATH.`** The name did not resolve. Give the full path to the executable.
- **Child process exits immediately.** Serial Studio drains any remaining output, shows a dialog titled `Process "<name>" stopped`, with the exit code, and disconnects. Run the child from a normal terminal first to confirm it starts.
- **Arguments with spaces.** The Arguments field splits on whitespace: wrap an argument that contains spaces in double quotes; single quotes are not special. Some programs read files relative to their working directory, so set **Working Dir** when yours does.
- **Permission denied on the pipe.** On Linux/macOS, the FIFO inherits filesystem permissions. `chmod 666 /tmp/mypipe` opens it to all users; tighter permissions require both reader and writer to share a user or group.
- **Data stops after the writer exits.** When the writer closes the pipe, Serial Studio disconnects and shows a **Pipe Closed** dialog. Click Connect again to wait for the next writer. See [Named pipe mode configuration](#named-pipe-mode-configuration) for the writer rules.
- **Pipe buffer fills up.** Linux pipes buffer 64 KB by default, and a writer that outruns Serial Studio blocks until the reader catches up. If the producer must never block, use a TCP socket (see [Drivers: Network](Drivers-Network.md)).
docs.title: Drivers-Process-IO#13

# Siemens S7comm Driver (Pro)

You have a Siemens S7-1200 on `192.168.0.1` and want the tank level stored at `DB5.DBD20` on a dashboard. In Serial Studio Pro you add that address as a variable, press **Connect**, and the value plots. A PLC keeps its values at numbered memory addresses; you tell Serial Studio which addresses to read. The S7comm driver is a read-only polling client for S7-300, S7-400, S7-1200 and S7-1500 controllers and compatible simulators. It cannot change the state of a running machine, because it has no write path at all.

## Quick start
docs.title: Drivers-S7#0

docs.body:
1. S7-1200 and S7-1500 only: enable PUT/GET and clear **Optimized block access** ([Controller-side prerequisites](#controller-side-prerequisites)). Skip this on S7-300 and S7-400.
2. In the Setup panel, choose **Siemens S7** as the bus type (Pro). The first time you pick a Pro feature, Serial Studio offers a free trial with a Yes/No prompt (it needs an internet connection).
3. Enter **Host** `192.168.0.1`, **Rack** `0` (the CPU's position in the rack) and **Slot** `1` (use slot `2` on an S7-300 or S7-400).
4. Click **Configure Variables…**, add a row with the name `Level` and the address `DB5.DBD20:REAL`, and close the dialog.
5. In the Setup panel, click **Create Project from Variables** and save the project when asked, then click **Connect**.
docs.title: Drivers-S7#1

docs.body:
The dashboard shows a plot titled `Level` (inside a group titled `DB5`). The driver polls every 200 ms and the plot moves whenever the value changes.

## When to use it instead of OPC UA

Use the [OPC UA driver](Drivers-OPC-UA.md) when the controller ships an OPC UA server. It is typed, browsable, and the server tells you what exists.

Use S7comm when it does not. That means an S7-300 or S7-400 with no OPC UA option, or a locked-down S7-1200 where the OPC UA licence was never bought. It also suits a commissioning session where you already have the symbol table in TIA Portal and want values in seconds. The trade is that you supply the addresses. Nothing on the wire can tell you whether `DB5.DBD20` is a REAL or four bytes of something else; you are the symbol table.
docs.title: Drivers-S7#2

docs.body:
## Addressing

An address names an area, a byte offset inside it and how wide the value is. Three examples:

- `DB5.DBD20`: data block 5, four bytes starting at byte 20 (the block number and byte offset are the ones TIA Portal shows for the variable).
- `MW10`: flag memory, two bytes starting at byte 10.
- `Q0.1`: bit 1 of output byte 0.

The width letter is `X` for a bit, `B` for a byte, `W` for a word (2 bytes) and `D` for a double word (4 bytes). With no type given, a `B`, `W` or `D` address is read as an unsigned number of that width and an `X` address as a bit. Two spellings are accepted, case-insensitively:
docs.title: Drivers-S7#3

docs.body:
| Form | Example | Reads |
|------|---------|-------|
| `DB<n>.DB{X\|B\|W\|D}<byte>[.<bit>]` | `DB5.DBD20` | Data block 5, four bytes at offset 20 |
| `{I\|E\|Q\|A\|M}[{X\|B\|W\|D}]<byte>[.<bit>]` | `MW10` | Flag memory, two bytes at offset 10 |

A bit index follows a second dot (`DB1.DBX0.3`, `Q0.1`), runs 0 to 7 and is valid only on a bit address. On `I`, `Q` and `M` the `X` may be left off when a bit index follows (`Q0.1` is `QX0.1`); `DB` addresses always need the width letter. An address with neither a width letter nor a bit index is refused. Data block numbers start at 1 (`DB0` is refused), and block numbers and byte offsets go up to 65535.
docs.title: Drivers-S7#4

docs.body:
To read the same bytes as a signed integer or a float, append the type:

```text
DB5.DBD20:REAL          four bytes at DB5 offset 20, IEEE 754 float
DB5.DBD24:DINT          the same width, signed 32-bit
MW10:INT                two bytes of flag memory, signed 16-bit
DB4.DBB10:STRING[32]    an S7 STRING of up to 32 characters
```

Declared types are `BOOL`, `BYTE`, `WORD`, `DWORD`, `INT`, `DINT`, `REAL` and `STRING`. A type is refused when its width does not match the address it is attached to, so `MW10:REAL` is rejected rather than silently reading two bytes of a four-byte float. `STRING` needs the `B` width and its declared length (1 to 254), and reads the S7 two-byte header plus the characters.
docs.title: Drivers-S7#5

docs.body:
In the second form, the German letters `E` (Eingang, input) and `A` (Ausgang, output) work as synonyms of `I` and `Q`.

Addresses are validated as you type them: the variable dialog shows the reason an address is refused, and the API returns the same reason instead of adding the variable.

## Configuration

The S7comm driver (Pro) is configured in the Setup panel with **Siemens S7** selected as the bus type. Connecting, sending and reading run on a thread the driver owns, so an unresponsive controller does not freeze the window.

### Controller-side prerequisites

The Siemens S7 driver (Pro) reads absolute memory, and a modern CPU has to be told to allow that. This is the usual reason a first connection fails.
docs.title: Drivers-S7#6

docs.body:
- **S7-1200 and S7-1500.** In TIA Portal, open the CPU's properties and check **Protection & Security → Permit access with PUT/GET communication from remote partner**. Without it the CPU accepts the TCP connection and then refuses the S7comm session.
- **Data blocks on S7-1200 and S7-1500.** Clear **Optimized block access** in each data block's properties. An optimized block has no stable byte layout, so `DB5.DBD20` names nothing the CPU can resolve.
- **S7-300 and S7-400.** No CPU setting is needed; these families answer PUT/GET reads as shipped.

### Setup panel fields

With **Siemens S7** selected in the Setup panel:
docs.title: Drivers-S7#7

docs.body:
1. **Host.** The controller's IP address or host name. The protocol's port (102) is implied.
2. **Rack** and **Slot.** Where the CPU sits in the rack. S7-1200 and S7-1500 CPUs are rack 0, slot 1; S7-300 and S7-400 CPUs in the standard central rack are rack 0, slot 2. Rack accepts 0-7 (default 0) and slot 0-31 (default 1). A wrong slot fails at the ISO connection step and a missing PUT/GET permission at the S7comm setup step ([Connection lifecycle](#connection-lifecycle)).
3. **Poll Interval (ms).** How often the whole variable list is read, and the frame rate of the source. Default 200 ms, clamped to 50-60000 ms.
4. **Variables.** The **Configure Variables…** dialog holds the list: a channel name and an address per row. The name is what the dashboard shows; leaving it empty uses the address itself. Up to 2048 variables can be configured. Names must be unique: a variable whose name is already in the list is ignored, and adding past 2048 does nothing.
5. **Create Project from Variables.** Builds a project from the list ([Generated project](#generated-project)).
docs.title: Drivers-S7#8

docs.body:
### Polling

Every poll of the S7comm driver (Pro) reads each variable in list order and compares it with the value the previous poll stored. Only variables whose value changed are sent on to the dashboard; the others keep their last value. If nothing changed, no frame is published.

Variables are read in batches of up to 20 items, further limited by the message length the controller agreed to when the session opened. A hundred addresses therefore cost at least five exchanges rather than a hundred. Each frame carries the time the poll started, so recordings and CSV exports show when the controller was read, not when the frame was drawn.
docs.title: Drivers-S7#9

docs.body:
A read that the controller refuses (a data block that does not exist, an offset past its end) is counted and named in the status, and the channel keeps its last value; the session stays up, because a bad address is a configuration error, not a dropped link. The link is declared lost only when an exchange fails outright; Serial Studio then disconnects.

### Generated project

**Create Project from Variables** builds the dashboard for you, so you do not write a frame parser. The generated project (titled `Siemens S7 Project`) has:
docs.title: Drivers-S7#10

docs.body:
- One source of type Siemens S7 carrying the host, rack, slot, interval and the variable list, so reopening the project reconnects without retyping the addresses.
- One group per data block, titled `DB<n>` (`DB5`), plus one group titled `Memory` for the `I`, `Q` and `M` areas. Each group uses the data grid widget.
- One dataset per variable: the variable's name as the title, plotting enabled for numeric types. Bit variables also appear as LEDs in an extra LED Panel group created after their group.
- A Built-In frame parser using the **Siemens S7 variables** template. Its schema is regenerated with the project; edit the variable list and generate again rather than editing the schema by hand.
docs.title: Drivers-S7#11

docs.body:
The project opens in the Project Editor for customization. The headless API command `io.s7.generateProject` performs the same generation without a save dialog.

### Connection lifecycle

Pressing **Connect** dials the controller and reports success or failure once. The dial has three steps, and a failure names the one that failed:

| Step | Fails when | Check |
|------|-----------|-------|
| TCP connection | The host is unreachable, refuses port 102, or stays silent | The IP address and the network |
| ISO connection | The controller refuses it; the error reads "check the rack and slot numbers" | Rack and slot |
| S7comm setup | The CPU will not open a session | PUT/GET and optimized block access |
docs.title: Drivers-S7#12

docs.body:
The TCP and ISO steps wait up to 5 s each; the S7comm setup waits 3 s. A silent host reports "The controller did not answer within 5 s" at the TCP step, and a refused connection shows the socket's own error. A silent ISO step reads "check the rack and slot numbers", and a silent setup reads "The controller did not answer the S7comm setup request". A session that drops after it was established makes Serial Studio disconnect; pressing **Connect** again polls the same variables.

The variable list is locked while a session is open, because the wire layout is sized when the session starts. Disconnect to edit it.
docs.title: Drivers-S7#13

docs.body:
## Command line

The S7comm driver (Pro) can be started from the command line:

```bash
SerialStudio --s7 192.168.0.1 --s7-rack 0 --s7-slot 1 \
  --s7-variable "DB5.DBD20:REAL:Level" \
  --s7-variable "DB1.DBX0.3:Running" \
  --s7-interval 200
```

Run it from a terminal, using the path of the Serial Studio executable on your system. `--s7-variable` takes `address[:TYPE][:name]` and repeats; `DB5.DBD20:REAL:Level` has the type `REAL` and the name `Level`. `--s7-rack` accepts 0-7 and `--s7-slot` 0-31 (default 1); `--s7-interval` defaults to 200. A spec that is not a valid address is skipped with a warning; if none are valid, Serial Studio does not connect. Without `--project`, Serial Studio generates a project from the variable list so the frames decode.
docs.title: Drivers-S7#14

docs.body:
## API

S7comm driver (Pro): the Socket API (the API Server is off by default; port 7777 when enabled) exposes the driver under `io.s7.*`: `getConfig`, `getStatus`, `setProperty`, `addVariable`, `removeVariable`, `clearVariables` and `generateProject`. `setProperty` takes a `key` and a `value` and accepts `host`, `rack`, `slot` and `pollInterval`. `getStatus` returns the session state and the pulled counters: successful reads, failed reads, refused items with the name of the last one, frames published and link drops. Each command, with its parameters, is listed under [S7comm Driver Commands](API-Reference.md#s7comm-driver-commands---pro-7).
docs.title: Drivers-S7#15

## Availability

The S7comm driver requires Serial Studio Pro. The first time you use a Pro feature, Serial Studio offers a free trial with a Yes/No prompt (it needs an internet connection to register); after the trial ends it offers activation or purchase. See [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md).

docs.body:
# UART / Serial Driver

Your board prints `Serial.println("23.5,1013");` at 115200 baud. To plot it in Quick Plot mode:

1. In the **Setup Panel**, select **UART/COM** from the Connection dropdown.
2. Pick the board under **Serial Port** (**COM Port** on Windows).
3. Set **Baud Rate** to the number in your `Serial.begin()` call. The default is 9600, so a 115200 sketch shows garbage until you change it.
4. Click **Connect**.

Two comma-separated values per line give two plots. [Protocol Setup Guides](Protocol-Setup-Guides.md) has the full walkthrough.

The UART driver covers USB-to-serial adapters, RS-232, RS-485 and Bluetooth Classic devices that the OS exposes as virtual COM ports. It is in the free edition, Connection Sequence included.
docs.title: Drivers-UART#0

docs.body:
## UART driver settings

With **UART/COM** selected as the connection in the Setup Panel, these fields appear. They map one-to-one onto UART parameters, and the driver wraps Qt's `QSerialPort`:
docs.title: Drivers-UART#1

docs.body:
| Setting | Controls | Default |
|---------|----------|---------|
| **Serial Port** (**COM Port** on Windows) | Which OS-level serial device to open (COM3, `/dev/ttyACM0`, etc.) | none selected |
| **Baud Rate** | Bits per second; presets 110, 150, 300, 1200, 2400, 4800, 9600, 19200, 38400, 57600, 115200, 230400, 256000, 460800, 576000 and 921600. The field accepts any positive rate typed in, so type a higher one if the device needs it | 9600 |
| **Data Bits** | 5 / 6 / 7 / 8 | 8 |
| **Parity** | None / Even / Odd / Space / Mark | None |
| **Stop Bits** | 1 / 1.5 / 2 | 1 |
| **Flow Control** | None / RTS/CTS / XON/XOFF; see [Flow control](#flow-control). Leave it on None unless the device needs otherwise | None |
| **Auto Reconnect** | After the port drops with a fatal error (unplug, resource loss), rescans once per second and reopens the same port name when it reappears. A manual Disconnect cancels the retry. Shown as Auto-Reconnect in the Project Editor | off |
| **Send DTR Signal** | Asserts the DTR line on connect. Leave it on unless your Arduino resets when you connect; see [Common pitfalls](#common-pitfalls) | on |
| **Hold RTS** | Asserts the RTS line on connect and holds it for the whole connection. Leave it off unless the device datasheet asks for RTS. Not applicable under RTS/CTS flow control, where the port driver owns RTS | off |
| **Connection Sequence** | Steps run on every open before any byte reaches the dashboard; see [Connection Sequence](#connection-sequence) | no steps |
docs.title: Drivers-UART#2

docs.body:
On Linux and macOS the **Serial Port** field is editable: type a device path missing from the list (for example `/dev/ttyAMA0`) and press Enter to register it. On macOS each adapter is listed once, as its `cu.*` device; the `tty.*` duplicates are hidden.

If your Arduino or ESP32 already streams on connect, you need nothing past this table and the pitfalls below. Skip the API and Connection Sequence sections.

## Common pitfalls
docs.title: Drivers-UART#3

docs.body:
- **The Arduino resets every time you connect.** Uno, Nano and other boards wire the USB-serial chip's DTR line to the reset pin through a capacitor, so asserting DTR on open reboots the sketch. Clear **Send DTR Signal** in the Setup Panel before connecting.
- **Garbled output.** Usually a baud-rate mismatch. Compare the sketch's `Serial.begin()` value with **Baud Rate**, then **Data Bits**, **Parity** and **Stop Bits** with the device's 8N1 setting. A 115200 stream read at 9600 looks like a cat walked across the keyboard.
- **The port opens but nothing comes through.** TX and RX may be swapped. Some adapters label pins from the host's point of view, some from the device's. The fix is usually to swap them physically.
- **Long cable runs drop bytes.** Past a few meters of TTL or about 15 m of RS-232, use an RS-485 transceiver at each end (up to 1200 m; see [RS-232 vs RS-485 vs TTL](#rs-232-vs-rs-485-vs-ttl)).
- **The device disappears mid-session on Linux.** `udev` may have renamed it; `/dev/ttyUSB0` can become `/dev/ttyUSB1` after a hot-unplug. A `udev` rule pinning the device by VID/PID to a stable symlink fixes it permanently.
- **The connection fails with "Connection Sequence failed at step ...".** See [When a step fails](#when-a-step-fails).
docs.title: Drivers-UART#4

docs.body:
## Controlling UART from the API

For scripting and automation only; the Setup Panel needs none of this. The UART settings are scriptable through the `io.uart.*` commands of the [JSON-RPC API](API-Reference.md). The API Server must be enabled; it is off by default and listens on port 7777.
docs.title: Drivers-UART#5

docs.body:
| Command | Arguments | Effect |
|---------|-----------|--------|
| `setDevice` | `device` (path) | Selects the port by device path |
| `setPortIndex` | `portIndex` (zero-based) | Selects the port by list position |
| `setBaudRate` | `baudRate` (bits per second) | Sets the saved **Baud Rate** |
| `setParity` | `parityIndex`: 0 None, 1 Even, 2 Odd, 3 Space, 4 Mark | Sets **Parity** |
| `setDataBits` | `dataBitsIndex`: 0 = 5, 1 = 6, 2 = 7, 3 = 8 | Sets **Data Bits** |
| `setStopBits` | `stopBitsIndex`: 0 = 1, 1 = 1.5, 2 = 2 | Sets **Stop Bits** |
| `setFlowControl` | `flowControlIndex`: 0 None, 1 RTS/CTS, 2 XON/XOFF | Sets **Flow Control** |
| `setDtrEnabled`, `setRtsEnabled`, `setAutoReconnect` | `dtrEnabled`, `rtsEnabled`, `autoReconnect` | Set **Send DTR Signal**, **Hold RTS** and **Auto Reconnect** |
| `setSequence` | sequence | Replaces the Connection Sequence |
| `listPorts`, `listBaudRates`, `getConfig`, `getSequence` | none | Read-only queries |
| `sendBreak` | `durationMs`, 1 to 10000 | Sends a BREAK on the open port |
| `setLiveBaudRate` | `baudRate` | Changes only the running rate; the saved **Baud Rate** stays, and the next connection opens at it again |
| `getLineStates` | none | Returns `cts`, `dsr`, `dcd`, `ri`, `rts` and `dtr` |
| `runSequence` | none | Re-runs the Connection Sequence; see [Running it again](#running-it-again) |
docs.title: Drivers-UART#6

docs.body:
The last four act on a connected port. Each takes an optional `sourceId` naming the Device in a multi-source project; without it they act on source 0. When the in-app AI issues a command that changes the port or a line, it sits behind the **Allow device control** toggle.

## Connection Sequence

Most Arduino and ESP32 boards stream as soon as the port opens and need no Connection Sequence. Use it only for devices that must be brought up first, such as a bus adapter that resets on a BREAK (the line held low longer than one byte time) or a GPS module that a configuration message switches to a faster baud. The **Connection Sequence** of a UART source performs that bring-up from Serial Studio itself, with no script and no vendor program. It is part of the free edition.
docs.title: Drivers-UART#7

docs.body:
The sequence is an ordered list of steps. Edit it with the **Connection Sequence…** button in the Setup Panel, or with the **Connection Sequence** row of a UART source in the Project Editor; both open the same editor. A project saves the sequence with its source, and the Setup Panel's sequence persists with the other serial settings. A project saved without one connects as it always did.

The sequence runs every time the port opens: from the Connect button, from `io.connect`, from the command line, and on an automatic reconnect. While it runs the Device is connecting, not connected. The dashboard receives no frames, **Auto-Execute on Connect** actions have not fired, the [Control Loop](Control-Loop.md) has not started, and writes from the API or the console are refused. The Device reports connected once the last step succeeds.
docs.title: Drivers-UART#8

docs.body: A sequence holds at most 128 steps.
docs.title: Drivers-UART#9

docs.body:
| Step | Parameters | What it does |
|------|------------|--------------|
| **Send BREAK** | Duration, 1 to 10000 ms | Holds the line in BREAK, then releases it. Bytes the device sends meanwhile are discarded, and the input buffer is cleared on release. |
| **Wait** | Duration, 0 to 600000 ms | Pauses. |
| **Set Control Line** | DTR or RTS, high or low | Drives a modem line. RTS is refused under RTS/CTS flow control. |
| **Send Data** | Data, Hex, line ending, checksum | Writes the data (text with `\r`/`\n` escapes, or hex bytes), then the line ending, then the checksum over both, in the order an action uses. |
| **Expect Reply** | Patterns, timeout (1 to 600000 ms), Continue If No Reply | Waits until the bytes received match one of the patterns. |
| **Clear Received Data** | none | Drops whatever the port has received so far. |
| **Set Baud Rate** | Rate, 1 to 15000000 | Changes the running rate. The saved **Baud Rate** is untouched, so every reconnection starts from it again. |
| **Set Flow Control** | None, RTS/CTS or XON/XOFF | Changes the running flow-control mode. |
docs.title: Drivers-UART#10

docs.body:
An **Expect Reply** pattern is a list of hex bytes. `??` matches any byte and a single `?` matches one hex digit, so `5?` accepts `50` to `5F`. Separate several acceptable replies with `|`: `55 | 5D ??` succeeds on either. The step looks at everything received since the previous matched reply (up to 4 KiB) and consumes through the match. A step with **Continue If No Reply** checked that times out leaves a console note and the sequence carries on.

The **Time Limit** (10000 ms by default, between 1 and 600000 ms) bounds the whole sequence. The editor refuses a limit smaller than the BREAK and Wait steps add up to.
docs.title: Drivers-UART#11

docs.body:
### Example: a bus adapter that resets on BREAK

Goal: bring an adapter up at 115200 baud with RTS/CTS flow control. The adapter powers up at 9600 baud, resets on a BREAK of at least 10 ms and answers with `55` or `5D` followed by a version byte. Two `15` bytes switch it to 115200 baud, and it streams only with RTS/CTS flow control on. With the Setup Panel at 9600 baud:

1. **Send BREAK**, 55 ms.
2. **Expect Reply** `55 | 5D ??` within 100 ms.
3. **Send Data** `15 15`, **Hex** checked.
4. **Wait** 20 ms.
5. **Set Baud Rate** 115200.
6. **Set Flow Control** RTS/CTS.

### When a step fails

A UART Connection Sequence step that fails ends the sequence and the connection attempt: an **Expect Reply** that times out, a write the port refuses, the port disappearing, or the time limit running out. The console and the log name the step by position and kind and quote what the device sent, cut to the first 32 bytes and ended with `...` when longer:
docs.title: Drivers-UART#12

docs.body:
```
Connection Sequence failed at step 2 (Expect Reply): no reply matched within 100 ms; received: 5A 00
```

There is no modal dialog. `received: nothing` points at power or wiring; bytes that match no pattern point at the wrong opening baud rate. With **Auto Reconnect** on, a port that disappears mid-sequence is retried like any dropped port; a device that answers wrongly is not.

### Connection Sequence in the console

The UART Connection Sequence (Setup Panel, **Connection Sequence…**) writes one line per step to the console, each prefixed `[Connection Sequence]`, and a final line reports the outcome. The bytes the device sends during the sequence appear as received data. None of them reach the frame parser, the dashboard or a recording.
docs.title: Drivers-UART#13

docs.body:
### Running it again

To re-run the UART Connection Sequence on a connected port, call `io.uart.runSequence`. It serves a device that was power-cycled while the port stayed open. The Device stays connected, frames pause until the run ends, and the outcome is written to the console; a failure also raises a notification. A Control Loop can issue the same command, along with `io.uart.sendBreak`.

### Connection Sequence limits

- The sequence opens at one baud rate. A device that powers up at a different rate in some units needs a second project, or a Control Loop that changes the saved rate and reconnects.
- Some USB serial adapters emit a fixed-length BREAK whatever duration is requested. The step reports success when the port accepts the request; it cannot measure what the adapter put on the wire.
- The steps have no branching or loops. Logic belongs in a [Control Loop](Control-Loop.md).
docs.title: Drivers-UART#14

docs.body:
## UART basics

UART stands for **Universal Asynchronous Receiver-Transmitter**. It is the small piece of hardware inside a microcontroller, a USB-to-serial chip, or a PC's chipset that converts parallel bytes into a sequential stream of bits and back. There is no clock line between the two ends; both sides agree in advance on how fast the bits will arrive, and the receiver synchronises itself to the start of each byte.

A UART is a peripheral, not a protocol. The protocol it implements is usually called *asynchronous serial* or just *serial*. When a datasheet says "speaks serial at 115200 8N1", it is describing UART parameters.
docs.title: Drivers-UART#15

docs.body:
### The frame

Every byte sent over a UART line is wrapped in a small fixed-shape frame. The line idles high. A low start bit tells the receiver to start clocking. The data bits follow, typically 8, least-significant first, then an optional parity bit and one or more high stop bits before the line returns to idle.

The most common configuration is **8N1**: 8 data bits, **N**o parity, **1** stop bit. The byte `0x4B` (`0100 1011`) sent as 8N1 looks like this, with the data bits least-significant first:

```text
idle 1 | start 0 | data 1 1 0 1 0 0 1 0 | stop 1
```

In 8N1 that is ten line bits per byte, a raw efficiency of 80%. The receiver samples each bit near the middle of its bit time.
docs.title: Drivers-UART#16

docs.body:
### Baud rate

**Baud rate** is the number of symbols per second on the line. For UART that is identical to bits per second: at 9600 baud, each bit lasts `1 / 9600 ≈ 104.2 µs`.

The presets are listed under [UART driver settings](#uart-driver-settings).

Both ends must agree. UARTs tolerate a few percent of clock mismatch between transmitter and receiver, but if the configured baud rates differ (for example 115200 vs 9600) the result is garbage or no data at all.

### Parity

A parity bit makes the total number of `1`s in the frame either always even or always odd. It detects single-bit errors but cannot detect two-bit errors and cannot correct anything. Leave it on **None** unless the device says otherwise: USB and short cables rarely flip bits, and a CRC in the application protocol covers the rest. **Even** and **Odd** set the count. **Space** and **Mark** force the parity bit to `0` and `1`, and survive on a few legacy buses.
docs.title: Drivers-UART#17

docs.body:
### Stop bits

The stop bit holds the line high for one or two bit-times after the last data bit. Choose **1 stop bit** unless the device explicitly requires something else.

### Flow control

Flow control lets the receiver tell the sender to pause when its buffer is full. UART has two schemes, plus the option of none:

- **Hardware flow control (RTS/CTS)** uses two extra wires. The receiver raises CTS (Clear To Send) when it can accept data and lowers it when it cannot. The sender checks CTS before each byte. Reliable, but the cable must include those lines.
- **Software flow control (XON/XOFF)** sends special characters in the data stream (`0x11` = XON, `0x13` = XOFF) to signal go/stop. This reserves those byte values, so it cannot be used with arbitrary binary data.
- **None** is the right choice when both sides are fast enough to never pause, or when the protocol layered on top provides its own back-pressure.
docs.title: Drivers-UART#18

docs.body:
For typical Arduino, ESP32, and STM32 telemetry, choose **None**. Hardware flow control matters with industrial equipment or sustained high-rate streams where the host cannot keep up at the application layer.

### RS-232 vs RS-485 vs TTL

UART is the protocol; the physical layer is separate. Serial Studio works with any of them as long as the OS exposes a serial port, but the differences matter when you choose hardware:
docs.title: Drivers-UART#19

docs.body:
- **TTL serial**: 0 V / 3.3 V (or 5 V) logic levels. What microcontroller pins drive directly. Short cables only.
- **RS-232**: ±3 V to ±15 V, single-ended, full-duplex over separate TX and RX wires. Cable lengths up to about 15 m. The classic 9-pin DE-9 connector found on PC serial ports.
- **RS-485**: differential signalling on two wires (A and B). Tolerates cable runs up to 1200 m and supports multi-drop buses (one master plus many slaves on the same pair). Native operation is half-duplex; a 4-wire variant supports full-duplex. This is the physical layer used by Modbus RTU and many industrial buses.
docs.title: Drivers-UART#20

docs.body:
A USB-to-serial adapter converts USB to TTL or RS-232 levels. To Serial Studio, all of them appear as a COM port on Windows or as `/dev/ttyUSB0` / `/dev/cu.usbserial-XXXX` on Linux and macOS.

## See also

- [Protocol Setup Guides](Protocol-Setup-Guides.md): step-by-step UART setup in the Setup Panel; the next step after this page.
- [Operation Modes](Operation-Modes.md): Quick Plot for plotting comma-separated values, or a project file to define your own frame format.
- [Troubleshooting](Troubleshooting.md): diagnostic steps for connection problems.
- [Communication Protocols](Communication-Protocols.md): overview of all supported transports.
- [Drivers: Network](Drivers-Network.md): TCP and UDP, the next step up when serial isn't enough.
