docs.body:
# Raw USB Driver (Pro)

If your board prints with `Serial.println` over a USB cable, you do not need this page. Arduino and ESP32 boards appear as a serial port, so use the [UART driver](Drivers-UART.md). Gamepads, joysticks and HID firmware belong to the [HID driver](Drivers-HID.md).

Raw USB is for the rest: a logic analyzer, an oscilloscope or a data-acquisition board whose datasheet says "uses bulk endpoint 0x81" and that never shows up as a COM port. Serial Studio opens such a device through **libusb** and reads the endpoint you pick.

Raw USB is a Pro feature (see [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md)). The first time you use a Pro feature, Serial Studio offers the Pro trial with a Yes/No prompt; registering the trial needs an internet connection.
docs.title: Drivers-USB#0

docs.body:
## Raw USB setup (Pro)

Raw USB needs Pro. On first use Serial Studio offers the Pro trial (Yes/No, needs internet); answering No leaves the feature locked, and after the trial ends it offers activation or purchase instead.

In the **Setup Panel**, select **USB Device** from the Connection dropdown. The default path takes four steps:

1. Pick your device from the **USB Device** dropdown.
2. Leave **Transfer Mode** on **Bulk/Interrupt Stream**.
3. Check the **IN Endpoint**. Serial Studio selects the first matching one, such as `EP 0x81 – Bulk IN (IF0, max 64 B)`, where `IF0` is interface 0. Pick another if the datasheet says so.
4. Click **Connect**.
docs.title: Drivers-USB#1

docs.body:
Raw bytes arrive from the endpoint. A [frame parser](Frame-Parser.md) or Quick Plot turns them into dashboard values, the same as on any other driver.

| Setting | Shown in | Values | Default |
|---------|----------|--------|---------|
| **USB Device** | all modes | `VID:PID – Manufacturer Product`; the list updates on libusb hotplug events, with a 2-second rescan where hotplug is unavailable | **Select Device** |
| **Transfer Mode** | all modes | **Bulk/Interrupt Stream**, **Advanced (Bulk + Control)**, **Isochronous** | **Bulk/Interrupt Stream** |
| **IN Endpoint** | all modes | the device's IN endpoints that fit the Transfer Mode | first match |
| **OUT Endpoint** | all modes | the device's OUT endpoints that fit the Transfer Mode | **None (Read-only)** |
| **Max Packet Size** | Isochronous | 1 to 49152 bytes | 1024, then pre-filled from the endpoint |
docs.title: Drivers-USB#2

docs.body:
The endpoint dropdowns and **Max Packet Size** lock while connected. Endpoint labels use `Bulk`, `Int` or `Iso` for the type, and add `ALT2` (for example `IF1 ALT2`) for a non-zero alternate setting.

The endpoint lists follow the Transfer Mode. **Isochronous** lists only isochronous endpoints; the other two modes list only bulk and interrupt endpoints. Changing the mode clears the selection and picks the first match. A device with no endpoint of the right type shows **No Usable IN Endpoints**, and **Connect** tells you which mode to switch to. Writes through the OUT endpoint time out after 1 second.
docs.title: Drivers-USB#3

docs.body:
### Transfer modes

| Mode | Transfer types | Use it for |
|------|----------------|------------|
| **Bulk/Interrupt Stream** | Bulk and interrupt IN/OUT, picked by the selected endpoint's type | Most devices: streaming data or small periodic reports |
| **Advanced (Bulk + Control)** | Bulk, plus vendor control transfers | Devices that need a vendor command to start streaming |
| **Isochronous** | Asynchronous isochronous IN | Fixed-rate streams where a few dropped packets are acceptable |

In the USB setup pane the mode is labeled **Advanced (Bulk + Control)**; the driver's generic property list labels it **Advanced Control**.
docs.title: Drivers-USB#4

docs.body:
Choosing **Advanced (Bulk + Control)** opens a Yes/No confirmation (default No), because a vendor control write can do anything the firmware allows, including bricking the device. The dialog appears once and Serial Studio remembers a Yes. Until you accept it in the setup pane, a project load or `io.usb.setTransferMode` with mode 1 is refused with an "Advanced USB mode refused" warning. The API call still returns success when refused, so read `transferMode` back.

In Isochronous mode, **Max Packet Size** is pre-filled from the selected endpoint, including the high-bandwidth multiplier (up to 3 x 1024 B on high speed). Change it only when the datasheet says otherwise.
docs.title: Drivers-USB#5

docs.body:
### Control transfers

With **Advanced (Bulk + Control)** selected and the device connected, a **Control Transfer** composer appears in the USB setup pane. A logic analyzer that stays silent until it gets a vendor command is waiting to be asked, and this is where you ask.

| Field | Format |
|-------|--------|
| **Request Type** (`bmRequestType`) | Hex. Bit 7 sets the direction: `0x80` and above is IN, below is OUT |
| **Request** (`bRequest`), **wValue**, **wIndex** | Hex |
| **Data** | OUT: hex bytes, such as `EF BE 00 00` |
| **Read Length** | IN: bytes to read |

The data length is 0 to 4096 bytes, and one control transfer runs at a time. A vendor "start streaming" write could be Request Type `40`, Request `01`, wValue `0001`, wIndex `0000` and no data. Click **Send Control Transfer**; the result appears in the composer.
docs.title: Drivers-USB#6

docs.body:
## Permissions and OS specifics

USB access is permission-controlled differently on each OS.

- **Linux.** By default only `root` can open arbitrary USB devices. Find your device's IDs with `lsusb` (the `ID` field) or in the **USB Device** dropdown. Create `/etc/udev/rules.d/99-myusbdevice.rules` containing the rule below, with your own VID and PID. `MODE="0666"` lets every local user open the device.

```
  SUBSYSTEM=="usb", ATTR{idVendor}=="1234", ATTR{idProduct}=="5678", MODE="0666"
  ```

Then reload the rules with `sudo udevadm control --reload-rules && sudo udevadm trigger`, and unplug and replug the device.
docs.title: Drivers-USB#7

docs.body:
Kernel drivers: Serial Studio enables libusb's auto-detach on Linux, so a kernel class driver bound to the interface (for example `cdc_acm`) is detached when the interface is claimed and re-attached on release.
- **Windows.** The standard class drivers (HID, CDC and so on) hold the device open and stop libusb from claiming it, so the device needs a WinUSB driver. In [Zadig](https://zadig.akeo.ie), choose the device, select **WinUSB** and click **Replace Driver**. The device then stops appearing as a normal COM port or HID device until you restore the original driver.
- **macOS.** A device that no OS class driver has claimed opens directly. When macOS has bound a kernel driver, opening or claiming the interface fails, and Serial Studio does not detach system drivers.
docs.title: Drivers-USB#8

docs.body:
For step-by-step setup, see the [Protocol Setup Guides, Raw USB section](Protocol-Setup-Guides.md).

## Common pitfalls
docs.title: Drivers-USB#9

docs.body:
- **Device not listed.** If `lsusb` does not show it either, the cable, hub or power is at fault. `lsusb -v -d VID:PID` prints the descriptors.
- **Device is listed but will not open.** Another driver or application has claimed it, or you lack permission. Follow [Permissions and OS specifics](#permissions-and-os-specifics) for your OS; on Linux, `dmesg | grep usb` shows kernel hints.
- **No data on the IN endpoint.** Pick the endpoint number the vendor documentation names. Some devices send nothing until they receive a vendor control write; use the [control-transfer composer](#control-transfers).
- **Bulk reads time out.** A timeout is not an error: the read loop retries every 100 ms. A connection that stays open with nothing arriving means the device is not sending on the selected IN endpoint. Any other read error (unplug, stall, overflow) closes the connection and shows "The USB device was disconnected or encountered a fatal read error."
- **Isochronous mode drops samples.** **Max Packet Size** is pre-filled from the endpoint, so dropped samples with the default usually mean a manual override, or a host that cannot grant the bandwidth because other isochronous devices share the hub.
docs.title: Drivers-USB#10

docs.body:
## Reference

### Threading

The driver runs two dedicated threads:

- **Event thread.** Pumps libusb's event loop, which libusb's async API and hotplug callbacks require.
- **Read thread.** Issues synchronous bulk or interrupt reads (64 KB buffer, 100 ms timeout) in Bulk/Interrupt Stream and Advanced (Bulk + Control) modes. In Isochronous mode, data arrives through a pool of eight async transfers (eight packets each) whose completion callbacks run on the event thread.

Bulk and interrupt blocks are stamped the moment the transfer returns and published from the read thread. Isochronous blocks are stamped in the completion callback and published after a hop to the main thread. Either way the frame pipeline picks them up from there. See [Threading and Timing Guarantees](Threading-and-Timing.md).
docs.title: Drivers-USB#11

docs.body:
### Remote API commands

With the API Server enabled (off by default, port 7777), the in-app AI assistant and external clients configure this driver through the `io.usb.*` scope:
docs.title: Drivers-USB#12

docs.body:
| Command | Parameters | Notes |
|---------|------------|-------|
| `io.usb.listDevices` | none | Returns `devices` array and `selectedIndex` (index 0 is the "Select Device" placeholder) |
| `io.usb.setDeviceIndex` | `deviceIndex` (0 to the device count; 0 = **Select Device**) | Out-of-range values return an `InvalidParam` error |
| `io.usb.setTransferMode` | `mode` (0 = Bulk/Interrupt Stream, 1 = Advanced (Bulk + Control), 2 = Isochronous) | Mode 1 is refused until the warning was accepted once in the setup pane (see [Transfer modes](#transfer-modes)); verify with `io.usb.getConfig` |
| `io.usb.setInEndpointIndex` | `endpointIndex` (0 = **Select IN Endpoint** placeholder, 1.. = endpoints) | Endpoint lists populate once a device is selected; index 0 cannot connect; out-of-range returns `InvalidParam` |
| `io.usb.setOutEndpointIndex` | `endpointIndex` (0 = **None (Read-only)**, 1.. = endpoints) | Out-of-range returns `InvalidParam` |
| `io.usb.setIsoPacketSize` | `size` (1 to 49152 bytes) | |
| `io.usb.getConfig` | none | Returns mode, indices, packet size, and both endpoint lists |
docs.title: Drivers-USB#13

docs.body:
Transport details are in the [API Reference](API-Reference.md); command safety tiers are in [AI Assistant](AI-Assistant.md#the-safety-tiers).

## USB background

The host always asks; a USB device never speaks first. Each device has **endpoints**: unidirectional buffers identified by a number and a direction (IN = device to host, OUT = host to device). Endpoint 0 is the control endpoint, and every device has it. Serial Studio reads the rest from the device's descriptors, so you only pick from the list.

Each endpoint has one of four **transfer types**:
docs.title: Drivers-USB#14

docs.body:
- **Control** carries configuration and vendor commands over endpoint 0.
- **Bulk** carries large data with error checking and guaranteed delivery, but no bandwidth guarantee. Most raw data-acquisition devices use it.
- **Interrupt** carries small periodic data with a guaranteed maximum latency. There are no hardware interrupts; the host polls.
- **Isochronous** carries time-sensitive streams with guaranteed bandwidth and no retransmission. A corrupted packet is lost.

A device is identified by a 16-bit **Vendor ID (VID)** and **Product ID (PID)**, listed together as `VID:PID`, for example `1234:5678 – Acme Logic Analyzer`. The USB-IF assigns VIDs; the vendor chooses PIDs.
docs.title: Drivers-USB#15

docs.body:
Standard-class devices (CDC, HID, mass storage) get a generic OS driver, which is why a USB-CDC microcontroller shows up as a COM port with no install. Vendor-specific devices skip the classes, and libusb lets an application talk to their endpoints directly.

## Further reading

- [Beyond Logic: USB in a NutShell](https://www.beyondlogic.org/usbnutshell/usb1.shtml)
- [USB Endpoint Types (Beyond Logic Chapter 4)](https://www.beyondlogic.org/usbnutshell/usb4.shtml)
- [libusb-1.0 API Reference](https://libusb.sourceforge.io/api-1.0/)

## See also
docs.title: Drivers-USB#16

docs.body:
- [Protocol Setup Guides](Protocol-Setup-Guides.md): step-by-step Raw USB setup.
- [Troubleshooting](Troubleshooting.md): WinUSB, udev, and permission diagnostics.
- [Drivers: UART](Drivers-UART.md): for USB-CDC virtual serial ports.
- [Drivers: HID](Drivers-HID.md): for HID-class devices.
- [Devices](Devices.md): driver capability summary across all transports.
- [Use Cases](Use-Cases.md): logic analyzers, scientific instruments, and bulk-endpoint devices.
docs.title: Drivers-USB#17

docs.body:
# Extensions

Your board already prints values. A color theme your whole team likes, a ready-made `.ssproj` for a common sensor, or a Python script that logs frames to a database was probably written by someone else already. Extensions are how you get it: open the **Extension Manager**, pick one, click **Install**.

There are five types:
docs.title: Extensions#0

docs.body:
- **Themes** change the look of the whole application, including code editor syntax colors.
- **Frame parsers** are JavaScript functions that decode a custom binary or text protocol. You only need one if your device sends something other than plain text lines.
- **Project templates** are ready-to-use `.ssproj` project files for common sensor setups.
- **Widgets** are QML dashboard visualizations that render live data like a built-in widget. A widget runs inside Serial Studio with the application's own privileges, so it asks for consent before it renders (see [Widget Extension Development](Widget-Extension-Development.md)).
- **Plugins** are external programs (Python, native binaries) that connect to the API Server to process or display live data.
docs.title: Extensions#1

docs.body:
Quickest test: **Extensions** > filter **Themes** > pick one > **Install** > choose it in **Preferences > General**.

Extensions are downloaded from online repositories and installed locally. Browsing and installing needs an internet connection, because the catalog is fetched from the repository each time you click **Refresh**.

## Opening the Extension Manager

Click the **Extensions** button in the toolbar. The Extension Manager has three views:

- **Grid view** lists available extensions, with a search field and a type filter. When the grid is empty, the catalog has not loaded: check your connection and click **Refresh**.
- **Detail view** shows the README, metadata, screenshot and the install and uninstall controls.
- **Repositories view** manages repository URLs. It opens from the **Repos** button, which exists only in the commercial (Pro) build; a trial or license does not add it to the free build (see [Managing repositories](#managing-repositories-pro)).
docs.title: Extensions#2

docs.body:
## Installing an extension

1. Open the Extension Manager.
2. Click **Refresh** to fetch the latest catalog.
3. Browse or search for an extension. Use the type dropdown to filter by Themes, Plugins, and so on.
4. Click an extension card to open the detail view.
5. Click **Install**. A progress bar shows download status.
6. Serial Studio makes the extension available according to its type:
docs.title: Extensions#3

docs.body:
| Type | After install |
|------|---------------|
| Theme | Appears in the theme dropdown in **Preferences > General**. **Get Themes…** beside the dropdown opens this catalog filtered to themes. |
| Plugin | Click **Run** in the detail view. |
| Frame parser | Copied to the [Extensions folder](#installed-extension-location) as a `.js` file. In the frame parser editor of the Project Editor, click **Open** in its toolbar (it imports a script file) and pick that file. |
| Project template | Copied to the [Extensions folder](#installed-extension-location) as an `.ssproj` file. Click **Open Project** in the toolbar to load it. |
| Widget | Restart Serial Studio. The widget then appears in the Project Editor's Widget list, where you pick a widget for a group or dataset. The first time it renders, a dialog asks you to allow it, because a widget runs with Serial Studio's own permissions. The answer is stored per package version, so an updated widget asks again. |
docs.title: Extensions#4

docs.body:
## Uninstalling an extension

1. Open the Extension Manager and find the installed extension (it shows an **Installed** badge).
2. For plugins: click **Stop** first if it is running. A process that is still writing to its folder does not enjoy being deleted.
3. Click the card, then click **Uninstall**.
4. If you were using the uninstalled theme, Serial Studio falls back to **Default**.

## Updating an extension

When a newer version is available, the card shows an **Update** badge. Click the card and press **Install** to update.
docs.title: Extensions#5

docs.body:
Serial Studio can also check for you. In **Preferences > Startup**, **Check for Extension Updates** looks for newer versions of installed extensions, and **Install Extension Updates Automatically** skips the question. Without the second option, a prompt lists the extensions and offers **Yes**, **No** and **Always update**. Choosing **Always update** turns on **Install Extension Updates Automatically**. With **Check for Extension Updates** off, nothing is checked. If you decline, Serial Studio does not ask about those extensions again until you restart it.

## Plugins

A plugin is a separate program that talks to Serial Studio while it runs: it receives live data, computes statistics, draws its own windows. Both ways of connecting belong to the API Server, a local network port Serial Studio opens so other programs can read your data. It is off by default. Turn it on with **Preferences > General > API & Plugins > Enable API Server**, or let **Run** do it when it asks.
docs.title: Extensions#6

docs.body:
- **gRPC (port 8888)** is high-performance binary streaming, recommended for real-time frame data. The gRPC server runs only while the API Server is enabled, and only in builds with gRPC support. See the [gRPC Server](gRPC-Server.md) docs.
- **TCP/JSON (port 7777)** is a JSON-based protocol. See the [API Reference](API-Reference.md) for details.

### Running a plugin

1. Install the plugin from the Extension Manager.
2. Click the plugin card to open the detail view.
3. Click **Run**. The plugin starts, and its output appears in the log panel.
4. Click **Stop** to terminate it.

### Plugin requirements
docs.title: Extensions#7

docs.body:
- The API Server must be enabled. If it is off when you click **Run**, Serial Studio shows an **API Server Required** prompt that offers to turn it on; answering **No** cancels the launch.
- Python plugins need Python installed.
- Plugins that use gRPC need the `grpcio` Python package. Repository plugins include a launcher script that installs it into a local virtual environment on first run.
- Running plugins are stopped when the dashboard goes away (the device disconnects or the file player closes) and when Serial Studio exits. They relaunch when the dashboard comes back, unless you stopped them by hand.
docs.title: Extensions#8

docs.body:
### Platform support

If a plugin is not available for your platform, the **Install** button is disabled and an **Unavailable** badge is shown.

> Building your own plugin? See the [Plugin Development](Plugin-Development.md) guide for the full `info.json` reference, code examples, state persistence, and distribution instructions.

## Repositories

A repository is a URL pointing to a `manifest.json` file that lists available extensions. Serial Studio is bundled with a default community repository, and **Refresh** downloads its catalog over the internet. Every edition can install from it; adding your own repositories is a Pro feature.
docs.title: Extensions#9

docs.body:
### Managing repositories (Pro)

The **Repos** button in the Extension Manager toolbar exists only in the commercial (Pro) build; the free build does not show it. With it you can add:

- Company-internal repositories on your intranet (served over HTTPS) or a private GitHub.
- Third-party collections hosted anywhere.
- A local folder, while you develop extensions.

To manage repositories:

1. Open the Extension Manager.
2. Click the **Repos** button in the toolbar.
3. Add URLs, click **Browse…** to pick a local folder, or remove existing entries. Accepted values are a local folder or an `https://` URL; plain `http://` is refused with "Repositories must be a local folder or an https:// URL." Adding or removing an entry refreshes the catalog immediately.
4. Click **Reset** to restore the default community repository. This also uninstalls every installed extension, stops running plugins and removes your custom repositories; a **Reset Extensions** confirmation asks first.
docs.title: Extensions#10

docs.body:
## Plugin state persistence

Plugin state, such as open windows and settings, is saved in the project file alongside widget layout data. Different projects can have different plugin setups.

A plugin has to ask for its state to be saved: Serial Studio never calls `extensions.saveState` on its own. State is restored when the plugin starts or when a new device connects. Plugins that were running when you closed Serial Studio start again the next time you connect a device or open a file, unless you stopped them yourself.

For details on using the state persistence API from code, see the [Plugin Development](Plugin-Development.md) guide.
docs.title: Extensions#11

docs.body:
## API access

The Extension Manager is available over the [API Server](API-Reference.md), which is off by default; enable it in **Preferences > General > API & Plugins** first. Connect on TCP port 7777, or on [gRPC](gRPC-Server.md) port 8888 in builds with gRPC support:
docs.title: Extensions#12

docs.body:
| Command                         | Description |
|---------------------------------|-------------|
| `extensions.list`               | List all available extensions. |
| `extensions.getInfo`            | Get details for a specific extension (`extensionId`). |
| `extensions.install`            | Install an extension by index (`addonIndex`). |
| `extensions.uninstall`          | Uninstall an extension by index (`addonIndex`). Destructive: removes the extension files irreversibly. Pass `dryRun:true` to preview the removal without committing it. |
| `extensions.refresh`            | Refresh catalogs from all repositories. |
| `extensions.saveState`          | Save plugin state to the project (`pluginId`, `state`). |
| `extensions.loadState`          | Load plugin state from the project (`pluginId`). |
| `extensions.listRepositories`   | List repository URLs. Pro only. |
| `extensions.addRepository`      | Add a repository URL (`url`). Pro only. |
| `extensions.removeRepository`   | Remove a repository by index (`index`). Pro only. |
docs.title: Extensions#13

docs.body:
The three repository commands are not registered at all in the free build.

## Installed extension location

Extensions are installed under `Extensions/` in your workspace folder, `Documents/Serial Studio` by default. Change the folder with **Workspace Folder** in **Preferences > General**. Each extension gets its own folder, `<type>/<id>/`:

```text
Documents/Serial Studio/Extensions/
  installed.json
  theme/my-theme/
    info.json
    my-theme.json
    code-editor/my-theme.xml
  plugin/my-plugin/
    info.json
    plugin.py
    run.sh
    run.cmd
```

## Creating extensions

This part is for extension authors. Installing only? You are done here.
docs.title: Extensions#14

docs.body:
### Repository structure

Directory names are convention; the `type` field in `info.json` decides what an extension is.

```text
my-repo/
  manifest.json
  theme/my-theme/
    info.json
    my-theme.json
    code-editor/my-theme.xml
  plugin/my-plugin/
    info.json
    plugin.py
    run.sh
    run.cmd
  frame-parser/my-parser/
    info.json
    my-parser.js
  project-template/my-template/
    info.json
    my-template.ssproj
  widget/com.example.level-bar/
    info.json
    LevelBar.qml
```

### `manifest.json`

The manifest lists paths to each extension's `info.json`:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "repository": "My Extensions",
  "extensions": [
    "theme/my-theme/info.json",
    "plugin/my-plugin/info.json"
  ]
}
```
docs.title: Extensions#15

docs.body:
### `info.json` format

Each extension has an `info.json` with metadata:

```json
{
  "id": "my-theme",
  "type": "theme",
  "title": "My Custom Theme",
  "description": "A dark theme with company branding.",
  "author": "Your Name",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "license": "MIT",
  "category": "Dark",
  "screenshot": "screenshot.png",
  "files": [
    "info.json",
    "my-theme.json",
    "code-editor/my-theme.xml"
  ]
}
```

#### Plugin `info.json`

Plugins add `entry`, `runtime`, and optionally `platforms` and `grpc` fields.

A plugin lists the platforms it supports in its `platforms` field; Serial Studio picks the matching entry. Matching tries the exact `os/arch` key first, then `os/*` for every architecture of one system, then a bare `*`. It reads `aarch64` as `arm64` and `amd64` as `x86_64`. Valid keys: `darwin/*` (always universal), `linux/x86_64`, `linux/arm64`, `windows/*`, `windows/x86_64`.
docs.title: Extensions#16

docs.body:
See the [Plugin Development](Plugin-Development.md) guide for the full reference and examples.

#### Widget `info.json`

Widgets add a `widget` block declaring the entity scope, the QML entry file, what data the widget accepts, and its settings. See the [Widget Extension Development](Widget-Extension-Development.md) guide for the full reference, the data model, and the trust model.

#### Field reference
docs.title: Extensions#17

docs.body:
| Field         | Required | Description |
|---------------|----------|-------------|
| `id`          | Yes      | Unique identifier (lowercase, hyphens; the widget example uses dots, as in `com.example.level-bar`). |
| `type`        | Yes      | `theme`, `frame-parser`, `project-template`, `widget`, or `plugin`. |
| `title`       | Yes      | Display name in the Extension Manager. |
| `description` | Yes      | Short description shown on the card. |
| `author`      | Yes      | Author name or organization. |
| `version`     | Yes      | Semantic version string (for example `"1.0.0"`). |
| `license`     | No       | License identifier (for example `"MIT"`). |
| `category`    | No       | Category for filtering. |
| `screenshot`  | No       | Relative path to a preview image. |
| `files`       | Yes      | Array of relative file paths to download/install. |
| `entry`       | Plugins  | Script or binary entry point. |
| `runtime`     | Plugins  | Interpreter command (for example `"python3"`). Empty for native binaries. |
| `terminal`    | Plugins  | `true` to launch in a system terminal window. |
| `grpc`        | Plugins  | `true` if the plugin uses gRPC streaming (port 8888) instead of TCP/JSON. |
| `platforms`   | Plugins  | Per-platform overrides for `entry`, `runtime`, and `files`. |
docs.title: Extensions#18

docs.body:
### Theme materials and lettering

To use a theme rather than write one, see **Preferences > General** or the quick test at the top of this page.

A Serial Studio theme extension (type `theme`) is a JSON color table: `title`, `translations`, `parameters` and `colors`. Five optional sections extend it (`fonts`, `materials`, `surfaces`, `styles`, `widgets`), and `parameters` accepts one new key, `icon-pack`. A theme without them looks exactly as it always did, and an older Serial Studio reads the same file as a color-only theme, so keep the color table complete.
docs.title: Extensions#19
Extensions#20

docs.body:
| Section | What it does |
|---------|--------------|
| `fonts` | Named lettering roles. `engraving` is used for dashboard widget titles and control legends. The family must already be installed on the computer; when it is not, or for text it has no glyphs for, the interface font is used. Leave the section out to keep the interface fonts. |
| `materials` | Named surfaces. `recipe` is `flat` (`color`), `gradient` (`top`, `bottom`), `brushed-metal` (`color`, `grain` from 0 to 1, `shade` from 0 to 1 for the top-to-bottom lighting, `bevel` true or false for the edge lines) or `glass` (`top`, `bottom`). |
| `surfaces` | Which material a part of the window is made of: `dashboard` (behind the widgets) and `widget` (the body of a dashboard widget). |
| `styles` | Per-control rules. `instrument.face` is the dial and bar-well color, apart from the plot area. `instrument.band-opacity` (0 to 1) is the strength of alarm bands on bars. `instrument.marker` is the color of a bar's value mark (`"level"` takes a darker shade of the bar's current color). `caption.active-lift` (for example 1.14) makes the focused dashboard window's caption lighter at the top; both states share the bottom color. |
| `widgets` | `"led": "lamp"` draws LED Panel indicators as panel lamps. Standard output buttons are drawn as panel push buttons; `"output": "plain"` keeps the flat button. |
| `parameters` | Beside `code-editor-theme` and `start-icon`, an optional `"icon-pack"` names the bundled icon pack the theme looks best with (`fluent`, `glass`, `outline`). It applies while the user's pack preference is *Follow theme*; a name this build does not bundle falls back to the standard set. A theme carries no icon artwork of its own. |
docs.title: Extensions#21

docs.body:
A theme is data. It selects recipes Serial Studio already has and cannot load a file or run anything. A name Serial Studio does not know is skipped with a warning in the log.

### Hosting

On GitHub, create a repository and share the raw manifest URL:

```text
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/your-org/extensions/main/manifest.json
```

For a local folder, click **Repos** in the Extension Manager toolbar (Pro), then **Browse…** to pick a folder that contains `manifest.json`. Any web server also works if it serves HTTPS, and relative paths in `files` resolve against the `info.json` URL. Plain `http://` URLs are refused.
docs.title: Extensions#22

docs.body:
# Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

If your Arduino already prints values with `Serial.println`, start with [I have an Arduino printing values](#i-have-an-arduino-printing-values-what-do-i-do).

Connection problems: see [Serial Studio doesn't detect my serial port](#serial-studio-doesnt-detect-my-serial-port).

## General

### What is Serial Studio?

Serial Studio is an open source tool for visualizing data from devices in real time. You can monitor sensors, debug hardware, and build custom dashboards without writing code.

It works with devices on a serial port, Bluetooth LE, network sockets, MQTT, Modbus, CAN Bus and more; the full list is under [What devices does Serial Studio support?](#what-devices-does-serial-studio-support).
docs.title: FAQ#0
FAQ#1

docs.body:
Two plots appear, one per value. `Serial.println` ends each line with a newline, and that newline is what tells Quick Plot where a sample stops. For the other modes, see [What data format should my device send?](#what-data-format-should-my-device-send).

### Is Serial Studio open source?

The core is open source, with two flavors:
docs.title: FAQ#2

docs.body:
1. **GPL version (open source).** Built from source under GPL-3.0. Includes core features, but leaves out Pro modules like MQTT, Modbus, CAN Bus, 3D plotting, and the Waterfall widget. The GPL build never contains Pro modules; the official binary contains them but locks them without a license or trial. Pro features are proprietary even though their source is visible in the repo.
2. **Official binary (proprietary).** Runs the free features without a license and with no time limit. Pro features unlock with a license, or with a 14-day trial that Serial Studio offers the first time you use one. A Yes/No prompt asks, and registering the trial needs an internet connection. Individual, team, and test-stand plans are available as monthly, yearly, or lifetime licenses; check current pricing at [serial-studio.com/pricing](https://serial-studio.com/pricing).
docs.title: FAQ#3

docs.body:
If you downloaded the installer from GitHub releases or serial-studio.com, you have the official binary. Pro features are proprietary, not open source. See the [License Agreement](License-Agreement.md) and [Free vs Pro](#free-vs-pro) for details.

### What platforms does Serial Studio support?

- **Windows:** Windows 10/11 (x64).
- **macOS:** macOS 14+ (universal binary: Intel and Apple Silicon).
- **Linux:** x64 via AppImage or Flatpak.
- **Raspberry Pi:** ARM64 (Ubuntu 24.04+ or equivalent).

### How is Serial Studio different from the Arduino Serial Plotter?

The Arduino Serial Plotter is good for quick debugging, but it only works with serial ports and basic plots.
docs.title: FAQ#4

docs.body:
Serial Studio reads BLE, MQTT, Modbus, CAN Bus and sockets as well as serial ports, draws 15+ widget types (gauges, maps, FFT, accelerometers) from a dashboard you design in the Project Editor, and records to CSV. Binary and custom protocols go through a JavaScript, Lua or Built-In frame parser.

See [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md) for a detailed comparison.

### Can I use Serial Studio for commercial projects?

**Official binaries:** yes, with a Pro license. Without one, the free features are for personal, educational, and open-source use, and the 14-day trial covers evaluation only. Commercial use covers business use, revenue-generating projects, client-facing systems, and grant- or privately-funded research.
docs.title: FAQ#5

docs.body:
**GPL build:** yes. A build compiled from source with GPL modules only is GPLv3 software, and the GPLv3 permits commercial use. It doesn't include Pro features like MQTT, Modbus, CAN Bus, or 3D visualization; businesses that need those, the official binaries, or email support buy a Pro license or evaluate with the 14-day trial.

See the [License Agreement](License-Agreement.md) for the full dual-licensing details.

### How do I cite Serial Studio in academic papers?

```
Spataru, A. (2025). Serial Studio: Open-Source Telemetry Dashboard and Data Visualization Tool.
GitHub. https://github.com/Serial-Studio/Serial-Studio
```
docs.title: FAQ#6

docs.body:
## Installation and setup

### How do I install Serial Studio on Windows?

1. Download `Serial-Studio-Pro-4.x.x-Windows.msi` from [GitHub releases](https://github.com/Serial-Studio/Serial-Studio/releases). A portable build (`Serial-Studio-Pro-4.x.x-Windows-Portable.zip`) is also published if you prefer no installer.
2. Install the [Microsoft Visual C++ Redistributable](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/windows/latest-supported-vc-redist) if prompted.
3. Run the installer.
4. On first launch, Windows may show an "Unknown developer" warning. Click "More Info → Run Anyway".

### How do I install Serial Studio on macOS?
docs.title: FAQ#7

docs.body:
**Option 1: official DMG (recommended).**

1. Download `Serial-Studio-Pro-4.x.x-macOS.dmg` (universal binary) from [GitHub releases](https://github.com/Serial-Studio/Serial-Studio/releases).
2. Open the DMG.
3. Drag Serial Studio into Applications.
4. Open it from Spotlight or Finder.

**Option 2: Homebrew (community-maintained).**

```bash
brew install --cask serial-studio
```

### How do I install Serial Studio on Linux?

**Recommended: AppImage.**

```bash
# Download from GitHub releases
chmod +x Serial-Studio-Pro-4.x.x-Linux-x64.AppImage
./Serial-Studio-Pro-4.x.x-Linux-x64.AppImage
```

**Alternative: Flatpak (GPLv3).**
docs.title: FAQ#8

docs.body:
```bash
flatpak install flathub com.serial_studio.Serial-Studio
flatpak run com.serial_studio.Serial-Studio
```

### Why can't I access serial ports on Linux?

Your user needs permission to open serial devices, which on most distributions means joining a group and logging out and back in. The steps, including the group name on Arch-based systems, are in [Serial port permissions](Linux-Installation.md#serial-port-permissions).

### How do I build Serial Studio from source?

**Prerequisites:**

- Qt 6.11.2, the version the project is built against.
- A C++20 compiler.
- CMake 3.20+.

**Linux build:**
docs.title: FAQ#9

docs.body:
```bash
sudo apt install libgl1-mesa-dev build-essential
mkdir build && cd build
cmake ../ -DPRODUCTION_OPTIMIZATION=ON -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build . -j$(nproc)
```

For macOS and Windows, see [Getting Started](Getting-Started.md).

## Devices and protocols

### What devices does Serial Studio support?
docs.title: FAQ#10

docs.body:
- **Serial ports:** UART, RS232, RS485 (via USB-serial adapter).
- **Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE):** GATT characteristics.
- **MQTT:** publish/subscribe for IoT (Pro).
- **Modbus TCP/RTU:** industrial PLCs and equipment (Pro). See [Modbus](Drivers-Modbus.md).
- **OPC UA:** PLCs and SCADA servers (Pro). See [OPC UA](Drivers-OPC-UA.md).
- **Siemens S7, EtherNet/IP, IEC 60870-5-104:** controller and substation clients (Pro). See [S7](Drivers-S7.md), [EtherNet/IP](Drivers-EtherNet-IP.md), [IEC 104](Drivers-IEC-104.md).
- **CAN Bus:** automotive and industrial networks (Pro).
- **TCP/UDP sockets, WebSocket and HTTP:** network-connected devices.
- **Audio input:** microphone, line-in (Pro).
- **Raw USB:** bulk and isochronous transfers via libusb (Pro).
- **HID devices:** gamepads, sensors, and custom USB HIDs via hidapi (Pro).
- **Process I/O:** pipe stdout from any program or named pipe into the dashboard (Pro).
- **CSV files:** replay previously recorded telemetry.
- **MDF4/MF4 files:** play automotive measurement files (CAN Bus, LIN, FlexRay, analog) (Pro).
docs.title: FAQ#11

docs.body:
### How do I connect to a serial port?

1. Plug in your device.
2. In the Device Setup panel, set **Connection** to **UART/COM**.
3. Pick your serial port from the dropdown.
4. Set the baud rate (9600 and 115200 are common).
5. Click **Connect**.

If you don't see your device, check drivers (FTDI, CH340, CP2102) and permissions (on Linux, see [Serial port permissions](Linux-Installation.md#serial-port-permissions)).

### Can I connect multiple devices at once?

Yes (Pro). Multi-device projects let you define several devices in a single project file, each with its own protocol, connection settings, and frame detection. For example, all at the same time you can connect:
docs.title: FAQ#12

docs.body:
- An Arduino over UART at 115200 baud.
- An ESP32 over Bluetooth LE.
- A PLC over Modbus TCP.

All devices feed into the same dashboard. Each source's data is routed to its own groups and widgets. CSV and MDF4 export captures every source in one file.

To set this up, open the Project Editor and add sources under the "Sources" section. Each source defines a bus type, connection parameters, and frame parsing rules.

### How do I connect via Bluetooth Low Energy?

1. Select **Bluetooth LE** as the Connection.
2. Wait for device discovery to finish.
3. Select your device and characteristic UUID.
4. Click **Connect**.
docs.title: FAQ#13

docs.body:
### How do I receive data via MQTT?

Pro only (MQTT is locked in the GPL build and in the official binary without a license or trial). You need a broker (Mosquitto, HiveMQ, AWS IoT) that your devices publish to.

1. In the Device Setup panel, set **Connection** to **MQTT Subscriber**.
2. Enter the broker **Hostname** and **Port** (for example `broker.hivemq.com` and `1883`).
3. Enter the **Topic Filter** to subscribe to (for example `sensors/temperature`).
4. Click **Connect**.

Each message on the topic is one frame, so a device publishing `23.5,67.2` plots two values. Credentials, TLS and Sparkplug are in [MQTT Subscriber](Drivers-MQTT.md).
docs.title: FAQ#14

docs.body:
### How do I use Modbus?

Pro only. Both Modbus TCP and Modbus RTU are supported.

**Modbus TCP:**

1. Set up a Modbus TCP server (industrial PLC, simulator, or Python script).
2. Select **Modbus** as the Connection.
3. Enter the server address (for example `192.168.1.100:502`).
4. Configure registers to read in your project file.
5. Click **Connect**.

**Modbus RTU:**

1. Connect your Modbus RTU device to a serial port.
2. Select **Modbus** as the Connection.
3. Pick the serial port and set baud rate, parity, and stop bits.
4. Configure registers to read in your project file.
5. Click **Connect**.
docs.title: FAQ#15

docs.body:
The Modbus PLC Simulator example has a full demo: open the **Examples** toolbar button (it downloads the example projects from GitHub on first use, so it needs an internet connection) or browse the [examples folder](https://github.com/Serial-Studio/Serial-Studio/tree/master/examples).

### How do I use CAN Bus?

Pro only.

1. Install CAN hardware drivers (or use VirtualCAN for testing).
2. Select **CAN Bus** as the Connection.
3. Choose a driver (VirtualCAN, SocketCAN, PEAK, Vector, and so on).
4. Select an interface and bitrate.
5. Import a DBC file to build the dashboard automatically.
6. Click **Connect**.
docs.title: FAQ#16

docs.body:
The CAN Bus example under **Examples** has step-by-step instructions. See also [CAN Bus](Drivers-CAN-Bus.md).

### How do I play MDF4/MF4 files?

Pro only. MDF4 (Measurement Data Format 4) is the recording format of automotive and industrial loggers.

1. Click the **Open MDF4** button in the toolbar.
2. Select your MDF4/MF4 file.

Serial Studio builds a dashboard from the channels in the file and shows playback controls (play, pause, seek). See [MDF4](MDF4.md) for supported channel types.

### How do I export data to MDF4 format?

Pro only.

1. In the Device Setup panel, turn on **MDF4 Recording** under Data Export.
2. Connect and receive data from any source.
docs.title: FAQ#17

docs.body:
Serial Studio writes the received data to a timestamped MDF4 file. See [MDF4](MDF4.md) for details.

### How do I connect via TCP/UDP?

1. Set **Connection** to **Network**, then set the socket type to TCP or UDP.
2. Enter the **Remote Address** (the device's IP address or hostname) and **Remote Port** (the device's listening port for TCP, or the port it sends to for UDP).
3. For UDP, also set the **Local Port** field — the port Serial Studio binds to receive datagrams. Set it to the port the device sends to (8080 in the example below). With `0` the OS picks a random port and nothing reaches Serial Studio.
4. Click **Connect**.
docs.title: FAQ#18

docs.body:
Example: a Python script sending UDP to Serial Studio:

```python
import socket
import time

temperature, humidity = 23.5, 61.0
sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
while True:
    data = f"{temperature},{humidity}\n"
    sock.sendto(data.encode(), ("127.0.0.1", 8080))
    time.sleep(1)
```

### What data format should my device send?

Serial Studio works in three modes, chosen with **Operation Mode** in the Device Setup panel. A frame is one line of data from your device.

**1. Console Only (No Parsing).**

- No parsing, no dashboard. Raw bytes flow straight to the terminal.
- Use it to check that the device is alive and that the baud rate and framing are correct.
docs.title: FAQ#19

docs.body:
**2. Quick Plot (Auto-Detected Format).**

- Send one line of values per sample, separated by comma, semicolon, tab or space (`23.5,67.2,1013.25\n`), or name:value pairs (`temp:23.5`).
- Serial Studio shows plots automatically.

**3. Parse via Project File.**

- Create a `.ssproj` project file with your dashboard layout in the Project Editor.
- The device sends raw data (CSV, binary, or a custom format).
- Serial Studio interprets it based on the project file and its optional Lua or JavaScript frame parser.

See [Operation Modes](Operation-Modes.md) and [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md) for more.
docs.title: FAQ#20

docs.body:
## Dashboard configuration

### How do I create a custom dashboard?

**Method 1: Project Editor (easy).**

1. Click **Project Editor** in the toolbar.
2. Click **New Project**.
3. Add groups (containers for your data).
4. Add datasets to each group.
5. Pick a widget for each dataset (gauge, plot, map, and so on).
6. Add units, min/max values, and labels.
7. Save the project file (`.ssproj`).
8. Load the project in Serial Studio.

**Method 2: edit JSON by hand.** Not recommended unless you're generating projects with scripts.

### What widgets are available?

**Free edition (also in Pro):**

- Line plots (single and multi-dataset).
- Bar charts.
- Gauges (circular and linear).
- Compass.
- Data grids and tables.
- Accelerometer (3-axis).
- Gyroscope (3-axis).
- FFT spectrum analyzer.
- GPS maps (ArcGIS / Esri map tiles).
- LED panel.
- Terminal.
- XY plots (parametric plots): set a plot's X axis to another dataset.
docs.title: FAQ#21

docs.body:
**Pro only:**

- 3D plots.
- Waterfall (scrolling spectrogram with order tracking).
- Image View (live JPEG/PNG camera feed widget).
- Canvas (scriptable Canvas2D-style widget).
- Output widgets: buttons, toggles, sliders, knobs, text fields, and the Output Panel (see [Output Controls](Output-Controls.md)).

### How do I export data to CSV?

1. In the Device Setup panel, turn on **CSV Spreadsheet** under Data Export.
2. Serial Studio saves all received data to a timestamped CSV file.
3. Turn the switch off to stop logging.

**CSV format:**

```
Elapsed (s),Group/Dataset 1,Group/Dataset 2,...
0.010000000,...
0.020000000,...
```
docs.title: FAQ#22

docs.body:
The first column is elapsed seconds with 9-decimal resolution. With multiple sources, the value columns are named `Source/Group/Dataset`.

### Can I change the application theme?

Yes. Click **Preferences → Theme** and pick one. [Preferences](Preferences.md) lists every setting in the dialog.

### Can I change the icon style?

Yes. **Preferences → Icon Pack** lists the bundled packs.
*Follow theme* (the default) uses the pack the theme names, or the standard set when it names none.
*Office* pins that standard set under every theme.
The colour icons of the toolbar, the Project Editor, the dashboard and the dialogs change; the button glyphs and window controls do not.
A mono pack is drawn in the theme's text colour.
The change applies immediately, without a restart.
docs.title: FAQ#23

docs.body:
### Can I turn off the interface animations?

Yes. Enable **Preferences → Startup → System → Reduce Motion**. Menus, dialogs, and buttons stop scaling, sliding, and bouncing; short fades remain. The change applies immediately, without a restart.

Reduce Motion is on by default when the rendering backend is **Software (Fallback)**, where every animated frame is drawn by the CPU. Dashboard widgets are not affected: gauge needles, bars, and compasses keep following the data.

### Does Serial Studio support HDR displays?

Yes, on macOS and Windows. Enable **Preferences → Startup → Graphics → HDR Output** and restart. Needles, lit lamps, and plot lines then glow brighter than the rest of the interface. See [HDR Output](Preferences.md#hdr-output).
docs.title: FAQ#24

docs.body:
### How do I calibrate or filter a dataset value?

Use a **Dataset Value Transform** (Pro; opening the Transform editor and connecting with a transform in the project both need a license or trial). Transforms can be written in Lua or JavaScript. Select any dataset in the Project Editor, click the **Transform** button in the toolbar, and write a `transform(value)` function:

```lua
function transform(value)
  return value * 0.01 + 273.15
end
```

The transform runs on every incoming frame and replaces the raw value everywhere: dashboard, plots, CSV export, and API. Built-in templates cover common operations like linear calibration, moving average, and unit conversion.
docs.title: FAQ#25

docs.body:
See [Dataset Value Transforms](Dataset-Transforms.md) for the full guide.

## Troubleshooting

### Serial Studio doesn't detect my serial port

**Windows:**

- Check Device Manager for the COM port number.
- Install the driver (FTDI, CH340, CP2102).
- Try a different USB cable (data, not charge-only).

**macOS:**

- Install a driver if needed (modern macOS includes most).
- Check `/dev/tty.usbserial-*` or `/dev/tty.usbmodem-*`.

**Linux:**

- Give your user serial access: see [Serial port permissions](Linux-Installation.md#serial-port-permissions).
- Check `/dev/ttyUSB*` or `/dev/ttyACM*`.
- Check permissions: `ls -l /dev/ttyUSB0`.
docs.title: FAQ#26

docs.body:
### I see garbled data or strange characters

**Baud rate.** This is the most common cause: a clean sensor at the wrong rate prints noise. Make sure Serial Studio's baud rate matches the device (9600 or 115200 are common).

**Data bits, parity, stop bits.** Default: 8N1 (8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit). Change **Data Bits**, **Parity** and **Stop Bits** in the UART section of the **Device Setup** panel; see [UART](Drivers-UART.md).

**Frame delimiters.** A frame is one line of data, and Serial Studio ends it at a newline (`\n`) by default. In Quick Plot mode, end lines with `\n` or `\r`; there is no setting to change. In Parse via Project File mode, set the source's **Frame Detection Method** and delimiters in the Project Editor.
docs.title: FAQ#27

docs.body:
### My plots look wrong or don't update

**Quick Plot mode:**

- Make sure each line is numbers, one line per sample (`val1,val2,val3\n`); a text-only line is ignored.
- Named values (`temp:23.5`) keep their channel even when a line omits one.
- End each frame with a newline (`\n`) or a carriage return (`\r`).

**Project File mode:**

- Check that the project file matches your data format.
- Check frame start/end sequences in project settings.
- Check the frame parser code.

### How do I parse binary or custom protocols?

Use a **frame parser**. Parsers can be written in JavaScript or Lua, or configured (not coded) as a Built-In template; see [Frame Parser Scripting](Frame-Parser.md). This JavaScript example is for binary frames, where `frame` is an array of byte values and each frame is two big-endian bytes; for CSV text, keep the default parser.
docs.title: FAQ#28
FAQ#29

docs.body:
### Serial Studio crashes or freezes

Report it as described in [How do I report a bug?](#how-do-i-report-a-bug). The [Problem Center](Problem-Center.md) and [Troubleshooting](Troubleshooting.md) cover the common causes.

### AppImage won't launch on Linux

**Error: `fuse: failed to exec fusermount`.**

The AppImage mounts itself through FUSE. Without it, extract and run the contents instead:

```bash
./Serial-Studio-Pro-*.AppImage --appimage-extract
./squashfs-root/AppRun
```

**Error: `version 'GLIBC_x.yy' not found`.**

Current packages bundle their own glibc and run on any distribution from the Debian 10 / RHEL 8 generation onward, so this error only appears with releases up to 4.0.3. Update to a newer release.

## Free vs Pro

### What features are in Free vs Pro?

Free means the unlicensed official binary and the GPL build; Pro means the official binary with a license or trial. Serial/UART, TCP/UDP, BLE, the standard widgets, Quick Plot, Project File mode, frame parsers and CSV export and playback are free. MQTT, Modbus, CAN Bus, OPC UA, S7, EtherNet/IP, IEC 104, audio, raw USB, HID, Process I/O, 3D, Waterfall, Image View, Canvas, output widgets, multi-device projects, dataset transforms, MDF4, the Historian and the AI Assistant are Pro. [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md) holds the complete table and is the authoritative list.

### How much does Pro cost?

Check current pricing at [serial-studio.com/pricing](https://serial-studio.com/pricing). Pro
is sold as monthly, yearly, or lifetime licenses, in these seat tiers:

- **Pro:** for individuals, 3 device activations.

Monthly and yearly plans renew until cancelled; the lifetime and Test Stand

docs.body:
### Can I try Pro features before buying?

Yes. The official binary runs the free features without a license. The first time you use a Pro feature, Serial Studio asks whether to start a 14-day trial with all Pro features enabled. Starting it needs an internet connection; it needs no account and no payment.

After 14 days:

- The next Pro feature opens a prompt that offers activation or purchase. Enter a license key to keep using Pro features.
- Or keep using the free features, with no time limit (MQTT, 3D, and the other Pro features lock).

### I'm a student or educator. Is there a discount?
docs.title: FAQ#33

docs.body:
There is no separate academic discount. For coursework and research that the core protocols and standard widgets support, the GPLv3 source build is free and covers that use. Universities and research institutions buy commercial licenses when they need Pro features, official binaries, or support, like any other organization.

### Can I use Pro features in open source projects?

If you have a Pro license, yes, you can use all features in your open source work.

Pro features are proprietary even though their source code is visible in the repo. If you ship your project under GPL and your users build Serial Studio from source, they won't get Pro features (MQTT, Modbus, CAN Bus, 3D, and so on) unless they buy licenses.

### Can Serial Studio control my Arduino (send data back)?

Yes. The Console panel has a send line: type text (or hex), pick a line ending, and Serial Studio writes it back to the connected device. You can also append a checksum to the outgoing bytes.

**Other options:**
docs.title: FAQ#39

docs.body:
- Add [Output Controls](Output-Controls.md) (Pro): buttons, toggles, sliders, knobs, and text fields on the dashboard. Each one runs a JavaScript template (GCode, SCPI, Modbus, NMEA, custom binary) that converts the control's state into outgoing bytes.
- Use a control loop. Each project can hold an Arduino-style script with `setup()` and `loop()` functions that runs in the background, so you can send commands on a timer or in response to incoming data, and drive the whole session from code. It uses the same scripting API as the frame parser.
- Write a [plugin application](https://github.com/Serial-Studio/Serial-Studio/tree/master/app/src/API) in your preferred language or framework that shares the device with Serial Studio.
- Use MQTT (Pro). Serial Studio can publish commands to MQTT topics that your device subscribes to.

## Advanced topics

### Can I integrate Serial Studio with my CI/CD pipeline?

Yes. Serial Studio accepts command-line options, including a `--headless` flag that runs without a GUI (server mode) and `--api-server` to expose the API server on startup. You can pass a project file, a connection (UART, TCP, UDP, Modbus, CAN Bus), and export options (CSV, MDF4) from the command line. For CI/CD:

- Drive a headless session from the command line, or
- Export CSV in real time, then run a script that watches the CSV file and validates the data.

Use either approach in CI/CD for hardware-in-the-loop testing.

### How do I contribute to Serial Studio?

See [README.md - Contributing](https://github.com/Serial-Studio/Serial-Studio#contributing) for guidelines.

**Quick start:**

1. Fork the repository.
2. Check the code style guidelines in the repo.

docs.body:
### Is there a command-line interface (CLI)?

Yes. Serial Studio accepts command-line options. Run it with `--help` to list them, or see the [Command-Line Interface](Command-Line-Interface.md) reference. Highlights:

- `--headless` runs without a GUI (server mode), and `--api-server` enables the API Server on startup (off by default; port 7777).
- You can pass a project file (`--project`), set up a connection (`--uart`, `--tcp`, `--udp`, and on Pro builds `--modbus-*` and `--canbus`), and enable exports (`--csv-export`, `--mdf-export`) from the command line.
- `--activate`/`--deactivate` manage a license key for CI/headless setup (Pro builds).

docs.body:
### Does Serial Studio have an API for external tools?

Yes. The API Server is off by default. Turn on **Enable API Server** in Preferences (General tab), or start with `--api-server`, and a JSON-RPC API with 440+ commands listens on TCP port 7777. The gRPC server (port 8888) and an MCP (Model Context Protocol) wrapper run on the same command surface, and only while the API Server is on. Scripts and AI agents can read live values, edit projects, manage sessions, and control exports. See [API Reference](API-Reference.md) and [gRPC Server](gRPC-Server.md).

### Does Serial Studio include an AI assistant?
docs.title: FAQ#44

docs.body:
Yes (Pro). The in-app AI Assistant is a bring-your-own-key chat panel that works with Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini, and other providers, including OpenAI-compatible local servers for offline use. Read-only commands run automatically, anything that mutates the project shows an Approve/Deny card, and device control (connect/disconnect, port settings) stays blocked unless you enable the **Allow device control** toggle. See [AI Assistant](AI-Assistant.md).

### Can Serial Studio run on Raspberry Pi?

Yes, if you have:

- A 64-bit OS (Ubuntu 24.04+ or equivalent).
- The ARM64 AppImage (from GitHub releases).
docs.title: FAQ#45

docs.body:
Performance depends on the Pi model and the connected display. Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 with 4 GB+ of RAM is a good starting point.

Alternatively, use the Pi as a data aggregator: collect sensor data and forward it to Serial Studio running on a desktop.

### Can I use Serial Studio for audio signal analysis?

Pro only (audio input).

1. Select **Audio** as the Connection.
2. Choose an audio input device (microphone, line-in).
3. Use the FFT plot to see the frequency spectrum.
4. Plot a channel with a line plot for the waveform.

See [Audio](Drivers-Audio.md).

### Can Serial Studio display live camera or image data?
docs.title: FAQ#46

docs.body:
Pro only (Image View widget).

Serial Studio can display live JPEG, PNG, BMP, or WebP images streamed from any connected device over any supported transport (UART, UDP, TCP, BLE, and so on).

The Image View widget runs an independent frame reader alongside the telemetry path. It scans the raw byte stream for image data without interfering with CSV or JSON telemetry in the same stream.

**Two detection modes:**

- **Autodetect (default).** No configuration needed. The widget automatically detects JPEG, PNG, BMP and WebP frames by their magic bytes (for example JPEG runs `FF D8 FF … FF D9`, PNG starts `89 50 4E 47` and ends with `IEND`). A good fit for embedded cameras streaming raw JPEG.
- **Manual delimiters.** Specify custom start/end byte sequences for proprietary framing (for example `$IMG_START$…$IMG_END$`). Configure them in the Project Editor group settings.
docs.title: FAQ#47

docs.body:
**Quick setup:**

1. In the Project Editor, add a new group and set its widget type to **Image View**.
2. Leave detection mode as **Autodetect** (works for most cameras with no setup).
3. Load your project and connect. The widget shows "Waiting for image…" until the first frame arrives.

**Mixed telemetry and image stream.**

You can send image data and telemetry (gauges, plots, and so on) over the same connection at the same time. The Image View widget extracts image frames by magic bytes. The normal telemetry parser ignores binary image data between its `frameStart`/`frameEnd` delimiters. See the **Camera Telemetry** example in `/examples` for a full Python + project file demo.

docs.body:
# File transmission (Pro)

Your board has a bootloader that waits for a firmware image on the serial port, or a sketch that reads configuration lines. File Transmission sends that file from Serial Studio over the connection that is already open. Typical jobs: flashing an image through a bootloader, loading a script onto a controller, replaying a list of AT commands.

The device has to be listening for the file. Serial Studio cannot make a board accept one: a sketch that only calls `Serial.println` ignores an XMODEM transfer.

The lowest-risk first transfer needs no handshake. Flash this sketch, which echoes each line it receives:
docs.title: File-Transmission#0
File-Transmission#1

docs.body:
## Send a file

1. Connect to the device.
2. Open **File Transmission** (see [Opening the File Transmission dialog](#opening-the-file-transmission-dialog)).
3. Pick the mode in **Transfer Protocol**.
4. Click **Select File...** and choose the file.
5. Adjust the settings the chosen mode shows (see the [Settings reference](#settings-reference)).
6. For XMODEM, XMODEM-1K, YMODEM and ZMODEM, make your device (the receiver) start waiting for the file. That is a bootloader or firmware action, not a Serial Studio setting. Then click **Begin Transmission**.

After you click **Begin Transmission**, the same button does the rest. In Plain Text and Raw Binary it reads **Pause Transmission** mid-transfer and **Resume Transmission** while paused. In the protocol modes it reads **Stop Transmission** and cancels the transfer. Closing the dialog clears the selected file.
docs.title: File-Transmission#2

docs.body:
## Choosing a mode

A CRC is a checksum the receiver uses to detect corrupted blocks. EOT is the end-of-transmission byte that closes an XMODEM-family transfer.

If your bootloader names a protocol, use that one. If you do not know, look for "XMODEM", "YMODEM" or "ZMODEM" in the bootloader's manual; if none is mentioned, use Plain Text for lines of text or Raw Binary for bytes the device parses itself.
docs.title: File-Transmission#3

docs.body:
| Mode        | Error detection  | Block size                | Pause/resume     | Best for |
|-------------|------------------|---------------------------|------------------|----------|
| Plain Text  | None             | One line                  | Yes              | Human-readable config files, AT commands |
| Raw Binary  | None             | 1,024 B (64-8,192 B)      | Yes              | Simple binary uploads without protocol overhead |
| XMODEM      | CRC-16           | 128 B                     | No               | Legacy devices, small files |
| XMODEM-1K   | CRC-16           | 1,024 B                   | No               | Legacy devices, larger files |
| YMODEM      | CRC-16           | 1,024 B                   | No               | Files where the receiver needs the filename and size |
| ZMODEM      | CRC-32           | 1,024 B (64-8,192 B)      | No               | Large files, unreliable links, modern firmware loaders (resumes from an offset after a crash) |
docs.title: File-Transmission#4

docs.body:
## Opening the File Transmission dialog

Connect to a device first. Then open the **Start** menu on the dashboard taskbar and choose **Tools** > **File Transmission**. If you pinned it under **Preferences** > **Taskbar** > **Pinned Buttons**, the taskbar button opens it too. In the console, the attach button in the send row (tooltip "Send a file to the connected device") opens the same dialog.

In a runtime-mode deployment the dialog opens only when the build was packaged with `--file-transmission` and Pro is active. The dialog closes when the connection drops.

## Transfer modes

### Plain text
docs.title: File-Transmission#5

docs.body:
In **Plain Text** mode (File Transmission, Pro), Serial Studio sends the file line by line as text, one line every **Transmission Interval**. A line that does not end with a newline gets `\n` appended; a line that already ends in `\r\n` keeps it. A device that needs a bare `\r` is not served by this mode.

Raise **Transmission Interval** if the device needs time to process each line before accepting the next (default 100 ms, range 0-10,000 ms). Pause and resume continue from where the transfer left off.

### Raw binary

In **Raw Binary** mode (File Transmission, Pro), Serial Studio sends the file in fixed-size blocks with no framing or error checking, for receivers that expect raw bytes and check integrity themselves.
docs.title: File-Transmission#6

docs.body:
**Block Size** (default 1,024 bytes, range 64-8,192) and **Transmission Interval** (default 100 ms, range 0-10,000 ms) set the pace. Throughput is block size divided by interval, so the defaults give about 10 KB/s; lower the interval for large files. The last block may be smaller than the configured size. Pause and resume work as in Plain Text.

### XMODEM

In **XMODEM** mode (File Transmission, Pro), Serial Studio uses a byte-oriented protocol older than most of the devices it talks to. It sends 128-byte blocks with CRC-16 error detection. The receiver starts the transfer by sending a `C` character to request CRC mode, so start the receiver first.
docs.title: File-Transmission#7

docs.body:
**Timeout** (default 10,000 ms, range 1,000-60,000) bounds each wait for the receiver, including the wait for that first `C`. **Max Retries** (default 10, range 1-100) is how many timeouts or NAKs a transfer tolerates before it gives up.

1. Serial Studio waits for the receiver to send `C`.
2. Each 128-byte block is sent with a sequence number and CRC-16 checksum.
3. The receiver answers ACK (success) or NAK (retransmit).
4. After the last block, Serial Studio sends EOT.

The last block is padded with `0x1A` (Ctrl-Z) up to the block size. XMODEM carries no file size, so the receiver cannot strip the padding; use YMODEM or ZMODEM when the exact size matters. Only CRC-16 mode is supported, not the legacy checksum mode.
docs.title: File-Transmission#8

docs.body:
### XMODEM-1K

In **XMODEM-1K** mode (File Transmission, Pro), Serial Studio uses XMODEM with 1,024-byte blocks, which cuts protocol overhead for larger files. It uses **Timeout** (default 10,000 ms) and **Max Retries** (default 10), waits for the receiver's `C` and pads the last block like XMODEM.

### YMODEM

In **YMODEM** mode (File Transmission, Pro), Serial Studio uses XMODEM-1K plus a metadata block that carries the filename and file size, so the receiver knows what it is getting before the data arrives. It uses **Timeout** (default 10,000 ms) and **Max Retries** (default 10).

1. Serial Studio sends block 0 with the filename and file size.
2. Data goes out in 1,024-byte blocks with CRC-16.
3. After the data, Serial Studio sends EOT twice, per YMODEM convention.
4. An empty block 0 signals end-of-batch.
docs.title: File-Transmission#9

docs.body:
The receiver can use the file size from block 0 to strip the padding from the last block. Filenames longer than 104 bytes are truncated in block 0.

### ZMODEM

In **ZMODEM** mode (File Transmission, Pro), Serial Studio uses a streaming protocol: it does not wait for an acknowledgment after each block, so link latency does not cap throughput. It uses CRC-32 and supports crash recovery.

Start the receiver first (for example, the bootloader's ZMODEM receive command), then click **Begin Transmission**.

**Block Size** sets the data subpacket size (default 1,024 bytes, range 64-8,192). **Timeout** (default 10,000 ms) and **Max Retries** (default 10) apply as in XMODEM.
docs.title: File-Transmission#10

docs.body:
- Data subpackets stream continuously without per-packet ACKs.
- A receiver restarting after an interrupted transfer can ask the sender to resume from a given byte offset (ZRPOS) instead of starting over.
- The file header carries the filename, size and modification time.

## If nothing happens

The usual cause is a receiver that is not waiting yet. Start the receiver on the device first, then click **Begin Transmission**. In the four protocol modes, Serial Studio waits up to **Timeout** for the receiver to start the transfer (a `C` in the XMODEM family), retries up to **Max Retries** times, then the status text shows "Transfer failed: Timeout: no response from receiver". Plain Text and Raw Binary have no handshake, so a device that is not listening misses the data. Clicking **Begin Transmission** at a sketch that only calls `Serial.println` is like handing a book to someone who is not in the room.
docs.title: File-Transmission#11

docs.body:
## Progress and log

During an active transfer, the dialog shows:

- **Progress: N%** with a progress bar.
- **Transfer speed.** Current throughput in B/s, KB/s, or MB/s.
- **Bytes sent / total.** Absolute byte counters.
- **Errors: N.** Number of protocol-level errors (NAKs, retries, timeouts). It appears after the first error and only counts in the protocol modes.
- **Status text.** Current protocol state or last event.

The **Activity Log** at the bottom of the dialog lists timestamped events: block transmissions, acknowledgments, errors, retries, and completion status. It keeps the most recent 200 entries. Click **Clear** to reset it.
docs.title: File-Transmission#12

docs.body:
## Settings reference

The dialog does not persist these settings; they return to the defaults below each time Serial Studio starts, and the dialog disables the controls while a transfer is active.

| Setting                | Applies to                              | Range             | Default    |
|------------------------|-----------------------------------------|-------------------|------------|
| Transmission Interval  | Plain Text, Raw Binary                  | 0-10,000 ms       | 100 ms     |
| Block Size             | Raw Binary, ZMODEM                      | 64-8,192 bytes    | 1,024 bytes|
| Timeout                | XMODEM, XMODEM-1K, YMODEM, ZMODEM       | 1,000-60,000 ms   | 10,000 ms  |
| Max Retries            | XMODEM, XMODEM-1K, YMODEM, ZMODEM       | 1-100             | 10         |
docs.title: File-Transmission#13

docs.body:
The ranges are the dialog's spin box limits. Block Size steps by 64 and Timeout by 1,000 ms.

## Tips

- If a slow receiver drops data, raise **Transmission Interval** (Plain Text, Raw Binary) or **Timeout** (protocol modes).
- On a noisy link, lower **Block Size** in ZMODEM so a failed subpacket resends less data.
