docs.body:
# Getting started with Serial Studio

## Overview

Your board prints numbers over USB and you want to see them as a plot. Serial Studio reads the stream, builds a dashboard from it, and runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux.

The shape is always the same: the device sends data, you pick how Serial Studio reads the stream (the **Operation Mode**: Quick Plot, Project File, or Console Only), and widgets appear. Serial/UART, TCP/UDP, and Bluetooth LE are free; the other drivers need Pro (see [Devices](Devices.md)). [Concepts](Concepts.md) explains the chain from device to dashboard on one page, and the [Glossary](Glossary.md) defines every term.
docs.title: Getting-Started#0

docs.body:
If your Arduino already calls `Serial.println`, install Serial Studio and jump to [Quick Plot](#your-first-connection-quick-plot-mode).

## Installation

### Windows

Download the installer from the [releases page](https://github.com/Serial-Studio/Serial-Studio/releases/latest) and run it. [Windows Installation](Windows-Installation.md) covers the unsigned-installer warning, the Visual C++ Redistributable, the portable ZIP, and the Microsoft Store edition.

### macOS

1. Download the DMG from the [releases page](https://github.com/Serial-Studio/Serial-Studio/releases/latest).
2. Open the DMG and drag Serial Studio into **Applications**.
docs.title: Getting-Started#1

docs.body:
Or install via Homebrew (community-maintained):

```bash
brew install --cask serial-studio
```

### Linux

Download the AppImage, DEB, or RPM from the [releases page](https://github.com/Serial-Studio/Serial-Studio/releases/latest), or install from Flathub (`com.serial_studio.Serial-Studio`). [Linux Installation](Linux-Installation.md) covers each package, signature verification, and the [serial port permissions](Linux-Installation.md#serial-port-permissions) a serial device needs.

### Building from source (GPL)

This is for contributors; the installers above are the normal route. Compiling needs Qt 6 and CMake (the project is built against Qt 6.11.2):
docs.title: Getting-Started#2

docs.body:
```bash
git clone https://github.com/Serial-Studio/Serial-Studio.git
cd Serial-Studio
cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build --config Release
```

The binary ends up in `build/`. On Windows the default Visual Studio generator is multi-config and ignores `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE`, so keep `--config Release` on the build step or configure with `-G Ninja`.

## Your first connection: Quick Plot mode

Quick Plot is the fastest way to get data on screen. The example uses an Arduino, but any device that prints numbers, one line per sample, over a serial port works.

### Step 1: prepare your device
docs.title: Getting-Started#3
Getting-Started#4

docs.body:
Plain comma-separated values work as well. A header row of the same width before the first data line, if present, supplies the channel names:

```
Temperature,Pressure,Humidity
23.5,1013.2,45.0
```

### Step 2: configure Serial Studio

1. Open Serial Studio.
2. In the Device Setup panel on the right edge of the window (drag its left edge to resize it), set **Operation Mode** to **Quick Plot (Auto-Detected Format)**.
3. Set **Connection** to **UART**.
4. Plug the board in first; the port list fills in. The field is labelled **COM Port** on Windows and **Serial Port** elsewhere. Examples: `COM3`, `/dev/ttyUSB0`, `/dev/cu.usbmodem*`. For an empty list, see [Serial port not showing up](#serial-port-not-showing-up-in-the-dropdown).
5. Set **Baud Rate** to `115200`, the value in the sketch.
docs.title: Getting-Started#5

docs.body:
### Step 3: connect

Click the **Connect** button in the toolbar. Then:

1. The Console shows the raw incoming lines, like this:

```
   temp:22.00, hum:60.00
   temp:22.03, hum:60.01
   ```

2. In Quick Plot mode, Serial Studio switches to the Dashboard once it parses a valid frame.
3. The Dashboard shows a Data Grid and a Multi-Plot with two traces, `temp` and `hum`.

Console empty? To check whether the board is sending anything, use [Console Only mode](#console-only-mode), or see [Common first-time issues](#common-first-time-issues). Console full of lines but no Dashboard after a few seconds? The lines are not in a shape Quick Plot accepts; see [Console shows data but no dashboard](#console-shows-data-but-no-dashboard).
docs.title: Getting-Started#6

docs.body:
### Step 4: explore the dashboard

- Click a widget's button in the taskbar at the bottom of the dashboard to bring it to the front (see [Toolbar & Button Reference](Toolbar-Reference.md#dashboard-taskbar)).
- Hover over plots to inspect values. Sine waves make it obvious when the plot is working; a flat line means the board stopped talking.
- Enable **CSV Spreadsheet** under **Data Export** in the Device Setup panel to record the session; replay it later with **Open CSV** in the toolbar.

### Step 5: keep it as a project

When the plot looks right, click **Menu** in the dashboard taskbar and choose **Save as Project**, then pick where to save it. Serial Studio disconnects, switches to Project File mode, and opens the project in the Project Editor. It does not reconnect; click **Connect** when you are ready. The project holds your connection settings and one dataset per channel, named from your labels. Rename channels, set units, and pick widgets in the Project Editor.
docs.title: Getting-Started#7

docs.body:
Quick Plot accepts a bare `\r`, but the saved project does not: it splits frames on `\n`, which covers `\n` and `\r\n` line endings. A device that ends lines with a bare `\r` needs its end delimiter changed in the Project Editor.

## Project File mode

Set **Operation Mode** to **Parse via Project File** (or click **Project Editor**) for Project File mode. Use it when Quick Plot's automatic channels are not enough: custom labels, units, widgets, or a binary frame. A `.ssproj` project file, built in the [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md), defines the device, its frame delimiters and decoder, the frame parser, and the datasets, groups, and widgets.
docs.title: Getting-Started#8

docs.body:
The [Project File tutorial](Project-File-Tutorial.md) builds a complete project from a sample sketch, step by step, and ends with the exact dashboard you should see. To start, click **Project Editor** in the toolbar (while disconnected, this switches Serial Studio to Project File mode), build the project, pick the device's connection in the Device Setup panel, and click **Connect**. The [Glossary](Glossary.md) defines frame, decoder, frame parser, and dataset.

## Let the device declare its dashboard (Arduino library)

If you write the firmware, the device can describe its own dashboard. The SerialStudio device library (Arduino, C and Python, in the `firmware/` directory of the Serial Studio repository) sends one declaration line with the channel names, units, ranges and widgets, and Serial Studio builds the dashboard from it on connect. For Arduino, install **SerialStudio** from the Library Manager, or copy `firmware/arduino` to `Arduino/libraries/SerialStudio`.
docs.title: Getting-Started#9
Getting-Started#10

docs.body:
## Console Only mode

Console Only is a diagnostic mode. Serial Studio doesn't try to parse anything; raw bytes from the device go straight to the terminal. Use it when you want to verify that a device is alive, check the baud rate and framing, or send commands interactively. If the console shows gibberish, the dashboard would only plot gibberish faster.

### Connect in Console Only mode

1. In the Device Setup panel, set **Operation Mode** to **Console Only (No Parsing)**.
2. Pick the **Connection** and configure it (port, baud rate, IP address).
3. Click **Connect**.
4. Raw bytes appear in the terminal. Toggle between Text and Hex display from the console toolbar.
5. Use the input box at the bottom of the console to send bytes back to the device.
docs.title: Getting-Started#11

docs.body:
There is no dashboard, and the CSV, Historian and MDF4 switches are disabled. Once the stream looks correct, switch to Quick Plot or Project File to visualize the data.

## Choosing an operation mode

- Printing numbers, one line per sample? Use **Quick Plot (Auto-Detected Format)**.
- Want your own widgets, labels, and units? Use **Parse via Project File**.
- Device silent or garbled? Use **Console Only (No Parsing)**.

[Operation Modes](Operation-Modes.md) compares the three in detail.

## Interface overview

The [Toolbar & Button Reference](Toolbar-Reference.md) maps every button.

### Toolbar (top of the window)
docs.title: Getting-Started#12

docs.body:
The toolbar holds the **Project Editor**, **Open Project**, and **Open CSV** buttons, **Open MDF4** (Pro), **Preferences**, **Examples**, **Help Center**, and the **Connect / Disconnect** button on the right. It has no driver buttons: pick the driver with the **Connection** selector in the Device Setup panel. The [Problem Center](Problem-Center.md) lists what is stopping data from reaching the dashboard.

**Examples** downloads example projects from GitHub on first open, so it needs an internet connection.

### Console view (center, default)

Before you connect, the console shows the edition details and a one-line hint on how to start. Once connected, it shows raw incoming data from your device, in Text or Hex. If no frame has been extracted 10 seconds after connecting in Quick Plot or Project File mode, the console prints a hint; it differs depending on whether any bytes arrived.
docs.title: Getting-Started#13

docs.body:
### Dashboard view (center, replaces the console)

Once Serial Studio parses at least one valid frame, the view switches from the Console to the Dashboard, which shows real-time widgets (plots, gauges, maps, grids) arranged according to your configuration. The [Widget Reference](Widget-Reference.md) lists them all.

### Device Setup panel (right side, collapsible)

The Device Setup panel is where you configure the connection:

- **Operation Mode.** **Console Only (No Parsing)**, **Quick Plot (Auto-Detected Format)**, or **Parse via Project File**, each with a tooltip describing what it expects.
- **Data Export.** The **CSV Spreadsheet**, **Historian Database** (Pro), and **MDF4 Recording** (Pro) switches, plus the console log.
- **Connection and its settings.** The link type, then its port, baud rate, or IP address.
docs.title: Getting-Started#14

docs.body:
Frame delimiters, the decoder, and the frame parser belong to a project and are set in the Project Editor. Drag the panel's left edge to give the Dashboard more space.

## Common first-time issues

The [Problem Center](Problem-Center.md) diagnoses most of these for you. Open it with the **Problem Center** button in the toolbar, or press **Ctrl+K** (**⌘+K** on macOS) outside the dashboard and pick `Problem Center`. **Connection Diagnostics** checks port permissions, drivers, and Bluetooth state, and the link checkers say whether bytes, frames, or values are the stage where data stops.

### Serial port not showing up in the dropdown
docs.title: Getting-Started#15

docs.body:
- **Windows:** Open Device Manager and check under "Ports (COM & LPT)". You may need a USB-to-serial driver: [CH340](http://www.wch-ic.com/downloads/CH341SER_EXE.html), [FTDI](https://ftdichip.com/drivers/vcp-drivers/), or [CP210x](https://www.silabs.com/developers/usb-to-uart-bridge-vcp-drivers).
- **Linux:** Your user needs access to serial devices; see [serial port permissions](Linux-Installation.md#serial-port-permissions). Check the device shows up with `ls /dev/ttyUSB*` or `ls /dev/ttyACM*`.
- **macOS:** Try a different USB port. Check System Settings for security prompts blocking the device. Your device usually appears as `/dev/cu.usbmodem*` or `/dev/cu.usbserial*`.
docs.title: Getting-Started#16

docs.body:
### No data showing in the console

- Check the baud rate matches your device configuration exactly.
- Make sure no other app has the port open. Two programs cannot share one serial port, and the Arduino IDE Serial Monitor is the usual squatter.
- Confirm the device is sending data. A logic analyzer or second terminal program is handy for verifying this.
- Try disconnecting and reconnecting.

### Console shows data but no dashboard

- In Quick Plot mode, make sure the device prints numbers, one line per sample. A text-only line is ignored by the dashboard, and a field that is not a number shows as text in the Data Grid and is not plotted.
- In Project File mode, check that your frame delimiters match what the device sends. Switch to Console Only mode to inspect the raw stream, then come back once you know the framing.
- If nothing parses, switch to Console Only. Wrong-looking raw bytes there mean a connection, baud, or wiring problem, not a parsing problem.
docs.title: Getting-Started#17

docs.body:
### Some widgets stop updating while others move

The parser returns fewer values than a dataset's frame index expects, so that dataset keeps its last value. The Problem Center names the affected datasets in a `short-frames` finding. See [Parser returns the wrong number of values](Troubleshooting.md#parser-returns-the-wrong-number-of-values).

### Garbled or corrupted data in the console

- Almost always a baud rate mismatch. Double-check both the device firmware and the Serial Studio setting.
- Also check data bits, parity, and stop bits match your device (the 8-N-1 default works for most).
docs.title: Getting-Started#18

docs.body:
## Next steps

- Build your own dashboard: the [Project File tutorial](Project-File-Tutorial.md), then the [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md). **Examples** in the toolbar opens working projects to copy from.
- Understand the model: [Concepts](Concepts.md), then [Operation Modes](Operation-Modes.md).
- Another device or protocol: [Devices](Devices.md), then [Communication Protocols](Communication-Protocols.md).
- Binary or non-standard frames: the [Frame Parser Reference](Frame-Parser.md), then [Deriving values](Derived-Values.md).
- Record and automate: [CSV Export and Playback](CSV-Export-Playback.md), then the [API Reference](API-Reference.md) for scripts and MCP on TCP port 7777.
- Get help: [Troubleshooting](Troubleshooting.md), the [FAQ](FAQ.md), and [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/Serial-Studio/Serial-Studio/discussions).
docs.title: Getting-Started#19

docs.body:
# Glossary

A quick reference for the terms used throughout Serial Studio and this documentation. Entries are alphabetical. Where a concept has its own page, the entry links to it. New here? Read [Quick Plot](#quick-plot), [Frame](#frame) and [Dataset](#dataset) first.

## Acquisition pipeline

The path your bytes take from the port to a widget on the dashboard, also called the data hotpath. It is built to keep up at 256 kHz+ without per-frame allocation. See [The Acquisition Pipeline](Data-Hotpath.md).

## Action

A user-defined command bound to a button on the dashboard or to an incoming trigger. Actions send bytes back to the device, run on a timer, or fire on a condition. See [Actions](Actions.md).
docs.title: Glossary#0

docs.body:
## Annotation

A labelled range of bytes in the console stream, produced by an annotation decoder rather than by the frame parser. Annotations carry a row, a class, and a text, and appear in the console's annotation views. See [Console Annotations](Console-Annotations.md).

## API server

The local TCP server on port 7777 (default) that external programs and plugins use to send JSON commands and read live data. It is off until you enable it in the preferences. See [API Reference](API-Reference.md).

## Baud rate

The speed of a UART link, in bits per second. Both ends must use the same value, or the Console shows garbage. Set it with **Baud Rate** in the Device Setup panel. See [Devices](Devices.md).
docs.title: Glossary#1

docs.body:
## Built-In parser (Native)

The no-code frame parser. You describe the frame layout with a JSON descriptor and Serial Studio parses it with parametrized C++ templates, so no Lua or JavaScript is needed. "Built-In" is the user-facing name; internal identifiers call it *Native*. See [Frame Parser Reference](Frame-Parser.md).

## Computed dataset

A dataset that takes its value from its [value transform](#value-transform) instead of from the frame, so it reads no frame index. A transform that never reads `value` makes its dataset computed. Older versions called these virtual datasets. See [Deriving values](Derived-Values.md).
docs.title: Glossary#2

docs.body:
## Connection

The link type a device uses (UART, Network, Bluetooth LE, or a Pro connection such as Modbus or CAN Bus), picked with the **Connection** selector in the Device Setup panel. See [Devices](Devices.md).

## Console

The panel that shows raw incoming bytes before any parsing, in ASCII or hexadecimal. It is also the full view in Console Only mode. Use it to confirm a device is sending data and that the baud rate is right and the frame delimiters match. See [Operation Modes](Operation-Modes.md).

## Control Loop

The optional `setup()` / `loop()` script that runs alongside a project to drive output, automate the device, or compute derived values. See [Control Loop](Control-Loop.md).
docs.title: Glossary#3

docs.body:
## CSV

Comma-separated values. The line `1,2,3` is what `Serial.println("1,2,3")` sends, and in Quick Plot it becomes three plots. See [Operation Modes](Operation-Modes.md).

## Dashboard

The grid of live widgets that replaces the Console once a frame parses into at least one dataset value. Widgets are arranged from the project file, or auto-generated in Quick Plot. See [Widget Reference](Widget-Reference.md).

## Dataset

A single named channel of data, such as one temperature or one axis of an accelerometer. A dataset maps a position in the frame to a value, a title, units, ranges, and a widget. Datasets live inside groups. See [Dataset Identity Model](Identity-Model.md).
docs.title: Glossary#4

docs.body:
## Dataset ID / Unique ID

A dataset carries three numbers that are easy to confuse, and mixing them up is the most common project-editing trap. The **dataset ID** is its slot inside its group (0, 1, 2...), used to address mutating API calls, and it is reassigned when datasets are reordered, inserted or deleted. The **unique ID** is a stable identifier that does not change when you edit the project; scripts and Variables tables use it as a key. The **frame index** says which field of the frame the value is read from (see [Frame index](#frame-index)). See [Dataset Identity Model](Identity-Model.md).
docs.title: Glossary#5

docs.body:
## Device

Anything Serial Studio reads data from: a board on a serial port, a network socket, a Bluetooth LE peripheral, a PLC, an MQTT broker, a process, or a file being played back. A project has one device, or several with Pro, and each device carries its own connection, frame detection, decoder and frame parser. See [Devices](Devices.md).

## Driver

The component that talks to one device (UART, TCP/UDP, Bluetooth LE, MQTT, Modbus, CAN Bus, Audio, USB, HID, Process I/O). Drivers stamp each frame with its arrival time at the source boundary. See [Devices](Devices.md).

## Extension

An add-on that extends Serial Studio: a theme, a frame parser, a project template, or a plugin (see Plugin). Extensions are browsed, installed, updated, and uninstalled from the **Extension Manager** dialog. See [Extensions](Extensions.md).
docs.title: Glossary#6

docs.body:
## Folder

A named, collapsible container in the Project Editor that organizes groups, Variables tables, or workspaces. Folders nest to any depth, are purely organizational, and exist in every edition. A leaf group folder also collapses into one aggregated dashboard workspace. See [Organizing with folders](Project-Editor.md#organizing-with-folders).

## Frame

One complete unit of data from the device, delimited by the frame-detection settings. The line `21.5,48` your Arduino prints is one frame. Each frame is parsed into dataset values that update the dashboard. See [Data Flow](Data-Flow.md).
docs.title: Glossary#7

docs.body:
## Frame detection / Delimiters

How Serial Studio decides where one frame ends and the next begins: End Delimiter Only, Start Delimiter Only, Start + End Delimiter, No Delimiters, or Fixed Length (every frame is the same number of bytes). `Serial.println("21.5,48")` ends with a newline, so End Delimiter Only with `\n` gives one frame per line. See [Data Flow](Data-Flow.md).

## Frame index

The 1-based position of a field within a parsed frame. A dataset reads its value from one frame index. Index 0 is reserved. See [Dataset Identity Model](Identity-Model.md).

## Frame parser

The logic that turns a raw frame into an ordered list of values. It can be the Built-In parser, a JavaScript `parse(frame)` function, or a Lua equivalent. See [Frame Parser Reference](Frame-Parser.md).
docs.title: Glossary#8

docs.body:
## Group

A container that holds related datasets and can show them together with a Group Widget. Groups organize the project tree. See [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md).

## Group Widget

The widget a group uses to show its datasets together, such as a Data Grid, Multi-Plot, Accelerometer, GPS Map, or 3D Plot. Some Group Widgets need datasets with specific tags: an Accelerometer needs exactly three datasets tagged X, Y and Z. Older versions called these composite widgets. See [Widget Reference](Widget-Reference.md).

## Historian

The Pro recording of each session into a database that can be browsed, searched and replayed. Older versions called it the Session Database. See [Historian](Historian.md).
docs.title: Glossary#9

docs.body:
## Macro

An ad-hoc JavaScript or Lua script, or a single typed command, run from the Macros window against the running application. Macros reach every registered API command in process, without the [API server](#api-server), and are not tied to a project. See [Macros](Macros.md).

## Notification

A Pro dashboard event of level Info, Warning or Critical, posted from scripts (frame parsers, transforms, the Control Loop), from alarm bands, or from the API. Events are grouped into free-form channels and shown in the Notification Log widget, with an optional native OS desktop notification. See [Notifications](Notifications.md).
docs.title: Glossary#10

docs.body:
## Operation mode

How a connection treats incoming data: **Console Only** (no parsing), **Quick Plot** (auto-plot each line of values in the format Serial Studio detects), or **Project File** (parse with a `.ssproj`). See [Operation Modes](Operation-Modes.md).

## Plugin

An external program (a Python script or a native binary) that connects to Serial Studio's [API server](#api-server) over TCP/JSON or gRPC to provide custom real-time data processing, visualization, or analysis. Plugins are installed from the Extension Manager and launched with its Run button. See [Extensions](Extensions.md).
docs.title: Glossary#11

docs.body:
## Pro / Free

Serial Studio ships in a free GPL edition and a commercial Pro edition. Pro adds output widgets, Modbus, CAN Bus, MDF4, 3D, Image View, Waterfall, file-transfer protocols and the Historian. For the edition of any other term, see [Pro vs Free Features](Pro-vs-Free.md).

## Problem Center

The window that lists standing diagnostics for the session: project mistakes, link conditions, script errors, and failed extensions, each with a cause and a remedy. **Connection Diagnostics** adds self-checks of the machine (port permissions, Bluetooth state, host reachability, audio access) to the same list. See [Problem Center](Problem-Center.md).
docs.title: Glossary#12

docs.body:
## Project file (`.ssproj`)

The JSON document that defines a dashboard: frame detection, groups, datasets, widgets, parser scripts, and transforms. Created and edited in the Project Editor. See [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md).

## Quick Plot

The zero-configuration mode that treats each line as a frame and each field of the line as a dataset, auto-creating one plot per field. `Serial.println("21.5,48")` gives two plots with no setup. See [Operation Modes](Operation-Modes.md).

## Setup panel

The collapsible panel titled **Device Setup**, where you choose the operation mode, configure the I/O interface, pick the device's Connection and settings, and enable export. See [Devices](Devices.md).
docs.title: Glossary#13

docs.body:
## Value transform

A per-dataset script (JavaScript or Lua) that calibrates, filters, or converts a value after parsing and before display. See [Dataset Value Transforms](Dataset-Transforms.md).

## Variables

Named values grouped into Variables tables that frame parsers, value transforms and scripts read and write, used for calibration constants and values shared between datasets. A Pro feature. Older versions called these data tables or shared memory. See [Variables](Variables.md).

## Widget

A visual element on the dashboard such as a Plot, Gauge, Compass, GPS Map, or Data Grid. Datasets and groups choose which widget renders them. See [Widget Reference](Widget-Reference.md).
docs.title: Glossary#14

docs.body:
## Workspace

A saved arrangement of which widgets are visible and how they are laid out on the dashboard, letting one project present different views for different tasks. See [Toolbar Reference](Toolbar-Reference.md#a-note-on-workspaces).

## User names and API names

Read this if you edit a `.ssproj` by hand or call the API. The UI and this manual use the names on the left. Project files, the API, and scripts keep older internal names, listed on the right, so existing projects and integrations keep working.
docs.title: Glossary#15

docs.body:
| Name in the UI and manual | Name in project files, the API and scripts |
|---------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| Device | source (`sources`, `sourceId`, `project.source.*`) |
| Built-In parser | Native (`frameParserLanguage` 2, native templates; the full numbering is 0 JavaScript, 1 Lua, 2 Native, 3 Expression) |
| Group Widget | group `widget` |
| Variables, Variables table, variable | data tables, table, register (`tableGet()`, `tableSet()`) |
| Computed dataset | virtual dataset (`virtual`) |
| Canvas Widget | painter (`"painter"`, `project.painter.*`) |
| Historian | sessions (`sessions.*`, the "Session Databases" folder) |
| Control Loop | control script |
docs.title: Glossary#16

docs.body:
## See also

- [Getting Started](Getting-Started.md) — install, connect, and read your first frame.
- [Concepts](Concepts.md) — the chain from device to dashboard on one page.
- [Dataset Identity Model](Identity-Model.md) — the index-versus-ID distinction in depth.
- [Data Flow](Data-Flow.md) — the full path from raw bytes to widgets.
- [FAQ](FAQ.md) — common questions.
docs.title: Glossary#17

docs.body:
# Historian (Pro)

You ran a test bench for a week and now want to look at Tuesday's run again. The Historian keeps every connected session, from connect to disconnect, in one SQLite file (a single-file database most languages can read) per project. A year of test flights is one file, not 400 CSVs.

You can browse, tag, annotate, export to CSV and replay any session through the dashboard. After a run, open **Historian**, pick the session and press **Replay**.

The Historian is a Pro feature. The first Pro feature you use makes Serial Studio offer the trial with a Yes/No prompt (it needs an internet connection); the trial never starts on its own. After a license or trial ends, Serial Studio stops opening the database. The file stays a standard SQLite database that any SQLite tool can read.
docs.title: Historian#0

docs.body:
## Turning recording on

1. Open or create a project. The project title names the database file.
2. Open the **Setup** pane.
3. Under **Data Export**, switch on **Historian Database** (Pro). The toggle is hidden in the free build and greyed out when the operation mode is Console Only (see [Operation Modes](Operation-Modes.md)).
4. Connect your device. Recording starts on connect, and each connection adds a new session to the project's database.
5. Disconnect. Recording stops and the session's end timestamp is written.

The session then appears in the Historian window. Serial Studio picks the path and creates the schema on first use. A background thread writes in batched transactions, so disk I/O does not block the data path.
docs.title: Historian#1

docs.body:
### File location

All sessions for a given project title live in a single `.db` file, grouped by project name:

```
<Workspace>/Session Databases/<Project Title>/<Project Title>.db
```

The workspace root is the folder set as the **Workspace Folder** in Settings. Project titles are sanitized so the filename is safe on every OS. Projects with no title fall back to `Untitled`. Sessions are separated inside the file by row, not by file.

## What gets recorded

A line like `25.3,1013` from `Serial.println` becomes two datasets, Temperature and Pressure, and each frame's values are stored with their time. "Final" values are what the dashboard shows, after any [dataset transform](Dataset-Transforms.md); "pre-transform" values are the same numbers before the transform ran. Both are stored, numeric and text.
docs.title: Historian#2

docs.body:
Each session also stores every raw byte that arrived on the driver exactly as received, and your [Variables](Variables.md), polled once a second with only the changed ones written. It keeps a snapshot of the project JSON as it was when recording started. That is how a session recorded with one version of the project replays faithfully later, even if the live project has changed.

Replay re-renders widgets from the stored final values. The raw byte stream is archived for inspection, CSV, or external analysis, but it is not re-parsed during replay.

## The Historian window

Open the Historian from the **Historian** button on the toolbar. Without an active Pro license or trial, the button shows the trial/activation prompt instead of the window. The window opens one project's database and lists every session recorded in that file, newest first.
docs.title: Historian#3

docs.body:
In operator mode (see [Operator Deployments](Operator-Deployments.md)) the Historian opens only while Historian Database is on, and it shows only the current project's database.

Select a session, then use the toolbar buttons (**Replay**, **Export CSV**, **Export PDF**, **Restore Project**, **Delete**; **Lock** applies to the whole file) to:
docs.title: Historian#4

docs.body:
- Replay it through the dashboard.
- Export it to CSV: final (post-transform) values, one column per dataset plus a timestamp column, written to the workspace.
- Generate an HTML or PDF report with a cover page, metadata, summary statistics and interactive plots. See [Session Reports](Session-Reports.md).
- Tag it with freeform labels such as `flight-test` or `anomaly`, and add notes. Tags are shared across every session in the project database, so one label can group sessions from different runs. In operator mode only the session being recorded accepts notes; completed sessions are read-only.
- Delete it, with its blocks, raw bytes, tags and table snapshots, in a single transaction.
docs.title: Historian#5

docs.body:
**Restore Project** extracts the project JSON embedded in the session into a standalone `.ssproj` file and opens it in the editor. **Lock** sets a password on the database that blocks session deletion until you unlock it with the same password. There is no password recovery, so store it somewhere safe.

## Replay

To replay a Historian session, select it in the Historian window and press **Replay**. Replay (Pro) plays the session back through the dashboard as if the device were connected, and drives MQTT and the API like a live connection. CSV, MDF4 and Historian recording are suppressed while any player (CSV, MDF4 or Historian replay) is open, so replaying a session writes no new export files.
docs.title: Historian#6

docs.body:
Play/Pause, previous/next frame and a progress slider work as in the [CSV player](CSV-Export-Playback.md).

When replay starts, Serial Studio saves the current operation mode and project path, and the session's embedded project is restored for the run. When replay ends, it restores the saved operation mode and project path. You can replay a session while your live project differs.

Replay is read-only. It does not modify the recorded session.

## Performance notes

Sessions are written in Write-Ahead-Logging (WAL) mode with `synchronous=NORMAL`. WAL lets the Historian and external tools read the database while a recording is running.
docs.title: Historian#7

docs.body:
| Setting                          | Value |
|----------------------------------|-------|
| Block queue                      | 8,192 entries |
| Flush threshold / interval       | 1,024 queued blocks or once per second |
| Raw-byte chunks per transaction  | up to 10,000 |
| Table-snapshot queue             | 1,024 entries |
| Table-snapshot rows per transaction | up to 1,000 |

When the disk falls behind and the block queue fills, the dropped blocks are counted in `sessions.frames_dropped`.

Databases grow linearly with data rate and session length. As a floor, each stored numeric value takes 8 bytes (float64), twice that with its pre-transform twin, plus the raw bytes. No retention policy exists: delete sessions in the Historian window or with the `sessions.*` API commands.
docs.title: Historian#8

docs.body:
## Choosing between CSV, MDF4, Historian and reports

| Goal                                                              | Best option               |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------|
| Hand a single file to a collaborator who uses Excel or pandas     | CSV export (free)         |
| Long recordings, high data rates, automotive toolchain            | [MDF4 export](MDF4.md) (Pro) |
| Archive every run of a project, then search, tag, or replay later | Historian (Pro)           |
| A shareable, printable summary with charts for a customer or lab notebook | Session report (Pro) |
docs.title: Historian#9

docs.body:
Session reports are rendered on demand from the database.

## Database format (for developers)

The Historian file is a standard SQLite 3 database: no custom container, no compression, no encryption. Any SQLite client can open it directly, so recorded sessions are usable from your own software without going through Serial Studio at all. The schema is created with `PRAGMA user_version = 4` and evolves additively (new columns and tables are added, existing ones are never renamed or reordered), so queries that name their columns keep working across application upgrades.

The database runs in WAL mode (see [Performance notes](#performance-notes)), so reading it while Serial Studio is recording is safe. Open it read-only from external tools (`file:...?mode=ro` in SQLite URI syntax): a second writer makes the recorder's transactions wait on the lock or fail with `SQLITE_BUSY`.
docs.title: Historian#10

docs.body:
The recording and the Historian can also be driven programmatically. The [API](API-Reference.md) exposes the `sessions.*` commands, such as `sessions.setExportEnabled`, `sessions.list` and `sessions.replay`, and the `--session-export` flag in the [Command-Line Interface](Command-Line-Interface.md) turns recording on at startup.

### Tables

| Table             | Contents |
|-------------------|----------|
| `blocks`          | Per-dataset final and pre-transform values for every published block |
| `raw_bytes`       | Every byte that arrived on the driver, as received |
| `table_snapshots` | Variables, captured on change at a 1 Hz poll; not a per-frame record |
| `sessions`        | Project title, start and end time, embedded project JSON (`project_json`), notes |
| `columns`         | Dataset title, group, units, widget type, virtual flag |
docs.title: Historian#11

docs.body:
Databases recorded by older versions store per-frame rows in `readings` (one row per dataset per frame, `raw_*` and `final_*` value pairs) and `stream_blocks` (float64 sample blobs encoded like `values_blob`) instead of `blocks`. Current builds still read those tables for replay and CSV export, but no longer write them; `sessions.capture_format` records which format a session uses (`2` for the block format, `1` or NULL for the legacy per-frame format).

### Timestamps

Every `*_ns` column is a 64-bit signed integer counting nanoseconds from the session's first recorded sample, not from the Unix epoch. The wall-clock anchor is `sessions.started_at`, an ISO 8601 local timestamp such as `2026-08-20T14:03:11`; add a `timestamp_ns` value to it to place a sample in calendar time. `sessions.ended_at` uses the same format. Within `raw_bytes`, timestamps are strictly increasing: entries that arrive in the same nanosecond are stepped forward by 1 ns so ordering is unambiguous.
docs.title: Historian#12

docs.body:
### Sample data: the `blocks` table

One row per dataset per published block, for frame-driven and stream-driven sources alike. Join `blocks` to `columns` on `(session_id, unique_id)` to resolve the dataset's title, group, units, and widget type.

| Column | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `session_id`, `unique_id`, `source_id` | Session, dataset, and stream source the row belongs to |
| `block_number` | Publication counter, increasing per session |
| `frames` | Number of samples encoded in the blobs of this row |
| `t0_ns`, `t_end_ns` | Timestamps of the first and last sample in the block |
| `dt_ns` | Sample period. Non-zero: sample *i* sits at `t0_ns + i * dt_ns`. Zero: the block is irregular and per-sample offsets live in `times` |
| `is_numeric` | 1 when every sample in the block is numeric |
| `min_value`, `max_value`, `sum_value`, `finite_count` | Precomputed statistics over the finite final values, NULL when the block has none |
docs.title: Historian#13

docs.body:
The sample payloads are binary blobs, all little-endian regardless of the recording machine:

| Column | Encoding |
|--------|----------|
| `values_blob` | `frames` IEEE-754 float64 values (8 bytes each): the final, post-transform values |
| `raw_values` | Same encoding, the pre-transform values; NULL when the block carries no pre-transform twin. Frame-driven sources always write it, so without a transform it duplicates `values_blob` |
| `texts` | `frames` entries, each a uint32 byte count followed by that many UTF-8 bytes: the final text values; NULL for numeric-only datasets |
| `raw_texts` | Same encoding as `texts`, the pre-transform text; NULL unless the dataset has both |
| `times` | `frames` int64 values: per-sample nanosecond offsets from `t0_ns`; present only when `dt_ns` is 0 |
docs.title: Historian#14

docs.body:
A blob whose length does not match `frames` (times 8 for the fixed-width blobs) is truncated or foreign; reject it rather than decoding past its end.

### Metadata tables
docs.title: Historian#15

docs.body:
- **`sessions`**: one row per recording. It also carries `app_version`, `capture_format`, `repro_class` (the verifier's reproducibility classification), `frames_dropped` and `overflow_bytes` (link-loss counters), `raw_sha256` and `readings_sha256` (integrity fingerprints checked by the built-in verifier), and `view_state` (the dashboard layout at recording time).
- **`columns`**: the per-session dataset catalog: `unique_id`, `title`, `group_title`, `units`, `widget`, `is_virtual`, plus `source_id` and `source_title` for stream sources.
- **`raw_bytes`**: `data` is the received byte stream as a BLOB, `device_id` distinguishes devices on multi-device links.
- **`table_snapshots`**: `table_name` and `register_name` (the column name for a Variables entry) identify the variable; exactly one of `numeric_value` or `string_value` is set.
- **`tags`** and **`session_tags`**: the tag catalog (labels unique, case-insensitive) and the session-to-tag join table.
- **`project_metadata`**: key/value store. `created_at` stamps database creation; `lock_password_hash` appears when the database is locked. The lock blocks deletion inside Serial Studio only; the file is not encrypted.
- **`verifications`**: append-only log of verifier runs with timestamp, application version, verdict, and detail JSON.
docs.title: Historian#16

docs.body:
### Reading a session from Python

To pull a dataset into your own tooling, decode the blobs directly. This reads the `Temperature` dataset of session 1.

```python
import sqlite3
import struct

db = sqlite3.connect("file:My Project.db?mode=ro", uri=True)

for sid, started in db.execute("SELECT session_id, started_at FROM sessions"):
    print(sid, started)

query = """
  SELECT b.t0_ns, b.dt_ns, b.frames, b.values_blob, b.times
  FROM blocks b
  JOIN columns c ON c.session_id = b.session_id AND c.unique_id = b.unique_id
  WHERE b.session_id = ? AND c.title = 'Temperature'
  ORDER BY b.t0_ns
"""
for t0, dt, frames, blob, times in db.execute(query, (1,)):
    values = struct.unpack(f"<{frames}d", blob)
    if dt:
        stamps = [t0 + i * dt for i in range(frames)]
    else:
        stamps = [t0 + off for off in struct.unpack(f"<{frames}q", times)]
```
docs.title: Historian#17

docs.body:
Each iteration yields one block: `values` holds the final values and `stamps` their session-relative timestamps in nanoseconds. The same pattern with `raw_values` recovers pre-transform values, and `texts` decodes by walking uint32 length prefixes.

## See also

- [Session Reports](Session-Reports.md): export sessions as self-contained HTML or PDF reports with charts.
