docs.body:
# Dataset Identity Model

Your board prints `25.3,1013.2,42`. Serial Studio splits that line into three values and shows each one as a dataset: the first has `index = 1`, the second `index = 2`, the third `index = 3`. That is all most projects ever need, and the Project Editor sets it for you.

You only need the rest of this page if you write transform scripts or call the API. There, mixing up `datasetId` and `uniqueId` reads the wrong dataset, or nothing. A transform script that reads a dataset by its stable id looks like this:

```js
var t = datasetGetRaw(4137);
```

## The identifiers

A dataset lives inside a group, which lives inside a source. `sourceId`, `groupId` and `datasetId` locate a dataset by position; `index`, `uniqueId` and `alias` do other jobs.
docs.title: Identity-Model#0

docs.body:
### `index`

`index` is the only identifier you set for ordinary dashboards. It is the 1-based position of the dataset's value in the parsed frame: with `25.3,1013.2,42`, the three datasets have `index = 1`, `2` and `3`. Counting starts at 1 because `0` is not a valid frame position; a dataset whose `index` is 0, negative or larger than the number of fields in the parsed frame is skipped and keeps its last value.

Select the dataset in the Project Editor and edit its index there. Several datasets can share one `index` to style the same raw value in different ways. `index` has no relation to `datasetId`, and the two often differ.
docs.title: Identity-Model#1

docs.body:
A short frame never clears or errors a dataset; it just stops updating. A widget that stays frozen while the others move has an `index` past the end of the frame.

### `sourceId`

`sourceId` is the zero-based index of the source a dataset reads from. A single-source project has only source `0`. Multi-source projects (Pro) number sources `0`, `1`, `2`… in the order they were added.

### `groupId`

`groupId` is the positional index of the group inside the project: `0` for the first group, `1` for the second, and so on. Adding, deleting, or reordering groups renumbers it, so it is not a stable identity. Groups also have a `uniqueId` that survives reorders (see [`uniqueId`](#uniqueid)). `project.group.get` accepts either one.
docs.title: Identity-Model#2
Identity-Model#3

docs.body:
`project.dataset.update` takes `groupId`, `datasetId` and the fields to change directly in `params`, not inside an `options` object.

### `uniqueId`

`uniqueId` is allocated from a per-project counter when a dataset is created, duplicated, or imported, and saved in the project file. Reordering, renaming, or moving a dataset between sources never changes it. Treat it as opaque: you cannot compute `(sourceId, groupId, datasetId)` from it, and you cannot predict the next value. Projects saved by older versions get their ids filled in once on load.

A duplicated or copy-pasted dataset receives a fresh `uniqueId`, so the original and the copy stay distinguishable.
docs.title: Identity-Model#4

docs.body:
Transform scripts and [Variables](Variables.md) tables use `uniqueId` because they need one key that is stable across sources. The `dashboard.getData` response lists each dataset with its `uniqueId`. The system table (`__datasets__`) uses it for its `raw:<uniqueId>` variable (the value as parsed) and `final:<uniqueId>` variable (the value after the dataset's [transform](Dataset-Transforms.md)).

### `alias`
docs.title: Identity-Model#5

docs.body: An `alias` is an optional name you set in the **Script Alias** field of the Project Editor's dataset form. It is empty by default and must be unique across the project. `datasetGetRaw(4137)` tells you nothing six months later; `datasetGetRaw("ATAM1-CH1")` does. A string argument is always an alias and a number is always a `uniqueId`, so the two never coerce into each other. Transform and frame-parser scripts accept it wherever they accept a `uniqueId`: `datasetGetRaw("ATAM1-CH1")` and `datasetGetFinal("ATAM1-CH1")` look up by alias, and the `__datasets__` table exposes `raw:<alias>` and `final:<alias>` variables next to the numeric ones. `uniqueId` stays the persisted identity that stored cross-references point at.
docs.title: Identity-Model#6

docs.body:
A duplicate alias is cleared 800 ms after you stop typing, and the editor reports it. An all-digit alias such as `123` gets a warning, because a quoted `"123"` is still looked up as an alias, not as `uniqueId` 123.

The Project Editor tree context menu has a **Seed Aliases from Titles** action that fills every empty alias from its dataset title, deduplicated, and leaves existing aliases untouched.

## Workspace refs: "groupId" there is a group `uniqueId`
docs.title: Identity-Model#7

docs.body:
Workspace widget refs store the group's `uniqueId` under the JSON key `groupId`. When you read workspace data (`project.workspace.get`) and see a "groupId" far larger than the number of groups, it is a group `uniqueId`, not a positional index. Those values come from the same counter as dataset `uniqueId`s, so a `groupId` larger than the group count is normal. Passing one to a positional-id command (`project.group.update`, `project.dataset.update`, `project.dataset.delete`) hits the wrong group or fails; resolve it with `project.group.get` and `uniqueId`.

Workspace IDs are a separate range: Overview is `1000`, All Data is `1001`, auto per-group workspaces start at `1002`, auto per-folder workspaces start at `3000`, and user workspaces start at `5000`.
docs.title: Identity-Model#8

docs.body:
## Where each ID is used

| ID          | Used by                                                                       |
|-------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `sourceId`  | `project.source.update`, `project.source.setFrameParserCode` (multi-source: Pro) |
| `groupId`   | `project.group.update`, `project.dataset.update`, `project.dataset.delete`    |
| `datasetId` | `project.dataset.update`, `project.dataset.setOptions`, `project.dataset.delete` |
| `index`     | Maps each slot of the parser's returned array to a dataset                    |
| `uniqueId`  | `dashboard.getData`, `dashboard.tailFrames`, `datasetGetRaw`, `datasetGetFinal`, `raw:<uniqueId>`, `final:<uniqueId>` |
| `alias`     | `datasetGetRaw("name")`, `datasetGetFinal("name")`, `raw:<alias>`, `final:<alias>` |
docs.title: Identity-Model#9

docs.body:
## Rule of thumb

> **Mutate by `(groupId, datasetId)`. Read by `uniqueId` or alias. Pick the frame value with `index`.**

## See also

- [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md): where datasets, groups, and sources are created and where their IDs come from.
- [Frame Parser Scripting](Frame-Parser.md): the parser that picks values out of the frame and assigns them to datasets by `index`.
- [Dataset Value Transforms](Dataset-Transforms.md): per-dataset scripts that read and write variables by `uniqueId`.
- [API Reference](API-Reference.md): the JSON-RPC surface that exposes mutating CRUD by `(groupId, datasetId)` and live reads by `uniqueId`.
docs.title: Identity-Model#10

docs.body:
# InfluxDB export (Pro)

You want your sensor readings on a Grafana panel that keeps updating while the capture runs, and keeps existing after you close Serial Studio. The InfluxDB sink sends every parsed sample to an InfluxDB 2.x server as it arrives. It does not work with InfluxDB 1.x. If the server is slow or down, the sink drops points; parsing and the dashboard carry on.

Typical uses: a Grafana dashboard for people away from the bench, or one shared history fed by several benches. To keep samples in a local file instead, see [CSV Export](CSV-Export-Playback.md), [MDF4](MDF4.md) or the [Historian](Historian.md).
docs.title: InfluxDB#0

docs.body:
## Quick setup

The sink writes the datasets of your project, so build the project first (see [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md)). A device printing `21.5,43,OK` with datasets titled Temperature, Humidity and Status produces the example line under [What gets written](#what-gets-written).
docs.title: InfluxDB#1

docs.body:
1. Install InfluxDB 2.x; it serves a web UI at `http://localhost:8086`. The first-start form asks for an organization name and a first bucket name. A bucket is where the points are stored.
2. Under API Tokens in the InfluxDB UI, create a token with write access to that bucket. Copy it then; InfluxDB shows it once.
3. In Serial Studio, open the Project Editor and select **Data Export** > **InfluxDB Sink** in the left tree.
4. Fill in **Server URL**, **Organization** and **Bucket**, then paste the token into **API Token**.
5. Switch **Enabled** on, then connect your device. The sink writes only while a device is connected.
6. The header bar above the form reads **Writing to InfluxDB** and its counter line reads `<n> written, ...` with `<n>` climbing. In the InfluxDB Data Explorer, look for the `serial_studio` measurement.
docs.title: InfluxDB#2

docs.body:
## Edition and licensing

InfluxDB export is a Pro feature (see [Pro vs Free Features](Pro-vs-Free.md)). Without a license or an active trial, **Enabled** stays off, even if the project file was saved with it on.

The first time you try to switch on **Enabled** (or any Pro feature), Serial Studio asks Yes or No whether to start the 14-day trial. The trial never starts on its own, and registering it needs an internet connection. After the trial ends, the prompt offers activation or purchase instead. An active trial unlocks the sink like a purchased license. A license that activates after the project has loaded switches the sink on without a reload.
docs.title: InfluxDB#3

docs.body:
## Where to configure it

**InfluxDB Sink** is a child of the **Data Export** node (Pro only) in the Project Editor's left tree, next to **MQTT Publisher**.

```
Project
├─ ...
├─ Data Export
│   ├─ MQTT Publisher
│   └─ InfluxDB Sink       <-- here
└─ ...
```

Selecting it opens a form with a **Publishing** section (**Enabled**) and a **Server** section (the other fields). The header bar above the form carries the live state and the counters:

- A green LED and **Writing to InfluxDB** once the endpoint has accepted a write, a red LED and **Not writing** otherwise. When the last write failed, the failure message replaces **Not writing**. A failure reads `Server answered HTTP <status>: <response body, first 1 KiB>` or `TLS verification failed: <reason>`. Redirects are not followed, so point the URL at the final `https` address.
- A counter line on the right, reading `<n> written, <n> dropped, <n> errors`.
docs.title: InfluxDB#4

docs.body:
## Form fields

| Field | Effect |
|-------|--------|
| **Enabled** | Master toggle. Writes while a device is connected. Stays off without a license or trial. |
| **Server URL** | Base URL of the InfluxDB server, for example `http://localhost:8086`. The sink appends the write path itself. |
| **Organization** | Name of the organization that owns the bucket, as InfluxDB shows it. |
| **Bucket** | Destination bucket. It must already exist; Serial Studio does not create it. |
| **Measurement** | The name your points are stored under. Defaults to `serial_studio`; leave it unless several projects share a bucket. An empty name, or one starting with `#`, falls back to the default, and surrounding whitespace is trimmed. |
| **API Token** | InfluxDB API token with write permission on the bucket. Write-only: after you paste a token the field clears, which is normal, and the placeholder reads `Stored; type a new token to replace it`. |
docs.title: InfluxDB#5

docs.body:
`Server URL`, `Organization`, `Bucket` and `Measurement` are saved in the project file. The token is not: Serial Studio keeps it, obfuscated, in this computer's settings, keyed by the server's host and port. Moving a project file to another machine carries the endpoint but not the token, and changing the host or port of the URL makes the stored token go missing, so re-enter it in both cases.

### The URL rule

A bearer token must not ride a cleartext connection to a remote host, so the sink accepts:

- `https` to any host.
- `http` only to `127.0.0.1`, `localhost` or `::1`.

Anything else is refused when the field is committed, and the header bar reports `Refused an insecure InfluxDB URL: use https, or http only for a loopback host`. The typed value is not kept. A LAN address on plain `http` is refused, even if it is your own desk; put TLS in front of it.
docs.title: InfluxDB#6

docs.body:
## What gets written

Each sample becomes one point, written as one line of InfluxDB line protocol:

```
serial_studio,source=0 Temperature=21.5,Humidity=43,Status="OK" 1757001600123456789
```

`Temperature`, `Humidity` and `Status` are dataset titles from the project, and the trailing number is the timestamp in nanoseconds.
docs.title: InfluxDB#7

docs.body:
- The measurement is the **Measurement** field, and `source` is the only tag. It carries the numeric source id, so several devices in one project stay separable inside a single measurement.
- **Field keys** are dataset titles. An empty title, or a title shared by two datasets, is qualified with the dataset's unique id (`Temperature_7`), so two datasets can never collapse onto one field key and overwrite each other.
- Field types: a number is written as a float, never as an integer or boolean, and text as a string. A dataset keeps the type of its first sample until the sink reopens. A string dataset is omitted from points that carry no text for it. NaN and infinity cannot be written, so they are skipped and counted in `fieldsSkipped`.
- **Timestamps** are the driver's capture times converted to wall-clock nanoseconds and sent with `precision=ns`. The conversion offset is sampled when the sink opens or the endpoint changes, so a system clock step mid-capture shifts later points until then.
docs.title: InfluxDB#8

docs.body:
Points accumulate into a batch and are POSTed to `<Server URL>/api/v2/write` with the organization, bucket and precision as query parameters and the token in an `Authorization: Token …` header. The sink POSTs at most once per drained set of blocks, and sooner when a batch reaches 512 KiB.

One request is outstanding at a time. If a batch is ready while a request is still in flight, that batch is dropped and counted. The sink drops rather than waits: a capture that stalls for a database is worse than a gap in a graph. A request that hangs is abandoned after 30 seconds so it cannot pin the slot.
docs.title: InfluxDB#9

docs.body:
## Statistics

The header counters and the API values are pulled on the one-second tick rather than pushed per point:

| Counter (API key) | Meaning |
|-------------------|---------|
| **written** (`pointsWritten`) | Points accepted by the server. |
| **dropped** (`pointsDropped`) | Points that never reached the bucket: a batch rendered while a request was still in flight, the points of a write the server rejected, and anything still queued when the sink closes. |
| **errors** (`httpErrors`) | HTTP failures. The most recent failure message, with the response body cut to 1 KiB, is shown in the header bar. |
| `fieldsSkipped` (API only) | Fields omitted from a point because the value was NaN or infinity. Not shown in the header bar. |
docs.title: InfluxDB#10

docs.body:
## API commands

Three [API](API-Reference.md) commands cover the sink. They need the API Server turned on (it is off by default, port 7777).

- `influx.setConfig` patches the endpoint with `url`, `org`, `bucket`, `measurement` and `token`. Every field is optional, so a call changes only what it names. The token goes to the same per-machine store as the form field; no command reads it back. A field of the wrong type, or an insecure URL, is rejected wholesale rather than coerced.
- `influx.setEnabled` takes `enabled` (boolean) and toggles the sink. Without a license or trial it reports `enabled=false`.
- `influx.getStatus` snapshots enabled and open state, the endpoint fields, whether a token is stored, the four counters (`pointsWritten`, `pointsDropped`, `fieldsSkipped`, `httpErrors`), and the last write error.
docs.title: InfluxDB#11

docs.body:
## Common pitfalls

- The URL was refused. `http` is accepted only for a loopback host. Use `https`, or an SSH tunnel to loopback.
- **Enabled will not stay on.** There is no valid license or active trial; see [Edition and licensing](#edition-and-licensing). The header shows **Not writing** and the counters do not move.
- A field is missing or has a `_<id>` suffix. An empty title, or one shared with another dataset, is written under a `_<id>` suffix (`Temperature_7`). Otherwise the values are NaN or infinity, counted in `fieldsSkipped`.
- Points fail with HTTP 422. The bucket already holds that field with a different type, so the points count under `dropped` and `errors`.
- **`dropped` climbs steadily while `errors` stays flat.** The server is slower than the capture. Reduce the sample rate, check the network path, or use a faster server.
- Nothing is written after moving the project or editing the URL. The token is stored per machine, keyed by host and port. Re-enter it.
docs.title: InfluxDB#12

docs.body:
## See also

- [MQTT Publisher](MQTT-Publisher.md): the other live outbound sink, including a line-protocol template for reaching InfluxDB through Telegraf instead of directly.
- [CSV Export & Playback](CSV-Export-Playback.md), [MDF4 Export & Playback](MDF4.md), [Historian](Historian.md): the local recording sinks.
- [API Reference](API-Reference.md): the `influx.*` commands.
- [Troubleshooting](Troubleshooting.md): general connection and data problems.
docs.title: InfluxDB#13

docs.body:
# MDF4 export and playback (Pro)

Switch on **MDF4 Recording**, connect your device, let it run for ten minutes, and a file called `2026-03-17_15-30-05.mf4` is waiting in `Documents/Serial Studio/MDF4/<project name>/`. MDF4 is a Pro feature. Open it later in a tool such as `asammdf`, or replay it in Serial Studio through the same data pipeline as a live connection.

MDF4 (Measurement Data Format 4, `.mf4`) is an [ASAM](https://www.asam.net/standards/detail/mdf/) binary log format used in automotive and test tools. Each project group gets its own set of columns with its own timestamps, so a 10 kHz vibration signal and a 1 Hz GPS signal share one file without padding. Serial Studio writes it uncompressed.
docs.title: MDF4#0

docs.body:
For text logging and the "which file format?" comparison, see [CSV Export & Playback](CSV-Export-Playback.md). For queryable, project-scoped session storage, see the [Historian](Historian.md).

## MDF4 export

### Turning export on

MDF4 export (Pro) is the **MDF4 Recording** switch under **Data Export** in the Setup panel, next to the CSV switch.

1. Connect your device.
2. In the Setup panel, under **Data Export**, turn on **MDF4 Recording**. You can also turn it on before connecting.
3. Let data flow, then disconnect.
4. Open the MDF4 folder described in [File location](#file-location) and find the `.mf4` file.
docs.title: MDF4#1

docs.body:
The switch is greyed out in Console Only mode. Without a Pro license no file is created: the first time you switch it on, Serial Studio offers the 14-day trial (a Yes/No prompt; registering the trial needs an internet connection), and after the trial expires the prompt offers activation or purchase instead. See [Pro vs Free Features](Pro-vs-Free.md). The setting is remembered between runs.

### File location

Serial Studio writes MDF4 files to `Documents/Serial Studio/MDF4/<Project Name>/` by default, named after the session start time. To move the workspace, see [CSV Export & Playback](CSV-Export-Playback.md).
docs.title: MDF4#2

docs.body:
```text
Serial Studio/MDF4/<Project Name>/<yyyy-MM-dd_HH-mm-ss>.mf4
```

For a session started at 3:30:05 PM on March 17, 2026, in a project named "Vehicle Test":

```text
Serial Studio/MDF4/Vehicle Test/2026-03-17_15-30-05.mf4
```

If that name is taken, Serial Studio appends `_2`, `_3` and so on, up to 64 attempts. A pause and resume within the same second therefore gives `..._2.mf4` instead of overwriting the first file.

To turn a file into CSV with Python:

```python
# pip install asammdf
from asammdf import MDF
MDF("2026-03-17_15-30-05.mf4").export(fmt="csv", filename="out.csv")
```

### Channels and metadata
docs.title: MDF4#3

docs.body:
Each project group becomes a channel group and each dataset becomes a channel, except Image View groups, which are not exported. A dataset called Temperature in the group Sensors appears as `Temperature` in channel group `Sensors`, plus a `Temperature (raw)` channel with the value before any [dataset transform](Dataset-Transforms.md). Channel names are written as UTF-8.

| Item | In the file |
|------|-------------|
| Channel group name | The group's title; `SourceName / GroupName` in multi-source projects |
| Unit | The dataset's `units` field |
| Data type | 64-bit float (8 bytes) for numeric datasets; fixed 256-byte UTF-8 string for text datasets |
| Time | The timestamp channel (`Time`, the MDF4 master channel): seconds from the file's start time, one per group |
| File header | Author (`Serial Studio`), description, subject (the project title), project (`Telemetry Data`) and start time |
docs.title: MDF4#4

docs.body:
Serial Studio writes only these. MDF4 itself supports conversion formulas and comments, but the exporter writes none, so scaling does not travel with the file.

### File lifecycle

One file covers one connected, unpaused stretch. Serial Studio creates it on the first frame received after export is on, and closes it on disconnect, pause, or when you turn export off. Resuming or reconnecting starts a new file with a new timestamp. If no frame arrives, no file appears.

### Background writing

Writing happens on a background thread so it does not slow the dashboard; the queue holds 8192 items and flushes every 1000 ms or at 1024 items. The export path never re-stamps frames, so CSV and MDF4 carry the same source timestamp (see [Threading and Timing Guarantees](Threading-and-Timing.md)).
docs.title: MDF4#5

docs.body:
### API and command line

To start MDF4 export from a script, run Serial Studio with `--mdf-export` (Pro; see the [Command-Line Interface](Command-Line-Interface.md)), or enable the API Server (off by default, port 7777). The [API](API-Reference.md) then exposes `mdf4Export.getStatus`, `mdf4Export.setEnabled` and `mdf4Export.close`.

## MDF4 playback

### Opening an MDF4 file

MDF4 playback (Pro) replays a recorded file without a device connected.

1. Click **Open MDF4** in the toolbar. It is disabled while you are connected, while a file is already open, and in operator (runtime) mode. Without a Pro license it triggers the same trial or activation prompt as export.
2. Pick a `.mf4` (or `.dat`) file. The dialog starts in the `MDF4` folder of your workspace.
3. The **MDF4 Player** dialog opens.
docs.title: MDF4#6

docs.body:
### How playback works

The MDF4 Player (Pro) feeds each frame through the same pipeline as a live connection: Frame Builder, then Dashboard and widgets. The player keeps the original timing between frames.

File export (CSV and MDF4) is suppressed while any player is open, so replaying a file does not re-record it.

### Player controls

In the MDF4 Player dialog, Space plays or pauses, Left and Right Arrow step one frame, and the progress slider seeks. The current timestamp shows above the slider as `HH:MM:SS.mmm`.

### Playing files from other tools

MDF4 playback (Pro) needs no setup for files recorded by Serial Studio: the `Time` channel is the clock and the `(raw)` channels are skipped. For files captured by other tools, the player assigns each channel group's data channels to the loaded project's datasets in file order, so the first channel feeds the first dataset. Load a project whose datasets are in the same order as the file's channels.
docs.title: MDF4#7

docs.body:
## Common pitfalls

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
|---------|---------------|
| No file appears | Export needs a live connection; the file is created on the first frame, not on the toggle. Console Only mode greys out the switch, and without a Pro license no file is created. |
| Files get large fast | An audio source at 48 kHz or a full CAN bus produces gigabytes per hour. Watch disk space; pausing or disconnecting closes the file and the next frame starts a new one. |
| Non-ASCII titles look garbled | Channel names are UTF-8; a tool that decodes names as ASCII garbles them. `asammdf` reads them correctly. |
docs.title: MDF4#8

docs.body:
## Further reading

- [ASAM MDF Standard (official site)](https://www.asam.net/standards/detail/mdf/)
- [asammdf Python library documentation](https://asammdf.readthedocs.io/)

## See also

- [CSV Export & Playback](CSV-Export-Playback.md): text-based logging and replay.
- [Historian](Historian.md): SQLite-backed project archive with built-in replay.
- [Drivers: CAN Bus](Drivers-CAN-Bus.md): connecting to a live CAN bus.
- [Pro vs Free Features](Pro-vs-Free.md): MDF4 export and playback are Pro features.
docs.title: MDF4#9

docs.body:
# MQTT Publisher (Pro)

Your ESP32 prints `21.4,43` over USB, and a Node-RED flow on another machine needs those numbers. The MQTT Publisher sends your device's data to an MQTT broker, a small server that relays messages to anything subscribed to a topic, so the second machine never talks to the device. It is the outbound side of Serial Studio's MQTT support; the [MQTT subscriber driver](Drivers-MQTT.md) is the inbound side. New to MQTT? [MQTT Topics & Semantics](MQTT-Topics.md) explains topics, QoS and retained messages in one page.

MQTT Publisher is a Pro feature. The first time you use a Pro feature without a license, Serial Studio offers a trial with a Yes/No prompt (registering the trial needs an internet connection). Without a license or an active trial, nothing is published and **Test Connection** reports that a commercial license is required. After a trial expires, the prompt offers activation or purchase. See [Pro vs Free Features](Pro-vs-Free.md).
docs.title: MQTT-Publisher#0

docs.body:
## Publish your first frame

You need a project that already parses your device's frames (see [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md)).

1. Install [Mosquitto](https://mosquitto.org) and start it. It listens on `127.0.0.1:1883` and includes the `mosquitto_sub` command used below.
2. In the Project Editor, select **MQTT Publisher** under **Data Export**.
3. Leave **Hostname** and **Port** at their defaults (`127.0.0.1`, `1883`) and set **Topic Base** to `sensors/demo`.
4. Set **Payload** to `Dashboard Data (JSON)` (the default is `Raw RX Data`) and turn on **Enable Publishing**.
5. Optionally click **Test Connection**, then connect your device.
docs.title: MQTT-Publisher#1

docs.body:
Watch the topic from a terminal:

```text
mosquitto_sub -t 'sensors/demo' -v
```

Each publish tick (10 per second by default) prints one line like this. The title and values come from your project, so yours will differ.

```text
sensors/demo {"title":"My Project","frameCount":3,"groups":[...]}
```

Test Connection only proves the broker accepts you. The terminal tells you whether data flows.

## Where to configure it

In the Project Editor, the **MQTT Publisher** node sits in the left tree under **Data Export** (a Pro-only node), next to the InfluxDB Sink. Selecting it opens a form-style editor.
docs.title: MQTT-Publisher#2

docs.body: The header bar above the form shows the live connection state (green LED + "Connected to broker" when up, red LED + "Not connected" otherwise) and five actions, all disabled until **Enable Publishing** is on:
docs.title: MQTT-Publisher#3

docs.body:
- **Test Connection.** Opens a throwaway connection with the current settings, waits up to five seconds, and reports the outcome in a message box ("MQTT broker reachable", "MQTT broker unreachable", or "MQTT publisher unavailable" without a license). It checks CONNECT only, publishes nothing, and does not test publish rights. It is independent of the live connection, so it is safe to run while the Publisher is connected. The probe forces **Clean Session** on and **Keep Alive** to 5 s, keeps your **Protocol Version**, and uses the Client ID with a `-probe` suffix. The live connection allows 15 s per attempt.
- **Edit Script.** Visible only when **Payload** is `Custom Script`. Opens the script editor dialog (see [Custom Script mode](#custom-script)).
- **Load CA Certs.** Enabled only when **Use SSL/TLS** is on. Adds PEM certificates from a folder to the in-memory trust store; the certificates are not saved with the project.
- **Client Certificate.** Enabled only when **Use SSL/TLS** is on. Picks the PEM certificate for mutual TLS.
- **Private Key.** Enabled only when **Use SSL/TLS** is on. Picks the matching PEM key; it defaults to the certificate file.
docs.title: MQTT-Publisher#4

docs.body:
The Publisher connects automatically whenever **Enable Publishing** is on and hostname and port are set. Changing any broker setting while connected triggers a disconnect-and-reconnect with the new values.

The same configuration is scriptable through the [API](API-Reference.md) commands `project.mqtt.publisher.getConfig`, `project.mqtt.publisher.setConfig`, and `project.mqtt.publisher.getStatus`. `setConfig` patches only the keys you pass.

## Form fields

### Publishing
docs.title: MQTT-Publisher#5

docs.body:
| Field | Effect |
|-------|--------|
| **Enable Publishing** | Master toggle. When off, Serial Studio publishes nothing. |
| **Payload** | Selects the wire format. Default `Raw RX Data`. See [Payload modes](#payload-modes) for the four options. |
| **Publish Rate (Hz)** | Messages per second, 1-30 (values outside are clamped), default 10. Frames that arrive between ticks go out together as one MQTT message. Broker I/O runs on its own worker thread, so a slow network never blocks frame parsing or the dashboard. |
| **Topic Base** | Base topic for the published payload. Required for traffic; when empty, the Publisher stays connected but publishes nothing. |
| **Script Topic** | (Visible only when **Payload** is `Custom Script`.) Topic the user script publishes to. Defaults to **Topic Base** when blank. |
| **Publish Notifications** | When on, dashboard notifications are mirrored to MQTT. |
| **Notification Topic** | (Visible only when **Publish Notifications** is on.) Topic used for notifications. Defaults to **Topic Base** when blank. |
docs.title: MQTT-Publisher#6

docs.body:
### Sparkplug

| Field | Effect |
|-------|--------|
| **Publish as Edge Node** | Publishes the datasets in the Sparkplug B namespace, with birth, death and rebirth handling, instead of the **Payload** you selected. See [Sparkplug](Drivers-MQTT.md#sparkplug). |
| **Group ID** | (Visible only when **Publish as Edge Node** is on.) Logical group of the edge node. Placeholder `Plant1`. |
| **Edge Node ID** | (Visible only when **Publish as Edge Node** is on.) Identifies the node inside the group. Placeholder `SerialStudio`. |
| **Device ID** | (Visible only when **Publish as Edge Node** is on.) Optional. When set, the datasets are published as a device of the node. |
docs.title: MQTT-Publisher#7

docs.body: ### Broker
docs.title: MQTT-Publisher#8

docs.body:
| Field | Effect |
|-------|--------|
| **Hostname** | Broker address (IP or hostname). Default `127.0.0.1`. |
| **Port** | TCP port. Default `1883` (plaintext); use `8883` for TLS. |
| **Custom Client ID** | Off by default: a fresh random 16-char id is generated on every project load. Turn this on only if your broker requires a stable identifier (e.g. an ACL keyed by client ID, or session persistence with `Clean Session = no`). When on, the **Client ID** row appears. |
| **Client ID** | (Visible only when **Custom Client ID** is on.) Identifier sent on CONNECT. The value is persisted with the project; the auto-generated id is not. |
| **Username / Password** | Optional authentication. The password is kept obfuscated in this machine's credential vault, never in the project file. The vault is keyed by hostname and port: changing either loads the credentials saved for that pair, and a project opened on another machine has no password. |
| **Protocol Version** | MQTT 3.1, 3.1.1, or 5.0. Default MQTT 5.0. |
| **Keep Alive (s)** | Seconds between PING packets when idle. Default 60. |
| **Clean Session** | Discard persistent session state on CONNECT. Default on. |
docs.title: MQTT-Publisher#9

docs.body:
### SSL / TLS

**Use SSL/TLS** is the master toggle. When on, these fields appear:
docs.title: MQTT-Publisher#10

docs.body:
| Field | Effect |
|-------|--------|
| **Protocol** | Negotiated TLS protocol family: TLS 1.2, TLS 1.3, TLS 1.3 or Later, DTLS 1.2 or Later, Any Protocol, or Secure Protocols Only (default). |
| **Peer Verify** | `None`, `Query Peer`, `Verify Peer`, or `Auto Verify Peer` (default). |
| **Verify Depth** | Maximum certificate chain length accepted. Default `10`; `0` = unlimited. |
| **Client Certificate** | Optional PEM certificate for mutual TLS (for example AWS IoT Core). The path is saved with the project. |
| **Private Key** | PEM key matching the certificate. Defaults to the certificate file. |
| **Key Passphrase** | Passphrase for an encrypted private key. Kept obfuscated in the machine's credential vault, never in the project file. |
| **ALPN (MQTT over port 443)** | Announces an ALPN protocol during the TLS handshake so a broker can serve MQTT on port 443 behind firewalls. |
| **ALPN Protocol** | (Visible only when **ALPN (MQTT over port 443)** is on.) Protocol name to announce; AWS IoT uses `x-amzn-mqtt-ca`. |
docs.title: MQTT-Publisher#11

docs.body:
For brokers using a private CA, click **Load CA Certs** in the header bar after enabling TLS.

## Payload modes

The **Payload** dropdown picks one of four modes. Start with `Dashboard Data (JSON)`: it carries dataset titles and values, so any consumer can read it. Use CSV for compact rows, Raw RX to forward bytes untouched, and Custom Script when the consumer needs an exact format. A frame is one line your device prints, such as `21.4,43`. With **Publish as Edge Node** on, the Sparkplug lane replaces all four.

| Mode | Topic | One message per tick holds |
|------|-------|----------------------------|
| Raw RX Data | **Topic Base** | The concatenated device bytes |
| Custom Script | **Script Topic**, else **Topic Base** | The concatenated script outputs |
| Dashboard Data (CSV) | **Topic Base**, plus a retained `<Topic Base>/header` | Multi-line CSV rows |
| Dashboard Data (JSON) | **Topic Base** | One aggregated JSON document |
docs.title: MQTT-Publisher#12

docs.body:
### Raw RX Data

In the MQTT Publisher (Pro), with **Payload** set to `Raw RX Data`, every chunk of bytes received from any active driver is republished to **Topic Base** unchanged. All chunks that arrived during one publish-rate tick are concatenated into a single publish.

Use this when the consumer wants to apply its own decoding, when you are tee-ing a serial device into existing MQTT infrastructure, or when the downstream tool is another Serial Studio instance subscribing to the topic.

### Custom Script

Set **Payload** to `Custom Script` (Pro) and write an `mqtt(frame)` function (in JavaScript or Lua) that receives the bytes of one frame (the same bytes the [Frame Parser](Frame-Parser.md) script sees) and returns the payload to publish, or `nil` / `null` to skip the frame. If your device prints `21.4,43` each line, `frame` holds those bytes.
docs.title: MQTT-Publisher#13
MQTT-Publisher#14

docs.body: Click **Edit Script** in the header to open the editor dialog. It has the same layout as the dataset-transform editor:
docs.title: MQTT-Publisher#15

docs.body:
- **Language** dropdown: JavaScript or Lua. The selection is stored in the project file.
- **Template** dropdown: ready-made starters for common integrations:
  - **Home Assistant Discovery + State**: publishes the auto-discovery config message and per-frame state updates.
  - **InfluxDB Line Protocol**: formats `measurement,tag=value field=value timestamp` lines suitable for a Telegraf `mqtt_consumer` input. Timestamps come from `os.time()`.
  - **Sparkplug B (NDATA)**: a JSON payload shaped like a Sparkplug data message, for a consumer that only needs the shape. For a real edge node, with protobuf payloads, aliases, birth and death certificates and rebirth handling, tick **Publish as Edge Node** instead of using this template ([Sparkplug](Drivers-MQTT.md#sparkplug)). Timestamps come from `os.time()`.
  - **AWS IoT / Azure IoT Shadow**: `{"state":{"reported":{...}}}` payload accepted by both clouds.
- Code editor with syntax highlighting, Ctrl-I to format the selection, Ctrl-Shift-I to format the document.
- Test row at the bottom: paste sample bytes in **Frame**, tick **Hex** if they are hex-encoded, click **Test**, and the dialog shows the string the script would publish (or the error). This runs in a disposable engine and never touches the live broker session.
- **Apply** saves the script into the project; **Cancel** discards changes.
docs.title: MQTT-Publisher#16

docs.body:
Limits:

- The script compiles lazily on the worker thread the first time a frame arrives after a code change.
- A frame whose script call fails is skipped; the rest of the batch still publishes.
- JavaScript and Lua calls both run under a 500 ms budget; a call that exceeds it is killed and that frame skipped.
- Lua runs in a sandbox limited to the `table`, `string`, and `math` libraries plus a restricted `os` table (`os.time`, `os.date`, `os.clock`, `os.difftime`); `load`, `loadfile`, and `dofile` are removed.
- **Test** uses the same sandbox, so sandbox errors show up there. It does not prove your script handles every real frame; confirm with a subscriber.
docs.title: MQTT-Publisher#17

docs.body:
### Dashboard Data (CSV)

In the MQTT Publisher (Pro), with **Payload** set to `Dashboard Data (CSV)`, you get one CSV row per parsed frame, with columns matching the project's dataset layout (same column order as the CSV export). Every frame that arrived during a publish-rate tick is concatenated into a single multi-line publish on **Topic Base**.

The CSV header is published once as a **retained** message on `<Topic Base>/header` (with Topic Base `sensors/demo`, that is `sensors/demo/header`), so any subscriber that joins later receives the schema immediately and can map column positions to dataset titles without having to know the project in advance. The header is republished automatically when the publisher detects a schema change or its broker configuration is re-applied.
docs.title: MQTT-Publisher#18
MQTT-Publisher#19

docs.body:
Use this when the consumer is another dashboard, a Node-RED flow, or a time-series store that already knows the project's dataset layout. The shape mirrors the [API Reference](API-Reference.md) `frame_now` payload but with array-valued samples for batch ingestion.

### Notifications

In the MQTT Publisher (Pro), when **Publish Notifications** is on, every event posted to the [Notification Center](Notifications.md) (alarm transitions, action confirmations, error messages) is also serialized to JSON and published to **Notification Topic** (or **Topic Base** if Notification Topic is blank). This is the fan-out point for alerting integrations and is independent of the **Payload** mode.
docs.title: MQTT-Publisher#20
MQTT-Publisher#21

docs.body:
The call returns `1` once the publish is queued for the worker, or `-1` if the Publisher is not connected or has no valid license. The actual broker send happens asynchronously on the worker thread, so the returned value is not the broker message ID. QoS is clamped to `0..2`.

Use **Custom Script** mode when the script's main job is shaping the publish payload; use `mqttPublish()` from a frame parser when the script's main job is parsing the frame and the publish is a side-effect.

## Common pitfalls
docs.title: MQTT-Publisher#22

docs.body:
- **Connected, but nothing arrives.** **Topic Base** is empty (the Publisher stays connected and publishes nothing) or **Enable Publishing** is off. **Test Connection** checks CONNECT only, so it passes either way.
- **Custom Script mode is selected but nothing publishes.** The script must define a function named exactly `mqtt(frame)` (not `parse`, not `publish`). Use **Test** in the editor to check a sample input.
- **Publisher and Subscriber on the same topic loop forever.** When the subscriber driver listens on the Publisher's **Topic Base**, the broker hands your own message back, the subscriber treats it as device data, and the Publisher sends it again, politely. Use different base topics, or disable one side.
- **Two instances on different machines hit "Client ID rejected".** Two Publishers need different client IDs. The default (**Custom Client ID** off) generates a fresh random id on every load, so this happens only when **Custom Client ID** is on with the same typed value on both machines.
- **TLS worked in the last session but fails after restarting Serial Studio.** Certificates added with **Load CA Certs** live in memory only. Load them again after every launch.
- **CSV consumers do not see the header.** They must also subscribe to `<Topic Base>/header`. The header is retained, so it arrives immediately on subscribe.
docs.title: MQTT-Publisher#23

docs.body:
# MQTT Topics & Semantics (Pro)

Your ESP32 publishes a reading to a broker, and Serial Studio subscribes to it and plots it:

```text
topic:   home/esp32-001/temperature
publish: mosquitto_pub -t home/esp32-001/temperature -m 23.5
filter:  home/esp32-001/#        (or home/+/temperature)
```

The broker is the server in the middle, and `mosquitto_pub` is Mosquitto's command-line tool, standing in for your ESP32 (on the board itself, an MQTT client library such as PubSubClient does the publishing).

To try it, install [Eclipse Mosquitto](https://mosquitto.org/) on your PC. In the main window's **Setup** pane, set the bus type to **MQTT Subscriber**, **Hostname** to `localhost`, **Port** to `1883` and **Topic Filter** to `home/esp32-001/#`, pick **Quick Plot** and connect, then run the `mosquitto_pub` line. The payload `23.5` is one number, so it becomes one plot.
docs.title: MQTT-Topics#0

docs.body:
The Pro [MQTT subscriber driver](Drivers-MQTT.md) takes data from a broker into Serial Studio. The Pro [MQTT Publisher](MQTT-Publisher.md) sends data from Serial Studio to a broker. This page defines the MQTT terms both use.

## MQTT overview

MQTT is a publish/subscribe protocol. The current version is 5.0; 3.1.1 is still common. Serial Studio supports 3.1, 3.1.1, and 5.0 on both of its MQTT surfaces and defaults to 5.0.

Publishers and subscribers do not connect to each other. They connect to a **broker**, a server that both Serial Studio and your device reach over the network, and the broker handles routing.
docs.title: MQTT-Topics#1

docs.body:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    P1[Publisher: Sensor A] -- "topic: factory/temp/A" --> Broker
    P2[Publisher: Sensor B] -- "topic: factory/temp/B" --> Broker
    P3[Publisher: Pump 1] -- "topic: factory/pumps/1" --> Broker
    Broker -- "subscribed: factory/temp/+" --> S1[Subscriber: Dashboard]
    Broker -- "subscribed: factory/#" --> S2[Subscriber: Logger]
    Broker -- "subscribed: factory/pumps/1" --> S3[Subscriber: Alarm]
```

Publishers send to a topic and subscribers register a pattern. Neither side knows the other exists, so you can add or remove either without touching the rest.

## Topics
docs.title: MQTT-Topics#2

docs.body:
Topics are hierarchical strings separated by `/`:

```text
factory/floor1/zone3/temperature
home/livingroom/sensors/humidity
serial-studio/devices/esp32-001/data
```

The broker does not enforce a schema; topics are just strings. Put the general scope first and the specific last, so one wildcard can select a whole branch.

Topic names are case-sensitive. `Sensors/Temperature` and `sensors/temperature` are two different topics; the broker will not route between them.

### Wildcards

Only subscribers can use **wildcards**, in the filter they register. Enter the filter in the subscriber driver's **Topic Filter** field (Project Editor: the source's Connection Settings; main window: **Setup** pane):
docs.title: MQTT-Topics#3

docs.body:
- `+` matches exactly one level. `factory/+/temperature` matches `factory/floor1/temperature` and `factory/floor2/temperature` but not `factory/floor1/zone3/temperature`.
- `#` matches the parent level and every level below it. `factory/#` matches `factory`, `factory/a` and `factory/a/b`. It must be the last character of the filter.

Neither wildcard matches a topic whose first level starts with `$`, such as `$SYS/#`. A common diagnostic trick is to temporarily subscribe to `#` (or `your/prefix/#`) and watch every non-`$` topic the broker routes. `mosquitto_sub -t '#' -v` does the same from a terminal.
docs.title: MQTT-Topics#4

docs.body:
Turning **Sparkplug** on in the subscriber replaces the filter with the Sparkplug namespace, so **Topic Filter** is ignored.

## Naming your own topics

Serial Studio does not create the subtopics below. The Publisher writes to the **Topic Base** you set, plus a retained `<TopicBase>/header` for the CSV column names. The layout here is a suggestion for your own devices:

```text
<project>/<device>/data
<project>/<device>/notify
```

Putting the project at the top makes it easy to scope subscribers and ACLs (per-user permission rules on the broker) per project. Putting the device next lets a single subscriber follow one device with `myproject/esp32-001/#` or watch the whole fleet with `myproject/+/data`.
docs.title: MQTT-Topics#5

docs.body:
Give each MQTT source in a project its own topic filter. If one filter matches several devices, Serial Studio cannot tell them apart unless the device identifies itself in the payload.

## Quality of Service (QoS)

MQTT publishes can carry one of three QoS levels:

| QoS | Name             | Guarantees |
|-----|------------------|-----------|
| 0   | At most once     | Fire and forget. The message is sent, and it's gone. No retransmission, no ack. May be lost. |
| 1   | At least once    | The publisher resends until the broker acknowledges. The subscriber may receive duplicates. |
| 2   | Exactly once     | Four-message handshake: PUBLISH, PUBREC, PUBREL, PUBCOMP. Guaranteed delivery, no duplicates. Slowest. |
docs.title: MQTT-Topics#6

docs.body:
For telemetry, QoS 0 is enough: if a temperature reading is lost, the next one is already on its way. Choose QoS 1 when a lost message is a problem but a duplicate is not; your application ignores the repeat. QoS 2 is for "must arrive exactly once" cases such as billing events and is rarely worth its cost for streaming data.

The Pro [subscriber driver](Drivers-MQTT.md) subscribes at QoS 0. The Pro [MQTT Publisher](MQTT-Publisher.md) publishes its built-in payload modes at QoS 0. In Sparkplug edge-node mode (**Publish as Edge Node**) it also registers its death certificate at QoS 1 and subscribes to its command topic at QoS 1. In the Publisher's script mode, the `mqttPublish()` hook can request any QoS from 0 to 2 and set the retain flag per message.
docs.title: MQTT-Topics#7

docs.body:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Publisher
    participant B as Broker

Note over P,B: QoS 0
    P-)B: PUBLISH

Note over P,B: QoS 1
    P->>B: PUBLISH
    B-->>P: PUBACK

Note over P,B: QoS 2
    P->>B: PUBLISH
    B-->>P: PUBREC
    P->>B: PUBREL
    B-->>P: PUBCOMP
```

## Retained messages

A publisher can mark a message as **retained**. The broker remembers the last retained message on each topic and delivers it immediately to any new subscriber. This is the way to signal "current state" rather than "events":

- `home/heating/setpoint` retained: the current setpoint, available to anyone who subscribes.
- `home/heating/events/setpoint-changed` non-retained: the change events, only seen by clients listening at the time.
docs.title: MQTT-Topics#8

docs.body:
Retained messages do not expire unless MQTT 5 message expiry is set. Publishing an empty payload to a topic with the retain flag clears the retained message.

Serial Studio's Publisher uses a retained message for the CSV header on `<TopicBase>/header`, so a subscriber that joins late still receives the column schema (see [MQTT Publisher](MQTT-Publisher.md)).

A retained message is delivered first on subscribe and looks like live data until the next publish arrives. The subscriber does not flag retained messages, so a stale value right after connecting is a retained one. Clear it by publishing an empty retained payload to that topic.
docs.title: MQTT-Topics#9

docs.body:
## Last Will and Testament

When a client connects, it can register a **Last Will** message: a topic, payload, and QoS that the broker publishes if the client disconnects ungracefully. Devices use it for presence: publish a retained "online" message on connect, and register a will of "offline" on the same topic.

The Pro subscriber driver registers no Last Will. The Pro MQTT Publisher registers one only in Sparkplug edge-node mode (**Publish as Edge Node**): an NDEATH message at QoS 1, not retained.

## Sessions and clean session

Leave **Clean Session** on unless you need the broker to hold messages while a client is offline. A persistent session means the broker remembers a client's subscriptions and queued messages across disconnects, keyed by the client ID. **Clean Session** is on by default in both the Pro subscriber driver (Setup pane) and the Pro MQTT Publisher (Project Editor, MQTT Publisher), so the broker forgets the client between connections.
docs.title: MQTT-Topics#10

docs.body:
To have the broker queue messages for an offline client, turn **Clean Session** off, set a fixed client ID, and publish to it at QoS 1 or 2 from your own device or from the Publisher's `mqttPublish()` hook (the built-in modes are QoS 0). The subscriber driver itself subscribes at QoS 0, so a subscriber source gets no queued messages whatever the setting.

## Keep alive

The keep-alive interval, set at CONNECT, is the longest the broker waits for a packet from the client. When the client is idle it sends a ping, so the timer resets. The subscriber driver sends pings only while **Auto Keep Alive** is on (the default; Project Editor only). If the broker hears nothing within 1.5 × keep-alive, it drops the connection and publishes the Last Will, if one is set.
docs.title: MQTT-Topics#11

docs.body:
**Keep Alive (s)** defaults to 60 in both the Pro subscriber driver (Setup pane) and the Pro MQTT Publisher (Project Editor, MQTT Publisher). The range is 0 to 65535. Pick a value shorter than the shortest idle timeout on the path (router, corporate firewall, mobile network); on flaky cellular links, use 30 or 15. `0` disables the mechanism, and the broker then notices a dead client only when TCP does.

## Client IDs

Every MQTT client on a broker needs a unique client ID. Serial Studio generates a random 16-character ID for each surface:

| Surface | ID | Where to change it |
|---------|----|--------------------|
| Pro subscriber driver | Kept until you change it | Setup pane, **Regenerate** |
| Pro MQTT Publisher | New on every project load, unless **Custom Client ID** is on | Project Editor, MQTT Publisher, **Custom Client ID** |
docs.title: MQTT-Topics#12

docs.body:
If two clients connect to the same broker with the same client ID, the broker disconnects the older one. Two Serial Studio instances on one broker need distinct client IDs, and so do two MQTT sources in one project.

## Popular brokers

For a first test, use [Eclipse Mosquitto](https://mosquitto.org/) on your PC: a single binary, easy to configure. For something bigger, [EMQX](https://www.emqx.io/) and [VerneMQ](https://vernemq.com/) scale out, and AWS IoT Core, Azure IoT Hub, HiveMQ Cloud and EMQX Cloud are managed.

Public test brokers such as `test.mosquitto.org` and `broker.hivemq.com` suit development only; check each site for its current ports. Do not use them for anything that should stay private. They are public.
docs.title: MQTT-Topics#13

docs.body:

# Macros

You want to send the same command to your board at the start of every session, or check the link state without clicking through three panels. The Macros window does that: type one command and read the reply, or save a short JavaScript or Lua script and run it whenever you need it.

## Overview

Every action in Serial Studio is a named command, such as `io.connect` or `project.dataset.add`. The Macros window runs them inside the app; no API server needs to be on.

Macros are available in every edition, GPL builds included. The window opens only in author mode: in a runtime-mode (operator) deployment the Macros command does nothing. The command catalog is whatever the running build registers; a command from a driver the build does not ship is not listed, and calling it returns the unknown-command error.
docs.title: Macros#0

docs.body:
Press **Ctrl+K** (**Cmd+K** on macOS) to open the [command palette](Command-Palette.md), type `Macros`, and press Enter. The **Macros** entry is in the **Tools** category and appears in the palette from both the main window and the dashboard. The main toolbar also has a **Macros** button, next to the Remote Attach and Problems buttons.

The left pane of the window is the command catalog: a search field, the command list grouped by scope, and a documentation panel for the selected command. The right pane holds two tabs, **Terminal** and **Script**.

A macro acts immediately: it can change your project and write to the connected device with no confirmation prompt. Macros run in the application as the local user, with no remote client in the loop.
docs.title: Macros#1

docs.body:
## Quick start

1. Press **Ctrl+K**, type `Macros`, and press Enter.
2. Open the **Script** tab. It is pre-filled with a JavaScript starter macro that calls `api.getCommands` and prints the first five command names (abbreviated here to one).
3. Click the **Run macro** button (the play icon). The window switches to the **Terminal** tab and prints output like this; `N` is the number of commands in your build. The starter ends each line with `\n`, so blank lines appear between entries:

```text
> [macro] run (js)
Hello from Serial Studio! N commands available.

api.getCommands - Returns every command the live server exposes ...
docs.title: Macros#2

docs.body:
...
[macro] finished
```

4. Switch back to **Script**, edit the macro, and run it again. Click **Verify macro** first to catch a syntax error without executing anything.

To talk to the board, connect the device from the main window, then replace the macro with this one. `apiCall(name, params)` runs one command and returns `{ ok: true, result: ... }` or `{ ok: false, error: "..." }`; the three lines check for the second form. `console.send` uses the Console's line ending and encoding settings. With no device connected it writes nothing but still replies `sent: true`, so check `io.getStatus` `isConnected` first if that matters:
docs.title: Macros#3

docs.body:
```javascript
const reply = apiCall("console.send", { data: "LED ON" })
if (!reply.ok)
  throw new Error(reply.error)
```

## Terminal tab

The Macros window's Terminal tab runs one command per line. The input row at the bottom takes a command name followed by an optional JSON object of parameters:

```text
io.getStatus
project.getStatus
project.group.add { "title": "Sensors", "widgetType": 5 }
```

The first two lines only read state. The third adds a group titled `Sensors` to the open project; `5` is the `NoGroupWidget` value of `widgetType`, a plain container for related datasets.
docs.title: Macros#4

docs.body: Whitespace after the name starts the parameters. The parameters must parse as a JSON object; a malformed object or a JSON array is refused with `Invalid parameter JSON` or `Parameters must be a JSON object` before anything is dispatched. Press Enter or click the **Run command** button to run the line. The scrollback echoes the line with a `>` prefix, then prints the reply as indented JSON in the same shape the API server sends over the wire, including the error object for an unknown command.
docs.title: Macros#5

docs.body:
While the first token is being typed, a completion popup opens above the input row. It lists every catalog name that starts with the token, then every name that contains it. **Up** and **Down** move through the popup, **Tab** or **Enter** accepts the highlighted name, and **Esc** closes the popup. Accepting a completion inserts the name together with a parameter skeleton: one key per parameter, prefilled with `""`, `0`, `false`, `[]`, or `{}` according to the parameter's type. Double-clicking a command in the catalog inserts the same skeleton.

With the popup closed, **Up** and **Down** recall earlier lines. History lives only for the current session. The **Clear output** button empties the scrollback, and the right-click menu offers **Copy**, **Select All**, and **Clear**.
docs.title: Macros#6

docs.body:
## Command catalog

The left pane of the Macros window is the command catalog. Its search field filters the list by command name and description. The list is grouped by scope, the part of the name before the first dot, and each row shows the verb after the dot with its description underneath. Selecting a row, or typing an exact command name in the Terminal tab's input row, fills the documentation panel below the list with the full name, the description, and every parameter as `name (type)`, with an asterisk after the parameters a command requires. A command without parameters shows `No parameters`.
docs.title: Macros#7

docs.body:
## Script tab

The Script tab holds the macro editor, a code editor with syntax highlighting for the selected language, and a toolbar. The toolbar buttons are icons; hover one to see the name used below.
docs.title: Macros#8

docs.body:
| Control | Effect |
|---------|--------|
| **JavaScript** / **Lua** | Selects the macro language and the highlighter. Switching replaces the starter macro with the other language's starter when the editor is empty or still holds an unedited starter; edited text is kept. |
| **Load macro** | Opens a `.js` or `.lua` file into the editor. Its suffix sets the language. |
| **Save macro** | Writes the editor text to a file. Its default suffix follows the selected language. |
| **Verify macro** | Compiles the text without running it and prints the verdict to the Terminal tab. |
| **Run macro** | Runs the text, switching to the Terminal tab for the output. Disabled while a macro is running. |
| **Stop macro** | Interrupts a running JavaScript macro. Disabled for Lua and while nothing is running. |
| **Clear editor** | Empties the editor and its undo history. |
docs.title: Macros#9

docs.body:
**Load macro** and **Clear editor** ask `Discard changes?` when the editor holds edits that have not been saved. Closing the window keeps the editor text and language for the rest of the session, so the draft is still there when the window is opened again; quitting the application discards it.

### What a run prints

Every run starts with a header line, `> [macro] run (js)` or `> [macro] run (lua)`, in the Terminal scrollback. Output from `console.log()` and `print()` follows as it is produced. When the script ends, the scrollback shows the value of the script's final expression (JavaScript) or of its `return` statement (Lua); a script that produces no value ends with `[macro] finished`.
docs.title: Macros#10

docs.body:
A failed run prints one line prefixed with `[macro]`:

| Message | Meaning |
|---------|---------|
| `[macro] Line 4: Error: boom` | A JavaScript macro threw or hit a runtime error on line 4. |
| `[macro] [string "macro"]:4: boom` | A Lua macro raised an error on line 4. |
| `[macro] Macro stopped by user` | **Stop macro** interrupted a JavaScript macro. |
| `[macro] Macro exceeded the 5000 ms script budget between API calls and was interrupted` | A JavaScript macro spent more than 5 s in script code without calling the host. |
| `[macro] macro exceeded the 30000 ms safety deadline` | A Lua macro ran for more than 30 s in total. |
| `[macro] Macro is empty` | The editor held only whitespace. |
docs.title: Macros#11

docs.body:
**Verify macro** prints `[macro] verify: no syntax errors` or `[macro] verify failed: <error>`. Both languages name the line: JavaScript as `Line 3: SyntaxError: Expected token ';'`, Lua as `[string "macro"]:3: '=' expected near 'x'`. Verify compiles the text without running it. A JavaScript source is compiled inside a function wrapper under a 2 s budget, so a top-level `return` passes Verify but fails at run time.

## JavaScript and Lua macros

Use JavaScript unless the macro needs `actionFire()` or a dashboard setter. A Lua macro runs on the main window thread and freezes the window until it returns, so one that loops forever holds the whole application for thirty seconds. A host call is any `apiCall`, `delay` or `deviceWriteAndWait`; it hands control back to Serial Studio. The two languages run under different execution models:
docs.title: Macros#12

docs.body:
| | JavaScript | Lua |
|---|---|---|
| Runs on | Its own worker thread. Window and dashboard stay responsive. | The main window thread. Everything else waits until the macro returns. |
| **Stop macro** | Interrupts at the next host call, sleep, or device wait, and within 5 s of pure script code. | Not available. |
| Time limit | 5 s of script time between host calls. Each `apiCall`, `delay`, and `deviceWriteAndWait` restarts the budget. | 30 s for the whole run. |
| `delay(ms)` | Sleeps the macro without blocking the interface; capped at 1 hour. | Not available. |
| Output | `console.log()`, `console.info()`, `console.warn()`, `console.error()`, and `print()` each write one line to the scrollback, arguments joined by a space. | `print()` writes one line, arguments joined by a tab. |
| Engine | A fresh engine per run; no variable survives into the next run. | A fresh state per run. The `ffi` and `jit` modules are removed and the JIT compiler is off. |
docs.title: Macros#13

docs.body:
A JavaScript macro that loops forever with no host call is interrupted by the 5 s budget on its own. A Lua macro in the same loop freezes the interface until the 30 s deadline ends the run, and host calls do not extend it. Split long work into several runs, or write it in JavaScript.

### SDK helpers inside a macro

Both languages preload `apiCall(method, params)`, `apiCallList()`, and the generated wrappers (`api.getCommands()`, `io.getStatus()`, `project.dataset.add(...)`, and the rest of the [SDK call surface](SerialStudio-SDK.md)). `apiCall` returns the same envelope in both: `{ ok: true, result: ... }` or `{ ok: false, error: "..." }`.
docs.title: Macros#14

docs.body:
The direct host helpers are not installed uniformly:

| Helper group | JavaScript macro | Lua macro |
|---|---|---|
| `apiCall`, `apiCallList`, generated wrappers | yes | yes |
| `delay`, `deviceWriteAndWait` | yes | no |
| `newFrame`, `refreshDashboard`, `dashboardTick`, `ensureDashboard` | yes | no |
| `tableGet` / `tableSet` and the handle variants | yes, routed through `apiCall` | yes |
| `notify*` (Pro) | yes, routed through `apiCall` | yes |
| `deviceWrite`, `actionFire`, dashboard setters (`clearPlots`, `setActiveWorkspace`, ...) | no | yes |

In JavaScript, `apiCall("console.send", { data: "..." })` takes the place of `deviceWrite()`. A macro that needs `actionFire()` or the dashboard setters runs in Lua. Calling an absent helper raises a `ReferenceError`.
docs.title: Macros#15

docs.body:
### Examples

Poll the link state once a second for five seconds (JavaScript):

```javascript
for (let i = 0; i < 5; ++i) {
  const reply = apiCall("io.getStatus")
  if (!reply.ok)
    throw new Error(reply.error)

console.log(reply.result.isConnected ? "link up" : "link down")
  delay(1000)
}
```

Count the commands in each scope (Lua):

```lua
local reply = apiCall("api.getCommands")
if not reply.ok then
  error(reply.error)
end

local scopes = {}
for _, cmd in ipairs(reply.result.commands) do
  local scope = cmd.name:match("^[^.]+")
  scopes[scope] = (scopes[scope] or 0) + 1
end

for scope, count in pairs(scopes) do
  print(scope, count)
end
```
docs.title: Macros#16

docs.body:
## Macro files

A macro is a plain text file with a `.js` or `.lua` suffix. The Macros window's **Load macro** and **Save macro** dialogs open in the `Macros` folder of the application data directory (created on first use); any other folder can be chosen from the dialog. Loading picks the language from the suffix: `.lua` selects Lua, anything else selects JavaScript. Saving writes the file atomically and prints `[macro] saved <name>`; loading prints `[macro] loaded <name>`.

## Limits

| Limit | Value |
|-------|-------|
| JavaScript script budget between host calls | 5000 ms |
| Lua run deadline | 30000 ms |
| `delay()` cap | 3600000 ms (1 hour) |
| Verify budget (JavaScript) | 2000 ms |
docs.title: Macros#17

docs.body:
A macro can call any command the catalog lists, including the mutating `project.*` commands. Commands that offer a `dryRun` parameter honor it from a macro as well.

## See also

- [API server](API-Reference.md) and [SDK](SerialStudio-SDK.md): remote programs reach the same commands through the API server; frame parsers, transforms and the Control Loop reach them through the SDK.
- [SDK Reference](SerialStudio-SDK.md): the `apiCall` envelope, the generated wrappers, and the helper groups.
- [API Reference](API-Reference.md): every command, its parameters, and the reply shapes the Terminal tab prints.
- [Control Loop](Control-Loop.md): the project-scoped script that runs for the life of a connection, the counterpart to an ad-hoc macro.
docs.title: Macros#18

# Notifications (Pro)

Your board prints a battery voltage. When it drops under 11 V you want a line on the dashboard saying so. A dataset is one value per frame, such as the battery voltage column. Its transform runs once per frame with that value. To place the code, select the dataset in the Project Editor, click **Transform** in the dataset toolbar and pick Lua or JavaScript (see [Dataset Value Transforms](Dataset-Transforms.md)). Paste one of these two versions, not both.

Lua version:

```lua
function transform(value)
  if value < 11.0 then
    notifyWarning("Power", "Battery low", string.format("%.2f V", value))
  end
docs.title: Notifications#0
Notifications#1

docs.body:
## Overview

Any caller posts an event, and the Notification Log widget lists events in time order, oldest at the top. An event has four fields:

| Field      | Type   | Purpose |
|------------|--------|---------|
| `level`    | int    | `0` = Info, `1` = Warning, `2` = Critical. |
| `channel`  | string | Free-form label such as `"Power"` or `"Engine"`. Spaces allowed. |
| `title`    | string | Short headline, shown in bold in the log. |
| `subtitle` | string | Optional detail line under the title, word-wrapped. |

[Alarm bands](Widget-Reference.md#alarm-bands) on a dataset post notifications automatically (channel `Alarms`); you do not call anything. A band-sourced row does not create a second annunciator point, because the band already drives it.
docs.title: Notifications#2

docs.body:
Channels are not declared up front; they exist once something posts to them. Channel names are case-sensitive.

## Where notifications come from

| Place | Where you write it | Entry point |
|-------|--------------------|-------------|
| Dataset transform | Project Editor, dataset, **Transform** | `transform(value)` |
| Frame parser | Project Editor, source, frame parser | `parse(frame)` |
| Output widget | Output widget script | `transmit(value)` |
| [Control Loop](Control-Loop.md) | Control Loop script | `setup()` and `loop()` |
| API Server | An external program | `notifications.post` |

The four script places in the table (transform, parser, output widget, Control Loop) all expose `notify`, `notifyInfo`, `notifyWarning`, `notifyCritical` and `notifyClear`, described in [The function family](#the-function-family). Use them in a parser to flag a malformed frame, in an output widget to log a clamped setpoint, or in the Control Loop to raise a communication-loss alarm.
docs.title: Notifications#3

docs.body:
The API Server is off by default. Enable it in **Preferences** (port 7777), then send `notifications.post` with `level`, `channel`, `title` and `subtitle`. The other notification commands are `notifications.resolve`, `notifications.list`, `notifications.listChannels`, `notifications.getUnreadCount`, `notifications.clearChannel`, `notifications.clearAll` and `notifications.markRead`. See [API Reference](API-Reference.md).

## The function family
docs.title: Notifications#4

docs.body:
| Function                                  | Level         | Purpose |
|-------------------------------------------|---------------|---------|
| `notify(level, channel, title, subtitle)` | caller chosen | Generic form. `level` is `0`, `1` or `2`, or the `Info`/`Warning`/`Critical` constants. |
| `notifyInfo(channel, title, subtitle)`    | `Info`        | Informational event. |
| `notifyWarning(channel, title, subtitle)` | `Warning`     | Worth attention, not critical. |
| `notifyCritical(channel, title, subtitle)`| `Critical`    | Alarm-class event. |
| `notifyClear(channel, title, subtitle)`   | `Info`        | Posts an Info event titled `Resolved: <title>` (just `Resolved` if the title is empty). The original row stays in the log. It also returns the matching alarm point on the annunciator to normal (see [Aural Alerts](Aural-Alerts.md)). |
docs.title: Notifications#5

docs.body:
### Argument overloads

`notifyInfo`, `notifyWarning`, `notifyCritical` and `notifyClear` accept one, two or three arguments. With one argument it is the title; with two it is title and subtitle; the channel then defaults to `"Dashboard"`. With three, the first is the channel. `notifyInfo("Ready", "System armed")` posts to `"Dashboard"` with title `"Ready"` and subtitle `"System armed"`.

The generic `notify()` starts with the level and then follows the same overloads for the remaining fields. The level constants are globals (`Info = 0`, `Warning = 1`, `Critical = 2`), so `notify(Critical, "Engine", "EGT exceeded", "1052 C")` equals `notifyCritical("Engine", "EGT exceeded", "1052 C")`.
docs.title: Notifications#6

docs.body:
## Examples

Paste these into the **Transform** field of a dataset (pick Lua or JavaScript in the Transform editor). The signatures are identical in frame parsers and output widgets. The battery-voltage example is in the page introduction.

A transform runs on every frame. Without a latch, a value stuck above 900 would post a row on every frame. A 10 kHz transform would otherwise fill the log with the same row ten thousand times a second. Latch the state, post once on entry, then post a `Resolved` event when the condition clears:

```lua
local latched = false

Notifications#8
Notifications#9
Notifications#10

docs.body:
## The Notification Log widget

The Notification Log is a Pro dashboard widget. Turn it on from **Start menu > Tools > Notifications** on the dashboard, or from the **Notifications** pinned shortcut on the taskbar (choose pinned shortcuts in **Preferences > Taskbar > Pinned Buttons**). The free build hides both.

| Element | Behaviour |
|---------|-----------|
| Rows | Icon, title, channel pill and timestamp, with the subtitle on a wrapped second line. Warning and Critical titles use the alarm color. The log follows new events unless you scrolled up. |
| Unread badge | Counts unread Warning and Critical events, capped at `99+`. Info events do not count. |
| **Filter by channel** | Case-sensitive substring match on the channel name, live as you type. |
| **Clear all notifications** | Wipes the in-memory history and the dedup window. |
docs.title: Notifications#11

docs.body:
There is one log per dashboard. It is not tied to any dataset group, and its position and size are saved with the project layout. With no events, it shows "No notifications yet".

The history is wiped on every dashboard reset: disconnect, project reload and playback stop. Events from the previous session do not bleed into the new one.

## OS desktop notifications

OS desktop notifications are a Pro feature. Open **Preferences**, select the **Notifications** tab (hidden in the free build) and turn on **System Notifications**. It is off by default.

With it on, Warning and Critical events raise a tray toast even when Serial Studio is not the foreground window. The toast shows the channel and title on one line and the subtitle on a second. Info events never produce a toast.
docs.title: Notifications#12

docs.body:
It needs a system tray; the condition is that the platform reports one. Where it reports none, no toast appears and the log still records the event. Some Linux desktops, stock GNOME for one, hide tray icons without an extension.

## Routing Qt log messages

Serial Studio's own critical errors appear in the log on a `System` channel, with the title `Critical` and the message as the subtitle. To see its warnings there too, turn on **Route Warnings to Notifications** on the same **Notifications** tab (title `Warning`). This setting is on the Pro-only **Notifications** tab. It is off by default because Qt and QML emit warnings often during normal operation. With **System Notifications** also on, routed events raise tray toasts like any Warning or Critical.
docs.title: Notifications#13

docs.body:
Events on the `System` and `Problems` channels never become alarm points on the annunciator, so a routed warning does not sound a siren.

## Rules and limits

| Rule | Value |
|------|-------|
| Ring buffer | The most recent 1024 events. Older ones drop as new ones arrive. |
| Deduplication | An event is dropped if the same `(level, channel, title, subtitle)` was posted in the last 100 ms, even with other events in between. A rising value in the subtitle (`"1049 C"`, then `"1050 C"`) is never collapsed. |
| Normalizing | Channel and title are trimmed. An event with both empty is ignored. Levels outside `0` to `2` clamp to Info or Critical. |
| Threads | `notify*` works from any engine. Off the GUI thread the event is queued to it, and Control Loop scripts reach the same bus through the `notifications.post` and `notifications.resolve` commands. |
docs.title: Notifications#14

docs.body:
Without an active Pro license (a GPL build, or an official binary with no license or trial):

| Engine | Result |
|--------|--------|
| JavaScript (parser, transform, output widget) | Checked when the script engine is created. The call throws `notify() requires a Pro license. See https://serial-studio.com/pricing`. |
| Lua | Checked on every call. The call does nothing, and Serial Studio logs one warning per session in the Console: `Script notify*() ignored: requires an active Serial Studio Pro license or trial`. |
| Control Loop and API Server | `notifications.post` and `notifications.resolve` are refused. |
docs.title: Notifications#15

docs.body:
The level constants `Info`, `Warning` and `Critical` are defined at every tier, so a Pro project still loads. Opening a project that uses `notify*` in the free edition shows the Pro-required overlay on the dashboard.

## See also

- [Dataset Value Transforms](Dataset-Transforms.md): where `notify*` is most often used.
- [Frame Parser Scripting](Frame-Parser.md): `parse(frame)` has the same notification API.
- [Aural Alerts](Aural-Alerts.md): Warning and Critical notifications become alarm points that sound and flash the master annunciator, and `notifyClear()` returns them to normal.
- [API Reference](API-Reference.md): `notifications.post`, `notifications.list` and the rest, for external drivers.
- [MQTT Publisher](MQTT-Publisher.md): the **Publish Notifications** option republishes every event on this bus to MQTT.
