# Offline Activation

The test rig sits behind a firewall that has never met a browser, so Serial
Studio cannot check your Pro license online. You export a small file from that
machine, trade it for a license file on any computer with a browser, and import
the result. Nothing else touches the network. The Pro trial prompt cannot help
here, because registering a trial needs the internet.

Offline activation works only with lifetime and Test Stand licenses. Monthly and
yearly subscriptions use [online activation](Pro-vs-Free.md#upgrading-from-free-to-pro),
which tolerates up to 30 days offline. A machine that connects now and then does
not need this page. The Test Stand tier includes 20 offline device activations.
docs.title: Offline-Activation#0

docs.body:
> **Warning:** activating an offline device permanently consumes one license
> seat. An air-gapped machine cannot report a deactivation, so the seat is never
> released and cannot be moved to another machine. A destroyed machine takes its
> seat with it. Plan your seats before activating.

## What you need

- A lifetime or Test Stand license key and the email address used to purchase
  it.
- The offline machine, with Serial Studio installed and no license active. The
  **Activate Offline…** button appears only while nothing is activated; on an
  online-activated machine, click **Deactivate** first.
- A second computer with a browser and internet access.
- A way to move small files between the two, such as a USB drive.
docs.title: Offline-Activation#1

docs.body:
## Steps

Two files cross the gap: a device file goes out, a license file comes back. The
app and its error messages call the license file a certificate; it is the same
`.sslic` file.

| File | Extension | Made by | Contents |
|------|-----------|---------|----------|
| Device file | `.ssmachine` | **Save Device File…** on the offline machine | Device ID, application name and version, timestamp. No personal data. |
| License file | `.sslic` | serial-studio.com/offline-activation | Signed certificate bound to the Device ID, with an **Expires** date. |

### 1. Save the device file

On the offline machine:
docs.title: Offline-Activation#2

docs.body:
1. Click **About** in the toolbar, then click **Manage License**.
2. In the Licensing dialog, click **Activate Offline…** to open the **Activate
   Offline** wizard.
3. Click **Save Device File…** and store the `.ssmachine` file.

The device file is a small JSON file with the Device ID, the application name
and version, and the time it was generated. It carries no personal information.
The Licensing dialog shows the same Device ID.

### 2. Get the license file

On a computer with internet access:

1. Go to
   [serial-studio.com/offline-activation](https://serial-studio.com/offline-activation).
   The wizard shows this address too, so you can type it on the other machine;
   ignore its **Open in Browser** button on the offline machine.
2. Upload the `.ssmachine` device file.
3. Enter the email address and license key from your purchase.
4. Download the `.sslic` license file the site returns.
docs.title: Offline-Activation#3

docs.body:
The site checks your license before it issues the file.

### 3. Import the license file

Move the `.sslic` file to the offline machine, then:

1. Reopen the wizard from **About → Manage License → Activate Offline…**.
2. Click **Import License File…** and select the `.sslic` file.

Pro features unlock immediately, and the import makes no network request. The
Licensing dialog now shows **Serial Studio Pro (Offline)** (the name follows
your license variant), the Device ID, and **Expires** as a date with the days
left, for example "(30 days left)".

With the API Server enabled (it is off by default), the `licensing.activateOffline`
command imports the same file from its `path` parameter. `licensing.getStatus`
reports `offlineActivated`, `offlineDaysRemaining` and `offlineExpiresAt`. The AI
Assistant cannot call `licensing.activateOffline`; it is in the Blocked tier.
docs.title: Offline-Activation#4

docs.body:
## How the license behaves

An offline Serial Studio Pro license behaves as follows.

- The license file (`.sslic`) is bound to the machine that produced the device file. It
  will not activate any other machine.
- The activation persists across restarts and needs no network.
- The certificate has its own **Expires** date, even on a lifetime license.
  With fewer than 14 days left the Licensing dialog adds "Your offline license expires soon.
  Request a new certificate to stay activated." After the date passes, the
  certificate fails verification the next time Serial Studio starts and Pro
  locks. To renew, repeat the Save, Get and Import steps from
  [Offline Activation](#steps) and import the new `.sslic` file.
- The Device ID comes from the operating system, not Serial Studio. It changes
  after an OS reinstall or a hardware replacement, and the old license file
  stops working.
docs.title: Offline-Activation#5

docs.body:
## Managing seats

To remove a Serial Studio Pro offline license from a machine, open **About → Manage License**, click
**Deactivate**, and confirm **Yes** at "Remove the offline license from this
device?". This deletes only the local certificate; the seat stays consumed. (Deactivating
an online activation does free its seat.) Copy the Device ID from the Licensing
dialog before you deactivate, or read it from the `.ssmachine` file (field
`machineId`).

To restore Pro on the same machine, import the same `.sslic` file again. Keep it
somewhere safe. If an offline machine is destroyed or decommissioned, email
alex@serial-studio.com with your license key and the Device ID.
docs.title: Offline-Activation#6

docs.body: ## Troubleshooting
docs.title: Offline-Activation#7

docs.body:
| Message | Cause | Fix |
|---------|-------|-----|
| "This certificate was issued for a different device." | The license file came from another machine's device file. | On the machine you are activating, repeat the Offline Activation steps: save a new device file, get a new license file at serial-studio.com/offline-activation, import it. |
| "The certificate file is malformed or unreadable." | You selected the `.ssmachine` file, or the `.sslic` copy is damaged or edited. | Select the `.sslic` file the site returned, or download it again. |
| "This certificate has expired." | The certificate is past its **Expires** date. | Get a new `.sslic` file at serial-studio.com/offline-activation with a fresh device file and import it. |
| "The certificate file is too large to be valid." | The file is over 64 KB, so it is not a license file. | Select the `.sslic` file the site returned. |
| "This certificate does not grant a valid license tier." | The certificate's signed tier field is missing or not one Serial Studio recognizes, usually a corrupted or hand-edited file. | Download the `.sslic` file again; if it repeats, email alex@serial-studio.com. |
| "Could not open the certificate file." | The file is unreadable (missing, locked, or no permission). | Copy the `.sslic` file to a local disk and select it again. |

# Operation modes

## Overview

Your board prints `23.5,60,1013` once per second. Quick Plot mode plots those three numbers the moment you connect. Console Only mode shows you the raw bytes instead, and Project File mode lets you design the dashboard yourself.

Those are the three operation modes in Serial Studio. Set the mode with **Operation Mode** in the **Device Setup** panel on the right side of the main window. Every mode works with every driver. UART, Network and Bluetooth LE are free; any other bus needs Pro, in every mode. See [Devices](Devices.md) for the driver list and [Pro vs Free Features](Pro-vs-Free.md) for the rest.
docs.title: Operation-Modes#0

docs.body:
If your board prints numbers, start with Quick Plot. All three modes are available in the free edition; individual features inside a project, such as multi-source, dataset transforms and Variables, need Pro.

## Console Only mode

Console Only is the Serial Studio mode that shows raw bytes in the terminal and builds no dashboard. To use it, set **Operation Mode** to "Console Only (No Parsing)" in the **Device Setup** panel.

Bytes go straight from the device to the terminal. Nothing is split into frames, plotted, or exported to CSV, and no frame parser runs. The terminal shows the stream as ASCII or hex, you can save the transcript to a file, and the input box still sends bytes back to the device.
docs.title: Operation-Modes#1

docs.body:
If the console shows `ÿÿ¿¿` instead of numbers, the baud rate is wrong. Change it in **Device Setup** and reconnect.

Use it to check baud rate, wiring and framing before you build a project, to see what a stream looks like when another mode parses it wrong, or to talk to a device with a text protocol such as AT commands.

## Quick Plot mode

Quick Plot is the Serial Studio mode that plots text lines with no project file and no script. To use it, set **Operation Mode** to "Quick Plot (Auto-Detected Format)" in the **Device Setup** panel, pick your port and baud rate, then connect.

### Example input
docs.title: Operation-Modes#2
Operation-Modes#3

docs.body:
```
Temperature,Humidity
23.5,60
23.6,59
23.7,59
```

Named values need no header row:

```
temp: 23.5, hum: 60
temp: 23.6, hum: 59
```

When the connection opens, Serial Studio reads each line, detects the format, and builds a dashboard with a Data Grid showing all current values, a Multi-Plot overlaying all channels on one time-series chart, and an individual plot per channel.

### Accepted shapes

Serial Studio detects the format from the first qualifying line, one where at least half the fields are numbers (or name:value pairs with numbers). Each value maps to one channel. A line ends at CR, LF, or CRLF. Semicolon-separated lines such as `23.5;60;1013` work the same way.
docs.title: Operation-Modes#4

docs.body:
| Shape | Example | Result |
|-------|---------|--------|
| Values separated by commas, semicolons, tabs or runs of spaces | `23.5,60,1013` or `23.5 60 1013` | One channel per value |
| Decimal comma under semicolon or space separation | `23,5;60` | Channels `23.5` and `60` |
| Named values, `name:value` or `name=value`, optional spaces after the delimiter | `temp: 23.5, hum: 60` | The names title the channels |
| Unit after a number | `23.5degC`, `1013hPa`, `45%` | The unit becomes the channel's unit and is stripped from the value |
| One-line JSON object | `{"t":23.5,"h":60}` | Nested objects flatten to dotted names (`imu.ax`), arrays to indexed names (`acc[0]`); strings, booleans and nulls are ignored |
| Line wrapped in `/*` and `*/` | `/* 23.5,60 */` | Parsed as its contents |
docs.title: Operation-Modes#5

docs.body: ### Edge cases
docs.title: Operation-Modes#6

docs.body:
- **Text lines.** A line with no numeric field (such as `WiFi connected`) never touches the dashboard. It still appears in the console.
- **Header detection.** For a positional stream, an all-text line before the first data line titles the channels, provided it has the same number of fields as that data line. Boot chatter with a different field count is ignored. Names on data lines take precedence, so a device already streaming `name:value` pairs when you connect keeps its labels.
- **Named streams.** Channels are keyed by name. A name missing from a line leaves that channel without a sample for that frame: plots show a gap and the Data Grid keeps the last value. A new name appends a channel. Positional streams rebuild the dashboard when the field count changes.
- **Format lock.** Once detected, the format stays fixed for the connection. It is re-evaluated only when a line has no numeric field under it but another format fits, such as boot chatter `uptime=1234` followed by `temp=23.5,hum=60`.
- **Field limit.** Quick Plot reads at most 512 fields per line; the rest of a longer line is dropped.
- **Device declarations.** A device that uses the SerialStudio library can send a declaration that builds the dashboard in place of format detection; see [Device Declarations](Device-Declarations.md). With **Preferences → Plotting → Quick Plot → Ask Devices for Their Dashboard** turned on (off by default), Serial Studio also asks for it on connect with one request line, `#ss?`. Console Only and Project File mode never send the request.
docs.title: Operation-Modes#7

docs.body:
### Save as Project

To keep the stream after the session, use **Save as Project** on the dashboard. The saved project's Built-In parser uses the Delimited text template for plain comma streams and the Line values template otherwise.

Known difference: in a saved project a missing named field repeats the previous value, where the live session leaves a gap.

### Limitations

Quick Plot has no manual format override (use Save as Project for anything the detector cannot settle) and no binary or hex input. Widgets, alarms, parser scripts and multi-source are Project File features; see the [Feature comparison](#feature-comparison).
docs.title: Operation-Modes#8

docs.body:
## Project File mode

Project File is the Serial Studio mode where a `.ssproj` file on the host defines the dashboard. To use it, set **Operation Mode** to "Parse via Project File" in the **Device Setup** panel, then load an existing project or build one in the Project Editor (the **Project Editor** button in the toolbar).

Say your device sends `23.5,60` followed by a newline. In the Project Editor:

1. Add two datasets, Temperature and Humidity (a dataset is one value on the dashboard). The first number lands in the first dataset, the second in the second.
2. Set the source's frame detection to **End Delimiter Only** and type `\n`.
3. The decoder already defaults to **Plain Text (UTF-8)**; connect.
docs.title: Operation-Modes#9

docs.body:
Where each setting lives in the editor is covered in [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md).

Beyond that, the `.ssproj` JSON file also holds the groups, widgets, alarms, FFT settings and actions. A Built-In template, or an optional `parse(frame)` function in Lua or JavaScript, turns arbitrary protocols into the array of values Serial Studio expects. A project can define several devices; see [Multi-source support](#multi-source-support) (Pro).

This mode gives access to every widget type and configuration option in Serial Studio, including alarms and FFT analysis.

### Frame detection methods

Serial Studio needs to know where one reading ends and the next begins; a delimiter is the byte or bytes that mark that. A source is one connected device, and frame detection is configured per source in the Project Editor.
docs.title: Operation-Modes#10

docs.body: If your device ends each line with a newline, choose **End Delimiter Only** and type `\n`; you can skip the rest of this section.
docs.title: Operation-Modes#11

docs.body:
| Method                      | API value | Behavior |
|-----------------------------|-----------|----------|
| **End Delimiter Only**      | 0         | A frame ends when the end delimiter is seen. The common choice for line-terminated CSV. |
| **Start and End Delimiter** | 1         | A frame begins at the start delimiter and ends at the end delimiter, for example `$DATA...;\n`. |
| **No Delimiters**           | 2         | All incoming data goes to the frame parser without splitting. For length-prefixed or fixed-size binary protocols where the parser finds the boundaries. |
| **Start Delimiter Only**    | 3         | A frame runs from one start delimiter to the next. Released only when the next start marker arrives (see Start Delimiter Only below). |
| **Fixed Length**            | 4         | Every frame is exactly **Frame Length** bytes. Details under Fixed Length below. |
docs.title: Operation-Modes#12

docs.body:
Delimiters can be plain text or hexadecimal byte sequences (toggle "Hexadecimal Delimiters" in the Project Editor). Fixed Length uses no delimiters, so the Project Editor hides the delimiter fields for it.

**Start Delimiter Only.** In Project File mode, the second occurrence of the delimiter becomes the start of the next frame, so a frame is released only once that next start marker arrives. The most recent frame sits buffered until then; for a slow or paused sender (a 1 Hz source, for example), the dashboard runs one frame behind.

**Fixed Length.** In Project File mode, every frame is **Frame Length** bytes, checksum included, from 1 to 524288. A source with a length outside that range falls back to No Delimiters.
docs.title: Operation-Modes#13

docs.body:
- The **Header Rule** (a mask and a value) selects the first byte of a frame: a byte starts a frame when `(byte & mask) == value`, and bytes before it are discarded.
- The **Body Rule** applies the same test to every other byte of the frame. A frame that fails it is dropped, and the search for the next header resumes at the offending byte.
- A mask of `00` turns a rule off. With no Header Rule the stream is assumed to be aligned and is cut every N bytes.
- If a checksum is set and fails, the reader drops one byte and searches for the next header (with a Header Rule), or drops the whole frame (without one).
docs.title: Operation-Modes#14

docs.body:
For example, a 5-byte frame whose first byte always has bit 7 set and whose other bytes never do uses Frame Length `5`, Header Rule mask `80` value `80`, and Body Rule mask `80` value `00`. If a byte is lost on the wire, the reader skips forward to the next byte with bit 7 set instead of staying misaligned.

### Decoder methods

The decoder determines how raw bytes are converted before being passed to the frame parser (or split as CSV).
docs.title: Operation-Modes#15

docs.body:
| Decoder                 | API value | Description |
|-------------------------|-----------|-------------|
| **Plain Text (UTF-8)**  | 0         | Bytes are decoded as UTF-8 text. The most common choice for ASCII/CSV protocols. |
| **Hexadecimal**         | 1         | Each byte is converted to a two-character hex string. For example, bytes `0x03 0xFF 0x02` become `"03ff02"`. |
| **Base64**              | 2         | Bytes are converted to a Base64 string. |
| **Binary (Direct)**     | 3         | Raw bytes arrive as a Lua table or JavaScript array of integers 0 to 255. |

### Frame parser script
docs.title: Operation-Modes#16
Operation-Modes#17

docs.body:
**Key behaviors:**

- The returned array is mapped to datasets by index. Datasets are numbered from 1 in the Project Editor, so element 0 goes to dataset 1, element 1 goes to dataset 2, and so on.
- `frame` is a string with the Plain Text, Hexadecimal and Base64 decoders, and an array of integers with Binary (Direct).
- Advanced returns: an array of arrays emits several frames from one call (`[[row1_val1, row1_val2], [row2_val1, row2_val2]]`), and `[scalar, [vec1, vec2, vec3]]` expands the inner array into separate dataset values.
- `parse()` takes exactly one argument; the two-argument `parse(frame, separator)` form from v2 projects is rejected when the script loads.
docs.title: Operation-Modes#18
Operation-Modes#19
Operation-Modes#20

docs.body:
## Picking the right mode

If the console shows gibberish, fix the baud rate before you blame the firmware. Start in Console Only to confirm the bytes make sense, move to Quick Plot once you see clean numbers one line per sample, and move to Project File when you need more control.

| Scenario                                                     | Recommended mode |
|--------------------------------------------------------------|------------------|
| Garbled stream, unknown baud rate, AT commands, a text CLI  | Console Only |
| Arduino or ESP32 printing numbers, one line per sample       | Quick Plot |
| Need gauges, bars, compass, GPS map, FFT, or alarms          | Project File |
| Custom binary protocol with length-prefixed packets          | Project File + Binary decoder + Lua/JS parser |
| Multiple sensors on different ports in one dashboard         | Project File (multi-source, Pro) |
| Production telemetry system with saved configuration         | Project File |
docs.title: Operation-Modes#21

docs.body: ### Feature comparison
docs.title: Operation-Modes#22

docs.body:
| Feature                     | Console Only        | Quick Plot       | Project File                  |
|-----------------------------|---------------------|------------------|-------------------------------|
| Setup effort                | None                | None             | Create project in editor      |
| Dashboard                   | No                  | Auto             | Custom                        |
| Frame detection             | None (raw stream)   | Line-based (auto)| Configurable per source       |
| Line format                 | N/A                 | Detected (see Accepted shapes) | Any (Built-In template or parser script) |
| Frame parser (Built-In/Lua/JS) | No               | No               | Yes                           |
| Dataset value transforms    | No                  | No               | Yes (Pro)                     |
| Variables (registers)       | No                  | No               | Yes (Pro)                     |
| Custom widgets              | No                  | No (plots only)  | Yes (project-defined)         |
| Alarms and LED indicators   | No                  | No               | Yes                           |
| FFT analysis                | No                  | No               | Yes                           |
| Multi-source                | No                  | No               | Yes (Pro)                     |
| CSV export                  | No                  | Yes              | Yes                           |
| MDF4 export                 | No                  | Yes (Pro)        | Yes (Pro)                     |
| Saved configuration         | No                  | No               | Yes (.ssproj file)            |
docs.title: Operation-Modes#23

docs.body:
## See also

- [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md): building and configuring a project file, including picking and configuring a Built-In template.
- [Frame Parser Reference](Frame-Parser.md): the Built-In template catalog and the Lua/JavaScript `parse()` API in detail.
- [Dataset Value Transforms](Dataset-Transforms.md): per-dataset value transforms applied after parsing.
- [Devices](Devices.md): the driver types available to any operation mode.
- [Pro vs Free Features](Pro-vs-Free.md): which drivers and dashboard features require a Pro license.

docs.body:
# Operator Deployments (Pro)

You built a dashboard on your bench. The person at the test rig should see it with one double-click: project loaded, device connected, no toolbar to wander into. That is a **deployment**, and Serial Studio writes it for you.

To make one:

1. Load the project.
2. Click **Deploy** in the toolbar (or run it from the command palette) to open **New Deployment**.
3. Keep the defaults and press **Save**.
4. Give the `.ssdeploy` file to the operator, who double-clicks it.

An *operator* is whoever runs the dashboard without editing it. A deployment is either a **deployment package** (`.ssdeploy`, the default **Format**), which carries the project inside it, or a **shortcut** (`.lnk`, `.app` or `.desktop`), which launches a project file on the same machine. Both open Serial Studio in [runtime mode](#runtime-mode): toolbar hidden, device connected on its own.
docs.title: Operator-Deployments#0

docs.body:
> **Deploy is a Pro feature.** The target machine needs the official Serial Studio binary; a build compiled from source under the GPL cannot launch a deployment. See [Licensing](#licensing).

> **Serial Studio must be installed on the target machine.** A shortcut records the absolute path of the executable and of the project file; if either moves, double-clicking fails with the OS's missing-file error. A package needs the install too, but not your paths.

## Shortcut files

With **Format** set to **Shortcut to the project file**, Serial Studio writes a native launcher for your platform. Fill in a name, optionally swap the icon, and choose where to save:
docs.title: Operator-Deployments#1

docs.body:
| Platform | File written          | Where it goes by default |
|----------|------------------------|--------------------------|
| Windows  | `.lnk` (shell-link binary) | Desktop, with the Serial Studio executable as the target |
| macOS    | `.app` bundle (Bash-launched, with custom `.icns`) | Desktop, opens via Finder/Dock |
| Linux    | `.desktop` (freedesktop.org Desktop Entry) | Desktop; move to `~/.local/share/applications/` to surface it in the launcher |

A shortcut hard-codes a single project file path plus the runtime flags you picked in the dialog. Double-clicking it relaunches Serial Studio with those exact arguments. A package opens with `--deployment` and needs no project path; **Desktop Shortcut** writes a launcher for it that is saved the same way.
docs.title: Operator-Deployments#2

docs.body:
The shortcut launch path: ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Project Editor
configured project"] --> B["Deploy dialog
name + icon + flags"] B --> C[".lnk / .app / .desktop
on the desktop"] C --> D["Serial Studio
--runtime --project foo.ssproj"] D --> E["Dashboard launches
(toolbar hidden, auto-connect)"] ``` The path and flags are captured when the shortcut is created. Editing the project later does not re-stamp the shortcut; it keeps pointing at the same file. ## The dialog **New Deployment** has three tabs, plus **Contents** when exporting a package. Open it with **Deploy** in the toolbar; the button is hidden once a project is running in runtime mode.
docs.title: Operator-Deployments#3

docs.body:
### General

In the **New Deployment** dialog (Pro), the General tab holds:
docs.title: Operator-Deployments#4

docs.body:
- **Format.** **Deployment package (.ssdeploy)** (the default) or **Shortcut to the project file**.
- **Project.** Read-only field showing the currently loaded project. In shortcut mode, use the folder button to switch projects without leaving the dialog. A project must be loaded for **Save** to enable.
- **Desktop Shortcut.** Package mode only: also writes a launcher for the package.
- **Name.** Defaults to the project's title. Used as the deployment filename and the displayed label in the operator's shell. Reserved characters (`\ / : * ? " < > |`) are replaced with `_` automatically when saving. The name is trimmed; an empty name saves as `Untitled Deployment`.
- **Icon.** Click the preview (or **Change Icon…**) to pick your own. macOS prefers `.icns`, Windows prefers `.ico`, Linux accepts SVG or PNG. Leave it alone to use the bundled deployment icon.
- **Theme.** Defaults to **Same as Serial Studio**, the theme set on the operator's installation. Pick a name from the dropdown to pin the deployment to that palette.
- **Fullscreen.** Launches the dashboard full-screen. Off by default.
- **Actions Panel.** On by default. Shows the dashboard's actions panel.
- **File Transmission.** Off by default. Lets the operator open the File Transmission dialog in runtime mode.
docs.title: Operator-Deployments#5

docs.body:
Pinning a theme suits kiosks that should always look the same, or paired light/dark deployments of one project. An unknown theme name on the target machine falls back to the host's saved preference with a warning. The [CLI reference](#cli-reference) maps each switch to its flag.

### Taskbar

In the **New Deployment** dialog (Pro), the Taskbar tab controls the dashboard taskbar in runtime mode.
docs.title: Operator-Deployments#6

docs.body:
- **Mode.** **Always shown** (default), **Auto-hide** (slides in near the bottom edge), or **Hidden**. Hidden removes the window minimize, maximize and close buttons and switches the dashboard to auto-layout, so it always fills the available area.
- **Search Bar.** On by default. Turning it off hides the taskbar search bar.
- **Pinned Buttons.** Which taskbar buttons stay pinned. **Notifications** and **Pause** are on by default; **Console**, **Clock**, **Stopwatch** and **File Transmission** are off. The File Transmission button needs the **File Transmission** switch on the General tab. The group is disabled when the mode is **Hidden**.
docs.title: Operator-Deployments#7

docs.body:
### Logging

In the **New Deployment** dialog (Pro), the Logging tab has a **Recorders** section of switches that pre-arm the export modules at startup. Each one enables the matching export, so recording starts the moment the device connects, with no extra clicks.

| Switch              | CLI flag              | What it does on launch |
|---------------------|-----------------------|------------------------|
| **CSV File**        | `--csv-export`        | Enables CSV export. |
| **MDF4 File**       | `--mdf-export`        | Enables MDF4 export. |
| **Historian**       | `--session-export`    | Enables Historian recording. |
| **Console Log**     | `--console-export`    | Enables Console export. |
docs.title: Operator-Deployments#8

docs.body:
The tab notes that recordings are saved in the Serial Studio workspace folder.

### Save

Press **Save**. A native Save dialog opens with the right file filter for your OS. Pick a location, and Serial Studio writes the file and reveals it in your file manager so you can move it onto a desktop, share it, or include it in an installer payload.

If anything goes wrong while writing the file, an inline error banner shows the OS error in the dialog. The dialog stays open so you can retry without losing your selections.

## Deployment packages
docs.title: Operator-Deployments#9

docs.body: In **New Deployment**, **Format** set to **Deployment package (.ssdeploy)** (the default) exports a **deployment package**: one `.ssdeploy` file holding the open project and the files it uses. These are alarm sounds, Canvas images, the widget extensions it uses, and any credentials and private keys you choose to include. The package also carries the runtime options from the dialog, its title, and its icon. Copy the file to any machine with a commercial (Pro) build of Serial Studio installed and double-click it. No paths from your machine are needed, and the project file can stay where it is.
docs.title: Operator-Deployments#10

docs.body:
| Shortcut to project file | Deployment package |
|--------------------------|--------------------|
| Points at a `.ssproj` on this machine | Carries the project and its files inside one file |
| Breaks if the project file moves | Does not depend on the project file path |
| The project stays readable JSON | The package is binary and does not show its content in a text editor |
| Editing the project updates every operator | Re-export the package after editing |

Use packages to hand a dashboard to someone else, such as a customer, a test lab or a demo laptop. Keep project shortcuts for in-house benches that share one centrally edited project.
docs.title: Operator-Deployments#11

docs.body:
> **Encoded, not encrypted.** A package is binary, so its content does not appear in a text editor. It is not encrypted: anyone who studies the file format can decode it. Do not treat a package as a way to keep secrets from a determined person.

### Contents tab

In package mode the dialog adds a **Contents** tab:
docs.title: Operator-Deployments#12

docs.body:
- **Carried Files.** Every file the package will carry, with its size. Canvas images are found by scanning the Canvas code for image file names. Use **Add Files…** for images whose path the code builds while it runs; they must sit inside the project folder.
- **External Dependencies.** Things the package cannot carry, such as programs the Process driver launches or web pages. The target machine must provide them.
- **Missing Files.** Referenced files that no longer exist. Export stays blocked until they are back.
- **Credentials and Private Keys.** Each password and private key the project uses, all excluded by default. Tick an item to carry it inside the package; the dialog then reminds you that anyone with the file can recover it. Excluded items are entered by the operator on first connect, through the same recovery dialog runtime mode always shows, and stay on that machine as usual.
docs.title: Operator-Deployments#13

docs.body:
Exporting a package needs a Pro license, the same as generating a shortcut; see [Licensing](#licensing). Turn on **Desktop Shortcut** on the General tab to get a launcher for the package as well. After the package is saved the dialog stays open and offers **Open Package**, so you can try the result right away.

### Opening a package

There are three ways to open a `.ssdeploy` file:

- Double-click it. The installers register the file type on Windows, macOS and Linux.
- Pick it in the **Open Project** dialog, or drag it onto the Serial Studio window.
- From a terminal, run `serial-studio --deployment demo.ssdeploy`.
docs.title: Operator-Deployments#14

docs.body:
A package always opens in a new window, so the window you are working in is left as it was. The dashboard opens in runtime mode with the package's options, title and icon.

A damaged package, or one changed after export, is refused with a message, and so is a package larger than 64 MiB. A package made by a newer version of Serial Studio names the version it needs.

### Sealed sessions
docs.title: Operator-Deployments#15

docs.body:
In Serial Studio Pro, a session opened from a `.ssdeploy` package is **sealed**: the operator can run the dashboard but cannot read, save, export or edit the project through any part of the app.
- The Project Editor, Preferences, Macros, the Problem Center, the AI assistant, the players, the Extension Manager and the Deploy dialog are unreachable, including from the command palette and keyboard shortcuts. A sealed session cannot re-export a package, so keep the source project.
- API, gRPC and MCP commands that would return or change the project answer `SEALED_SESSION`. Live data, device control, exports, alarms and window layout keep working, so integrations that read data still run. The same rule applies to the project's own scripts when they call the API.
- Live frames and mirror viewers carry the layout and values but no script source, so Canvas widgets appear as placeholders on a mirror viewer.
- Nothing from the package is written to disk in readable form. There are no backups, no project autosave and no copy in the settings. Historian recordings keep what replay needs but not the scripts, so Canvas widgets replay as placeholders and **Verify** and **Regress** report the recording as sealed.
- Only the widget extensions inside the package load; extensions installed on the machine do not. The usual extension consent prompt appears the first time.
docs.title: Operator-Deployments#16

docs.body:
## Licensing

Generating a shortcut or exporting a package needs a Pro license. Without one, the first use of a Pro feature offers a trial through a Yes/No prompt; the trial never starts on its own, and accepting it needs an internet connection. Once the trial has expired, the prompt offers activation or purchase instead. If you decline the trial or it has expired, **Save** fails with "A Pro license is required to generate shortcuts."

Opening a deployment is a separate matter: any official (Pro) build launches it, and the license matters only at connect time. A package without Pro content connects without a license. A package that uses Pro features asks for a license (or an accepted trial) when it connects. A GPL build cannot open either kind. Compare [Pro vs Free Features](Pro-vs-Free.md#operator-deployment-generation).
docs.title: Operator-Deployments#17

docs.body:
## Runtime mode

Shortcuts and packages both run in runtime mode: every shortcut adds `--runtime`, and a package reaches the same mode through `--deployment`. Runtime mode adjusts the dashboard for unattended, operator use:
docs.title: Operator-Deployments#18

docs.body:
| Behaviour                             | Effect |
|---------------------------------------|--------|
| Toolbar                               | Hidden from launch. The Setup, Console, and Project Editor buttons are not visible. |
| Project loading                       | Loads the project immediately, in Project mode, with no project picker: the file passed via `--project` for a shortcut, the project inside the package for a package. |
| Auto-connect                          | Once the interface loads, Serial Studio connects on its own, provided the device configuration is valid and it is not already connected. |
| Failed initial connect (4 s grace)    | If no connection is established within 4 seconds of launch, the **Device Unavailable** dialog is shown. |
| User-initiated disconnect             | Disconnecting from the dashboard quits Serial Studio; it counts as "I'm done." |
| Device-initiated drop                 | Shows the **Connection Lost** dialog. The operator can **Reconnect**, pick a different device, or **Quit**; the dashboard layout is preserved underneath. |
| Project file missing at launch (shortcuts only) | A pre-flight check runs before the QML loads. If the project file is missing, a "Project file not found" dialog is shown and offers to **Delete Shortcut** (when `--shortcut-path` is provided) or **Quit**. |
docs.title: Operator-Deployments#19

docs.body:
Runtime mode changes only the chrome. The data pipeline, frame parsers and exports behave as usual, and so does the API Server (off by default, port 7777; gRPC on port 8888 runs only while the API Server is enabled). Sealed packages additionally restrict project-reading commands; see [Sealed sessions](#sealed-sessions).

### The recovery dialog

In Pro runtime mode, the recovery dialog is the only part of the setup UI an operator sees, and only while there is no connection. When the first connection fails, the **Device Unavailable** dialog opens. When an active connection drops, the **Connection Lost** dialog opens. Both have two pages:
docs.title: Operator-Deployments#20

docs.body:
1. **The first page** shows a warning icon, a one-line headline ("The connection to your device was lost." or "Serial Studio couldn't reach your device."), and three buttons: **Quit**, **Pick Different Device**, and **Reconnect** after a drop or **Try Again** after a failed first connect. The dialog closes itself when a connection is re-established, so the operator can leave it open and come back.
2. **The second page**, opened by **Pick Different Device**, has a bus-type combo plus the Hardware setup pane. It lets the operator choose a different port or device without exposing the rest of the toolbar. Press **Connect** when ready.
docs.title: Operator-Deployments#21

docs.body:
## CLI reference

A shortcut is a saved invocation of `serial-studio` with these flags. The same command can be run by hand, dropped into a service unit, or scripted in CI (the full flag list lives in [Command-Line Interface](Command-Line-Interface.md)):

```sh
serial-studio \
    --project /path/to/project.ssproj \
    --runtime \
    --fullscreen \
    --csv-export \
    --mdf-export \
    --session-export \
    --console-export \
    --shortcut-path /path/to/deployment.lnk
```

Flags marked (Pro) exist only in commercial builds; a GPL build rejects the whole command above.

The cleanup treats macOS `.app` bundles as directories (recursive remove) and Windows `.lnk` / Linux `.desktop` as plain files. Nothing else on disk is touched.

## Tips for kiosk-style setups

Pair the deployment with a project lock: a locked `.ssproj` plus runtime mode limits the editor surface available at the workstation. See [Project Lock](Project-Lock.md). When one `.ssproj` serves several machine variants, declare a [workspace profile](Project-Editor.md#workspace-profiles) per variant and start each bench with `--profile <name>`, so the operator only sees that variant's workspaces and you keep a single project file. On a dedicated display, combine **Fullscreen** with the OS's autostart hook to bring the dashboard up on boot.
docs.title: Operator-Deployments#25

docs.body:
A deployment shortcut on Linux (`.desktop`) appears in the application menu once you save it to `~/.local/share/applications/`. If the entry does not show up, run `update-desktop-database ~/.local/share/applications`.

A deployment `.lnk` on Windows that keeps showing the previous icon after you regenerate it is the icon cache: sign out and back in, or rebuild it with `ie4uinit.exe -show`.

A deployment `.app` on macOS may ask for confirmation on first launch because it is unsigned. Right-click it and choose **Open**.

An update that overwrites the Serial Studio executable in place keeps shortcuts working; one that moves it means regenerating them.

## Frequently asked

**Does the deployment include Serial Studio itself?**
No. A shortcut or package needs the official (Pro) build of Serial Studio installed on the target machine, because a build compiled from source under the GPL cannot launch it. Install Serial Studio first, then copy the deployment over. See [Licensing](#licensing).

**Can a deployment launch in Quick Plot or Console-Only mode?**
Not via the dialog. Deployments target Project mode, which is the intended use.

**Does the deployment bundle the project file inside it?**
A shortcut does not; see [When the project file goes missing](#when-the-project-file-goes-missing). A [deployment package](#deployment-packages) does.
docs.title: Operator-Deployments#27

docs.body:
**Can I edit a deployment after creating it?**
A shortcut, yes. Windows `.lnk` exposes Properties → Target. The macOS `.app` keeps a small Bash launcher at `Contents/MacOS/<bundle-name>` (the executable named in `Info.plist`'s `CFBundleExecutable`). Linux `.desktop` files are plain text. All three can be edited by hand to adjust the flags. A package is not meant to be edited: change the project and export it again.

**Will the deployment work on a machine without a Pro license?**
It launches on any official (Pro) build without a license. Connecting needs a license, or an accepted trial, only if the project uses Pro features. A build compiled from source under the GPL cannot launch it. See [Licensing](#licensing).
docs.title: Operator-Deployments#28

docs.body:
**What if the machine has several devices and the deployment points at one of them?**
The **Pick Different Device** page of the recovery dialog lets the operator switch without leaving runtime mode. Auto-connect is a starting point, not a hard wire.

The first send without a license or trial shows the trial offer, a Yes/No prompt (registering a trial needs an internet connection); see [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md). docs.title: Output-Controls#2

docs.body:
The function decides the bytes, so the same slider can drive a plain-text command, a JSON payload or a binary packet. Binary payloads are byte-strings built with `String.fromCharCode`.

While a slider or knob is dragged, Serial Studio sends at most one value every 50 ms. The most recent value is held and sent when the interval ends. An Emergency Stop press skips the wait.

## Output Control Types

### Button

Sends a single command on click, or latches on and off when **Toggle Button** is enabled. A Button passes `1` to `transmit()`, or `1` / `0` when latching; see [Writing a Transmit Function](#writing-a-transmit-function). The separate [Toggle](#toggle) control is a switch widget; Toggle Button makes a Button latch, and both send `1` and `0`.
docs.title: Output-Controls#3

docs.body:
| Property | Default | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| Button Icon | (none) | Icon shown next to the caption |
| Colorize Icon | off | Tint the icon with the button color |
| Button Color | Automatic | Custom fill color; automatic uses the group accent color |
| Button Size | Normal | Small, Normal, Large or Extra Large |
| Button Style | Standard | Standard, Illuminated Push Button, Emergency Stop or Selector Switch |
| Toggle Button | off | Stay pressed between clicks and send `1` (on) / `0` (off) |
| On Label | (empty) | Caption while latched; falls back to the widget label |
| Off Label | (empty) | Caption while released; falls back to the widget label |
docs.title: Output-Controls#4

docs.body:
A latching button is filled with the button color while it is on and drawn as a plain
button while it is off, so its state is readable without opening the device. It sends
the same values as a Toggle, so a transmit function written for one works for the other.

Button Size scales the button, its icon and its caption together, and the Output Panel reserves a proportionally larger cell for it.

#### Button Style

Button Style sets what the button is. It is stored in the project and works under every
theme; the theme only decides how a Standard button is painted.
docs.title: Output-Controls#5

docs.body:
| Style | Behavior |
|-------|----------|
| Standard | The button described above. |
| Illuminated Push Button | A round colored head in a metal ring. It sends what a Standard button sends, and its head is lit while a latching button is on. |
| Emergency Stop | A red mushroom head on a yellow ring. One press latches it and sends `1`. A second, separate press releases it and sends `0`. |
| Selector Switch | Converts the button into a Knob set to **Rotary Selector** with two positions, labelled from On Label and Off Label (`OFF` and `ON` when empty), Min 0 and Max 1. `transmit()` receives `0` or `1`; see [Knob Style](#knob-style). |
docs.title: Output-Controls#6

docs.body:
An Emergency Stop always latches, so Toggle Button is fixed on:

- A press latches it and sends `1`. A second, separate press sends `0`.
- The press is sent at once, without the 50 ms pacing delay other control changes get.
- A release is ignored for a moment after the press, so a double-click cannot press and release it.
- If the transmit function returns nothing for `0`, the release sends nothing.
- With no [state source](#state-feedback) the button starts released each time the dashboard opens; bound to one, it shows what the equipment reports.
- When there is no connection to send on, the head shows **NOT SENT**.
docs.title: Output-Controls#7

docs.body:
> **An on-screen emergency stop is a command sent over the data link.** It reaches the
> equipment only if the computer, Serial Studio, the connection and the device firmware
> are all working. It is never a substitute for a hardwired emergency-stop circuit.

### Slider

Sends a numeric value from a draggable slider.

| Property | Default | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| Min | 0 | Lower bound of the slider range |
| Max | 100 | Upper bound of the slider range |
| Step | 1 | Increment between discrete positions |
| Decimals | Automatic | Decimals shown for the value; automatic shows two when Step is below 1, otherwise none |
| Units | (empty) | Suffix shown after the value, such as `%` or `rpm` |
| Initial Value | 0 | Starting position |
docs.title: Output-Controls#8

docs.body:
The value passed to `transmit()` is a number inside [Min, Max]. Transmissions occur continuously while dragging, at the rate in [How Output Controls Work](#how-output-controls-work). Keyboard and wheel behavior is in [Limits](#limits).

### Toggle

Binary on/off switch.

| Property | Default | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| Initial Value | 0 | Starting state (0 = off, 1 = on) |
| On Label | (empty) | Caption while on; falls back to the widget label |
| Off Label | (empty) | Caption while off; falls back to the widget label |

Passes `1` to `transmit()` when switched on, `0` when switched off.
docs.title: Output-Controls#9

docs.body:
When there is room for it, a toggle is drawn as a lever switch: the handle points up for on and
down for off, with the On and Off labels above and below it. A theme that asks for the plain
look keeps the switch.

### Text Field

Accepts typed input and sends it. The **Input** property selects how the typed text is read.

| Property | Text | Number |
|----------|------|--------|
| Value passed to `transmit()` | The typed string | The typed number |
| Interaction | Press Enter or click Send | Press Enter or click Send |
| Range | None | Min to Max, checked before `transmit()` runs |
| Use cases | AT commands, debug console, custom queries | Setpoints, duty cycles, servo angles |
docs.title: Output-Controls#10

docs.body:
A Number field adds the same numeric properties as a slider:

| Property | Default | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| Min | 0 | Lowest value the field accepts |
| Max | 100 | Highest value the field accepts |
| Step | 1 | Increment for the arrow keys and the mouse wheel |
| Decimals | Automatic | Decimals shown when the field displays a value |
| Units | (empty) | Suffix shown beside the field |
| Quantize to Step | off | Snap a typed value to the nearest Step, counted from Min, before the range check |

A value outside Min to Max, or text that is not a number, is out of range: nothing is transmitted, the field keeps what was typed, and a message under the field names the allowed range. The message clears on the next accepted value. After a send the field shows the value that was accepted.
docs.title: Output-Controls#11

docs.body:
Keyboard and wheel editing of a Number field is described in [Limits](#limits). A Text-mode field still clears after sending.

#### Text Field Style

Text Field Style sets how the field looks and how it is used. **Text Field Size** scales the
field, its text and its Send button with the same four sizes a button has.
docs.title: Output-Controls#12

docs.body:
| Style | Input | Behavior |
|-------|-------|----------|
| Standard | Text or Number | The field and Send button described above. |
| Readout Display | Number | The value in large digits on a dark display, with its units. With a state source it shows the reported value, otherwise the last value sent. Click it to type a new value; Enter sends and Escape cancels. |
| Keypad Entry | Number | Clicking the field opens a numeric keypad for touch screens. The sign key appears only when Min is below zero, and the point only when Decimals is not 0. Enter sends the value through the same range check as typing. |
| Command Line | Text | A dark command prompt. Enter sends and clears the line. Up and Down recall the last 20 lines sent from this field during the session. |
| Compact | Text or Number | The field without the Send button. Enter sends. |
docs.title: Output-Controls#13

docs.body:
A style that does not match the Input setting is greyed in the list and the field draws as
Standard. The style is kept, so switching Input back restores it.

### Knob

Rotary dial for continuous setpoint adjustment. It has the same numeric properties as Slider (Min 0, Max 100, Step 1, Decimals Automatic, Units empty, Initial Value 0) and is displayed as a circular dial. The value passed to `transmit()` is a number inside [Min, Max].

A knob is drawn as a pointer knob with a detent mark per Step (eleven marks when there are more
than 24 steps). Drag it round, or use the wheel or the arrow keys, with Shift for ten steps. A
theme that asks for the plain look keeps the dial.
docs.title: Output-Controls#14

docs.body:
#### Knob Style

Set **Knob Style** to **Rotary Selector** to draw the knob as a selector switch with one
labelled position per Step from Min to Max. Three positions are Min 0, Max 2, Step 1;
**Position Labels** takes their names, separated by commas (`Off, Low, High`). The transmit
function receives the selected position's value, so a `switch` on it gives each position its
own payload.

Turn on **Spring Return** for a selector that only holds a position while it is pressed, like a
jog switch. The position under the pointer, or the one an arrow key moves to, is sent when you
press. When you let go, the selector goes back to its **Initial Value** position and sends that
value once. Releasing it at rest sends nothing, and the mouse wheel does not move it.
docs.title: Output-Controls#15

docs.body:
A selector with a state source shows the position the device reports. The report can be a
position's value (`2`) or one of the position labels (`Hand`, in any letter case). A report that
matches no position shows the selector as unknown rather than pointing between two marks.
Showing a reported position never sends anything.

## Creating Output Controls

The steps are in the [Overview](#overview): open the Project Editor, click **Button**, **Slider**, **Toggle**, **Text Field** or **Knob** in its toolbar (see [Toolbar & Button Reference](Toolbar-Reference.md)), then **Edit Code** to write the transmit function.
docs.title: Output-Controls#16

docs.body:
Output controls live inside **Output Panel** groups. You can also click **Output** in the toolbar to add an empty Output Panel first, then add controls to it. A new control goes into the selected Output Panel, or the first one in the project. Each Output Panel can hold multiple controls of mixed types, packed automatically into as many columns as fit the available width.

## The Transmit Function

Every output control has a JavaScript `transmit(value)` function that defines how interactions become device commands. Variables declared outside `transmit()` persist across calls.

### Writing a Transmit Function
docs.title: Output-Controls#17

docs.body:
Select the control and click **Edit Code** in the Project Editor toolbar. The transmit function opens in its own window, with the template list, import, validation and testing all in its header, a live preview of the control beside the code, and a status line that reports whether the script compiles and defines `transmit(value)` as you type.

A script that does not compile, or that never defines `transmit(value)`, is not saved: the project keeps the last version that worked, and closing the window with a broken script asks before discarding it.

The preview drives the real control through its own range, step size and labels, and shows the exact bytes the script produces. It never transmits: nothing reaches a connected device from the preview, so a relay or PWM script is safe to exercise with hardware attached.
docs.title: Output-Controls#18

docs.body:
The function takes `value`, and optionally `token` (see [Acknowledged Commands](#acknowledged-commands)), and returns a string:

```javascript
function transmit(value) {
  return "CMD " + value + "\r\n";
}
```

| Control | `value` |
|---------|---------|
| Button | `1` |
| Toggle, latching Button | `0` or `1` |
| Slider, Knob, Number Text Field | A number |
| Text-mode Text Field | A string |

The return value must be a string. Returning an empty string sends nothing. For binary protocols, build a byte-string with `String.fromCharCode(...)` (see the Binary Packet template); returning a plain array of numbers transmits nothing. Payloads are capped at 65536 bytes, and a `transmit()` call that runs longer than 500 ms is stopped by a watchdog. Both conditions abort the transmission and flash a red border on the control; hover the control to see the error message.
docs.title: Output-Controls#19

docs.body:

Select one from the template dropdown and customize it for your device. Full code is shown below for the four most common; the others are summarized in a table.

#### Simple Command

Sends plain text with a line terminator. Adapts to the widget type automatically.

### Importing from File

Click **Import** in the transmit function window's header to load a `.js` file from disk. This is useful for sharing transmit functions across projects or version-controlling them separately.

## Examples

### Motor Speed Controller

Control motor speed with a slider and a stop button.

| Control | Type | Properties |
|---------|------|------------|
| Speed | Slider | Min: 0, Max: 100, Units: "%" |
| Stop | Button | Button Style: Emergency Stop |

Speed transmit function:
```javascript
function transmit(value) {
  return "SPD " + Math.round(value) + "\r\n";
}
```

Stop transmit function. The release (`0`) sends nothing. An on-screen stop is never a substitute for a hardwired one; see [Button Style](#button-style):
```javascript
function transmit(value) {
  return value === 1 ? "ESTOP\r\n" : "";
}
```

docs.body:
## Protocol Helper Functions

Every output widget's JavaScript engine includes built-in helper functions for Modbus and CAN Bus protocols. These handle binary byte-packing so you don't have to construct raw bytes manually. The checksum helpers (`checksum`, `checksumHex`, `checksumAlgorithms`) are available too, so a protocol that trails its payload with a CRC appends `checksum('CRC-16-MODBUS', payload)` instead of carrying its own table; see [Checksum Helpers](Frame-Parser.md#checksum-helpers).

### Modbus Helpers

Every Modbus helper takes an optional trailing `unit` (1 to 247). When given, the payload is prefixed with `0xFF 0x83 <unit>` and the Modbus driver writes to that device instead of the connection's own unit, which is how a control commands the second device on a shared RS-485 bus. A unit outside 1 to 247 is ignored and the write goes to the connection's own unit.
docs.title: Output-Controls#30

docs.body:
#### `modbusWriteRegister(address, value, unit)`

Writes a 16-bit integer to a single holding register.

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `address` | Number | Register address (0x0000–0xFFFF) |
| `value` | Number | Value to write; rounded, then wrapped to 16 bits (-1 sends 65535). Not clamped. |
| `unit` | Number | Optional, 1 to 247 |

```javascript
function transmit(value) {
  return modbusWriteRegister(0x0001, value);
}
```

#### `modbusWriteCoil(address, on, unit)`
docs.title: Output-Controls#31

docs.body:
Writes the ON/OFF convention (ON = 0xFF00, OFF = 0x0000) to a holding register. This helper is presently an alias for `modbusWriteRegister()`: it packs the same 4-byte holding-register write and does not issue a native Modbus coil write (function code 5/15) — the driver always targets holding registers (function code 6/16). Use it when a downstream PLC program maps that holding register to a physical relay or coil; it will not work against a device that expects an actual coil write.

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `address` | Number | Holding register address (0x0000–0xFFFF) |
| `on` | Boolean/Number | Truthy = ON, falsy = OFF |
| `unit` | Number | Optional, 1 to 247 |
docs.title: Output-Controls#32
Output-Controls#33

docs.body:
#### `modbusWriteRegisters(address, values, unit)`

Writes an array of 16-bit integers to consecutive holding registers starting at `address`. Each element is rounded and wrapped to 16 bits like `value` above. `unit` is optional, 1 to 247.

```javascript
function transmit(value) {
  return modbusWriteRegisters(0x0020, [1, Math.round(value)]);
}
```

### CAN Bus Helpers

#### `canSendFrame(id, payload)`

Sends an arbitrary CAN frame with the given identifier and payload.

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `id` | Number | CAN identifier. 0 to 0x7FF is sent as an 11-bit standard id; anything higher is masked to 29 bits (0x1FFFFFFF) and sent as an extended id |
| `payload` | Array or String | Payload bytes as an array of numbers (0–255), or a raw string. The helper adds a length byte after the id |

## Multi-Source Projects

In projects with multiple devices, the target device is determined by the source of the Output Panel group a control belongs to, not by a per-control property. Every control in a group transmits to that group's source. To send to a different device, place the control in an Output Panel group assigned to that source.

## Output Controls vs. Actions

Output controls and [Actions](Actions.md) both send data to connected devices:

| Feature | Output Controls | Actions |
|---------|----------------|---------|
| Widget types | 5 (button, slider, toggle, text, knob) | Button only |
| Data formatting | JavaScript `transmit()` function | Fixed TX Data + EOL |
| Continuous values | Yes (slider, knob) | No |
| Timer/auto-repeat | No | Yes (5 timer modes) |
| Auto-execute on connect | No | Yes |
| License | Pro | Free |
docs.title: Output-Controls#38

docs.body:
## Limits

In Serial Studio Pro, a Slider, Knob or Number Text Field enforces the Min and Max set in the Project Editor before the transmit function runs. `transmit()` never receives a value outside that range, whether it came from the pointer, the keyboard or an API client driving the dashboard, so the function needs no range check of its own. The slider and knob cannot be moved past either end; a Number field refuses the value and says so.

Step also moves a control from the keyboard. With a slider, knob or Number field focused, the arrow keys and the mouse wheel move the value by one Step, or by ten with Shift held. In a Number field they edit the text and Enter sends. The wheel acts only on the focused control, so scrolling a panel never moves a setpoint.
docs.title: Output-Controls#39

docs.body:
The limits are part of the project, and `project.outputWidget.get` reports them (`inputKind`, `minValue`, `maxValue`, `stepSize`, `units`) so a remote client knows the range before it drives a control. The console and the API's raw write are not controls and stay unrestricted. The limits guard against a typing mistake; they do not check what the device accepts.

## State Feedback

In Serial Studio Pro, an output control can show the equipment's reported state. In the Project Editor, select the control, open **State Feedback** and set **State Source**. By default an output control shows the state **you** last set it to. The equipment can change on its own: an interlock trips, someone uses a local panel, a command is refused. The control keeps showing your last click and quietly says something untrue about the machine.
docs.title: Output-Controls#40

docs.body:
Bind a control to a **state source** and it shows what the equipment reports instead. Set **State Source** to a dataset (one named value from your device's frame) or a table variable, then pick the source itself.

A load bank makes the case. Stopping the bank also stops its cooling fan, because the two are interlocked in the equipment rather than in Serial Studio. Bind the fan's control to the dataset carrying fan status and it stops claiming the fan is running the moment the bank goes down.

### On Value

For a toggle or a latching button, **On Value** decides which readings mean on.

Leave it empty and any non-zero number means on. That works for a dataset reporting `1` and `0`, but a device reporting text like `RUN` and `STOP` carries no number at all, so it would read as off even while running — fill in `RUN` and the control matches it exactly, comparing as text or as a number automatically.
docs.title: Output-Controls#41

docs.body:
Anything more involved (a bit within a status word, a threshold, hysteresis) belongs in the dataset's own [transform](Dataset-Transforms.md), which already exists for exactly this. Produce a clean `0` or `1` there and leave **On Value** empty.

### Waiting and No Data

A bound control shows three states rather than two.

**live**: the source is reporting, and the control shows what it says.

**waiting…**: you acted and the equipment has not confirmed yet. **Confirm Within (ms)** sets how long this lasts (default 3000, capped at 120000); a contactor may close in well under a second while a fan takes several. During this window the control keeps showing what you asked for, and feedback does not override it. The wait ends as soon as the source reports the state you asked for, and otherwise when **Confirm Within** runs out, even if the device has stopped sending data.
docs.title: Output-Controls#42

docs.body:
**no data**: the source has not reported, or has gone quiet. The control dims and says so, because showing "off" when the truth is "we have not heard" is the failure this feature exists to remove.

Feedback never transmits. Reflecting equipment state is not an operator action, so a bound control cannot command itself in a loop. Dragging a bound slider is also never interrupted: feedback is held until you let go.

If you delete the dataset or variable a control was bound to, the project still loads and the control still works — it stops correcting itself, and the Problems list reports it.

## Acknowledged Commands
docs.title: Output-Controls#43
Output-Controls#44

docs.body:
The token counts up from 1, wraps after 32767 and is never 0. A script that ignores `token` works as before.

### The Reply Convention

A text frame carries the reply as its last three fields, and the device repeats the latest reply in every frame until the next command arrives:

```
42,18,0,OK
42,19,2,above limit
```

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| Token | The number the command carried. A reply with any other token is ignored. |
| Code | `0` acknowledges the command; any other number refuses it. |
| Message | Optional text shown beside a refusal. It holds no separator character. |
docs.title: Output-Controls#45

docs.body:
Each field is an ordinary dataset; hide them with **Hide on Dashboard** if they are not for display. Under **State Feedback**, pick **Reply Token**, then **Result Code** and the optional **Reply Message**. A reply needs both a token and a code. **Confirm Within (ms)** sets how long the control waits, with a floor of 100 ms for a reply.

The dashboard reads the datasets once per display tick, so a reply sent once and not repeated can be missed under load and then reads as unanswered.

### The Three Outcomes

| Readout | Meaning |
|---------|---------|
| acknowledged | The device echoed the token with code 0. |
| refused: *message* | The device echoed the token with another code. The control also shows its red border and tooltip. |
| unanswered | **Confirm Within** ran out with no reply carrying the token, whether frames kept arriving or the device went silent. |
docs.title: Output-Controls#46

docs.body:
While the reply is outstanding the control shows **waiting…**. A control with a state source as well holds what you asked for after an acknowledgement until the source confirms it or the window ends; after a refusal it returns to the reported state at once.

Controls that share a Reply Token dataset share one token counter, so two of them never wait on the same number. The outcome lasts as long as the control's tile does: switching workspaces drops it, and the next command starts over.

The `examples/Acknowledged Commands` example pairs an Arduino sketch with a Blink button and a Setpoint field; the sketch refuses a setpoint above 80 although the control accepts up to 100.
docs.title: Output-Controls#47

docs.body:
## Common Mistakes

### Controls Do Not Appear on Dashboard

**Symptom:** Output controls are configured in the Project Editor but do not appear on the dashboard.

**Fix:** Connect the device. Output panels appear on the dashboard only while a device is connected or a replay is open. Also verify that the controls are inside an Output Panel group.

### Commands Not Received by Device

**Symptom:** The control is visible and interactive, but the device does not respond.
docs.title: Output-Controls#48

docs.body:
**Fix:**
1. Check the **Console** view to confirm data is being sent.
2. Verify the transmit function returns a properly terminated string (most devices expect `\r\n`).
3. In multi-source projects, confirm the control is in an Output Panel group assigned to the correct device.
4. Confirm the sketch reads the port and that its baud rate matches the connection; a line the sketch never reads looks like a dead control.
5. Output controls are a Pro feature. The first send without a license or trial shows the trial offer; if you decline or the trial has expired, nothing is sent and the control shows no error. See [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md).
docs.title: Output-Controls#49

docs.body:
### Slider Sends Too Many Commands

**Symptom:** The device is overwhelmed or the serial buffer overflows while dragging a slider.

**Fix:** A slider sends at most 20 values per second, one per 50 ms. If your device still cannot keep up, increase Step, which reduces how many distinct values a drag produces. A `transmit()` call cannot delay a send; returning an empty string skips that value.

### Transmit Function Not Saved

**Symptom:** Closing the transmit function window shows the message "No transmit function is defined."

**Fix:** The script does not compile or does not define `transmit(value)`. Define `function transmit(value)` that returns a string; the status line in the window reports when it does.
docs.title: Output-Controls#50

docs.body:
### Red Border on a Control

**Symptom:** The control flashes a red border after a send.

**Fix:** Runtime errors raised during a transmit (watchdog timeout, a script exception, or an oversize payload) flash a red border on the control for a few seconds; hover it to read the error message.

## Tips

For protocols beyond the built-in [Protocol Helper Functions](#protocol-helper-functions), define your own helper functions next to `transmit()` in the same script. A helper is only a function: if the dashboard sends the wrong bytes, the Console shows them before the device does.

## See Also
