docs.body:
# Protocol Setup Guides

An Arduino running `Serial.println("1,2,3")` at 115200 baud is the shortest path: select **UART/COM**, pick the port, set **Baud Rate** to 115200 and click **Connect** in the toolbar. The console then shows the raw text, and [Getting Started](Getting-Started.md#your-first-connection-quick-plot-mode) turns it into plots. Quick Plot mode needs no project: it expects comma-separated values ending in a newline, which is what `Serial.println("1,2,3")` sends.

The **Setup Panel** is the **Device Setup** panel on the right edge of the window, where you pick a driver and set its connection fields. Project-level settings, such as the MQTT Publisher, live in the Project Editor.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#0

docs.body:
UART, Network and Bluetooth LE are free; the rest need Pro. OPC UA, EtherNet/IP, S7 and IEC 104 have their own pages: [OPC UA](Drivers-OPC-UA.md), [EtherNet/IP](Drivers-EtherNet-IP.md), [S7](Drivers-S7.md), [IEC 104](Drivers-IEC-104.md). For protocol selection, see [Communication Protocols](Communication-Protocols.md); for the driver model, see [Devices](Devices.md).

Sections marked Pro need a Pro license. The first time you use a Pro feature, Serial Studio offers a trial with a Yes/No prompt (internet connection required); see [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md).

## Serial/UART Setup

**License:** Free
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#1

docs.body:
**Prerequisites:** Device connected via USB or RS-232/RS-485 adapter. Driver installed if required (CH340, FTDI, CP210x).

### Steps
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#2

docs.body:
1. In the **Setup Panel**, select **UART/COM** from the Connection dropdown.
2. Select the COM port (Windows), `/dev/ttyUSBx` / `/dev/ttyACMx` (Linux), or `/dev/cu.usbserial-*` (macOS) from the **COM Port** dropdown.
3. Set the **Baud Rate** to match your device. Default: 9600. Common values: 9600, 115200, 921600. The field is editable, so rates not in the list can be typed directly.
4. **Data Bits** defaults to 8, **Parity** to None, **Stop Bits** to 1, and **Flow Control** to None; change any of these to match your device.
5. Leave **Send DTR Signal** enabled (the default) if your device uses DTR, the line Arduino boards use to reset on connect, for reset signaling; disable it if a DTR pulse resets your device unexpectedly.
6. Optionally enable **Auto Reconnect** (off by default) to reconnect when the device is unplugged and re-plugged.
7. Click **Connect**.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#3

docs.body:
### Troubleshooting

- **Port not listed:** On Linux, see [Serial port permissions](Linux-Installation.md#serial-port-permissions). On Windows, install the appropriate USB-serial driver. On all platforms, try a different USB cable or port.
- **No data after connecting:** Confirm the baud rate matches `Serial.begin()` on the device. If text shows in the console but nothing plots, Serial Studio did not see a newline-terminated line of comma-separated values; see [Frame Parser](Frame-Parser.md). Try toggling **Send DTR Signal**.
- **Garbled data:** Garbled characters are the sound of two devices speaking at different speeds. Double-check the baud rate in the device documentation.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#4

docs.body:
Full driver reference: [UART](Drivers-UART.md).

## TCP Network Setup

**License:** Free

**Prerequisites:** Device and computer on the same network, or device accessible over the internet. Device IP address and port number known.

### Steps

1. In the **Setup Panel**, select **Network** from the Connection dropdown.
2. Set the **Socket Type** to **TCP**.
3. Enter the **Remote Address** (IP address or hostname of the device). Default: `127.0.0.1`.
4. Enter the **Remote Port** the device is listening on. Default: 23, a placeholder; set the port your device listens on.
5. Click **Connect**.

Serial Studio resolves the hostname when it dials. An unresolvable host shows up as a connection error, not a disabled **Connect** button.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#5

docs.body:
Serial Studio is a TCP client only: it dials out to a listening server and never accepts inbound connections. If the device expects to push data to a listener, run a small TCP relay in front of Serial Studio, or switch to UDP.

### Troubleshooting

- **Connection refused:** Verify the device is listening on the specified port. Ping the device to confirm network reachability. Check firewall rules on both ends.
- **Connection times out:** The device may be on a different subnet or behind a NAT. Verify the IP address.

Full driver reference: [Network](Drivers-Network.md).

## UDP Network Setup

**License:** Free
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#6

docs.body:
**Prerequisites:** Device IP address and port number known. For receiving, the device must be sending to your computer's IP.

### Steps

1. In the **Setup Panel**, select **Network** from the Connection dropdown.
2. Set the **Socket Type** to **UDP**.
3. Enter the **Remote Address** (IP address of the device, or multicast group address). Default: `127.0.0.1`.
4. Enter the **Remote Port** (the destination port when Serial Studio writes data back). Default: 53, a placeholder; set the port your device receives on. This field is hidden while **Multicast** is checked.
5. Set the **Local Port** to the port your computer should bind to for receiving data. Use `0` (the default) for automatic port assignment; bind a fixed port when the device sends to a known destination.
6. Optionally enable **Multicast** if the remote address is a multicast group (e.g., `239.x.x.x`). Serial Studio joins the group on connect.
7. Click **Connect**.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#7

docs.body:
### Troubleshooting

- **No data received:** Check that the device is sending to your computer's IP and the correct local port. Check firewall rules: UDP is often blocked by default. If you're using multicast, verify the device and this computer are on the same multicast-capable network segment.
- **Data from wrong source:** UDP is connectionless. Any device sending to your bound port will be received. Use firewall rules or application-level filtering if needed.

Full driver reference: [Network](Drivers-Network.md).

## Bluetooth LE Setup

**License:** Free

**Prerequisites:** Computer with Bluetooth 4.0+ adapter. BLE device powered on and in advertising mode (not connected to another host).
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#8

docs.body:
### Steps

1. In the **Setup Panel**, select **Bluetooth LE** from the Connection dropdown.
2. Ensure Bluetooth is enabled on your computer. Serial Studio starts scanning for BLE devices as soon as the driver is selected.
3. Your device appears in the **Device** dropdown within a few seconds; if it does not, see Troubleshooting below.
4. Select your device from the dropdown.
5. If the device exposes multiple GATT services, select the appropriate **Service** from the dropdown.
6. Select the **Characteristic** that carries your telemetry data (typically a notify characteristic, one that pushes new values to Serial Studio). Your firmware's documentation or a BLE scanner app lists which characteristic notifies; the one that sends your readings is the one to pick.
7. Click **Connect**.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#9

docs.body:
### Troubleshooting

- **Device not found:** Ensure the device is advertising and not already paired with another host. Move the device closer. Restart Bluetooth on your computer. On macOS, grant Bluetooth permission to Serial Studio in System Settings.
- **Connected but no data:** Verify you selected the correct service and characteristic. The characteristic must support notifications or indications. Check that the device is actively sending data.
- **Adapter not available:** On Linux, ensure `bluetoothd` is running and the user is in the `bluetooth` group.

Full driver reference: [Bluetooth LE](Drivers-Bluetooth-LE.md).
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#10

docs.body:
## MQTT Setup (Pro)

**License:** Pro

**Prerequisites:** Access to an MQTT broker. Broker hostname, port, and credentials (if any). Topic filter (subscriber) or base topic (publisher).

Your sensors already publish to a broker, or you want Serial Studio to publish to one. MQTT has two surfaces in Serial Studio; both can run in the same project.

- **Subscriber (per-source driver).** Treats a broker topic as if it were a serial or network device. Configured under **Devices** in the Project Editor, exactly like UART or Network. Use this when the data already lives on a broker.
- **Publisher (per-project).** Pushes parsed frames, raw bytes, or notifications out to a broker. Configured under the **MQTT Publisher** node in the Project Editor (directly below Devices). Use this when Serial Studio is the producer and downstream tools subscribe.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#11

docs.body:
### Subscriber: add an MQTT source

For a single-device setup, select **MQTT Subscriber** from the Connection dropdown in the **Setup Panel** and fill in the same fields there. For multi-device projects:
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#12

docs.body:
1. Open the Project Editor.
2. Add a new source under **Devices** (or pick an existing one) and set its **Bus Type** to **MQTT Subscriber**.
3. Under **Connection Settings**, enter:
   - **Hostname** and **Port** (`1883` plaintext, `8883` TLS; default `1883`).
   - **Username** / **Password** if the broker requires authentication.
   - **Client ID** (auto-generated; click **Regenerate** to pick a new one).
   - **Topic Filter**. Examples: `sensors/#`, `device/+/telemetry`, `mydevice/data`. Connecting is blocked while this is empty, unless Sparkplug is enabled.
   - **Version** (MQTT 3.1, 3.1.1, or 5.0).
   - **Clean Session** on (default) for interactive use.
4. To use TLS, enable **Use SSL/TLS** and pick an **SSL Protocol** and **Peer Verify** mode. For a private CA, set **CA Certificates** to **Load From Folder…** and pick the directory holding the PEM files.
5. Configure frame detection on the source. Each MQTT message preserves payload boundaries, so set the source's frame detection method to **No Delimiters**: each MQTT message becomes one frame.
6. Save the project and click **Connect** in the toolbar.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#13

docs.body:
Repeat with another source set to **MQTT Subscriber** to add a second broker connection (or a second topic on the same broker). Each MQTT source has its own broker session, credentials, and TLS configuration.

See [MQTT Subscriber](Drivers-MQTT.md) for the full protocol primer.

### Publisher: configure the project-level publisher
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#14

docs.body:
1. Open the Project Editor and select **MQTT Publisher** in the left tree.
2. Under **Publishing**, turn on **Enable Publishing**.
3. Pick **Payload**:
   - **Dashboard Data (JSON)** publishes each parsed frame as compact JSON.
   - **Dashboard Data (CSV)** publishes each parsed frame as a CSV row.
   - **Raw RX Data** republishes the bytes that arrived on any active driver, unmodified.
   - **Custom Script** publishes the value returned by the `mqtt(frame)` script hook.
4. Set **Publish Rate (Hz)**, how often the publisher emits (1-30 Hz, default 10).
5. Set **Topic Base**. The Publisher silently produces no traffic when this is empty.
6. Turn on **Publish Notifications** to mirror dashboard events to MQTT; set **Notification Topic** if you want them on a separate topic from the frame stream (it defaults to the Topic Base when empty).
7. Under **Broker**, fill in hostname, port, credentials, protocol version, and keep-alive.
8. For TLS, enable **Use SSL/TLS** and pick a protocol, peer-verify mode, and verify depth. Use **Load CA Certs** in the header bar to add PEM certificates for a private CA.
9. Click **Test Connection** in the header bar to probe the broker without disturbing the live session. The result appears in a message box.
10. Click **Connect** in the header bar to open the publishing session.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#15

docs.body:
See [MQTT Publisher](MQTT-Publisher.md) for the full reference, including the `mqtt(frame)` script hook for frame parsers.

### Troubleshooting

- **Connection fails:** Verify broker address and port. Test with a standalone MQTT client (e.g., MQTT Explorer, `mosquitto_sub`) to confirm the broker is reachable. On the Publisher form, **Test Connection** does the same probe inside Serial Studio.
- **Subscribed but no messages:** Topic names are case-sensitive. Verify the topic filter matches what the device publishes to. Use `#` as the topic filter to receive all messages for debugging.
- **TLS handshake failure:** Verify the CA certificate matches the broker's certificate chain. After loading a new CA, disconnect and reconnect (or run **Test Connection**) to apply it.
- **Publisher and a subscriber loop on the same topic:** Publishing to a topic the project also subscribes to creates an echo. Use different base topics, or disable one side.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#16

docs.body:
## Modbus RTU Setup (Pro)

**License:** Pro

**Prerequisites:** RS-485-to-USB adapter connected to the computer. Device wired to the RS-485 bus with correct polarity (A-to-A, B-to-B) and 120-ohm termination resistors at each end.

### Steps
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#17

docs.body:
1. In the **Setup Panel**, select **Modbus** from the Connection dropdown.
2. Set the **Protocol** to **Modbus RTU**.
3. Select the **Serial Port** corresponding to your RS-485 adapter.
4. Set the **Baud Rate** to match the device (common: 9600, 19200, 115200).
5. Set **Parity** (commonly Even for Modbus), **Data Bits** (usually 8), and **Stop Bits** (usually 1).
6. Set the **Slave Address** (device address on the bus, 1-247; default 1).
7. Click **Configure Register Groups…** and add one or more groups, each specifying:
   - **Register Type**: Holding Registers (0x03, 16-bit read/write values at numbered addresses), Input Registers (0x04, 16-bit read-only values), Coils (0x01, single read/write bits), or Discrete Inputs (0x02, single read-only bits).
   - **Start Address**: The first register to read (0-65535).
   - **Register Count**: How many consecutive registers to read (1-125).
   - **Slave Address**: optional per-group unit (1-247). Leave it empty to use the Slave Address from the Setup Panel, which is how you poll several units on one bus.
8. Set the **Poll Interval (ms)**. Default: 100 ms, which polls at 10 Hz; the range is 50-60000 ms and values outside it are clamped.
9. Click **Connect**.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#18

docs.body:
### Generate Project from Register Groups

Once you have configured your register groups, you can auto-generate a Serial Studio project file instead of building one by hand:

1. In the Setup Panel with **Modbus** selected, click **Configure Register Groups…** and add your groups.
2. Click **Generate Project** in the **Modbus Register Groups** dialog.
3. Serial Studio asks you to save the `.ssproj` file.
4. The Project Editor opens for further customization.

The generated project includes one group per register block, one dataset per register/coil, and a generated Lua frame parser. See [How Multi-Group Polling Works](#how-multi-group-polling-works) for details on the frame parser.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#19

docs.body:
### Troubleshooting

- **No response:** Verify the slave address matches the device. Check RS-485 wiring polarity. Confirm the baud rate and parity match the device settings. Ensure termination resistors are in place.
- **Timeout errors:** Increase the poll interval. Reduce the number of registers per group. Check the physical bus for noise or excessive cable length.
- **CRC errors:** Almost always a wiring issue: swapped A/B lines, missing termination, or ground loop.

Full driver reference: [Modbus](Drivers-Modbus.md).

## Modbus TCP Setup (Pro)

**License:** Pro

**Prerequisites:** Device connected to the network with a known IP address and Modbus TCP port.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#20

docs.body:
### Steps

1. In the **Setup Panel**, select **Modbus** from the Connection dropdown.
2. Set the **Protocol** to **Modbus TCP**.
3. Enter the **Host** (device IP address or hostname).
4. Enter the **Port** (Serial Studio prefills 5020; standard Modbus TCP devices listen on 502).
5. Set the **Slave Address** (usually 1 for TCP gateways, but may vary).
6. Click **Configure Register Groups…** and add one or more groups: **Register Type** (Holding, Input, Coils or Discrete Inputs), **Start Address** (0-65535), **Register Count** (1-125) and an optional per-group **Slave Address**.
7. Set the **Poll Interval (ms)**. Default: 100 ms; the range is 50-60000 ms and values outside it are clamped.
8. Click **Connect**.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#21

docs.body:
### Troubleshooting

- **Connection refused:** Verify the device is listening on the specified port. Check firewall rules. Confirm the IP address is correct.
- **Connection times out:** The dial gives up after 5 seconds; check the IP address and routing.
- **No data:** Verify the slave address, register type, start address, and count match the device's register map documentation.

## Modbus Register Map Import (Pro)

**License:** Pro

A register map file describes every register of a device. Serial Studio reads it and generates a project with register groups, datasets, a Lua frame parser and dashboard widgets.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#22

docs.body:
### Supported Formats

Serial Studio auto-detects the format from the file extension and accepts **CSV**, **XML**, and **JSON** files.

### How to Import

1. In the **Setup Panel**, select **Modbus** from the Connection dropdown.
2. Click **Import Register Map…**.
3. Select a CSV, XML, or JSON register map file.
4. Review the registers in the **Modbus Register Map Preview** dialog.
5. Click **Create Project**. Serial Studio asks you to save the `.ssproj` file.
6. The register groups are also loaded into the Modbus driver automatically.

### CSV Format

CSV is the most common format for Modbus register maps. Most PLC vendors, SCADA tools, and device datasheets can export or be converted to this format.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#23

docs.body: **Columns** (header row required, order is flexible; only `address` is required, and `name` is the first one to add):
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#24

docs.body:
| Column        | Aliases                                           | Required | Default    |
|---------------|---------------------------------------------------|----------|------------|
| `address`     | `addr`, `register`, `reg`                         | Yes      | None       |
| `name`        | `label`, `tag`                                    | No       | Register N |
| `type`        | `register_type`, `function`, `fc`                 | No       | holding    |
| `dataType`    | `data_type`, `format`                             | No       | uint16     |
| `units`       | `unit`, `eng_units`                               | No       | None       |
| `min`         | `minimum`, `range_min`                            | No       | 0          |
| `max`         | `maximum`, `range_max`                            | No       | 65535      |
| `scale`       | `factor`, `multiplier`                            | No       | 1.0        |
| `offset`      |                                                   | No       | 0.0        |
| `description` | `desc`, `comment` (used as name if no name column)| No       | None       |
| `slave`       | `unit_id`, `unitid`, `device`                     | No       | connection's unit |
| `bit`         | `bit_index`                                       | No       | whole word |
| `rw`          | `access`, `writable`                              | No       | read-only  |
| `order`       | `word_order`, `byte_order`                        | No       | abcd       |
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#25

docs.body: The last four columns describe how the device is wired rather than what a register holds:
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#26

docs.body:
- **`slave`**: the unit the register lives on. Registers from different units become separate polled blocks, each read from its own unit, and the generated parser tells the replies apart by the unit byte they carry. Leave it empty for a single-device bus. (`unit` alone still means the units column.)
- **`bit`**: a bit index inside a holding or input register (0 = least significant). The row becomes a light in the block's LED Panel group, following that bit; the rest of the word stays untouched.
- **`rw`**: `w`, `rw`, `write`, `yes` or `true` marks the register writable. A writable row also produces an output control in a generated Controls panel that writes the register (a toggle for coils and bit rows, a slider for numeric registers) and reads its state back from the block's table. A single write covers at most 123 registers.
- **`order`**: the word/byte order of a 32-bit or 64-bit value: `abcd` (big-endian, the default), `cdab` (word swap), `badc` (byte swap) or `dcba` (little-endian). `big`/`little`/`swap` are accepted as aliases.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#27

docs.body:
**Register type values:** `holding` (or `0x03`, `3`, `hr`), `input` (or `0x04`, `4`, `ir`), `coil` (or `0x01`, `1`), `discrete` (or `0x02`, `2`, `di`).

**Data type values:** `uint16`, `int16`, `uint32`, `int32`, `uint64`, `int64`, `float32`, `float64`, `bool`. Unknown types fall back to `uint16`; `bool` defaults its range to 0-1.

The same four optional fields are accepted as XML attributes and JSON keys under the same names (`slave`, `bit`, `rw`, `order`).

Lines starting with `#` are treated as comments and skipped.

A complete map is in [Example Files](#example-files).

### Converting Vendor Data to CSV
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#28

docs.body:
Most Modbus device documentation provides register maps as tables in PDF or Excel. To convert:

1. **Identify the columns:** Look for register address, name/description, data type, and units.
2. **Map register types:** Holding registers (function code 03), input registers (04), coils (01), discrete inputs (02).
3. **Note multi-register values.** A 32-bit value (`float32`, `uint32`, `int32`) occupies two consecutive 16-bit registers; a 64-bit value occupies four. Set the address to the first register and Serial Studio reads the rest as one value.
4. **Add scaling if needed:** If the device stores temperature as raw value × 0.1, add `scale,0.1` to the CSV.
5. **Save as `.csv`** with UTF-8 encoding.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#29

docs.body:
### XML Format

Two layouts are supported:

**Flat (type as attribute):**

```xml
<modbus>
  <register address="0" type="holding" name="Temperature" dataType="uint16" units="°C" min="0" max="150" scale="0.1"/>
  <register address="0" type="coil" name="E-Stop"/>
</modbus>
```

**Nested (type from parent element):**

```xml
<modbus>
  <holding-registers>
    <register address="0" name="Temperature" dataType="uint16" units="°C"/>
  </holding-registers>
  <coils>
    <register address="0" name="E-Stop"/>
  </coils>
</modbus>
```

Supported parent tags: `holding-registers`, `input-registers`, `coils`, `discrete-inputs` (with or without hyphens).
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#30
Protocol-Setup-Guides#31

docs.body:
### What Gets Generated

The importer produces:
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#32

docs.body:
- **Register groups** loaded into the Modbus driver (ready to connect immediately).
- **Project groups.** One Data Grid group per contiguous block of same-type registers, plus one workspace per group and an Overview workspace.
- **Variables tables.** One table per block, with one variable per entry; the parser publishes values into the tables and each dataset reads its value back through a small Lua transform, so datasets never depend on parser channel order.
- **Datasets.** One per register entry, with name, units, min/max, a plot toggle, and widget type (LED with an alarm band for booleans, gauge for temperatures/pressures, bar for percentages). Plots and gauges open on demand from the Data Grid rows instead of crowding the dashboard.
- **Frame parser.** A commented, editable Lua parser with one declarative spec line per register. It extracts values from Modbus protocol frames, handles data types (uint16, int16, float32, ...), and applies scaling/offset. See [How Multi-Group Polling Works](#how-multi-group-polling-works) for details on how the parser handles multiple register groups.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#33

docs.body:
### Example Files

A hydraulic test stand register map in CSV:

```csv
address,name,type,dataType,units,min,max,scale,offset
0,Temperature,holding,uint16,°C,0,150,0.1,0
1,Pressure,holding,uint16,PSI,0,5000,1,0
2,RPM,holding,uint16,RPM,0,3000,1,0
3,Valve Position,holding,uint16,%,0,100,0.1,0
4,Flow Rate,holding,float32,GPM,0,50,1,0
6,Motor Load,holding,uint16,%,0,100,0.1,0
7,Vibration,holding,uint16,mm/s,0,50,0.1,0
0,Pump Inlet Temp,input,int16,°C,-40,150,0.1,0
1,Pump Outlet Temp,input,int16,°C,-40,150,0.1,0
2,Ambient Temp,input,int16,°C,-40,80,0.1,0
0,E-Stop,coil,bool,,0,1,,
1,Motor Run,coil,bool,,0,1,,
2,Valve Open,coil,bool,,0,1,,
3,Alarm Active,coil,bool,,0,1,,
0,Door Sensor,discrete,bool,,0,1,,
1,Level Switch,discrete,bool,,0,1,,
```
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#34

docs.body:
The same map in JSON uses the flat layout (`"registers": [...]`) with one object per row, for example `{"address": 4, "type": "holding", "name": "Flow Rate", "dataType": "float32", "units": "GPM", "min": 0, "max": 50}`. In XML it is the nested layout with one `<register .../>` element per row under `<holding-registers>`, `<input-registers>`, `<coils>` and `<discrete-inputs>`.

## How Multi-Group Polling Works

Modbus (Pro) polls register groups in order, and the generated Lua frame parser decodes each reply.

### Driver Side

Each poll tick, the Modbus driver polls group 0, then 1, then 2, and so on in list order, and emits one frame per response.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#35

docs.body:
### Parser Side

The Modbus frame parser matches each reply to a register block by its function code (the second byte of the response) and keeps the other blocks' last values in their Variables tables. For two groups, holding registers carry function code `0x03` and coils `0x01`, so each reply updates only its own block's datasets. If a response times out, the parser keeps that block's previous values and resynchronizes on the next matching reply.

### Practical Considerations

- **Customization:** The generated Modbus parser is editable Lua. Each register is one line in the `BLOCKS` spec (`name`, `offset`, `type`, optional `scale`/`shift`); to add a register, add a line there plus a matching table variable and a dataset that reads it back with `tableGet()`. For larger changes, adjust the register groups and regenerate the project.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#36

docs.body:
## CAN Bus Setup (Pro)

**License:** Pro

**Prerequisites:** CAN-to-USB adapter (PEAK PCAN, Kvaser, CANable, SocketCAN-compatible) connected and drivers installed.

### Steps

1. In the **Setup Panel**, select **CAN Bus** from the Connection dropdown.
2. Select the **CAN Driver** (backend). The Qt plugins are `socketcan` (Linux), `peakcan`, `vectorcan`, `systeccan`, `tinycan`, and `virtualcan`; Serial Studio adds its own `canable_gsusb` (CANable USB), `slcan` (Serial CAN), and `seeed_usbcan` (Seeed / Waveshare) backends.
3. Select the **Interface** from the dropdown (e.g., `can0`, `PCAN_USBBUS1`).
4. Set the **Bitrate** to match the CAN network exactly. Default: 500000. Common values: 125000, 250000, 500000, 1000000 bps.
5. Optionally enable **Flexible Data-Rate** if the network uses CAN FD frames. **Listen-Only** (passive monitoring) and **Loopback** (self-test) are off by default.
6. Click **Connect**.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#37

docs.body:
To skip writing a project by hand, click **Import DBC File…** under **DBC Database**: the importer generates a complete project from a CAN signal database (see [Auto-Generating Projects](Auto-Generating-Projects.md)). Without a DBC, frames reach the [frame parser](Frame-Parser.md) as binary records (ID, DLC, payload); decode them with the **Binary (Direct)** decoder and your own parse function.

### Linux SocketCAN Preparation

Before connecting in Serial Studio, bring up the CAN interface from a terminal:

```bash
sudo ip link set can0 type can bitrate 500000
sudo ip link set up can0
```

For CAN FD, add the data bitrate:
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#38

docs.body:
```bash
sudo ip link set can0 type can bitrate 500000 dbitrate 2000000 fd on
sudo ip link set up can0
```

### Troubleshooting

- **No messages received:** Verify the bitrate matches the network exactly. Even a slight mismatch causes all frames to be rejected. Check CAN-H/CAN-L wiring and termination (120 ohm at each bus endpoint; measure approximately 60 ohm between CAN-H and CAN-L).
- **Interface not listed:** Ensure the adapter driver is installed. On Linux, verify the interface is up with `ip link show can0`. On Windows, check Device Manager for the CAN adapter.
- **Error frames only:** Bitrate mismatch, missing termination, or bus contention. Check all physical connections.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#39

docs.body:
Full driver reference: [CAN Bus](Drivers-CAN-Bus.md).

## Audio Input Setup (Pro)

**License:** Pro

**Prerequisites:** Audio input device (microphone, line-in, audio interface) connected and recognized by the OS.

### Steps

1. In the **Setup Panel**, select **Audio** from the Connection dropdown.
2. Select the **Input Device** from the dropdown (lists all detected audio capture devices).
3. Select the **Sample Rate**. Common: 44100 Hz, 48000 Hz. Available rates depend on the device.
4. Leave **Normalization** ticked (the default) to get samples as floats in the -1.0 to 1.0 range; the driver then picks the sample format itself and the **Sample Format** selector is hidden.
5. If you unticked **Normalization**, select the **Sample Format**. Options, as supported by the device: Unsigned 8-bit, Signed 16-bit, Signed 24-bit, Signed 32-bit, Float 32-bit.
6. Select the **Channels** layout (Mono, Stereo, or a multichannel layout, depending on the device).
7. Click **Connect**.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#40

docs.body:
Audio data flows into the pipeline as PCM samples, which can be visualized with Plot, FFT Plot, and Waterfall widgets.

### Troubleshooting

- **No audio detected:** Verify the input device is selected correctly in the dropdown. Check the OS audio settings to confirm the input is not muted and the level is adequate. On macOS, grant Microphone permission.
- **Distorted signal:** Reduce the input gain in OS audio settings. Use a line-in input instead of a microphone input when connecting sensors.
- **Wrong sample rate options:** The available sample rates are reported by the hardware. If the rate you need is not listed, try a different audio interface.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#41

docs.body:
Full driver reference: [Audio](Drivers-Audio.md).

## Raw USB Setup (Pro)

**License:** Pro

**Prerequisites:** USB device with accessible bulk, control, or isochronous endpoints. On Linux, appropriate `udev` rules. On Windows, a WinUSB-compatible driver (installable via Zadig).

### Steps
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#42

docs.body:
1. In the **Setup Panel**, select **USB Device** from the Connection dropdown.
2. Pick the device from the **USB Device** dropdown. Devices are listed as `VID:PID – Manufacturer Product`.
3. Select the **Transfer Mode**:
   - **Bulk/Interrupt Stream** (default): Standard synchronous bulk or interrupt IN/OUT. Works for most devices.
   - **Advanced (Bulk + Control)**: Bulk transfers plus vendor-specific control transfers. A confirmation dialog appears before enabling, since incorrect control requests can crash or damage hardware.
   - **Isochronous**: Asynchronous isochronous transfers for fixed-rate streaming.
4. Select the **IN Endpoint** (for reading data from the device).
5. Select the **OUT Endpoint** (for writing data to the device), if applicable.
6. For Isochronous mode, set the **Max Packet Size** to the maximum transfer size reported by the selected endpoint (prefilled from the endpoint descriptor).
7. Click **Connect**.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#43

docs.body:
### Troubleshooting

- **Device not listed:** On Linux, add a `udev` rule granting your user access to the device's VID/PID, then run `sudo udevadm control --reload-rules && sudo udevadm trigger`. On Windows, use Zadig to install a WinUSB driver for the device. On macOS, the device should appear if no kernel driver has claimed it.
- **Permission denied:** On Linux, verify the `udev` rule is correct and the user is in the appropriate group. Running as root is a quick test but not recommended for production.
- **No data:** Verify the correct IN endpoint is selected. Check that the device firmware is sending data on that endpoint.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#44

docs.body:
Full driver reference: [USB](Drivers-USB.md).

## HID Setup (Pro)

**License:** Pro

**Prerequisites:** USB HID-class device (gamepad, joystick, custom HID firmware, sensor) connected.

### Steps

1. In the **Setup Panel**, select **HID Device** from the Connection dropdown.
2. Wait for device enumeration. HID devices are re-enumerated every 2 seconds automatically.
3. Pick the device from the **HID Device** dropdown. Devices are listed as `Product Name (VID:PID)`.
4. Click **Connect**.
5. Once connected, the **Usage Page** and **Usage** fields show which HID collection is active, which helps when a device exposes several interfaces.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#45

docs.body:
### Troubleshooting

- **Device not listed:** On Linux, add a `udev` rule for `hidraw` access: create a file in `/etc/udev/rules.d/` with `KERNEL=="hidraw*", SUBSYSTEM=="hidraw", MODE="0666"` (or a more restrictive rule targeting your VID/PID). On Windows and macOS, HID devices are generally accessible without additional configuration.
- **No data:** Verify the device is actively sending HID reports. Some HID devices only send reports when there is a state change (e.g., button press on a gamepad).

Full driver reference: [HID](Drivers-HID.md).

## Process I/O Launch Mode Setup (Pro)

**License:** Pro
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#46

docs.body:
**Prerequisites:** A script or executable that writes data to stdout in a format Serial Studio can parse.

### Steps

1. In the **Setup Panel**, select **Process** from the Connection dropdown.
2. Set the **Mode** to **Launch Process**.
3. Enter the **Executable** path, or click **Browse** to select it. Bare command names are resolved through the PATH.
4. Enter **Arguments** (command-line arguments for the process), if any.
5. Optionally set the **Working Dir** for the process.
6. Click **Connect**.

Serial Studio spawns the process, reads its merged stdout and stderr, and feeds the output into the data pipeline. You can write to the process's stdin via the console.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#47

docs.body:
### Troubleshooting

- **Process not found:** Verify the executable path is correct. On Linux/macOS, ensure the script has execute permission (`chmod +x script.py`). For Python scripts, you may need to specify `python3` as the executable and the script path as an argument.
- **No data:** Ensure the script flushes its stdout (Python: use `flush=True` in `print()` or run with `python3 -u`). Buffered output will not appear until the buffer fills.
- **Process crashes immediately:** Check the working directory and arguments. Review the console output for error messages from the process.

Full driver reference: [Process I/O](Drivers-Process-IO.md).
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#48

docs.body:
## Process I/O Named Pipe Setup (Pro)

**License:** Pro

**Prerequisites:** An external process writing data to a named pipe (FIFO on Linux/macOS, `\\.\pipe\Name` on Windows).

### Steps

1. In the **Setup Panel**, select **Process** from the Connection dropdown.
2. Set the **Mode** to **Named Pipe**.
3. Enter the **Pipe Path**, or click **Browse** to select it.
   - Linux/macOS: `/tmp/myfifo`. Serial Studio creates the FIFO automatically if it doesn't already exist.
   - Windows: `\\.\pipe\MyPipeName`. The external process must create the named pipe before you connect.
4. Optionally click **Pick Running Process…** to choose a running process from a list.
5. Click **Connect**.
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#49

docs.body:
Serial Studio opens the named pipe for reading and streams data into the pipeline. The external process must open the pipe for writing.

### Troubleshooting

- **Cannot open pipe:** On Windows, the pipe must be created by the writing process before Serial Studio connects. On Linux/macOS, Serial Studio creates the FIFO itself if it's missing; if opening still fails, check that the path is writable and not already claimed by another process.
- **No data:** Ensure the external process is actively writing to the pipe. A pipe delivers nothing until a writer has it open.

Full driver reference: [Process I/O](Drivers-Process-IO.md).
docs.title: Protocol-Setup-Guides#50

docs.body:
# Remote Dashboard

The hardware is on a test stand in another room, and you want its dashboard on your desk. Remote Dashboard does that: the Serial Studio next to the hardware is the *publisher*, the one on your desk is the *viewer*, and the viewer shows the same groups, datasets, and live values. Remote Dashboard is in both the free and Pro editions; no license is needed on either side.

The view is read-only. Nothing you do on the viewer reaches the device, and the viewer's own project on disk is never modified. The device stays plugged into the publisher; the viewer only needs a network route to it. The link uses Serial Studio's API Server (a network port, 7777 by default), which is off until you turn it on.
docs.title: Remote-Dashboard#0

docs.body:
## Try it on one machine

1. Open **Preferences**, **General** tab, **API & Plugins** group, and turn on **Enable API Server**.
2. Open a project so there is a dashboard to show. Do not connect a device: attaching is refused while a local device is connected.
3. Run the **Remote Dashboard** command from the [command palette](Command-Palette.md) (**Ctrl+K**, **Cmd+K** on macOS).
4. Leave Host `127.0.0.1`, Port `7777`, Token empty, and press **Attach**.

Local connections need no token. With no device connected, expect the status line "connected, the remote is not producing data": a one-machine test shows the layout, not live values. For live values, run the viewer on a second machine and follow the next two sections.
docs.title: Remote-Dashboard#1

docs.body:
## Publisher: allow incoming viewers

Viewers on the same machine need only step 1; another machine also needs step 2.

1. Turn on **Enable API Server** (**Preferences**, **General** tab, **API & Plugins** group). It is off by default. The **API Server Port** field below it sets the port (1024-65535, default 7777).
2. Turn on **Allow External API Connections** and copy the **API Access Token** below it. A confirmation dialog, **Allow External API Connections?**, appears; press **Yes** (**No** leaves the toggle off). The token field stays disabled, and read-only, until the toggle is on. Read [Trust model](#trust-model) first: the link is not encrypted.
docs.title: Remote-Dashboard#2

docs.body:
With **Allow External API Connections** off, the server listens on loopback only. Turning **Enable API Server** off also turns **Allow External API Connections** off, so switch it back on after re-enabling the server.

The refresh button next to the token generates a new one and invalidates the old one.

The viewer needs the publisher's LAN address, for example `192.168.1.20`, and TCP port 7777 (or your port) allowed through the publisher's firewall.

The publisher accepts at most 32 simultaneous viewers, the API server's client limit. The `API/MaxViewers` key in the application settings can only lower that cap, and `0` refuses viewers while leaving the rest of the API available. There is no UI field for it.
docs.title: Remote-Dashboard#3

docs.body:
## Viewer: attach

Before attaching, the publisher must have **Enable API Server** on, plus **Allow External API Connections** and a token if the viewer is another machine (see [Publisher](#publisher-allow-incoming-viewers)).

1. Run the **Remote Dashboard** command from the [command palette](Command-Palette.md) (**Ctrl+K**, **Cmd+K** on macOS). The **Attach to Remote Dashboard** dialog opens.
2. Fill in the connection fields:

| Field | Meaning | Default |
|-------|---------|---------|
| Recent | The 12 most recent `host:port` endpoints; selecting one fills the fields below, including the token used with it | shown once an endpoint has been used |
| Host | Host name or IP address of the publisher | `127.0.0.1` |
| Port | The publisher's API Server Port (**Preferences**, **General**, **API & Plugins**) | `7777` |
| Token | The publisher's API Access Token; required only for connections from another machine | empty |
docs.title: Remote-Dashboard#4

docs.body:
3. Press **Attach**.

A viewer cannot attach while its own device connection or a recording is active. The dialog shows "Disconnect the local device or close the open recording first." and **Attach** stays disabled.

The status line shows the link state:

| Status text | What to do |
|-------------|------------|
| Not attached. | Nothing yet; press **Attach**. |
| Attached to *host:port* - live, *N* datasets at *N* Hz. | Values are flowing. |
| Attached to *host:port* - connected, the remote is not producing data. | The link is up but the publisher is producing no data. Connect a device or open a project on the publisher. |
| Attached to *host:port* - no response, the link may be down. | Heartbeats stopped. Check that the publisher is running and that host, port, and token are right. The viewer keeps the last values and recovers when the link returns. |
docs.title: Remote-Dashboard#5

docs.body:
If an attach fails, the status line shows the failure reason instead.

While attached, the toolbar's **Connect** button is replaced by a **Remote Dashboard** button. Click it to reopen the dialog and press **Detach**. Detach restores whatever the viewer was doing before: its own project, operation mode, and connection state.

The viewer asks for 60 Hz; the publisher grants the lower of that and its own dashboard refresh rate, between 1 and 60 Hz. The status line shows the negotiated rate.

Endpoints and their tokens are remembered in the viewer's application settings, and the dialog reopens with the last used publisher filled in.
docs.title: Remote-Dashboard#6

docs.body:
## Headless publisher

Only needed for a machine with no screen, such as an embedded PC. `serial-studio` is the installed application executable (see [Command Line Interface](Command-Line-Interface.md)). Provision the publisher from the command line:

```bash
serial-studio --headless --api-server --api-external --api-token-file /etc/serial-studio/token
```

`--api-external` is the non-interactive form of the **Allow External API Connections** toggle and skips its confirmation dialog. The token must be at least 32 hexadecimal characters; `openssl rand -hex 16` makes one. `--api-port <port>` replaces 7777 and accepts 1-65535, wider than the Settings field's 1024-65535. With no token source, the publisher generates a token.
docs.title: Remote-Dashboard#7

docs.body:
Pass the token with `--api-token-file <path>` or the `SS_API_TOKEN` environment variable. `--api-token <token>` also works but shows the token in the process list of the machine.

## What a Remote Dashboard viewer receives

The publisher sends its project document (groups, datasets, titles, units) and the live values the dashboard displays. It does not send raw frames. On the viewer, the console is empty, and CSV/MDF4 export, the MQTT publisher, and the Historian record nothing; record on the publisher. If the publisher's project changes while attached, the viewer picks up the new layout.

FFT Plot, Waterfall, and 3D Plot are unavailable on a viewer: they need every raw sample, and the link carries only displayed values. Those widgets show "Not available on a Remote Dashboard."
docs.title: Remote-Dashboard#8

docs.body:
The project is sent whole, but the viewer strips the publisher's logic when it loads it (see [Trust model](#trust-model)).

## Trust model

On a home or lab network this is fine; across the internet, tunnel it. The link is not encrypted, so use Remote Dashboard on a trusted network, or through an SSH tunnel or a VPN when it must cross an untrusted one. Keep **Allow External API Connections** off when no remote viewer is expected.

A viewer only displays. A spoofed publisher can make it show a wrong number. It cannot make it run anything. Before the viewer loads the publisher's project it removes the frame parsers, dataset transforms and transform libraries, the Control Loop, the output widgets' transmit functions, every source's connection settings, and the MQTT publisher and InfluxDB blocks. The viewer parses nothing, writes to no device, and opens no connection of its own.
docs.title: Remote-Dashboard#9

docs.body:
Canvas widgets (user-written drawing scripts) still draw, but their script runs on a draw-only surface that cannot call the API or reach devices, files, or processes. See [Canvas widget](Canvas-Widget.md#canvas-code-on-a-remote-dashboard).

Known exposures:

- Anyone who can capture the traffic can read the telemetry and the project document, including its scripts and connection settings. The token authorizes the connection but does not protect what travels over it.
- A token holder can also issue API commands on the publisher. There is no read-only token.
- Remembered tokens are stored in the viewer's application settings, encrypted under a machine-specific key. This is obfuscation, not a vault: anyone running as the viewer's user can still attach with them. A settings file copied to another machine yields no token.
docs.title: Remote-Dashboard#10

docs.body:
## See also

- [API Reference](API-Reference.md) — the API server, token handling, and external access.
- [Command Line Interface](Command-Line-Interface.md) — headless and provisioning flags.
- [Operator Deployments](Operator-Deployments.md) — locking down the watching station.
docs.title: Remote-Dashboard#11
SerialStudio-SDK#0

docs.body:
Every script in a project has the SDK already loaded, so `io.writeData` needs no import. The script kinds are a [frame parser](Frame-Parser.md), a [dataset transform](Dataset-Transforms.md), a [Control Loop](Control-Loop.md) (a script that runs on its own timer) and an [Output widget](Output-Controls.md)'s `transmit()`. You write them in the [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md); the Control Loop has its own node under **Project Scripts**. Plain plotting needs no script at all, so skip this page until you want to write to the device or react to a value.

Pro covers `notify*`, `mqttPublish`, dataset transforms, Variables tables (`tableGet`/`tableSet` and handles) and Output widgets (`transmit()`). Frame parsers, the Control Loop, `io.*`, `deviceWrite`, the encoders and the checksums are free. See [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md).
docs.title: SerialStudio-SDK#1
SerialStudio-SDK#2

docs.body:
The protocol encoders and the checksum helpers never reach the registry, so they return their value directly instead of an envelope. `deviceWriteAndWait()` returns its own `{ ok, ... }` object (see [`deviceWrite()` and `deviceWriteAndWait()`](#devicewrite-and-devicewriteandwait)).

## Byte payloads and the encoding enum

Any argument that carries **bytes to the device** takes a trailing encoding constant so you never base64-encode by hand:

| Constant | Value | You pass | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SerialStudio.Text` | 2 | a UTF-8 string | `"READ\r\n"` |
| `SerialStudio.Hex` | 1 | a hex string | `"5600030C"` |
| `SerialStudio.Base64` | 0 | a base64 string | `"VgADDA=="` |
docs.title: SerialStudio-SDK#3

docs.body:
```javascript
io.writeData("READ\r\n", SerialStudio.Text);             // text bytes
io.writeData("DEADBEEF", SerialStudio.Hex);              // 4 raw bytes
io.ble.writeCharacteristic("fff1", "01FF", SerialStudio.Hex);
```

## How a wrapper maps to a command

The SDK is one generated file per language, `SerialStudio.js` and `SerialStudio.lua`, loaded into every script engine at startup. It wraps a single primitive, `apiCall(method, params)`, which calls the same command registry the [network API](API-Reference.md) exposes over TCP. So `io.ble.writeCharacteristic("fff1", "5600030C", SerialStudio.Hex)` is a readable spelling of:
docs.title: SerialStudio-SDK#4

docs.body:
```javascript
apiCall("io.ble.writeCharacteristic",
        { characteristicUuid: "fff1", data: "<base64 of 5600030C>" });
```

Any command in the [API Reference](API-Reference.md) works from a script. Every call can fail (a wrong UUID, a disconnected device, a Pro-only command on a Free build), so check `ok`. `apiCall` has no allow-list, rate limit or payload cap.

## The result envelope

Every SDK call that reaches the command registry returns the same object. Check `ok` before trusting `result`.

| Field | When set | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `ok` | always | `true` on success, `false` otherwise. |
| `result` | success | The command-specific payload. Absent when the command returns nothing. |
| `error` | failure | Human-readable message. |
| `errorCode` | failure | Machine-readable code, for example `INVALID_PARAM`, `MISSING_PARAM`, `UNKNOWN_COMMAND` or `METHOD_NOT_ALLOWED`. |
docs.title: SerialStudio-SDK#5
SerialStudio-SDK#6

docs.body:
### Device I/O (`io.*`)

The wrappers mirror the bus tree. The ones you reach for most:

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `io.writeData(data, encoding)` | Write raw bytes to the active connection (any bus). |
| `io.getStatus()` | `{ isConnected, paused, ... }`. |
| `io.getLatestFrame(options?)` | The most recent raw frame (see [`newFrame()`](#seedecideact-helpers) for the deduplicated once-per-arrival form). |
| `io.connect()` / `io.disconnect()` | Open / close the configured connection. |
| `io.setPaused(paused)` | Pause/resume the data stream. |
| `io.ble.writeCharacteristic(uuid, data, encoding)` | Write to a specific BLE characteristic. |
| `io.ble.selectServiceByUuid(uuid)` / `io.ble.setNotifyCharacteristic(uuid)` | Wire up a BLE service/notify by UUID from a script. |
docs.title: SerialStudio-SDK#7

docs.body:
Every other `io.*` command (audio, CAN, Modbus, network, process, USB, HID configuration) is also a wrapper: type `io.` in the editor and autocomplete lists the namespace.

### `deviceWrite()` and `deviceWriteAndWait()`

`deviceWrite(data, sourceId?)` is the data-first form of `io.writeData`. It exists in the frame parser, transforms and Output widgets, but **not in the Control Loop**, which uses `io.writeData` instead (see [Where each surface lives](#where-each-surface-lives)). `sourceId` defaults to the first source.
docs.title: SerialStudio-SDK#8

docs.body: `deviceWriteAndWait(data, timeoutMs, until, source?)` (Control Loop and [Macros](Macros.md); elsewhere it returns `{ ok: false, error: "unsupported here" }`) writes, then **blocks the worker thread** (never the GUI) until a reply satisfies `until` or `timeoutMs` elapses. `timeoutMs` is clamped to 0..30000. `source` defaults to `0`. `until` is a terminator string, an expected byte count (number), or `undefined` for the first non-empty reply. It returns `{ ok, data, bytesRead, timedOut }`, or `{ ok: false, error }` when the write fails. It is the clean way to drive a request/response instrument without juggling `newFrame()` state.
docs.title: SerialStudio-SDK#9

docs.body:
```javascript
var reply = deviceWriteAndWait("*IDN?\n", 1000, "\n");   // SCPI query
if (reply.ok && !reply.timedOut)
  console.log("Instrument: " + reply.data);
```

### Variables tables (`tableGet` / `tableSet`)

The Variables tables are the cross-script blackboard (see [Variables](Variables.md)): constants and computed variables that hold their value across frames. All four script kinds read and write them with the same two calls:

| Function | Returns | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `tableGet(table, variable)` | value or `undefined` | `tableGet(t, r) || fallback` works for missing variables. |
| `tableSet(table, variable, value)` | none | Stages the new value into the live runtime. An undefined/nil value is ignored. |
To read another dataset, `datasetGetRaw(uniqueId | alias)` and `datasetGetFinal(uniqueId | alias)` return its pre- and post-transform value. A number argument is a uniqueId; a string argument is the dataset's alias. They are not available in the Control Loop.
docs.title: SerialStudio-SDK#10

docs.body:
In a Control Loop these calls marshal to the GUI thread, so each costs a round-trip: read once per `loop()` pass, not in a tight inner loop.

### Dashboard control

Available in the frame parser, transforms and Output widgets. The Control Loop reaches the same commands through `apiCall("dashboard....")`; the direct functions below do not exist there.

| Function | Effect |
|---|---|
| `clearPlots()` | Wipe plot history. |
| `setPlotPoints(n)` | Set the visible plot window length. |
| `setTerminalVisible(v)` / `setNotificationLogVisible(v)` | Toggle dashboard panels. |
| `setClockVisible(v)` / `setStopwatchVisible(v)` | Toggle the clock / stopwatch. |
| `setActiveWorkspace(idOrName)` | Switch the active workspace. |
docs.title: SerialStudio-SDK#11

docs.body:
The JavaScript-only [See/Decide/Act helpers](#seedecideact-helpers) are available in every script kind.

### Actions

`actionFire(actionId)` triggers a configured [Action](Actions.md) (a saved one-shot command) by id. Use it to reuse a command you already defined in the UI instead of re-encoding the bytes in script. It is not available in the Control Loop; there, call `apiCall` with the method name from the [API Reference](API-Reference.md).

### Notifications (Pro)

`notify(level, ...)`, `notifyInfo(...)`, `notifyWarning(...)`, `notifyCritical(...)`, and `notifyClear(...)` post to the [Notifications](Notifications.md) center. Each accepts `(title)`, `(title, subtitle)`, or `(channel, title, subtitle)`. `level` is `Info`, `Warning`, or `Critical` (globals `0/1/2`). With one or two arguments the channel is `Dashboard`.
docs.title: SerialStudio-SDK#12

docs.body:
On a build without Pro (see [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md)) the result depends on the script kind:

- JavaScript frame parser, transform and Output widget: the call throws `Error("notify() requires a Pro license. ...")`. Wrap it in `try`/`catch` if the script must run everywhere.
- Control Loop: the call returns `{ ok: false }`, so check `ok`.
- Lua: the call does nothing and logs a warning once.

```javascript
notifyCritical("Watchdog", "No frames for 2 s");
notifyClear("Watchdog");   // clears the Watchdog title on the Dashboard channel
```

### MQTT (Pro)

`mqttPublish(topic, payload, qos, retain)` publishes to the configured broker from the frame parser, transforms and Output widgets. It does not exist in the Control Loop. See [MQTT Publisher](MQTT-Publisher.md) and [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md).
docs.title: SerialStudio-SDK#13

docs.body:
### Protocol encoders (pure helpers)

These build a wire-format byte string and **return it directly** (no envelope). They are how Output widgets and parsers craft Modbus/CAN frames without bit-twiddling. Pair them with `deviceWrite()` / `io.writeData(..., SerialStudio.Base64)` to send, or `return` them from an Output widget's `transmit()`.
docs.title: SerialStudio-SDK#14

docs.body:
| Function | Produces |
|---|---|
| `modbusWriteRegister(address, value, unit?)` | 16-bit holding-register write (4 bytes). `value` is rounded and truncated to 16 bits. |
| `modbusWriteRegisters(address, values, unit?)` | Several consecutive registers: the address, then 2 bytes per value. |
| `modbusWriteCoil(address, on, unit?)` | Coil ON=`0xFF00` / OFF=`0x0000` (4 bytes). |
| `modbusWriteFloat(address, value, unit?)` | Big-endian IEEE-754 float across two registers (6 bytes). |
| `canSendFrame(id, payload)` | CAN frame from a byte array or string payload. An `id` up to `0x7FF` is a standard frame: 2 id bytes, a length byte, the payload. A larger `id` is a 29-bit extended frame: 4 id bytes (the first has bit `0x80` set), a length byte, the payload. An extended `id` is masked to 29 bits. The payload length is not checked: you supply at most 8 bytes. |
| `canSendValue(id, value, bytes?)` | CAN frame carrying a big-endian numeric value, rounded to an integer (default 2 bytes; above 4 the high bytes come out wrong). |
docs.title: SerialStudio-SDK#15

docs.body:
The optional `unit` (1 to 247) adds a 3-byte `FF 83 <unit>` prefix that sends the write to that Modbus unit instead of the connection's own. An out-of-range `unit` is ignored. The byte counts above are without the prefix.

### Checksums (pure helpers)

The frame reader's checksum library is exposed to every engine, so a script never carries its own CRC table. `data` is a binary string (one character per byte, the same convention the encoders above return) or an array of byte values; in Lua a plain string is already bytes, and a table of numbers works too.
docs.title: SerialStudio-SDK#16

docs.body:
| Function | Produces |
|---|---|
| `checksum(algorithm, data)` | The digest bytes as a binary string in wire order: `CRC-16-MODBUS` little-endian, every other multi-byte algorithm big-endian. Append it to a payload as-is. |
| `checksumHex(algorithm, data)` | The same digest as lowercase hex, for comparing against a text frame's trailer. |
| `checksumAlgorithms()` | The algorithm names: `XOR-8`, `MOD-256`, `CRC-8`, `CRC-16`, `CRC-16-MODBUS`, `CRC-16-CCITT`, `Fletcher-16`, `CRC-32`, `Adler-32`. |

An unknown algorithm or a `data` argument that is neither a string nor an array raises an error in the script (a `TypeError` in JavaScript, a Lua error in Lua). Data longer than 1 MiB (1048576 bytes) is rejected the same way.
docs.title: SerialStudio-SDK#17
SerialStudio-SDK#18

| `apiCall` / `apiCallList` | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| `delay` | no-op | no-op | yes | no-op |
| `deviceWriteAndWait` | returns `{ ok: false }` | returns `{ ok: false }` | yes | returns `{ ok: false }` |
| See/Decide/Act (JavaScript only) | yes | yes | yes | yes |

docs.body:
The Control Loop runs on its own worker thread, so it reaches the application only through `apiCall`, which is marshalled to the GUI thread. That is why its direct helpers are missing; use `io.writeData` and `apiCall` instead. [Macros](Macros.md) get the same worker-thread surface as the Control Loop.

### Output widget scripts

- `transmit()` runs from a user action on the widget (a knob turn, a button press), not from an arriving frame, so `newFrame()` has nothing new to read.
- `delay()` does nothing and `deviceWriteAndWait()` returns `{ ok: false, error: "unsupported here" }`.
- `transmit()` is always JavaScript. The Lua/JavaScript choice applies only to the frame parser.
docs.title: SerialStudio-SDK#20

docs.body:
## See/Decide/Act helpers

Four JavaScript-only helpers for closed-loop automation: read the latest data, decide in plain code, act through the SDK. They have no Lua equivalent. The [Control Loop](Control-Loop.md) page covers the model in full; the SDK surface is:

| Function | Returns | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `newFrame(sourceId?)` | frame or `null` | The latest frame, **once per arrival** (`null` if nothing new). Carries `text`, `values`, `sourceId`, `timestampMs`, `ageMs`, `sequence`. |
| `refreshDashboard()` | envelope | Re-run dataset transforms from the last values and repaint (**view only**, no export). |
| `dashboardTick()` | envelope | Same render, but also fans the synthesized frame to the export sinks (CSV/MDF4/Session/MQTT). Seeds structure before the first device frame. |
| `ensureDashboard(spec)` | summary | Declaratively create any group/dataset in `spec` that does not exist yet; existing items are untouched, and a repeated identical spec is free. |
docs.title: SerialStudio-SDK#21
SerialStudio-SDK#22
SerialStudio-SDK#23
SerialStudio-SDK#24

docs.body:
return v;                          // datasets still get both channels
}
```

> `notifyCritical` and `notifyClear` need Pro. On a Free build they throw (see [Notifications (Pro)](#notifications-pro)), so wrap them in `try`/`catch` or leave them out.
>
> Call the SDK only on the **state transition** (the `if`), never on every frame. `parse()` runs on the acquisition pipeline's processing thread, so each `apiCall` adds time to every frame and can make the stream fall behind. There is no rate limit to save you, and a parser that fires on every frame is a quick way to build a busy pipeline.

### 4. Dataset transform: calibrate against a live table variable
docs.title: SerialStudio-SDK#25
SerialStudio-SDK#26
SerialStudio-SDK#27

docs.body:
```javascript
var fps = apiCall("dashboard.getFps", {});
if (fps.ok)
  console.log("Dashboard at " + fps.result.fps + " FPS");
```

## Lua notes

Lua matches the JavaScript surface except for the points below.

- The envelope is a Lua table: `local r = io.getStatus(); if r.ok then ... end`.
- The encoding enum is `SerialStudio.Hex` / `.Text` / `.Base64`, the same constants as in JavaScript.
- Wrappers are global functions with dotted names (`io.writeData`, `io.ble.writeCharacteristic`); optional arguments go in a trailing table.
- The See/Decide/Act helpers (`newFrame`, `refreshDashboard`, `dashboardTick`, `ensureDashboard`) do not exist in Lua.
- The checksum helpers are native globals in every Lua engine: `checksum(algorithm, data)` returns the digest as a byte string (`s:byte(1, -1)` unpacks it), `checksumHex` the hex form, and `data` may be a string or a table of byte values.
docs.title: SerialStudio-SDK#28

docs.body:
```lua
function transform(value)
  local slope = tableGet("Calibration", "adc_slope") or 1.0
  return value * slope
end
```

## Handles: the fast path for table-heavy parsers

`tableGet` and `tableSet` look a variable up by name on every call. A **handle** is a number that points straight at the variable, so resolving a name once and reusing the handle skips the lookup on every read and write.

| Function | Returns | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `tableHandle(table, variable)` | handle (number), or `-1` | Resolve once, at script load. `-1` means the variable does not exist. |
| `tableHandleMany(table, variables)` | array of handles | Resolve several variables of one table in a single call. |
| `tableGetH(handle)` | value or `undefined` | Read by handle. A stale or invalid handle returns `undefined`. |
| `tableSetH(handle, value)` | none | Write by handle. A stale, invalid, or constant-variable handle is ignored, as is an undefined/nil value. |

# Session Reports (Pro)

You recorded a bench run last Tuesday and a customer wants it as a document, not a database. Session Reports (Pro) turns a session from the [Historian](Historian.md) into a file with a cover page, the min, max and mean of every value, and one chart per value.

Official builds with the embedded browser engine export a PDF. Builds without it export a single self-contained HTML file. There is no format switch: the build decides. If the dialog in step 4 is titled **Generate PDF Report**, your build exports PDF; if it is titled **Generate Report**, it exports HTML.

Each comma-separated value your device prints becomes a dataset in Serial Studio, and the report calls it a parameter. A session with temperature and humidity gives a cover page, a table with one row per value, and one chart page each.
docs.title: Session-Reports#0

docs.body:
Session Reports are a Pro feature, like the Historian. Without a license, the first use offers the Pro trial with a Yes/No prompt (it needs an internet connection); see [Pro vs Free Features](Pro-vs-Free.md). The export stays unavailable until a license or trial is active.

## Generating a report

A session is one recording of a connection, from connect to disconnect. Reports read the session from the Historian database, not the live project, so you can regenerate one from an archived session after the project has changed. The Historian list stays empty until you record one: switch on **Historian Database** under **Data Export** in the project setup, then connect your device (see [Historian](Historian.md)).
docs.title: Session-Reports#1

docs.body:
1. Open the Historian with the **Historian** button on the toolbar.
2. Select a recorded session.
3. Click **Export PDF** in the session detail toolbar (tooltip: "Generate a PDF report for the selected session"). The button keeps this name on every build.
4. The **Generate PDF Report** dialog opens (titled **Generate Report** on builds without the embedded browser engine). The defaults work, so you can skip straight to the next step. To brand or trim the report, see [Options](#options).
5. Click **Export PDF** in the dialog (**Export HTML** on builds without the embedded browser engine).
6. Confirm the destination in the **Save PDF Report** (or **Save HTML Report**) dialog.
docs.title: Session-Reports#2

docs.body:
The Save dialog is pre-filled with:

```text
<Workspace>/Reports/<Project Title>/<Document title or session_ID>.pdf
```

The workspace root is the **Workspace Folder** set in Settings → General. The file name is your document title if you set one, otherwise `session_` followed by the session ID.

## What's in the report

The report has four sections, switched on and off in the **Sections** row of [Options](#options). The **Datasets** tab of the dialog selects which datasets appear.
docs.title: Session-Reports#3

docs.body:
| Section | Contents |
|---|---|
| **Cover page** | Logo, company name, document title, project name, author, generation date, plus the session ID, duration, sample count, parameter count and start/end timestamps |
| **Test information** | Project title, the same session figures, tags, and session notes |
| **Measurement summary** | Per-parameter table with sample count, min, max, mean, and standard deviation. Non-numeric datasets show `—` for numeric columns |
| **Parameter trends** | One Chart.js line chart per numeric dataset, each starting its own page when printed. With two or more datasets, a screen-only overlay chart (hidden on print, so absent from a PDF) draws them on one set of axes |
docs.title: Session-Reports#4

docs.body:
The statistics are computed over every recorded sample, not the downsampled series the charts show.

## Options

The dialog remembers its settings between runs. They are stored per user, not per project.
docs.title: Session-Reports#5

docs.body:
| Tab | Field | Values and default |
|---|---|---|
| **Branding** | **Company**, **Document title**, **Author** | Free text, empty by default |
| **Branding** | **Logo** | PNG, JPG, or SVG, embedded inline so an HTML report stays self-contained |
| **Page** | Page size | A0–A6, B4, B5, Letter, Legal, Executive, Tabloid or Ledger; default A4. Reports always print in landscape |
| **Page** | Line width | 0.5 to 3.0, default 1.4 |
| **Page** | Line style | Solid (default), dashed, or dotted |
| **Sections** | Cover page, Test information, Measurement summary, Parameter trends | All on by default |
| **Sections** | **Annotate min, max, and mean values on plots** | Off by default; overlays those statistics on each chart |
| **Datasets** | Dataset checkboxes | Search box, **Expand All** and **Collapse All**, and a checkbox per group, folder or dataset |
docs.title: Session-Reports#6

docs.body:
At least one dataset must stay selected. Otherwise the export button is disabled and the dialog shows "Select at least one dataset to include." Turning off **Parameter trends** leaves a report without charts.

## How charts are rendered

Charts use **Chart.js 4.x**, bundled inside Serial Studio, so no network access is needed. For a PDF, Serial Studio loads the report in an off-screen browser page, waits for Chart.js to finish, and prints that page to PDF. Charts are static in a PDF. An HTML report keeps hover tooltips and the overlay chart. Series colors cycle through HSL hues starting at 210°, 48° apart, at 68% saturation and 36% lightness.
docs.title: Session-Reports#7

docs.body:
### Downsampling

Each chart holds at most 10,000 points. Longer series are split into 2,500 equal-count buckets that keep the first, minimum, maximum and last sample of each, then topped up with evenly spaced samples to 10,000. Peaks and valleys survive. Shorter series are plotted whole. The limit is not configurable.

For the full-resolution data, export the session to CSV from the Historian instead (see [CSV Export & Playback](CSV-Export-Playback.md)).

### Numeric formatting

Axis tick labels show up to three decimals, with trailing zeros dropped. Magnitudes below 0.001 or at or above 1,000,000 switch to scientific notation with two decimals (`1.23e-4`); zero stays plain. The time axis shows whole seconds for steps of 1 s or more, and one decimal below that.
docs.title: Session-Reports#8

docs.body:
## Performance

A PDF export is slower than HTML, because the off-screen browser has to render every chart before printing, and sessions with many datasets take longest. An HTML export still runs the database read and the 10,000-point downsampling first.

## See also

- [Historian](Historian.md): where sessions are recorded and browsed.
- [CSV Export & Playback](CSV-Export-Playback.md): for full-resolution tabular exports.
- [Pro vs Free Features](Pro-vs-Free.md): full list of Pro-only features.
docs.title: Session-Reports#9

# Threading and Timing Guarantees

Your Arduino prints 1000 lines a second with `Serial.println`. The dashboard redraws about 60 times a second, and every one of those 1000 lines still reaches the CSV file when export is on (see [CSV Export and Playback](CSV-Export-Playback.md)), with the time it arrived. A frame is one line or packet your device sends.

Serial Studio is soft real-time: it has no latency or jitter bounds, so keep closed-loop control off it.

## Practical advice

### When timing matters and Serial Studio is fine

Logging telemetry from a test stand or a vehicle, where a few milliseconds of uncertainty vanish against the length of the run. Audio-rate capture (48 kHz) with the Audio driver (Pro). CAN Bus (Pro) and Modbus (Pro) monitoring, which run well below the pipeline's headroom. Recording sessions with the [Historian](Historian.md) (Pro) and loading the original timestamps back into Python or MATLAB.
docs.title: Threading-and-Timing#0

docs.body:
### When you should look elsewhere

- **Closed-loop control.** Anything that needs a deterministic response of a millisecond or less from sensor read to actuator write. Use a real-time OS or a microcontroller.
- **Hard-deadline data acquisition.** If a single missed frame is unacceptable, you need a kernel-bypass DAQ stack (DAQmx, RT-Linux), not a Qt application. Nothing in Serial Studio yields when a frame takes too long: a 50 ms transform on one frame makes that frame take 50 ms.
- **Sub-millisecond cross-source synchronization.** All sources share one steady clock, but each chunk is stamped when its driver receives it. Skew between two sources is the difference in their OS and bus latency plus any event-loop delay, and Serial Studio neither measures nor corrects it.
docs.title: Threading-and-Timing#1

docs.body: ### Behavior that looks like a timing problem
docs.title: Threading-and-Timing#2

docs.body:
| Symptom | Cause | What to do |
|---------|-------|------------|
| CSV timestamps come in clumps | Frames extracted from one read share the chunk's timestamp, within nanoseconds (see [Timestamp ownership](#timestamp-ownership)) | Nothing. The clump is the arrival time of the read, which is all the driver measured. |
| The dashboard looks laggy at 100 kHz | The dashboard redraws at the UI refresh rate on purpose, not at the input rate | The rate is set under **Plotting > UI Refresh Rate (Hz)** in [Preferences](Preferences.md) (default 60, range 1 to 240). Open the CSV or the Historian (Pro) for full-rate data. |
| A widget skips frames | Widgets sample the latest data on each redraw, not per frame | Nothing. Export and the Historian see every frame. |
| The dashboard updates late or in jumps while a [dataset transform](Dataset-Transforms.md) is active | Transforms run on the pipeline thread, so a heavy one (regex, JSON parsing, tight Lua loops) delays every block flush behind it. The window stays responsive; only the data is late. | Profile it. For expensive per-frame math, work offline against the Historian database. |
docs.title: Threading-and-Timing#3

docs.body:
## What is and isn't guaranteed

### Guaranteed
docs.title: Threading-and-Timing#4

docs.body:
- **Order.** Frames reach every consumer in the order the driver produced them.
- **No frame loss while the CPU keeps up.** If it can't, frames are lost in one of two ways. [FrameReader](Data-Hotpath.md) drops frames, writes `[FrameReader] Frame queue full -- frame dropped (total N)` to the application log, and posts a **Frames dropped** notification, throttled to once every 5 seconds. Separately, if every block in the pool is still held by a consumer, the pipeline does not allocate; it drops blocks, writes `[FrameBuilder] Block pool exhausted ... dropping blocks` to the log and posts a **Block pool exhausted** notification, once. Data is then missing from the display and from recordings. The usual cause is a consumer that is not draining: a slow API client, a stalled recording or a heavy widget. To get back under the limit, lower the baud rate or data rate, simplify the parser or transform, or close widgets and recordings you don't need.
- **No per-frame allocation in the pipeline.** Parsed values are written into reused buffers, so memory use stays flat at any data rate. Details: [The Acquisition Pipeline](Data-Hotpath.md).
- **Consumers don't block each other.** A slow MQTT publish or a failing CSV write doesn't block the pipeline or the dashboard. Each consumer has its own worker thread and its own queue.
docs.title: Threading-and-Timing#5

docs.body:
### Not guaranteed

There is no upper bound on the time from acquisition to dashboard. The dashboard adds up to one refresh period (16.7 ms at the default 60 Hz), and a slow Lua transform on a loaded machine adds more. Frame-to-frame spacing on the dashboard is whatever Qt's event loop schedules, since widgets sample the latest data on each tick of the UI refresh rate (**Plotting > UI Refresh Rate (Hz)** in [Preferences](Preferences.md)).

Timestamps come from `std::chrono::steady_clock`, not `system_clock`. They measure durations and order events, but they aren't synchronized to NTP, so they don't line up with external systems by absolute time.
docs.title: Threading-and-Timing#6

docs.body:
## Threading model in practice

You don't need this section to use Serial Studio; it explains why a slow parser can't freeze the window. Every driver's bytes land on one dedicated processing thread, the pipeline thread (owned by `IO::PipelineHost`). `FrameReader`, the frame parser engines and `FrameBuilder` all live there. The drivers differ in where they read bytes before the hop.

| Where the driver reads bytes | Drivers |
|------------------------------|---------|
| Its own I/O thread | HID (Pro), USB (Pro), Process I/O (Pro), Audio (Pro), EtherNet/IP (Pro), S7 (Pro) |
| The GUI thread, through Qt's event loop | UART, Network, Bluetooth LE, CAN Bus (Pro), Modbus (Pro), MQTT (Pro) |
docs.title: Threading-and-Timing#7

docs.body:
OPC UA (Pro) and IEC-104 (Pro) are not in the table; see [Devices](Devices.md) for where they sit. The built-in gs_usb CAN backend is an exception to its row: it reads on its own thread. In every case the data crosses to the pipeline thread by a queued connection, once per received chunk, not once per frame. One read or socket notification can carry many frames, and splitting it is `FrameReader`'s job on the pipeline thread.
### FrameReader and FrameBuilder run on a dedicated pipeline thread

Delimiter scanning, decoding, `parse()`, transforms and staging values into a block all run as plain function calls on that one thread, so none of it pays a cross-thread cost per frame. Only two rates cross a thread boundary on the frame path: the chunk rate coming in from the driver, and the display-tick rate going out to the GUI. A slow transform stalls the pipeline thread, never paint and input handling.
docs.title: Threading-and-Timing#8

docs.body:
### Consumers run on worker threads

Everything that consumes a parsed frame, except the dashboard, runs off the pipeline thread on its own worker:

- CSV export (Free).
- MDF4 export (Pro).
- InfluxDB export (Pro).
- Historian (Pro). The SQLite writer batches inserts, and raw bytes go through a second queue.
- MQTT publisher (Pro).
- API Server, off by default, port 7777. Its TCP client sockets are serviced on the server's own worker thread, so a slow client can't stall the pipeline.
- gRPC server, port 8888. It runs only while the API Server is enabled.

The pipeline thread flushes a shared, trimmed copy of the current block into each consumer's queue and moves on, one copy per flush rather than one per frame, and only while at least one such consumer is active. A blocked consumer can fill its own queue, but it can't back-pressure the producer.
docs.title: Threading-and-Timing#9

docs.body:
### Dashboard runs on the GUI thread

The dashboard drains finished blocks on each UI refresh tick and renders whatever has accumulated since the last tick. At the 256 kHz benchmark rate and the default 60 Hz tick, one redraw covers about 4,300 frames, delivered as several blocks because each flushes at 64 samples (frame mode) or 4096 (stream mode). Consumers drain their own queues independently of the dashboard.

## Timestamp ownership

A frame's timestamp is set once, at the driver boundary, and never overwritten. Each chunk is stamped when the driver receives it, and the dashboard, CSV, MDF4, the Historian, MQTT, the API and gRPC all use that stamp.
docs.title: Threading-and-Timing#10

docs.body:
- **One chunk, many frames.** The spacing between frames inside one chunk (`frameStep`) defaults to 1 ns. N frames extracted from one UART or network read therefore carry timestamps within nanoseconds of each other; the driver never measured their real spacing. Only Audio (from the device sample rate) and CAN Bus (from the span of each batched burst) set a real `frameStep`.
- **Audio back-dates.** When miniaudio hands over a buffer of N samples at sample rate `sr`, the first sample carries its true acquisition time rather than the time the OS called the audio callback.
- **Tie-breaking.** Export workers don't re-stamp. When two frames share a timestamp they add a minimal offset so exported times strictly increase (`monotonicFrameNs`). This is a tie-breaker, not a clock.
docs.title: Threading-and-Timing#11

docs.body:

Your board prints `23.5,48.1` once a second and you want to see it. docs.body:
The Start menu's Export submenu mirrors these switches. It calls the Console Log switch **Console Transcript**; they are the same recorder.

### Console Log file location

Console Log is a Pro feature. Each transcript is written under the workspace's `Console/<subfolder>/` directory, where `<subfolder>` is the project title (Project File mode), `Quick Plot`, or `Console` (Console Only mode). The file is named `yyyy_MMM_dd HH_mm_ss.txt`, with `_deviceN` appended for a multi-device Console Only session. ANSI escape sequences are stripped before writing, and the file is UTF-8 with a byte-order mark.
