docs.body:
The **Settings** popup holds the **Show Timestamp**, **Echo**, **Emulate VT-100** and **ANSI Colors** checkboxes (ANSI Colors is enabled only while VT-100 emulation is on), a **Scrollback Lines** field (default 1000, range 100 to 100000) and a **Cyclic Send Interval (ms)** field.

With **Emulate VT-100** on, keystrokes typed into the console view are translated to VT-100 escape sequences (the terminal protocol used by shells and menu-driven firmware) and sent to the connected device, turning the console into an interactive terminal.

### A note on workspaces

Custom workspaces (Pro, Project File mode): a **workspace** is a saved arrangement of dashboard windows. Each project includes a default workspace. Add your own to keep different views of the same data (an overview screen, a diagnostics screen) and switch between them from the Start menu or the taskbar's workspace switcher. Free builds use the auto-generated workspaces.

**Ctrl+K** opens the [Command Palette](Command-Palette.md), a searchable grid of every workspace alongside the dashboard's tools and open widgets. Type to filter, move with the arrow keys, press Enter to switch, or Escape to close.

docs.body:
# Troubleshooting

The Console shows text and the dashboard stays empty, or the numbers are wrong. Start with the [Problem Center](Problem-Center.md): press **Ctrl+K**, then type `Problem Center`. It lists the project mistakes, link conditions, and script errors Serial Studio detected, each with a remedy. **Connection Diagnostics** (also in **Ctrl+K**) checks port permissions, Bluetooth state, and host reachability for you.

## Arduino prints values but the dashboard is empty

Take the smallest case: a sketch that ends each reading with a newline.

```cpp
void setup() { Serial.begin(115200); }
void loop() { Serial.println("1.5,2.5,3.5"); delay(100); }
```
docs.title: Troubleshooting#0

docs.body:
Work down this list and stop at the first step that fails.

1. In the **Setup Panel**, select **UART/COM** as the connection, pick the board under **Serial Port** (**COM Port** on Windows), and set **Baud Rate** to the number in `Serial.begin()`. The default is 9600.
2. Set **Operation Mode** to **Quick Plot (Auto-Detected Format)**. The sketch's comma-separated line then plots with no project.
3. Click **Connect** and look at the Console. If the text appears there but the dashboard stays empty, the link works and the problem is framing or parsing: continue with [Frames not being detected](#frames-not-being-detected) and [Data shows as "0" or "NaN"](#data-shows-as-0-or-nan).
4. If the Console stays empty, the bytes never arrive: continue with [Connected but no data appearing](#connected-but-no-data-appearing).
docs.title: Troubleshooting#1

docs.body:
A line ending in `\n` is a frame, and the comma-separated values in it are the dataset values. The [Getting Started](Getting-Started.md) guide shows this end to end in Quick Plot mode, and [Data Flow](Data-Flow.md) defines frames, decoders, and parsers.

## Installation Issues

### Windows: "Missing VCRUNTIME140.dll" or similar error

Windows reports that the Visual C++ runtime is missing. Install the **Microsoft Visual C++ Redistributable** from [Microsoft's download page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/windows/latest-supported-vc-redist) and start Serial Studio again.

### macOS: "App is damaged and can't be opened" or "Unidentified developer"
docs.title: Troubleshooting#2

docs.body:
macOS blocks the app because of its quarantine flag. For the "damaged" error, clear the flag in Terminal and open the app again. Substitute the bundle name shown in /Applications (for example `Serial-Studio-GPL3.app` for the GPL build).

```bash
xattr -cr "/Applications/Serial-Studio-Pro.app"
```

For "unidentified developer", open **System Settings > Privacy & Security** and click **Open Anyway** next to the Serial Studio message, or right-click the app and select **Open**.

### Linux: AppImage won't run ("Permission denied")

The downloaded file is not marked executable. Mark it and run it:
docs.title: Troubleshooting#3

docs.body:
```bash
chmod +x Serial-Studio-*.AppImage
./Serial-Studio-*.AppImage
```

### Linux: AppImage error "fuse: failed to exec fusermount"

The AppImage mounts itself through FUSE and the host has no working FUSE setup. Extract it and run the contents directly:

```bash
./Serial-Studio-*.AppImage --appimage-extract
./squashfs-root/AppRun
```

### Linux: Serial port permission denied

Opening the port fails with "permission denied". Your user must belong to the group that owns serial devices: `dialout` on most distributions, `uucp` on Arch-based systems.

```bash
sudo usermod -a -G dialout $USER
```
docs.title: Troubleshooting#4

docs.body:
Log out and back in, then run `groups` to confirm. [Serial port permissions](Linux-Installation.md#serial-port-permissions) has the details.

## Connection Issues

Run **Connection Diagnostics** first (**Ctrl+K**, then `Connection Diagnostics`). It reports denied serial port permissions with the exact command to run, a switched-off or unpermitted Bluetooth adapter, and a network host that does not resolve or refuses the port. See [Problem Center](Problem-Center.md#connection-diagnostics).

### Serial Port

#### Port not visible in dropdown

In the **Setup Panel**, select **UART/COM** as the connection first; the port list belongs to that driver. If the board is still missing, the operating system does not see it either:
docs.title: Troubleshooting#5

docs.body:
- **Windows:** open Device Manager (Win+X, then Device Manager) and look under "Ports (COM & LPT)". A yellow warning icon means the driver is missing. Common ones: [CH340/CH341](https://www.wch-ic.com/downloads/CH341SER_EXE.html), [FTDI](https://ftdichip.com/drivers/vcp-drivers/), and [CP210x](https://www.silabs.com/developers/usb-to-uart-bridge-vcp-drivers).
- **Linux:** run `ls /dev/tty* | grep -E 'ttyUSB|ttyACM'`. If the port is listed but cannot be opened, see [Serial port permission denied](#linux-serial-port-permission-denied).
- **macOS:** run `ls /dev/tty.*` and look for `usbmodem` or `usbserial`.
docs.title: Troubleshooting#6

docs.body:
Also try another cable and another USB port. A charge-only cable powers the board and shows nothing else.

#### "Failed to open port" error

Another program holds the port until you close it. Close the Arduino IDE Serial Monitor, PuTTY, Screen, Minicom, Tera Term, and any second Serial Studio instance. If nothing else is running, unplug the device, wait a few seconds, plug it back in, and reselect the port. On Linux, check [the permission fix](#linux-serial-port-permission-denied).

#### Connected but no data appearing

Check these in order:
docs.title: Troubleshooting#7

docs.body:
1. **Baud Rate** matches the device. The default is 9600; a sketch with `Serial.begin(115200)` needs 115200. If you do not know the rate, try 9600, 19200, 38400, 57600, and 115200.
2. The selected port is the right one. Unplug the device and see which entry disappears.
3. The device is transmitting. Open the same port in another terminal, or check the sketch calls `Serial.println()`.
4. In the UART setup, **Send DTR Signal** is on by default. Clear it if opening the port resets your board; many Arduino boards reset when DTR changes. If a native-USB board stays silent, leave it on.
5. The Console shows text but the dashboard stays empty: the frame delimiters do not match. See [Frames not being detected](#frames-not-being-detected).
docs.title: Troubleshooting#8

docs.body:
#### Garbled or unreadable console output

Data arrives, but the Console shows nonsense instead of readable text. Random accented characters, or a scatter of `?` and diamond symbols, mean the UART clock and the device disagree on bit timing: match **Baud Rate** to the device.

If the text is readable except for the same few characters, wrong in the same places every time (a degree symbol that always shows as two odd characters), the bytes arrive intact and the device sends non-ASCII characters. Changing the baud rate does not help. Run **Hex Display** from **Ctrl+K** to see the raw bytes.

### Network Socket (TCP/UDP)
docs.title: Troubleshooting#9

docs.body:
See [Network Sockets](Drivers-Network.md) for every field.

#### Cannot connect to TCP socket

1. Confirm **Remote Address** and **Remote Port** match the device, and that **Socket Type** is TCP, not UDP. `ping <ip-address>` checks the address.
2. Test the listener from a terminal: `telnet <ip-address> <port>`. "Connection refused" means the device is not listening; a hang usually means a firewall is dropping the connection.
3. Allow Serial Studio through the firewall: Windows Defender Firewall (Allow an app), macOS System Settings > Privacy & Security > Firewall, or `sudo ufw allow <port>` on Linux.
4. Check that the computer and the device are on the same network.
docs.title: Troubleshooting#10

docs.body:
#### UDP not receiving data

**Local Port** is the usual cause: it defaults to `0`, and then the OS picks a random port and nothing reaches Serial Studio. Set it to the port the device sends to.

If that is already right:

- Check the device sends to this computer's current IP. DHCP may have changed it (`ipconfig` on Windows, `ip addr` on Linux and macOS).
- Allow Serial Studio through the firewall; UDP is blocked more often than TCP.
- Run Wireshark to see whether the datagrams arrive at all.

### Bluetooth LE

See [Bluetooth LE](Drivers-Bluetooth-LE.md) for every field. Bluetooth LE is available in both editions.
docs.title: Troubleshooting#11

docs.body:
#### BLE device not found during scan

Many BLE peripherals stop advertising once a phone or another app connects to them. Disconnect the device elsewhere, power-cycle it, and keep it within a metre or two of the computer. Then check that the computer's Bluetooth is on, and run **Connection Diagnostics** (**Ctrl+K**), which reports a switched-off or unpermitted adapter.

#### Connected to BLE but no data

Select the **Service**, then the **Characteristic** that carries the telemetry, the one with the Notify property. Serial Studio enables notifications on a characteristic when you select it (it writes the CCCD descriptor), so there is nothing to switch on by hand. A characteristic that is Indicate-only, or has no CCCD, delivers nothing. Serial Studio does not show characteristic properties, so check them in the firmware.
docs.title: Troubleshooting#12

docs.body:
## Dashboard & Visualization Issues

The [Problem Center](Problem-Center.md) lists the project mistakes behind most empty or wrong widgets: a dataset with no frame position, two datasets reading the same index, a plot axis pointing at a deleted dataset, or an inverted range. Each finding has a **Go To** button that opens the Project Editor at the item to fix.

### Data shows as "0" or "NaN"

A dataset shows 0 or NaN when its frame index points past the parser's output or at the wrong value. The first value your parser returns feeds the dataset with frame index 1, the second feeds index 2, and so on. [Parser returns the wrong number of values](#parser-returns-the-wrong-number-of-values) shows how to find the mismatch.
docs.title: Troubleshooting#13

docs.body:
If the indices are right, the parser itself is failing: errors appear in the Console, and [Parser function not working](#parser-function-not-working) shows how to log what it receives. Also check that the raw frames in the Console match the format the parser expects.

### Widgets not displaying or showing errors

- **Wrong data for the widget:** the Accelerometer widget needs exactly 3 datasets (X, Y, Z) and the GPS widget needs latitude and longitude. A gauge cannot show text and a bar is a poor fit for unbounded values. [Widget Reference](Widget-Reference.md) lists the requirements per widget.
- **Broken widget:** delete the widget from the project and add it again with a fresh configuration.
docs.title: Troubleshooting#14

docs.body:
### Dashboard layout broken after update

Loading a project saved by an older Serial Studio version resets a customized workspace layout to the automatic one, on purpose: an empty custom layout is worse than an automatic one. Rearrange the workspaces and save the project. If datasets or widgets are missing rather than moved, report it as a bug.

## Frame Parsing Issues

While connected, the [Problem Center](Problem-Center.md) tells the two failure stages apart: `bytes-without-frames` means the delimiters do not match the stream, `frames-without-values` means frames arrive but the parser returns nothing, and `script.parser` findings show the parser's own errors or that the watchdog switched it off for overrunning its time budget.
docs.title: Troubleshooting#15

docs.body:
### Frames not being detected

The Console shows bytes arriving, but the dashboard receives no frames. The delimiters in the project do not match what the device sends.
docs.title: Troubleshooting#16

docs.body:
1. Open the Console and look at the bytes. Delimiters are case-sensitive and a stray space counts; the Console's **Hex Display** command (**Ctrl+K**) shows hidden characters.
2. A plain `Serial.println` ends each line with `\r\n`, and the project's default end delimiter `\n` covers it. A device that ends lines with a bare `\r` needs its end delimiter changed in the Project Editor.
3. Frame delimiters, decoder and parser are set per source in the Project Editor (click **Project Editor** in the Setup Panel): the **Frame Detection Method**, **Frame Start Delimiter** and **Frame End Delimiter** fields. **Test With Sample Data** lets you paste a frame and adjust detection until it splits correctly.
4. For binary protocols, **No Delimiters** treats each captured chunk as one frame, which suits length-prefixed protocols; the parser must find the boundaries inside it.
docs.title: Troubleshooting#17

docs.body:
### Parser returns the wrong number of values

**Problem:** some widgets stop updating while others keep moving, or a widget never shows a value, although frames arrive.

**Cause:** each dataset reads one frame index, the 1-based position of its value in the parser's output. When the parser returns fewer values than a dataset's index, that dataset receives nothing and keeps its last value, so it looks frozen rather than empty. The usual reasons are a device that sends fewer fields than the project expects, a separator that does not match, or frame indices that are off by one (the first value is index 1, not 0).
docs.title: Troubleshooting#18

docs.body:
**How to find it:**

1. Open the [Problem Center](Problem-Center.md). A `short-frames` warning names each affected device, the number of values its frames carry, the highest frame index the project maps, and the datasets that receive nothing. **Go To** opens the first of them.
2. In the Project Editor, open the device's frame parser page and click **Test With Sample Data**. Paste one real frame. Expand a row: each value is labelled with its frame index and the dataset that reads it, and datasets whose index the frame does not reach are listed as not in this frame.

**Fix:** make the device send every expected value, correct the parser or its separator, or set the affected datasets' frame index to the position of their value in the frame.
docs.title: Troubleshooting#19
Troubleshooting#20

docs.body:
2. **Return an array** (a table in Lua), not a string: `return [1, 2, 3];` works, `return "1,2,3";` does not.
3. **Match the decoder.** The source's **Decoder** (Project Editor, source settings; default Plain Text) sets the type of `frame`. Plain Text, Hexadecimal and Base64 give a string; Binary (Direct) gives a byte array, 0-indexed in JavaScript and 1-indexed in Lua. The table is in [Frame Parser Scripting](Frame-Parser.md). A string function on a byte array produces the error in [Parse error: "string expected, got table"](#parse-error-string-expected-got-table--framesplit-is-not-a-function).
docs.title: Troubleshooting#21

docs.body:
### Parse error: "string expected, got table" / "frame.split is not a function"

The Console repeats one of these on every frame:

- Lua: `bad argument #1 to 'byte' (string expected, got table)`
- Lua: `attempt to index a table value (local 'frame')`
- JavaScript: `TypeError: frame.split is not a function` (or `frame.match`, `frame.charCodeAt`)

The source uses the **Binary (Direct)** decoder, which hands `parse()` the frame as raw byte values (a 1-indexed table in Lua, an array in JavaScript), but the parser code was written for a string input.

1. Index the bytes directly instead of using string functions:
docs.title: Troubleshooting#22
Troubleshooting#23

docs.body:
```lua
   function parse(frame)
     if #frame < 4 then return {} end
     local value = bit.lshift(frame[1], 8) + frame[2]  -- big-endian uint16
     return { value }
   end
   ```

3. Or switch the decoder to Plain Text or Hexadecimal in the Project Editor if the device sends text. The decoder and the parser must agree on the frame type; the decoder table is in [Frame Parser Scripting](Frame-Parser.md).

### Dataset transform not working

**Problem:** You applied a `transform(value)` function but the dashboard still shows raw values.

**Debugging steps:**

1. **Check the function is named `transform`.** It has to be exactly `function transform(value)` (Lua) or `function transform(value) {` (JavaScript). The name is case-sensitive.
docs.title: Troubleshooting#24

docs.body:
2. **Click Apply in the transform editor.** Changes are only saved when you click Apply. Closing the dialog without Apply discards changes.

3. **Test with the built-in Test area.** Enter a raw value in the Input field and click Test. If you see an error, fix the function before applying.

4. **Handle non-numeric datasets.** The transform receives the raw value as a number when it parses as numeric, otherwise as a string. A non-numeric value like "N/A" is passed to `transform()` as a string, not skipped, so make sure your function handles the string case.

5. **Check the Problem Center.** A transform that produces errors raises a `script.transform` warning there ([Problem Center](Problem-Center.md)). The compiler's own message goes to the application log, so it is visible in a terminal only if you launch Serial Studio from one.
docs.title: Troubleshooting#25
Troubleshooting#26

docs.body:
For a Lua parser, the Fast mode described in [Frame Parser Scripting](Frame-Parser.md) runs much faster but disables the watchdog.

## CSV Player Issues

### Cannot open CSV file

Serial Studio's own exports always open, so record a short session and compare your file with it. The player expects a header row and a first column that holds elapsed time or a timestamp it can recognise: `Elapsed (s)` in Serial Studio's exports, a column with the unit in the name such as `time(ms)`, or date/time strings. Exports are UTF-8 with a byte-order mark. A multi-source file also needs the project that produced it loaded first. [CSV Export & Playback](CSV-Export-Playback.md#opening-a-csv-file) has the accepted formats.
docs.title: Troubleshooting#27

docs.body:
### Playback is choppy

The CSV Player replays at the original capture speed; there is no playback-speed control. For very large or high-rate files, split the file into smaller segments or keep only the columns you need.

## Pro Feature Issues

### MQTT connection fails

MQTT is a Pro feature. See [MQTT Subscriber](Drivers-MQTT.md) and [MQTT Publisher](MQTT-Publisher.md). Run **Test Connection** on the Publisher form to probe broker reachability without disturbing live publishing.

Two instances or sources sharing one client ID kick each other off. If the IDs are distinct, check the broker address and port, the credentials, and the TLS certificates.
docs.title: Troubleshooting#28

docs.body:
### Modbus connection fails

Modbus is a Pro feature. Check, in order:

- **Slave Address** matches the device (1-247, default 1).
- **Register Type**, **Start Address**, and **Register Count** match the device manual.
- RTU: baud rate, parity, and RS-485 wiring polarity. TCP: IP address and port.

See [Modbus RTU Setup](Protocol-Setup-Guides.md#modbus-rtu-setup-pro) and [Modbus TCP Setup](Protocol-Setup-Guides.md#modbus-tcp-setup-pro).

### CAN Bus issues

CAN Bus is a Pro feature. Check the bitrate against the bus, termination resistors at both ends, that the adapter is recognized, and that the DBC file loads without format errors. See [CAN Bus Setup](Protocol-Setup-Guides.md#can-bus-setup-pro).
docs.title: Troubleshooting#29

docs.body:
### A Pro feature shows a trial or activation prompt

This applies to Serial Studio Pro in the official binary. The first time you use a Pro feature, Serial Studio asks **Start your free 14-day Serial Studio Pro trial?** with **Yes** and **No**. Registering the trial needs an internet connection. Answer **No** and the feature stays unavailable until you use it again and say Yes.

**Trial ended:** the prompt offers **Activate License** or **Get Serial Studio Pro** instead. The trial is not offered a second time on the same machine; the free features keep working.

**Transforms and Variables:** a project containing a dataset transform or a Variables table needs Pro to connect, and the prompt lists how many. Right-click the dataset and choose **Remove Transform**, or delete the table, to run the project for free.
docs.title: Troubleshooting#30

docs.body:
**Check status:** click **About** in the toolbar, then **Manage License**, to open the Licensing dialog. While a trial runs, the Console welcome text shows the days remaining. After it ends, it shows `Pro trial expired. Free features remain fully functional.`

**Activate a key:** paste it in the Licensing dialog and click **Activate**. Activation needs an internet connection.

**Trial rules:** one 14-day trial per version and per machine; reinstalling does not reset it, and a new Serial Studio release starts a fresh one ([Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md)).

**Compiled from source:** a build with only the GPL modules has no Pro features and cannot activate. Install the official binary from [serial-studio.com](https://serial-studio.com).
docs.title: Troubleshooting#31
Troubleshooting#32

docs.body:
Without the `shift()` cap, `history` grows forever. Long sessions with a long plot history also hold more points.

### Slow frame rate / laggy dashboard

3D Plot is the only widget that renders a real 3D scene; swap it for a Plot or a Gauge where a full 3D view is not needed.

The dashboard redraws at 60 Hz by default. **UI Refresh Rate (Hz)** on the Settings dialog's plotting page accepts 1 to 240. A very high data rate still adds CPU load parsing and updating datasets between redraws.

## Getting More Help
docs.title: Troubleshooting#33

docs.body: Ask questions on [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/Serial-Studio/Serial-Studio/discussions). For a bug, search the [issues](https://github.com/Serial-Studio/Serial-Studio/issues) first, closed ones included, then [open a new one](https://github.com/Serial-Studio/Serial-Studio/issues/new) with the details listed under [Reporting Bugs Effectively](#reporting-bugs-effectively). [DeepWiki](https://deepwiki.com/Serial-Studio/Serial-Studio) answers questions from the repository, though its answers may differ from this manual. Pro license holders can email alex@serial-studio.com with their order email.
docs.title: Troubleshooting#34

docs.body:
## Reporting Bugs Effectively

Include these in an issue:

**System Information:**
- [ ] Serial Studio version and build. The toolbar's **About** button shows `Version 4.0.3 (abcdef1)`; click that line to copy the full build identity, commit included. A build compiled locally reads `local build` instead of a commit.
- [ ] Operating system and version
- [ ] How you installed (official binary, compiled from source, AppImage, etc.)

**Problem Description:**
- [ ] Clear description of the problem
- [ ] Steps to reproduce (numbered list)
- [ ] Expected behavior
- [ ] Actual behavior

**Additional Information:**
- [ ] Screenshots or screen recording (if applicable)
- [ ] Console output (copy from console panel)
- [ ] Sample project file (if project-specific)
- [ ] Sample data (a few frames or CSV file)
docs.title: Troubleshooting#35

docs.body:
**Example Good Bug Report:**

```text
## Problem
Dashboard widgets show "NaN" instead of values

## System
- Serial Studio v4.0.3 (a1b2c3d)
- Windows 11 Pro
- Official binary installer

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Connect Arduino Uno via USB (COM3)
2. Configure: Baud 115200, delimiter: \n
3. Load attached project file
4. Open dashboard

## Expected
Gauges should show temperature values (20-30 C)

## Actual
All gauges show "NaN"

## Additional Info
- Console shows the parser error text
- Attached: project.json, sample_data.csv
- Screenshot: screenshot.png
```

Use-Cases#0

docs.body:
The setups below start from that same line and show what changes when the link, the data or the dashboard gets bigger. Each one names its edition. They are sketches of working configurations, not validated or certified designs, and Serial Studio is not a medical device.

## Editions

UART, TCP/UDP, Bluetooth LE, the three operation modes, the Project Editor, frame parsers and CSV export are free. MQTT, Modbus, CAN Bus, OPC UA, Audio, Raw USB, HID, Process I/O, multi-device projects, output controls, MDF4, dataset transforms, computed datasets, Variables and the 3D Plot, Waterfall, Image View and Canvas widgets need Pro; WebSocket, HTTP and the API Server are free. The complete list is in [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md). The official binary offers a 14-day trial the first time you use a Pro feature, through a Yes/No prompt; registering the trial needs an internet connection. After it expires, the same prompt offers activation or purchase.
docs.title: Use-Cases#1

docs.body:
## Over serial (UART)

### Joint angles from a robot arm

A 6-DOF arm on an Arduino Mega prints `10.5,42.0,-3.2,88.1,0.0,12.7` (six joint angles) at 50 Hz. In Quick Plot, that is six plots, a Multi-Plot and a Data Grid with nothing to configure. To add an XY plot of the end-effector or bars with threshold colors, use **Save as Project** on the dashboard and add the widgets in the [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md); bar colors come from alarm bands on the dataset.

Edition: Free (UART, Quick Plot, Parse via Project File).

### Classroom weather station

Fifteen groups build an Arduino Uno with a DHT22 and a BMP180 and print temperature, humidity and pressure as comma-separated values. Everyone starts in Quick Plot. A group that wants gauges and labels switches to "Parse via Project File" and builds a project in the Project Editor; one project file serves every lab station. CSV export gives the data to Python or a spreadsheet for the write-up.
docs.title: Use-Cases#2

docs.body:
Edition: Free.

### Greenhouse with a binary sensor frame

An Arduino Mega packs eight soil-moisture readings, temperature, humidity and a light level into a binary frame. A [frame parser](Frame-Parser.md) in JavaScript converts the bytes to values, and the dashboard shows the moisture as a Bar widget and the climate as plots. Switching the irrigation relay from the dashboard needs [output controls](Output-Controls.md) (Pro) with a transmit function; without them, the firmware decides when the relay switches. The relay does not care who asked.

Edition: Free for the dashboard (UART, frame parser); Pro for output controls.
docs.title: Use-Cases#3

docs.body:
### Radio telemetry from a rocket, balloon or UAV

A 433 MHz or 900 MHz radio module on the ground station shows up as a serial port. The airborne side sends altitude, acceleration, battery voltage and GPS coordinates as lines of text. Serial Studio plots them, draws the GPS Map track, and logs everything to CSV for the recovery team. Values such as a predicted landing point or remaining flight time come from the firmware, or from a [computed dataset](Derived-Values.md#computed-dataset) (Pro) that combines other datasets.

Edition: Free; Pro for computed datasets.

## Over Bluetooth LE

### Mobile robot with an ESP32
docs.title: Use-Cases#4

docs.body:
An ESP32 notifies one BLE characteristic with a line such as `lat,lon,battery,ax,ay,az` at 20 Hz. Serial Studio connects as the BLE central, subscribes to that characteristic, and shows the position on a GPS Map, the battery as a Gauge and the IMU on the Accelerometer and Gyroscope widgets. See [Bluetooth LE](Drivers-Bluetooth-LE.md) for the firmware side. When the robot leaves BLE range, an ESP32 publishing the same values to an MQTT broker lets a Pro dashboard keep watching.

Edition: Free over BLE; Pro for the MQTT fallback.

### Gait insoles

An Arduino Nano 33 BLE in each shoe sends four force-sensor readings per insole. The dashboard overlays left and right on Multi-Plots and exports CSV for later analysis. Stride metrics are calculated by the firmware or after export.
docs.title: Use-Cases#5

docs.body:
Edition: Free (Bluetooth LE).

## Over TCP and UDP

### Race car and competition robot

A Raspberry Pi with a CAN hat reads the car's bus and forwards a text line per sample, over a Wi-Fi hotspot, to the pit-lane laptop. A competition robot's RoboRIO or Jetson sends JSON the same way. In the **Device Setup** panel, choose the Network driver; Serial Studio listens on a TCP or UDP socket; a frame parser maps each JSON field to a dataset, and the dashboard shows tire temperatures, brake pressure, PID terms or battery current beside each other.

Edition: Free (TCP or UDP, frame parser). The Pi does the CAN decoding; to decode CAN in Serial Studio itself, see [ECU signals from a DBC file](#ecu-signals-from-a-dbc-file).
docs.title: Use-Cases#6

docs.body:
### Software-defined radio spectrum

GNU Radio computes magnitudes from an RTL-SDR dongle and sends them as UDP packets. The FFT Plot shows the spectrum; the Waterfall widget (Pro) adds the time axis for repeaters and satellite passes.

Edition: Free (UDP) for the FFT Plot; Pro for Waterfall.

## MQTT

### Twenty sensors in a forest

Each ESP32 with a BME280 publishes a reading to an MQTT broker over Wi-Fi or 4G. In the **Device Setup** panel, choose the MQTT driver; Serial Studio subscribes with a topic filter such as `sensors/+/data` through the [MQTT subscriber](Drivers-MQTT.md). The bytes do not say which node sent them, so each node includes its own id in the payload. A frame parser reads the id and fills that node's dataset group; with 20 nodes the project holds 20 groups. GPS Map widgets mark the node positions, and CSV export feeds the seasonal analysis.
docs.title: Use-Cases#7

docs.body:
The same pattern covers a home energy monitor: an ESP32 with current sensors publishes to a Mosquitto broker on a Raspberry Pi, and a power figure (volts times amps) is a computed dataset. An accumulated kWh needs a Variables table that remembers the running total between frames, or the firmware can send it.

Edition: Pro (MQTT, computed datasets, Variables).

## Industrial buses

### Modbus PLC monitoring
docs.title: Use-Cases#8

docs.body: A line has several PLCs, and engineers need register values on one screen. Serial Studio polls as a Modbus master over Modbus TCP or Modbus RTU. In **Configure Register Groups…** you add one group per block of Holding Registers, Input Registers, Coils or Discrete Inputs, and each group can name its own slave address. Each poll produces a binary frame; set the source decoder to **Binary (Direct)** and use a frame parser to turn register bytes into datasets. See [Modbus](Drivers-Modbus.md). A water-quality probe with an RS485 output works the same way when it speaks Modbus RTU through a USB-RS485 adapter; if it prints text, use the UART driver instead.
docs.title: Use-Cases#9

docs.body:
Edition: Pro (Modbus).

### OPC UA tag browser

PLCs and gateways that already publish an OPC UA address space need no tag-list export. You enter `opc.tcp://host:port`, browse the address space and tick the tags to monitor, whole folders included, up to 2048 channels. Serial Studio generates the project from the selection and subscribes to the tags. Login is anonymous or username/password. See [OPC UA](Drivers-OPC-UA.md) for security policies and timestamps.

Edition: Pro (OPC UA).

## CAN and MDF4

### ECU signals from a DBC file

An ECU engineer imports a DBC file and the dashboard shows decoded signals by name, such as `Engine_RPM` and `Vehicle_Speed`, for every message ID at once. The adapter can be PEAK PCAN, SocketCAN on Linux, a Qt-supported Vector interface, or `virtualcan` for testing; CAN FD is available when the adapter supports it. Export the session to MDF4 for CANalyzer or CANape. See [CAN Bus](Drivers-CAN-Bus.md).
docs.title: Use-Cases#10

docs.body:
Edition: Pro (CAN Bus, DBC import, MDF4 export).

### Bluetooth OBD-II (ELM327) adapter

This is a different path from CAN Bus: pair it in the operating system so it appears as a COM port, connect with the free UART driver, and decode its AT-command replies in a frame parser.

Edition: Free (UART, frame parser).

### Replaying an MDF4 file

The **Open MDF4** toolbar button replays a `.mf4` file through the same pipeline as a live connection, at the original timing, with Play/Pause, frame stepping and a seek slider. A file recorded by Serial Studio replays with no setup. A file from another tool maps each channel group's data channels onto the loaded project's datasets in file order, so load a project whose datasets match the file's channel order. Playback shows one file at a time, and CSV and MDF4 export are off while a player is open. See [MDF4](MDF4.md).
docs.title: Use-Cases#11

docs.body:
Edition: Pro (MDF4 playback).

## Other Pro drivers and multi-device projects

### Simulation dashboard from a child process

A physics simulation prints `position,velocity,energy` to stdout. With the Process I/O driver in **Launch Process** mode, Serial Studio starts the program, you answer Yes to the launch-consent prompt, and the values plot live. **Named Pipe** mode reads from a FIFO instead; use Launch mode when the dashboard must write back to the process, for a parameter sweep. See [Process I/O](Drivers-Process-IO.md).

Edition: Pro (Process I/O).

### Gamepad plus robot feedback

The HID driver reads a USB gamepad's axes and buttons through hidapi. In a multi-device project, a second source receives the robot's IMU and motor values over BLE. Joystick axes become plots, buttons light up in an LED Panel, and one CSV export holds both sources for post-match review; its rows are sparse, with empty cells where a source had no sample.
docs.title: Use-Cases#12

docs.body:
Edition: Pro (HID, multi-device projects).

### Two drones on one dashboard

Drone A sends over a 900 MHz radio modem on UART, drone B over UDP on Wi-Fi. A multi-device project gives each its own source, parser and groups, so GPS, attitude and battery sit side by side. MDF4 export writes one file; each project group becomes a channel group named `SourceName / GroupName`. [Output controls](Output-Controls.md) in an Output Panel group per drone send commands: a slider whose transmit function builds `"THR " + value + "\r\n"`, a knob for yaw and a toggle for the camera. The throttle range, yaw range and command strings are example settings. A return-home command belongs on an Emergency Stop button style, which latches.
docs.title: Use-Cases#13

docs.body:
Edition: Pro (multi-device projects, output controls, MDF4 export).

### USB instruments beside serial sensors

Bench instruments that expose bulk USB endpoints but no serial port connect through the Raw USB driver (libusb). In a multi-device project they sit next to a serial-sensor source, and MDF4 export keeps both in one file.

Edition: Pro (Raw USB, multi-device projects, MDF4 export).

## More setups at a glance
docs.title: Use-Cases#14

docs.body:
| Setup | Link | What the dashboard shows | Edition |
|-------|------|--------------------------|---------|
| Pendulum lab with Arduino Nano and MPU6050 | UART | X/Y/Z acceleration plots, FFT Plot for the resonance peak | Free |
| Smart beehive: HX711 scale and DS18B20 on a LoRa node | LoRa gateway to serial | Weight and temperature trends | Free |
| Air-quality nodes: PMS5003 and GPS on an ESP32 | MQTT | Readings on a GPS Map | Pro (MQTT) |
| CNC spindle load and axis positions | Modbus RTU, or serial with a frame parser | Spindle RPM, load, X/Y/Z positions | Pro for Modbus; Free over serial |
| Single-sensor UART setups: conveyor encoder, MAX6675 reflow oven | UART | Belt speed and pulse count, or temperature against time with CSV for the process record | Free |
| EV battery pack: BMS cell voltages | UART | 96 cell voltages in a Bar widget, pack current and temperatures | Free |
| Antenna analyzer: NanoVNA | USB serial | SWR sweep plot; a Smith chart is a Canvas script you write, no template ships | Free; Pro for Canvas |
| APRS tracker: TNC with decoded packets | UART | Station positions on a GPS Map, text in the console | Free |
| Biosignals: AD8232 ECG, MAX30102 oximeter | UART or BLE | Waveform and FFT Plot; SpO2 and BPM computed by the firmware | Free |
| Solar array: INA219 on an ESP32 | UART or MQTT | Voltage, current, watts | Free; Pro for MQTT |
| Aquarium: pH, temperature and conductivity | UART | Gauges with alarm bands for out-of-range values | Free |
| HVAC ducts: DS18B20 on supply and return | Wi-Fi (TCP) | Supply, return and outdoor temperatures; the differential is a computed dataset | Free; Pro for computed datasets |
| Dyno: ELM327 OBD-II adapter | COM port via UART | RPM, throttle and coolant plots; an XY power curve needs both axes as datasets in the stream | Free |
docs.title: Use-Cases#15

docs.body:
## Custom visualizations (Canvas)

Canvas lets you draw a widget with a short JavaScript script, or start from a bundled template. In the [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md), click **Canvas** in the toolbar to add a Canvas group, add datasets, click **Edit Code**, then click **Template** in the code editor to pick one. The script defines `paint(ctx, w, h)` and, optionally, `onFrame()` once per dashboard tick; a 250 ms watchdog stops a call that does not return. Every Canvas entry below is Pro. See [Canvas Widget](Canvas-Widget.md) for the full list of templates.

### Phosphor-style oscilloscope
docs.title: Use-Cases#16

docs.body:
The built-in line plot has no persistence trace, no afterglow and no XY mode. The `Oscilloscope` template draws channels on a phosphor-green CRT background with a 10 x 8 graticule, a glow under each trace and a crisp line on top. The `XY scope (Lissajous)` template plots two synchronous channels against each other.

### Artificial horizon

A flat attitude indicator is simpler than the 3D Gyroscope widget. The `Artificial horizon` template binds two datasets, pitch and roll in degrees. Sky and ground rotate with roll and slide with pitch, a pitch ladder marks every 10°, and a fixed aircraft symbol stays in front. The source can be any stream that provides pitch and roll in degrees.
docs.title: Use-Cases#17

docs.body:
### Lab-equipment mimic

When the dashboard replaces an analog meter, operators should not relearn the panel. Start from the `Dial gauge` template, set the green, amber and red zone thresholds, and replace the face colors and tick marks. A smoothing filter in `onFrame()` makes the needle sweep instead of snapping to each new value.

### Audio VU meter and bargraphs

The `Audio VU meter` and `Bars with peak hold` templates draw segmented LED-style bars with peak markers: saturated segments are active, pastel segments are inactive, and a peak marker holds for a set interval before it decays. Pair them with the [Audio driver](Drivers-Audio.md) (Pro) to read a microphone or line input.
docs.title: Use-Cases#18

docs.body:
### Polar diagnostics for rotating machinery

The `Polar plot` template draws (angle, magnitude) pairs as rays on a polar grid with range rings and 30° spokes. Put it next to a Waterfall widget (Pro) for order-tracking spectra on the same dashboard.

## Starting your own

Print one line of numbers, run Quick Plot, and check that the values arrive. Then save the stream as a project, and add widgets, a frame parser or a different driver as the data needs them. The toolbar's **Examples** button downloads example projects from GitHub the first time you open it, so it needs an internet connection.
docs.title: Use-Cases#19

docs.body: To add a use case to this page, open a GitHub issue or send a pull request. For help with a setup, see the [FAQ](FAQ.md), [Troubleshooting](Troubleshooting.md) or [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/Serial-Studio/Serial-Studio/discussions).
docs.title: Use-Cases#20

docs.body:
# Variables (Pro)

Your Arduino prints a raw ADC count, three datasets need the same volts-per-count slope, and you would rather not paste that number into three scripts. Variables, a Pro feature of the Project Editor (Project Editor > Variables), hold it once, in a table saved with the project. A variable has a name and a default value, and stores a number or a string:

| Table `calibration` | Permissions | Default |
|---------------------|-------------|---------|
| `slope`             | Read-Only   | `0.01`  |

A **transform** is a small Lua or JavaScript function attached to a dataset in the Project Editor. It receives the parsed value and returns the value to display; see [Dataset Value Transforms](Dataset-Transforms.md). This one multiplies every value by the slope:
docs.title: Variables#0
Variables#1

docs.body:
**Edition.** Creating, duplicating or importing a table, and adding a variable, need a Pro license or an active trial. So does connecting with a project that defines a table. The first time you use a Pro feature without a license, Serial Studio asks whether to start the Pro trial (it needs an internet connection to register); declining leaves the feature locked, and once a trial has ended the prompt offers activation or purchase instead. Deleting the table is free and lets the project connect again. See [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md#dataset-transforms-variables-and-custom-workspaces).

## Defining tables in the Project Editor
docs.title: Variables#2

docs.body:
Variables (Pro), Project Editor > Variables. **Add Variables Table** and **Add Variable** need a Pro license or trial (see Edition above).

1. Open the project in the Project Editor.
2. Select the **Variables** node in the tree.
3. Click **Add Variables Table** and give it a name, for example `calibration` or `runtime`.
4. Select the table and click **Add Variable**. Type a name; the new variable is Read/Write with a default of `0`. Then set:
docs.title: Variables#3

docs.body:
| Field             | Accepts                                    | Effect                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------|--------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Variable Name** | text; a duplicate gets a `_2` suffix       | The name transforms pass to `tableGet()` and `tableSet()`.                                                                  |
| **Permissions**   | Read-Only, Read/Write                      | Read-Only is a constant; Read/Write is a computed variable ([Variable types](#variable-types)).                                                     |
| **Default Value** | a number or a string                       | The value at project load. A constant keeps it all session; a computed variable starts there and holds what transforms write. |
docs.title: Variables#4

docs.body:
Tables are saved with the project file, so anyone who opens it gets the same tables and defaults.

The table toolbar also has **Insert Constant**, which adds a physical constant (speed of light, standard gravity, gas constants) as a Read-Only variable, and **Import** and **Export**, which move a table to and from CSV. The file starts with the header `name,permissions,value`. Permissions accepts `read-only` or `read-write` (also `read/write`, `rw`, `computed`). Import needs Pro.

The same edits are scriptable: the `project.dataTable.*` commands add, rename and delete tables and variables, and read or write a variable's live runtime value from outside a transform. See the [API Reference](API-Reference.md#data-table-commands-13).
docs.title: Variables#5

docs.body:
### Naming rules

- Table and variable names are case-sensitive and free-form.
- Runs of whitespace collapse to one space, so a name typed with two spaces does not match the string in your script. Short ASCII names without spaces keep scripts readable.
- A duplicate table name gets a numeric suffix (`Calibration 2`); a duplicate variable name gets `_2`.
- A new table's name has any `/` removed, because `/` joins a folder to a table in its full path.
- Do not name a table `__datasets__`; the name belongs to the system table.

## Variable types

A variable is one of two types, picked with the **Permissions** field. This manual calls them a **constant** (Read-Only) and a **computed variable** (Read/Write); the editor only shows Read-Only and Read/Write, and a computed variable has nothing to do with a [computed dataset](Dataset-Transforms.md#computed-datasets).
docs.title: Variables#6

docs.body:
A constant is written at project load and is fixed for the session. It is for configuration: sensor slopes, offsets, thresholds, full-scale ranges. `tableSet()` cannot modify it.

A computed variable behaves like ordinary memory. Once a transform writes a value it stays until the next write, which matches how state lives in embedded systems: filter states, integrators, edge counters, latched flags. To start each frame from a known value, write it with `tableSet()` at the top of an early transform.

## The transform API

Four functions read and write variables. Lua and JavaScript have the same names and semantics; a missing value is `nil` in Lua and `undefined` in JavaScript. For transforms that touch the same variables on every value, `tableGetH` and `tableSetH` resolve a name once to a handle; see [Fast table access with handles](SerialStudio-SDK.md#handles-the-fast-path-for-table-heavy-parsers).
docs.title: Variables#7

docs.body:
| Function                             | Arguments                                   | Returns                                                         |
|--------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------|
| `tableGet(table, variable)`          | table name, variable name                   | the value, or nil/undefined if the variable doesn't exist       |
| `tableSet(table, variable, value)`   | table name, variable name, number or string | nothing; ignored if the variable is a constant or doesn't exist |
| `datasetGetRaw(uniqueId \| alias)`   | integer uniqueId or alias string            | the value, or nil/undefined for an unknown dataset              |
| `datasetGetFinal(uniqueId \| alias)` | integer uniqueId or alias string            | the value, or nil/undefined for an unknown dataset              |
docs.title: Variables#8

docs.body:
A `uniqueId` is the integer shown next to each dataset in the Project Editor tree; see the [Dataset Identity Model](Identity-Model.md).

- A table filed in a folder is addressed by its full path: `tableGet("sensors/calibration", "slope")`.
- A string argument to `datasetGetRaw` and `datasetGetFinal` is always an alias, even if it looks like a number, so `datasetGetFinal("10")` looks for an alias named `10`.
- An unknown ID, alias or variable returns nil and logs a warning once.

Publish a value from one transform and consume it in another:

```lua
-- Earlier dataset writes a shared value
function transform(value)
  tableSet("runtime", "pack_current", value)
  return value
end
```
docs.title: Variables#9

docs.body:
```lua
-- Later dataset reads it
function transform(value)
  local i = tableGet("runtime", "pack_current")
  return value * i
end
```

See [Dataset Value Transforms](Dataset-Transforms.md#table-api) for the per-language reference, including the JavaScript equivalents.

## Processing order and visibility

A dataset sees the final values of the datasets listed above it in the Project Editor tree: earlier groups first, then earlier datasets inside the same group. For everything below it, it sees whatever the previous frame left behind. If dataset B depends on dataset A, list A before B.

Each dataset is processed in one pass before the next: its raw value is written to the system table, its transform runs, and its final value is written. So `datasetGetRaw(uid)` is current only for the running dataset and those above it. Computed variables written by earlier transforms are visible to later ones in the same frame and on every later frame, until the next write.
docs.title: Variables#10

docs.body:
## The system table

Serial Studio builds one table called `__datasets__` from your project. You don't define it. The Project Editor shows it as a read-only **Dataset Values** node under Variables, listing each dataset's unique ID and its `datasetGetFinal()` access code. It mirrors every dataset as two variables:

| Variable           | Contents                                                             |
|--------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `raw:<uniqueId>`   | Raw value from the frame parser, before the dataset's transform runs |
| `final:<uniqueId>` | Final value after the dataset's transform has run                    |
docs.title: Variables#11

docs.body:
A dataset with a **Script Alias** is also exposed as `raw:<alias>` and `final:<alias>`. Outside a transform, read it with `tableGet("__datasets__", "final:ATAM1-CH1")`; inside one, use `datasetGetFinal("ATAM1-CH1")`, which returns the same value.

## Common use cases

### Sensor calibration constants

Several datasets share one calibration, and every firmware revision, lab recalibration or field swap would otherwise mean editing each transform by hand. Store the calibration in constants, so a recalibration is one edit in the Project Editor. The same pattern covers per-deployment unit factors such as `m_to_ft` or `counts_per_rev`. This recipe is also the shipped calibration transform template: open the transform editor's template picker and start there.
docs.title: Variables#12

docs.body:
Table `calibration`:

| Variable | Permissions | Default | Purpose              |
|----------|-------------|---------|----------------------|
| `slope`  | Read-Only   | `0.01`  | V per ADC count      |
| `offset` | Read-Only   | `0.0`   | Zero-offset in volts |

```lua
function transform(value)
  local slope  = tableGet("calibration", "slope")
  local offset = tableGet("calibration", "offset")
  return slope * value + offset
end
```

### Thresholds and alarm limits

Store warning and critical levels in constants and let a transform return a status code (0 ok, 1 warning, 2 critical) for you to plot or display. For coloring a widget by level, see [Alarm bands](Widget-Reference.md#alarm-bands).
docs.title: Variables#13

docs.body:
Table `limits`:

| Variable  | Permissions | Default |
|-----------|-------------|---------|
| `warn_lo` | Read-Only   | `10`    |
| `warn_hi` | Read-Only   | `80`    |
| `crit_lo` | Read-Only   | `0`     |
| `crit_hi` | Read-Only   | `95`    |

```lua
function transform(value)
  local wl = tableGet("limits", "warn_lo")
  local wh = tableGet("limits", "warn_hi")
  local cl = tableGet("limits", "crit_lo")
  local ch = tableGet("limits", "crit_hi")
  if value <= cl or value >= ch then return 2  -- critical
  elseif value <= wl or value >= wh then return 1  -- warning
  else return 0 end  -- ok
end
```
docs.title: Variables#14

docs.body:
Pair this with a [computed dataset](Dataset-Transforms.md#computed-datasets) so the status gets its own channel without consuming a frame index.

### Derived quantities from other datasets

To compute power from voltage and current, create a computed dataset whose transform reads both channels with `datasetGetFinal()`. Both source datasets must be listed above it in the Project Editor tree (see [Processing order and visibility](#processing-order-and-visibility)). Here voltage has unique ID 10 and current has 11:

```lua
function transform(value)
  local v = datasetGetFinal(10)
  local i = datasetGetFinal(11)
  if v == nil or i == nil then return 0 end
  return v * i
end
```
docs.title: Variables#15

docs.body:
If the source datasets have aliases, the transform reads them by name, which stays readable in a large project: `datasetGetFinal("voltage")` and `datasetGetFinal("current")`. The same shape fits IMU acceleration magnitude, RMS of three phase currents and torque times angular velocity.

### Cross-dataset scratch pad

When two transforms need the output of an expensive calculation (an FFT peak, a filtered value, a CRC), compute it once in an earlier dataset, publish it to a computed variable and read it from the later datasets. The writing dataset must be listed above the readers. The value persists, so readers see what the earlier transform last wrote, in this frame or carried over from the previous one.
docs.title: Variables#16

docs.body:
The same pattern carries a "data valid" flag: one transform sets `probe_ok` to 0 or 1 after a range check, the others branch on it, and one out-of-range channel taints several derived channels. Declare `probe_ok` with a default of `1`, or every reader sees invalid data until the probe's transform has run once.

Table `runtime`:

| Variable     | Permissions | Default |
|--------------|-------------|---------|
| `filtered_v` | Read/Write  | `0`     |

A variable always reads as its default before the first write, never as nil. Seed on `info.frameNumber == 1`, not on a nil test. `info.frameNumber` counts frames per source, so in a multi-source project seed a shared variable from one source only.
docs.title: Variables#17

docs.body:
```lua
-- Earlier dataset: compute and publish
function transform(value, info)
  local f = tableGet("runtime", "filtered_v")
  if info.frameNumber == 1 then f = value end
  local smoothed = 0.9 * f + 0.1 * value
  tableSet("runtime", "filtered_v", smoothed)
  return smoothed
end
```

```lua
-- Later dataset: consume without recomputing
function transform(value)
  return value - tableGet("runtime", "filtered_v")
end
```

### Tunable filters and cross-frame state

Put the knob (cutoff, alpha, window size) in a constant and the filter's running state in a computed variable. Configuration stays separate from state, and you re-tune the filter without touching its code. The same split serves integrators, derivatives, edge counters, peak detectors and latched alarms, because a computed variable keeps its value between frames.
docs.title: Variables#18

docs.body:
An exponential moving average, with `ema_alpha` Read-Only (default `0.1`) and `ema_state` Read/Write in table `filters`:

```lua
function transform(value, info)
  local alpha = tableGet("filters", "ema_alpha")
  local ema   = tableGet("filters", "ema_state")
  if info.frameNumber == 1 then ema = value end
  ema = alpha * value + (1 - alpha) * ema
  tableSet("filters", "ema_state", ema)
  return ema
end
```

A discrete-time derivative `dT/dt` of the dataset with unique ID 2 (the temperature), using `info.timestampMs` and `info.frameNumber`, which restarts at 1 after a disconnect (see [Dataset Value Transforms](Dataset-Transforms.md)). Table `runtime` holds `last_temp` and `last_t_ms`, both Read/Write with default `0`:
docs.title: Variables#19

docs.body:
```lua
function transform(_, info)
  local T = datasetGetFinal(2)
  if T == nil then return 0 end

local prevT  = tableGet("runtime", "last_temp")
  local prevTs = tableGet("runtime", "last_t_ms")

tableSet("runtime", "last_temp", T)
  tableSet("runtime", "last_t_ms", info.timestampMs)

if info.frameNumber == 1 then return 0 end
  local dt = info.timestampMs - prevTs
  if dt <= 0 then return 0 end
  return (T - prevT) / (dt / 1000)
end
```

## Rules and limitations
docs.title: Variables#20

docs.body:
1. `tableSet()` on a constant is ignored and Serial Studio logs a `[DataTableStore]` warning to the application log. Constants are frozen at project load.
2. A variable holds one number or one string, such as a device serial number. For a vector, use several variables or several datasets.
3. A Variables table is not a settings dialog. For a knob that changes while you watch the data, use an Output widget.
4. Tables are shared across all sources in a project. Each source processes its frames on its own, so a transform reading a value another source writes gets the latest write, with no ordering guarantee between sources.
5. Variables were called Data Tables before the rename. The API namespace is still `project.dataTable.*` and the project file still stores them under the `registers` key.
docs.title: Variables#21

docs.body:
## See also

- [Dataset Value Transforms](Dataset-Transforms.md): how to write the `transform(value)` function and call the table API.
- [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md): where tables are defined.
- [Data Flow](Data-Flow.md): where transforms and tables sit in the overall pipeline.
- [Frame Parser Scripting](Frame-Parser.md): `parse(frame)` produces the raw values that transforms consume.
- [API Reference](API-Reference.md#data-table-commands-13): the `project.dataTable.*` commands.
