# Widget Extension Development

## Table of Contents

- [Overview](#overview)
- [Package Structure](#package-structure)
- [The Widget QML File](#the-widget-qml-file)
- [Installing and Testing](#installing-and-testing)
- [Trust Model](#trust-model)
- [info.json Reference](#infojson-reference)
- [ExtensionDataModel Reference](#extensiondatamodel-reference)
- [Configuration Settings](#configuration-settings)
- [When a Package Fails to Load](#when-a-package-fails-to-load)
- [Distribution](#distribution)

## Overview

You have a tank level on dataset 3 and want a horizontal bar the built-in widgets do not offer. A
widget extension is how you add it without rebuilding Serial Studio: a JSON description and one QML
file (Qt's UI language, so you need to read basic QML). If you only want to use a widget someone
else wrote, see [Extensions](Extensions.md).
docs.title: Widget-Extension-Development#0

docs.body:
A dataset is one value from your device's frames, such as the tank level; a group is a set of
related datasets. You define both in the [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md).

Once installed, the widget appears in the Project Editor's widget list for a dataset or a group,
whichever the package declares, and it behaves like a built-in: you can place it in workspaces,
freeze it, and pop it out.

**Compass** and **Data Grid** are included with Serial Studio and use this same format, so they make good
working examples. They are bundled, so they skip the consent prompt described in
[Trust Model](#trust-model).
docs.title: Widget-Extension-Development#1

docs.body:
Widget extensions are not a Pro feature; GPL and commercial builds load them alike.

A widget extension runs with the same privileges as Serial Studio itself and there is no sandbox.
Read [Trust Model](#trust-model) before installing a package you did not write.

## Package Structure

A package is a folder with two files:

```text
com.example.level-bar/
  info.json
  LevelBar.qml
```

The same package, with a working `config` block and comments in the QML, ships in the source tree
under
[`examples/widget-extension/`](https://github.com/Serial-Studio/Serial-Studio/tree/master/examples/widget-extension)
(`info.json`, `LevelBar.qml`, `README.md`).
docs.title: Widget-Extension-Development#2

docs.body:
Installed packages live in the workspace folder, outside the application bundle, so updating or
moving Serial Studio leaves them installed. With the default workspace folder, that is:

- macOS and Linux: `~/Documents/Serial Studio/Extensions/widget/com.example.level-bar/`
- Windows: `Documents\Serial Studio\Extensions\widget\com.example.level-bar\`

Create the folders if they do not exist yet. The workspace folder is the one set in Serial Studio's
settings. `info.json` is described in [info.json Reference](#infojson-reference); the QML file is
the next section.

## The Widget QML File

This is a complete `LevelBar.qml`. Save it next to the `info.json` from
[info.json Reference](#infojson-reference) and the two files are an installable package. It draws a bar scaled between the dataset's declared minimum
and maximum, with the title above it:
docs.title: Widget-Extension-Development#3

docs.body:
```qml
import QtQuick
import QtQuick.Controls
import SerialStudio

Item {
  id: root

required property color color
  required property string widgetId
  required property var windowRoot
  required property ExtensionDataModel model

readonly property real span: Math.max(model.maxValue - model.minValue, 1)
  readonly property real fill: Math.max(0, Math.min(1, (model.value - model.minValue) / span))

Column {
    anchors.fill: parent
    anchors.margins: 8
    spacing: 6

Label {
      text: model.title + ": " + model.text
      color: root.color
      width: parent.width
      elide: Text.ElideRight
    }
docs.title: Widget-Extension-Development#4

docs.body:
Rectangle {
      width: parent.width
      height: 24
      color: "#20000000"
      border.color: root.color

Rectangle {
        height: parent.height
        color: root.color
        width: parent.width * root.fill
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Pick it for the tank dataset and the bar fills as the level rises.

The entry file declares four required properties, and Serial Studio sets all four when it creates
the widget:

| Property | What it carries |
|----------|-----------------|
| `model` | The live data; see [ExtensionDataModel Reference](#extensiondatamodel-reference). |
| `color` | The dashboard's accent colour for this widget. |
| `windowRoot` | The window the widget is inside, for dialogs and pop-ups. |
| `widgetId` | The widget's persistence key. |
docs.title: Widget-Extension-Development#5

docs.body:
You do not poll or subscribe: the `model` properties update by themselves, so any binding that
reads them redraws.

**Import surface.** A package may import `QtQuick`, `QtQuick.Controls`, and `SerialStudio`.
Serial Studio's own QML components are compiled into the application and cannot be imported from a
package folder; ship anything else you need inside your package.

## Installing and Testing
docs.title: Widget-Extension-Development#6

docs.body:
1. Copy the package folder into the `Extensions/widget/` folder of your workspace (see
   [Package Structure](#package-structure) for the path).
2. Restart Serial Studio, or change the workspace folder, so the catalog is rescanned. Do the same
   after every edit to the QML or `info.json`. Installing a package through the extension manager
   (see [Extensions](Extensions.md)) rescans on its own.
3. Open the project that has your tank level dataset, select the dataset in the Project Editor, and
   pick **Level Bar** from its **Widget** list. A group-scope package appears in a group's list
   instead.
4. Connect the device, or play a CSV, to see the widget move. The first time the package runs, a
   consent dialog appears; choose Allow. It asks before running your own code, which is polite if
   slightly redundant.
docs.title: Widget-Extension-Development#7

docs.body:
Everything after this section is lookup. You can stop here for a first widget.

## Trust Model

**A widget extension runs inside Serial Studio with the same privileges as Serial Studio itself.**
Its QML shares the application's QML engine, so it can read your files and use the network. There
is no sandbox and no permission list.

Serial Studio hides its internal QML names (the `Cpp_*` ones) from installed packages, but the
engine is shared, so that prevents mistakes, not malice.
docs.title: Widget-Extension-Development#8

docs.body:
What Serial Studio does instead is ask. Before a package you installed runs for the first time, a
dialog states what it is, who published it, where it lives on disk, and that it runs with the
application's privileges. Declining leaves the package installed and inert; its tile on the
dashboard says "This widget is installed but has not been allowed to run." and offers a **Review
and Allow…** button. The decision is remembered per package version, so an update asks again.
Packages bundled with the application skip the dialog.

Install widget packages the way you would install any program: from a source you trust.
docs.title: Widget-Extension-Development#9

docs.body:
## info.json Reference

```json
{
  "id": "com.example.level-bar",
  "type": "widget",
  "title": "Level Bar",
  "description": "A horizontal level bar for a single numeric dataset.",
  "author": "Your Name",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "license": "MIT",
  "category": "Instruments",
  "files": ["info.json", "LevelBar.qml"],
  "widget": {
    "apiVersion": "1.0",
    "hostCompat": ">=1.0 <2.0",
    "scope": "dataset",
    "qml": "LevelBar.qml",
    "icon": "widgets/bar",
    "readsStringValues": false,
    "accepts": {
      "datasets": { "min": 1, "max": 1 },
      "value": "numeric"
    },
    "defaultSize": { "width": 360, "height": 120 },
    "config": [],
    "dependencies": { "required": [], "optional": [] },
    "experimental": false
  }
}
```
docs.title: Widget-Extension-Development#10

docs.body:
The keys outside the `widget` block are the standard extension metadata described in
[Extensions](Extensions.md). A widget manifest is rejected unless it has a non-empty `id` and
`title`, `"type": "widget"`, and a `widget` block. The `widget` block is specific to this type:
docs.title: Widget-Extension-Development#11

docs.body:
| Key | Required | Description |
|-----|----------|-------------|
| `apiVersion` | No | Manifest format the package was written against. A package declaring a newer major version than the host, or a version that does not parse, is not loaded. The host's widget API version is 1.0. |
| `hostCompat` | No | Host widget-API range the package supports, as space-separated comparators (`">=1.0 <2.0"`). Omitted or `"*"` means any version. |
| `scope` | No | `"dataset"` (default) or `"group"`. Any other value is treated as `"dataset"`. Decides which Project Editor widget list offers the package. |
| `qml` | Yes | The entry file, relative to the package folder. It may not point outside the folder. |
| `icon` | No | Either a built-in icon identifier (`"widgets/bar"`) or a file inside the package (`"icon.svg"`). A file path that points outside the package is ignored and the built-in fallback icon is used. |
| `accepts` | No | `datasets.min` (default 1) and `datasets.max` (default unlimited) bound the number of datasets; a `max` below `min` is raised to `min`. A missing or negative `max` means unlimited; a negative `min` is treated as 0. `value` is `"numeric"`, `"string"`, or `"any"` (the default). A dataset or group that does not match is not offered the widget. |
| `readsStringValues` | No | Set `true` when the widget renders text values rather than numbers. Serial Studio only pushes string values to widgets that ask for them. |
| `defaultSize` | No | Width and height of the pop-out window, in pixels. Defaults to 400 x 300; each axis is clamped to 48-8192. |
| `config` | No | Declared settings, at most 128; see [Configuration Settings](#configuration-settings). |
| `dependencies` | No | Other extension packages this one needs, at most 64. A missing **required** dependency stops the widget from loading and is reported; a missing optional one is only reported. |
| `experimental` | No | Marks the package as work in progress. |
| `replaces` | No | Reserved for packages bundled with Serial Studio. Any other package that declares it is refused. |
docs.title: Widget-Extension-Development#12

docs.body:
The `id` is also the value stored in a project's group or dataset `widget` field, so keep it
stable across versions. Use a reverse-domain identifier. These identifiers of built-in widgets are
reserved and rejected: `datagrid`, `map`, `gps`, `gyro`, `gyroscope`, `multiplot`,
`accelerometer`, `plot3d`, `image`, `painter`, `webview`, `barpanel`, `terminal`, `clock`,
`stopwatch`, `notification-log`, `led-panel`, `ledpanel`, `bar`, `gauge`, `compass`, and `meter`. A package that claims one is refused in every build, and a package can never replace or
unlock a Pro widget.

## ExtensionDataModel Reference
docs.title: Widget-Extension-Development#13

docs.body:
The model republishes what the dashboard already resolved, on the dashboard's own update tick, so
it updates at the dashboard's rate rather than once per frame. A package never touches an
application object to read data. Most widgets need only `title`, `value`, `text`, `units`,
`minValue` and `maxValue`; the rest of the table is for the cases that need it.
docs.title: Widget-Extension-Development#14

docs.body:
| Property | Type | Description |
|----------|------|-------------|
| `title` | string | Display title of the dataset or group, including a user's rename. |
| `value` | double | Numeric value of the dataset (the first dataset for a group). |
| `text` | string | The same value formatted the way the dashboard formats it: the dataset's label when one matches, otherwise the number with its units. |
| `label` | string | The dataset's value label for the current value, or empty when the dataset has no label for it. `value` keeps the number. |
| `stringValue` | string | The raw value as text. |
| `units` | string | Declared units. |
| `isNumeric` | bool | Whether the current value parsed as a number. |
| `minValue`, `maxValue` | double | Declared display range. |
| `decimalPoints`, `displayFormat` | int, string | Declared formatting. |
| `alarmsDefined`, `alarmTriggered`, `alarmSeverity` | bool, bool, int | Alarm-band state. |
| `datasetCount` | int | Number of datasets behind the widget. |
| `datasets` | model | Per-dataset rows for group-scope widgets; the roles are listed below. |
| `groupId`, `sourceId`, `uniqueId` | int | Identity of the entity the widget renders. |
| `groupScope` | bool | True for a group-scope package. |
| `extensionId` | string | The package's own identifier. |
| `config` | map | Current values of the declared settings. |
| `paused` | bool | Writable. While true, the model stops publishing new values. A package sets it to freeze its own display; the bundled Data Grid does. |
docs.title: Widget-Extension-Development#15

docs.body:
The `datasets` model exposes one row per dataset with these roles:

| Role | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `title`, `text`, `label` | Display title, formatted value, and value label, as above. |
| `value`, `numericValue` | The dataset's value; use `numericValue` when you need the number. |
| `isNumeric`, `units`, `minValue`, `maxValue`, `decimalPoints`, `displayFormat` | Same meaning as the model properties of the same name. |
| `uniqueId`, `index` | Identity and position of the dataset. |
| `alarmsDefined`, `alarmSeverity` | Alarm-band state. |
| `widgets` | The other dashboard widgets showing the same dataset, as `{ windowId, icon, title }` maps. |
docs.title: Widget-Extension-Development#16

docs.body:
The model emits `updated()` when a value changes, and QML property bindings pick that up.

## Configuration Settings

A widget extension declares user-editable settings in the `widget.config` array of its `info.json`,
and Serial Studio renders the settings form. You write no UI:

```json
"config": [
  { "id": "barColor", "type": "choice", "label": "Bar colour",
    "default": "green", "options": ["green", "amber", "red"] },
  { "id": "showValue", "type": "bool", "label": "Show numeric value", "default": true },
  { "id": "smoothing", "type": "double", "label": "Smoothing",
    "default": 0.25, "min": 0, "max": 1 }
]
```
docs.title: Widget-Extension-Development#17

docs.body:
Each entry takes these keys:

| Key | Required | Description |
|-----|----------|-------------|
| `id` | Yes | The name you read the value by. |
| `type` | Yes | `bool`, `int`, `double`, `string`, or `choice`. |
| `label` | No | Text shown in the form. Defaults to the `id`. |
| `description` | No | Longer explanation of the setting. |
| `default` | No | The initial value. |
| `min`, `max` | No | Bounds for numeric settings. |
| `options` | For `choice` | The list of allowed values. It may not be empty. |

An entry with no `id`, an unsupported `type`, or a `choice` without options is reported as "Widget
extension declares an unusable setting".
docs.title: Widget-Extension-Development#18

docs.body:
Read a value with `model.config["barColor"]` and write one with
`model.setConfigValue("barColor", "amber")`.

Values are stored per project, next to the rest of the per-widget settings, and are saved with the
project file. Users reach the form from the widget's caption menu (**Widget Settings…**) on the
dashboard, or, for a dataset-scope widget, from the **Widget Settings** section of the dataset form in the
Project Editor. A group-scope widget's settings are reached from the caption menu. The caption
menu entry is hidden when a package declares no settings.

## When a Package Fails to Load

A package that cannot render never disappears silently. The widget slot shows a placeholder
with the cause and an **Open Problem Center** button, and the [Problem Center](Problem-Center.md)
lists a matching entry under these titles:
docs.title: Widget-Extension-Development#19

docs.body:
| Problem Center title | Cause |
|----------------------|-------|
| Widget extension manifest cannot be read | The `info.json` file could not be opened. |
| Widget extension manifest is not valid JSON | The manifest could not be parsed. |
| Widget extension manifest is not usable | The manifest is missing `id`, `title`, `"type": "widget"`, or the `widget` block. |
| Widget extension declares an unusable setting | A `config` entry has no `id`, an unsupported `type`, or an empty `choice` list. |
| Widget extension uses a reserved identifier | The package `id` is a built-in widget identifier. |
| Widget extension may not replace a built-in widget | A package that is not bundled declares `replaces`, a key reserved for bundled packages. |
| Widget extension needs a newer manifest format | `apiVersion` does not parse, or its major version is newer than the host's. |
| Widget extension is not compatible with this version | `hostCompat` excludes this build. |
| Widget extension has no usable QML file | The declared entry is missing, or points outside the package. |
| Widget extension is already registered | Another package with the same `id` is already loaded, so this copy is ignored. |
| Widget extension is missing a required extension | A required dependency is not installed, or its version is out of range. |
| Widget extension is missing an optional extension | An optional dependency is not installed. The widget still loads. |
| Widget extension failed to load | The QML did not compile, or errored while being created. The message carries the QML error. |
docs.title: Widget-Extension-Development#20

docs.body:
Two causes show only on the placeholder tile. "The package is not installed, or has not been
allowed to run." means a project names a package that is missing or not yet allowed on this
machine. "This widget is installed but has not been allowed to run." comes with a **Review and
Allow…** button, which reopens the consent dialog.

## Distribution

Widget packages are hosted and installed exactly like every other extension type: add
`widget/<id>/info.json` to a repository `manifest.json` and point the extension manager at it. See
[Extensions](Extensions.md) for repository layout, hosting, and per-platform files.
docs.title: Widget-Extension-Development#21
Widget-Extension-Development#22

docs.body:
# Widget reference

## Overview

Your board prints `21.5,48` once a second. In the [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md) each value becomes a **dataset**, and datasets live in a **group**. A dataset shows one value and a group shows several together. To give the first dataset a gauge, select it in the Project Editor and set its **Widget** to Gauge, with a range. The project file stores that as the JSON below. You never have to edit it by hand, and the keys on this page are project-file keys.

```json
{ "title": "Temperature", "units": "C", "widget": "gauge", "widgetMin": 0, "widgetMax": 100 }
```
docs.title: Widget-Reference#0

docs.body:
The gauge sweeps to 21.5 on a 0 to 100 dial, with C beneath it.

Widgets come in three kinds:

- **Group widgets** display the datasets of one group, such as a GPS map or a data grid. Choose the widget type when you add the group with **Add Group**.
- **Dataset widgets** display a single value: Plot, FFT Plot, Waterfall (Pro), Bar, Gauge, Compass, Meter. Click **Plot**, **FFT Plot** or **Waterfall** on the dataset toolbar in the Project Editor. Bar, Gauge, Compass and Meter are chosen in the dataset's **Widget** setting.
- **Utility widgets** (Clock, Stopwatch, Terminal) belong to no group. Turn them on from the dashboard taskbar or the Start menu.
docs.title: Widget-Reference#1

docs.body:
New to Serial Studio? [Getting Started](Getting-Started.md) takes you from a first connection to a first dashboard.

## Picking the right widget

For a single number from your Arduino, start with [Plot](#plot); add a [Gauge](#gauge) once you know the range. Group widgets need several datasets in one group.
docs.title: Widget-Reference#2

docs.body:
| Data type                                                                     | Recommended widget         |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------|
| Temperature                                                                   | [Gauge](#gauge), [Plot](#plot), or [Bar](#bar) |
| Pressure, voltage, signal level                                               | Plot, Gauge, [Meter](#meter), or Bar |
| Several related signals overlaid on one chart                                 | [Multi-Plot](#multi-plot) (group) |
| GPS coordinates                                                               | [GPS Map](#gps-map) (group) |
| Acceleration (X, Y, Z)                                                        | [Accelerometer](#accelerometer) (group) |
| Orientation angles (yaw, pitch, roll); for angular rate (deg/s) see Gyroscope | [Gyroscope](#gyroscope) (group) |
| Heading or bearing                                                            | [Compass](#compass)        |
| Audio or vibration frequency                                                  | [FFT Plot](#fft-plot)      |
| Time-frequency / spectrogram                                                  | [Waterfall](#waterfall-pro) (Pro) |
| Boolean status flags                                                          | [LED Panel](#led-panel) (group) |
| Many related channels, color by severity                                      | [Bar Panel](#bar-panel) (group) |
| Mixed numeric and text values                                                 | [Data Grid](#data-grid) (group) |
| 3D trajectory or position                                                     | [3D Plot](#3d-plot-pro) (group, Pro) |
| Live camera or image stream                                                   | [Image View](#image-view-pro) (group, Pro) |
| Custom instrument mimic or layout no widget covers                            | [Canvas](#canvas-pro) (group, Pro) |
| Embedded web page / map / 3D model                                            | [Web View](#web-view) (group) |
| Wall-clock time / session timestamp                                           | [Clock](#clock) (utility)  |
| Manual elapsed-time / lap timing                                              | [Stopwatch](#stopwatch) (utility) |
| Raw text stream, typing to the device                                         | [Terminal](#terminal) (utility) |
docs.title: Widget-Reference#3

docs.body:
## Group widgets

### Data Grid

- Widget key: `"datagrid"`.
- Displays all datasets in a tabular format with titles, values, and units.
- Best for: overview of multiple channels, status monitoring.
- Configuration: none required beyond adding datasets to the group.
- Pause freezes the grid. Resume shows the current values immediately and discards what arrived while paused.

### Bar Panel
docs.title: Widget-Reference#4

docs.body:
- Widget key: `"barpanel"`.
- One labeled bar per dataset in the group: title, alarm-band-zoned track, live value.
- Alarm bands are always drawn in full as muted zones on each track; the fill takes the active band's color (green while normal, yellow/red as the value crosses band edges).
- **Bar Style** (group key `barPanelStyle`: empty = Auto, `horizontal`, or `vertical`) in the Project Editor: Auto (default, picks by panel shape), Horizontal (labeled rows), or Vertical (rake-style columns).
- Datasets with **Hold Min/Max Markers** enabled show tick marks at the lowest and highest values observed since the last data reset.
- Best for: monitoring many related channels at a glance (temperatures, pressures, EGT rakes) where color should mean severity and nothing else.
- Configuration: set `widgetMin`/`widgetMax` per dataset for the track range; define alarm bands for severity coloring.
docs.title: Widget-Reference#5

docs.body:
### Multi-Plot

- Widget key: `"multiplot"`.
- Overlays multiple dataset curves on shared axes, with per-curve visibility toggles and an auto-scaling Y-axis.
- Best for: comparing related signals (for example a 3-axis accelerometer over time).
- Configuration: switch **Plot** on for each dataset in the group (project-file key `graph: true`).

### GPS Map

- Widget key: `"map"` (the Project Editor writes this for new GPS Map groups; `"gps"` is also accepted).
- Tile-based map that plots the trajectory path and shows latitude, longitude, and altitude. The view follows the latest position; zoom and pan with the mouse.
- Best for: vehicle tracking, drone telemetry, field measurements.
- Requires: datasets with latitude, longitude, and optionally altitude.
- Needs an internet connection for map tiles. Previously viewed areas are cached.
- Only the first base map style is free; the additional styles in the **Base Map** dropdown require Pro.
docs.title: Widget-Reference#6

docs.body:
### Gyroscope

- Widget key: `"gyro"` (also accepts `"gyroscope"`).
- Attitude indicator showing yaw, pitch, roll.
- Best for: IMU visualization, drone orientation, robotics.
- Requires: exactly 3 datasets, in group order yaw, pitch, roll.
- Expects absolute angles in degrees. If your sensor only provides angular rates (deg/s), integrate them with the **Integrate Rate to Angle** transform template.

### Accelerometer

- Widget key: `"accelerometer"`.
- 3-axis acceleration visualization with a computed total G-force: pitch, roll, peak G and magnitude, over a configurable max G range.
- Best for: vibration analysis, impact detection, motion sensing.
- Requires: exactly 3 datasets, in group order X, Y, Z acceleration.
docs.title: Widget-Reference#7

docs.body: ### LED Panel
docs.title: Widget-Reference#8

docs.body:
- Widget key: `"ledpanel"`.
- One multi-state indicator light per dataset in the group, with the dataset title beside it.
- With alarm bands defined, each light takes the color of the band the value sits in, shows the band's `label` next to the title, and flashes while a band marked `blink` is active. Outside every band, the light is off (annunciator-panel behavior).
- Without bands, the light falls back to a single threshold: on (dataset color) when the value meets or exceeds `ledHigh` (default 80).
- Every dataset in the group is a light, **Hide on Dashboard** included, exactly as every dataset in a Bar Panel group is a row. To show a value both in a Data Grid and as a light, add it to both groups; datasets may share a Frame Index.
- Best for: status flags, limit indicators, digital I/O states, annunciator panels.
- Configuration: set the group widget to **LED Panel**, then either define `alarmBands` (see [Alarm bands](#alarm-bands)) or set `ledHigh` on each dataset.
- Projects saved by an earlier version flagged individual datasets with `led: true` instead. On load, each group that had lights gains a `<Group> LEDs` group right after it holding copies of those datasets, saved workspaces keep pointing at the panel, and the project is marked modified so you can save the new form. A flagged dataset that was also hidden showed no light and is not copied.
docs.title: Widget-Reference#9

docs.body:
### 3D Plot (Pro)

- Widget key: `"plot3d"`.
- 3D scatter and trajectory visualization.
- Orbit or free-camera navigation.
- Optional anaglyph stereo (red/cyan 3D glasses).
- Interpolation support.
- Best for: 3D position tracking, spatial data, point clouds.
- Recommended: 3 datasets tagged x/y/z; any axis without a tagged dataset renders at 0.
- Renders through Serial Studio's custom QPainter-based 3D pipeline. No GPU or OpenGL driver required. Runs on low-end hardware including Raspberry Pi.
- Pro. The first use offers a free trial (internet needed); see [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md).

### Image View (Pro)
docs.title: Widget-Reference#10

docs.body:
- Widget key: `"image"`.
- Live JPEG/PNG/BMP/WebP image streaming from the device.
- Autodetect or manual frame delimiter configuration.
- Independent frame reader per widget. Image frames and CSV telemetry coexist in the same byte stream.
- Export, zoom, and image filter toolbar controls.
- Best for: camera feeds, thermal imaging, visual inspection.
- Group-level configuration fields:
  - `imgDetectionMode`: `"autodetect"` (default, uses format magic bytes) or `"manual"` (user-defined delimiters).
  - `imgStartSequence`: hex start delimiter (manual mode only).
  - `imgEndSequence`: hex end delimiter (manual mode only).
- No datasets required inside the group. The widget reads raw image bytes directly from the transport stream.
- Pro. The first use offers a free trial (internet needed); see [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md).
docs.title: Widget-Reference#11

docs.body: ### Canvas (Pro)
docs.title: Widget-Reference#12

docs.body:
- Widget key: `"painter"`.
- User-scripted dashboard widget. The script defines a JavaScript `paint(ctx, w, h)` callback (and an optional `onFrame()` callback) that renders directly into the widget's bitmap on every dashboard tick.
- Eighteen templates ship, one of them blank. Examples: Oscilloscope, Dial gauge, Polar plot, Radar sweep, Artificial horizon and Heatmap; the full list is under [Built-in templates](Canvas-Widget.md#built-in-templates).
- The script reads the group's datasets through a `datasets` global and dashboard tick metadata through `frame.number` / `frame.timestampMs`.
- Best for visualizations not covered by any built-in widget: instrument mimics, project-specific layouts, lab-equipment-style readouts.
- Repaints at the dashboard refresh rate (60 Hz by default, configurable 1-240 Hz). A 250 ms watchdog terminates the script if a single call does not return.
- See the [Canvas Widget](Canvas-Widget.md) reference for the full API.
- Pro. The first use offers a free trial (internet needed); see [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md).
docs.title: Widget-Reference#13

docs.body:
### Web View

- Widget key: `"webview"`.
- Embeds a web page inside a dashboard group, backed by Qt WebEngine (Chromium).
- The only configuration is a URL, set in the group's settings in the Project Editor.
- Group-level configuration fields:
  - `webViewUrl`: the address to load.
- No datasets required inside the group.
- Best for: embedding a live map, a 3D model viewer, a hardware vendor's web dashboard, or any HTML content alongside your telemetry. The ISS Tracker example uses it to show a NASA glTF model of the station.
- Requires a build compiled with Qt WebEngine. On builds without it, the widget shows a "Web View Unavailable" placeholder instead of failing to load the project.
docs.title: Widget-Reference#14

docs.body:
## Dataset widgets

Bar, Gauge, Compass and Meter each have two pages; see their sections.

### Plot

- One per dataset with **Plot** switched on in the Project Editor (project-file key `graph: true`).
- Single-curve 2D time-series line chart with an auto-scaling Y-axis, or a fixed range with `plotMin` and `plotMax`.
- Optional custom X-axis from another dataset (`xAxis`), which enables XY/scatter plots.
- Pause stops appending samples and keeps the history you already have.
- Best for: individual signal monitoring, trend analysis.

### FFT Plot
docs.title: Widget-Reference#15

docs.body:
- One per dataset with **FFT Plot** switched on in the Project Editor (`fft: true`).
- Real-time frequency spectrum analysis via Fast Fourier Transform (KissFFT).
- Configurable FFT window size: 8 to 262144 samples (powers of 2). Default 256.
- Selectable window function applied before the transform to reduce spectral leakage (15 options, from Rectangular to Flat Top). Default Blackman-Harris. The same window is used by the Waterfall widget.
- Configurable sampling rate determines the frequency axis (default 100 Hz).
- Configurable frequency range via `fftMin` and `fftMax`.
- [Frequency markers](#frequency-markers) name frequencies or ranges on the plot and show their live level.
- Best for: vibration frequency analysis, audio spectrum, signal quality.
- Configuration fields: `fftSamples` (window size), `fftWindow` (window function), `fftSamplingRate` (Hz), `fftMin`, `fftMax`.
docs.title: Widget-Reference#16

docs.body: ### Waterfall (Pro)
docs.title: Widget-Reference#17

docs.body:
- One per dataset with **Waterfall** switched on in the Project Editor (`waterfall: true`).
- Scrolling time-frequency plot (spectrogram). Each row is one FFT magnitude spectrum, with the newest row drawn at the top and older rows scrolling down.
- Reuses the dataset's [FFT Plot](#fft-plot) settings (`fftSamples`, `fftWindow`, `fftSamplingRate`, `fftMin`, `fftMax`). The Waterfall caps the transform at 65536 samples; a larger `fftSamples` is clamped. Enable both `fft: true` and `waterfall: true` if you want the FFT plot alongside the waterfall.
- Magnitude is converted to dB. The dynamic range (`minDb` / `maxDb`) is adjustable from the widget toolbar.
- Built-in color maps, sequential: Viridis, Inferno, Magma, Plasma, Turbo, Jet, Hot, Cividis, Cubehelix, SDR Classic, Grayscale, Grayscale (Inverted). Diverging (mid-scale neutral, so an idle spectrogram reads as the low-end color rather than black): Spectral, Red/Blue, Coolwarm.
- Mouse wheel to zoom, drag to pan, hover for a frequency/time readout. Reset view from the toolbar.
- Configurable history depth: 16 to 4096 stored rows.
- Draws the same [frequency markers](#frequency-markers) as the FFT Plot.
- **Y-axis source.** Defaults to elapsed time. Set `waterfallYAxis` to another dataset's `uniqueId` to drive the Y axis from that dataset's value instead. This is typically used for order-tracking plots (for example RPM vs. frequency).
- Best for: vibration order tracking, audio spectrograms, RF band monitoring, transient frequency events.
- Configuration fields: `waterfall: true`, `waterfallYAxis` (0 = time; otherwise the `uniqueId` of the dataset to use as the Y axis), plus the FFT fields listed in this section.
- Pro. The first use offers a free trial (internet needed); see [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md).
docs.title: Widget-Reference#18

docs.body:
### Bar

- Widget key: `"bar"`.
- Horizontal bar gauge with min/max range, current value and units, and color-banded alarm zones with per-band severity (Info / OK / Warning / Critical).
- Two pages: analog display and large digital readout. Swipe horizontally or use the page dots at the bottom; each tile remembers its page in the project file.
- Best for: bounded values such as a tank level or a battery percentage.
- Configuration fields (project-file keys): `widgetMin` (default 0), `widgetMax` (default 0), `alarmBands` (array; see [Alarm bands](#alarm-bands)). Swapped min and max values are put in order.
docs.title: Widget-Reference#19

docs.body:
### Gauge

- Widget key: `"gauge"`.
- Circular or arc gauge display with colored outer-rim arc segments for each alarm band.
- Two pages: analog display and large digital readout; swipe or use the page dots.
- Configuration fields (project-file keys): `widgetMin` (default 0), `widgetMax` (default 0), `alarmBands`.

### Compass

- Widget key: `"compass"`.
- Heading indicator (0 to 360 degrees) that converts a numeric heading to a cardinal direction (N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW).
- Two pages: analog display and large digital readout, which adds the cardinal direction; swipe or use the page dots.
- Configuration: none beyond the value itself (0 to 360).
docs.title: Widget-Reference#20

docs.body:
### Meter

- Widget key: `"meter"`.
- Analog half-arc meter with a sweeping needle, tick marks, colored arc bands, and value readout.
- Two pages: analog display and large digital readout; swipe or use the page dots.
- Configuration fields (project-file keys): `widgetMin` (default 0), `widgetMax` (default 0), `alarmBands`.

## Alarm bands

An alarm band is a value range with a color and a severity. This gauge draws an 80 to 100 Warning zone on the dial and raises a Warning when the value gets there:

```json
{ "title": "Coolant", "widget": "gauge", "widgetMin": 0, "widgetMax": 120,
  "alarmBands": [ { "min": 80, "max": 100, "severity": 2, "label": "Hot" } ] }
```
docs.title: Widget-Reference#21

docs.body: Edit bands with the **Alarm Bands** button in the dataset toolbar (next to **Transform**). It opens a dialog with presets (Tachometer, Speedometer, Engine Temperature, Pressure, Battery Voltage, Fuel Level, Signal Strength, CPU / System Load, OK / Warning / Critical, Indicator (On / Off), Fault Indicator), a per-band color picker, severity selector, blink toggle, and a live preview strip.
docs.title: Widget-Reference#22

docs.body: Bar, Gauge, Meter, Bar Panel, and LED Panel widgets render alarm bands. Bands are always drawn in full: muted zones along the bar track (Bar / Bar Panel) or arc segments on the dial rim (Gauge / Meter). The fill or needle takes the active band's color, so a value in the normal range reads as a green signal. A value outside every band takes the nearest band's severity, so overrange data renders as critical rather than unclassified. LED Panel entries light in the active band's color. The tachometer convention (white below normal, green operating range, yellow caution, red redline) is one setup; any combination of ranges and colors is allowed.
docs.title: Widget-Reference#23

docs.body:
Bands take effect only on a dataset that one of these widgets shows: a dataset with a Bar, Gauge, or Meter widget, or any dataset in a Bar Panel or LED Panel group. **Hide on Dashboard** removes the first case, because a hidden dataset gets no widget of its own; Bar Panel rows and LED Panel lights are unaffected. On any other dataset (a plot-only dataset, for example) the bands are kept in the project file but are not drawn, post no notification, and raise no [alarm point](Aural-Alerts.md). Assigning one of the widgets again brings them back.

Three dataset options in the Widget Settings control when bands alert:
docs.title: Widget-Reference#24

docs.body:
| Option (project-file key)                      | Effect | Default |
|------------------------------------------------|--------|---------|
| **Suppress Alarms** (`suppressAlarms`)         | Bands stay drawn, but the dataset posts no notification, raises no alarm point and plays no sound. A redline that should be seen but not heard is the usual case. | Off |
| **Alarms only while visible** (`alarmsWhileVisible`) | The dataset alerts only while a widget showing it is on screen. **Suppress Alarms** wins when both are on. | Off |
| **Alarm Deadband** (`alarmDeadband`)           | Hysteresis in the dataset's units: an active band holds until the value leaves it by more than the deadband. | 0 |
docs.title: Widget-Reference#25

docs.body:
**Alarms only while visible.** The bands stay drawn and the dataset keeps recording, but a notification, an alarm point and a sound happen only while a widget showing the dataset is on screen. A widget showing the dataset counts as on screen when all of these hold:

- It sits on the active tab of the main dashboard (Dashboard pane shown) or of an external dashboard window.
- The window is not minimized.
- The widget itself is neither minimized nor closed.

An open pop-out counts, and so does a frozen dashboard. Revealing the dataset while its value already sits in a Warning or Critical band counts as entering the band, so the point and the notification arrive at once. Hiding it removes the point, and nothing is recorded for the time it was hidden. One project can carry several device profiles on their own workspaces this way: only the profile the operator is looking at alerts.
docs.title: Widget-Reference#26

docs.body:
**Alarm Deadband.** A value that hovers on a band edge would enter and leave the band on every frame, raising a point each time. The hold only ever delays a step down: a move into a more severe band takes effect immediately, so a deadband never postpones a Critical. A temperature with a Warning band at 80 and a deadband of 1 alarms at 80.0 and clears at 78.9, not at 79.9.

**Band schema.** Under the dataset's `alarmBands` array, each entry is an object:
docs.title: Widget-Reference#27

docs.body:
| Field      | Type   | Required | Notes |
|------------|--------|----------|-------|
| `min`      | double | yes      | Lower bound of the band (inclusive). |
| `max`      | double | yes      | Upper bound of the band (inclusive: a value is in the band when `min <= value <= max`). |
| `severity` | int    | yes      | `0` = Info, `1` = OK, `2` = Warning, `3` = Critical. Drives the default color. Only `2` and `3` raise a notification on entry. |
| `color`    | string | no       | Hex override (`"#rrggbb"`). When empty, the severity's theme color is used (theme switches re-tint live). |
| `label`    | string | no       | Optional human-readable name. Surfaces in the band-edge notification subtitle and next to the dataset title on LED panels. |
| `blink`    | bool   | no       | When `true`, LED panels flash the LED while the value sits in this band. Defaults to `false`. |
| `sound`    | string | no       | WAV file played instead of the priority's default when the value enters this band (see [Aural Alerts](Aural-Alerts.md)). Relative paths resolve against the project file's folder. Omitted when empty. |
docs.title: Widget-Reference#28

docs.body: Severity is a separate scale from [notification](Notifications.md) `level` (`0` = Info, `1` = Warning, `2` = Critical): band severity 2 posts level `Warning` (1) and severity 3 posts level `Critical` (2).
docs.title: Widget-Reference#29

docs.body:
Bands may have gaps, may overlap, and need not cover the full range. Overlaps resolve to the FIRST matching band in list order, not the last. A gap only leaves the painted track/background uncolored: the bar fill or needle itself still takes a band's color, clamped to whichever band is nearest.
**Notifications and aural alerts.** Entering a Warning or Critical band also raises an alarm point on the master annunciator, the bell in the taskbar tray (see [Aural Alerts](Aural-Alerts.md)); leaving it returns the point to normal. When the value enters a band with severity ≥ Warning, Serial Studio posts a notification on the "Alarms" channel, with the band's `label` in the subtitle. Alarm tracking runs per dataset at the dashboard level, so notifications fire even when the widget displaying the dataset is hidden or not instantiated. The 3 second cooldown is tracked per dataset and per severity tier: a dataset's Warning is suppressed by its own Warning or Critical within 3 seconds, a Critical only by its own Critical, so escalating from Warning to Critical always posts.
**Legacy compatibility.** Project files written by older Serial Studio releases carry `alarmEnabled` / `alarmLow` / `alarmHigh` instead of `alarmBands`. On load, those are converted to two `Warning`-severity bands (`[widgetMin..alarmLow]` and `[alarmHigh..widgetMax]`). The legacy keys are not written back; re-saved projects carry only `alarmBands`. For canvas scripts (Pro), `dataset.alarmLow` and `dataset.alarmHigh` remain readable as derived values (first / last `Warning+` band edges) so existing scripts keep working.
docs.title: Widget-Reference#30

docs.body:
## Frequency markers

A frequency marker names a frequency or a range on a dataset's FFT Plot and Waterfall and shows the live level there, which keeps a known line in view: mains hum, a resonance, the band where a bearing defect appears. Markers are free on the FFT Plot. The Waterfall is Pro (see [Pro vs Free](Pro-vs-Free.md)).

In the [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md), select a dataset with FFT or Waterfall enabled and click **Freq. Markers** on the dataset toolbar. The **Frequency Markers** dialog holds one row per marker, and a strip at the bottom previews them from 0 Hz to the top of the range.
docs.title: Widget-Reference#31

docs.body:
| Column | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **Start (Hz)** | Frequency of a point marker, or the low edge of a band. A row left at 0 is dropped on **Apply**. |
| **End (Hz)** | High edge of a band. Left empty, or not above **Start (Hz)**, the row is a point marker. |
| **Warn (dB)**, **Alarm (dB)** | Levels from -200 to 100 at which the marker changes color. Left empty, the level is off. |
| **Color** | Click to choose a color; right-click to return to the automatic color. |
| **Label** | Name shown on the marker. Without one, the marker shows its frequency. |

Frequencies stop at half the FFT sampling rate, shown as **Frequency range** at the top of the dialog. **Preset** replaces the table with a watchlist and skips any entry above that range: **Mains Hum (50 Hz + harmonics)**, **Mains Hum (60 Hz + harmonics)**, or **Octave Bands (31.5 Hz - 16 kHz)**.
docs.title: Widget-Reference#32

docs.body:
On the dashboard a point marker is a vertical line and a band is a shaded region. Each marker carries a chip with its name and its peak level in dB, measured on the spectrum as displayed: inside the band, or within two FFT bins either side of a point marker. On the FFT Plot, clicking a chip highlights that marker and dims the others. **Show Frequency Markers** on the widget toolbar hides or shows them all; the FFT Plot offers this button only when the dataset has markers.

**The levels only change the color.** A peak at or above **Warn (dB)** draws the marker in the theme's Warning color, and at or above **Alarm (dB)** in its Critical color. A marker raises no alarm point, notification, or sound. For an alert you can hear, use [alarm bands](#alarm-bands) on a Bar, Gauge, or Meter.
docs.title: Widget-Reference#33

docs.body:
In the project file, markers are the dataset's `fftMarkers` array. This dataset is sampled at 2000 Hz, so its range ends at 1000 Hz:

```json
"fftMarkers": [
  { "freq": 50, "label": "Mains", "color": "#ffb300" },
  { "freq": 120, "endFreq": 180, "label": "Bearing", "warningDb": -40, "alarmDb": -20 }
]
```

On load, an entry whose `freq` is not above 0 is dropped, an `endFreq` not above `freq` makes a point marker, and a `warningDb` above `alarmDb` swaps the two. The API commands are `project.dataset.getFFTMarkers` and `project.dataset.setFFTMarkers` in the [API Reference](API-Reference.md).
docs.title: Widget-Reference#34

docs.body:
## Utility widgets

Terminal, Clock and Stopwatch are dashboard-level utility widgets, free in every build. They are not attached to any group or dataset. Toggle them with the **Console**, **Clock** and **Stopwatch** buttons on the dashboard taskbar, or from the **Start menu**. Each remembers between sessions whether it was on; all three start off.

### Terminal

- Shows the raw text stream from the device, with VT-100 emulation and ANSI colors.
- Keystrokes typed into it go to the connected device.
- The taskbar calls it **Console**.

### Clock

- Page 0 is an analog face, page 1 a digital readout (12-hour time and date). Driven by the system clock, ticks once per second.
- The active page is remembered between sessions.
- Best for: visible session timestamps in screen recordings, lab/operator dashboards.
docs.title: Widget-Reference#35

docs.body:
### Stopwatch

- Single-page widget: large `HH:MM:SS.mmm` readout, **Start/Stop**, **Lap**, **Reset** buttons, and a scrollable lap table.
- Local-only timing; data is not persisted to the project, transmitted, or sent to the device.
- Best for: bench testing, run/test timing during a session.

## Dataset fields reference

Every dataset in a project file supports these visualization-related fields:
docs.title: Widget-Reference#38

docs.body:
| Field              | Type   | Default | Description |
|--------------------|--------|---------|-------------|
| `index`            | int    | 0       | Frame offset index (column position in CSV data). |
| `title`            | string | (none)  | Human-readable display name. |
| `units`            | string | (none)  | Measurement units (for example "m/s", "degC"). |
| `widget`           | string | `""`    | Dataset widget type: `"bar"`, `"gauge"`, `"compass"`, or `"meter"`. |
| `graph`            | bool   | false   | Enable time-series plot. |
| `fft`              | bool   | false   | Enable FFT spectrum plot. |
| `waterfall`        | bool   | false   | Enable waterfall (spectrogram) plot. Pro. |
| `waterfallYAxis`   | int    | 0       | Waterfall Y-axis source: 0 = time, otherwise the `uniqueId` of another dataset (order tracking). |
| `log`              | bool   | false   | Enable logging to file. |
| `overviewDisplay`  | bool   | false   | Show in the overview/status bar. |
| `plotMin`          | double | 0       | Plot Y-axis minimum (0 = auto-scale). |
| `plotMax`          | double | 0       | Plot Y-axis maximum (0 = auto-scale). |
| `widgetMin`        | double | 0       | Widget (bar/gauge/meter) minimum. |
| `widgetMax`        | double | 0       | Widget (bar/gauge/meter) maximum. |
| `displayTickCount` | int    | 5       | Major-tick count on the dial scale (0 = auto-fit to widget size). Editor label "Tick Count". |
| `displayFormat`    | string | `"0d"`  | Decimal places on analog widget ticks and captions; Hexadecimal and Binary apply wherever the value is shown as text. Editor label "Label Format". |
| `decimalPoints`    | int    | -1      | Fixed decimal places for the value display; overrides `displayFormat` (-1 = auto). Editor label "Decimal Points". |
| `extremeHold`      | bool   | false   | Shows tick marks at the lowest and highest values observed since the last data reset. Editor label "Hold Min/Max Markers". |
| `ledHigh`          | double | 80      | Light-on threshold for a dataset in an LED Panel group (used only when `alarmBands` is empty). |
| `alarmBands`       | array  | `[]`    | Colored value bands for bar/gauge/meter widgets, LED panels, and bar panels; ignored on any other dataset. Each entry: `{min, max, severity, color?, label?, blink?}`; see [Alarm bands](#alarm-bands). Legacy `alarmEnabled` / `alarmLow` / `alarmHigh` keys from older releases are still read and migrated to bands on load, but no longer written. |
| `suppressAlarms`   | bool   | false   | Keeps the dataset's alarm bands drawn but stops its band notifications, alarm points, and sounds. Written only when true. Editor label "Suppress Alarms". |
| `alarmsWhileVisible` | bool | false   | The dataset's alarm bands notify, raise alarm points, and sound only while a widget showing it is on screen (see [Alarm bands](#alarm-bands)); `suppressAlarms` wins when both are set. Written only when true. Editor label "Alarms only while visible". |
| `alarmDeadband`    | double | 0       | Hysteresis in the dataset's units: the active alarm band holds until the value leaves it by more than this; escalation is never delayed. Must be >= 0; written only when positive. Editor label "Alarm Deadband". |
| `fftSamples`       | int    | 256     | FFT window size (power of 2, 8 to 262144). The Waterfall clamps it to 65536. |
| `fftWindow`        | int    | 5       | FFT window function, applied to both the FFT plot and the waterfall: 0 = Rectangular, 1 = Bartlett, 2 = Hann, 3 = Hamming, 4 = Blackman, 5 = Blackman-Harris, 6 = Nuttall, 7 = Blackman-Nuttall, 8 = Flat Top, 9 = Welch, 10 = Bartlett-Hann, 11 = Bohman, 12 = Cosine, 13 = Lanczos, 14 = Parzen. |
| `fftSamplingRate`  | int    | 100     | FFT sampling rate in Hz. |
| `fftMin`           | double | 0       | FFT frequency axis minimum. |
| `fftMax`           | double | 0       | FFT frequency axis maximum. |
| `fftMarkers`       | array  | none    | [Frequency markers](#frequency-markers) drawn on the FFT Plot and Waterfall. Written only when not empty. |
| `labels`           | array  | none    | Value-to-text table, entries `{"value": <integer>, "text": <string>}`. Editor button "Labels"; see the [Project Editor](Project-Editor.md). |
| `labelsDefault`    | string | ""      | Text shown for a value no `labels` entry lists; empty shows the number. Editor row "Any other". |
| `xAxis`            | int    | -2      | X-axis source: `-2` = time (default), `-1` = sample count (the **Samples** choice in the X-Axis Source combo), or the `uniqueId` of another dataset for an XY plot. |

docs.body:
# gRPC server

## What gRPC does in Serial Studio

The gRPC server is in the free edition and needs no license.

Your Arduino prints values and Serial Studio plots them. gRPC is for the next step: a program of your own, in Python, Go, C++ or any other language, that reads those frames (one line of values from your device, parsed into fields) or controls Serial Studio. You do not need it to build a dashboard.

Serial Studio exposes its whole command set over gRPC, a binary protocol, on port 8888. A command is a named action such as `io.getStatus`, which reports whether a device is connected. Any command available on the [TCP/JSON API](API-Reference.md) (port 7777) also runs over gRPC.
docs.title: gRPC-Server#0

docs.body:
## Turning gRPC on

Port 8888 stays closed until the API Server is on, and the API Server is off by default. Until then a client gets "connection refused".

1. Click **Preferences** in the toolbar.
2. On the **General** tab, scroll to the **API & Plugins** section.
3. Turn on **Enable API Server**.

The toggle takes effect immediately. The TCP/JSON server opens on the port set in **API Server Port** (1024-65535, default 7777), and the gRPC server opens on port 8888 with it. The gRPC port is fixed and does not follow **API Server Port**. Turning the toggle off closes both. If another program already holds port 8888, Serial Studio shows an "Unable to start gRPC server" dialog ("Failed to bind to ...") and the gRPC server stays off.
docs.title: gRPC-Server#1

docs.body:
> **Built from source?** gRPC is compiled in only with `-DENABLE_GRPC=ON`, and the CMake default is `OFF`. Without it, port 8888 never opens and the **Export Protobuf File** row is missing from **API & Plugins**. "Connection refused" on 8888 means the API Server toggle is off or the build lacks gRPC.

## Quick start (grpcurl)

[grpcurl](https://github.com/fullstorydev/grpcurl) is a command-line gRPC client. Download [`serialstudio.proto`](https://github.com/Serial-Studio/Serial-Studio/blob/master/doc/grpc/serialstudio.proto) into the current folder first: the server does not offer reflection, so grpcurl needs the file to know the service.
docs.title: gRPC-Server#2

docs.body:
```bash
# List available commands
grpcurl -plaintext -import-path . -proto serialstudio.proto \
  -d '{}' localhost:8888 serialstudio.SerialStudioAPI/ListCommands

# Execute a command
grpcurl -plaintext -import-path . -proto serialstudio.proto \
  -d '{"command":"io.getStatus","id":"1"}' \
  localhost:8888 serialstudio.SerialStudioAPI/ExecuteCommand

# Stream frames (Ctrl+C to stop)
grpcurl -plaintext -import-path . -proto serialstudio.proto \
  -d '{}' localhost:8888 serialstudio.SerialStudioAPI/StreamFrames
```

`ListCommands` returns every command name you can pass to `ExecuteCommand`. The [API Reference](API-Reference.md) describes each one. `io.getStatus` reports whether a device is connected. `StreamFrames` prints nothing until a device sends data.
docs.title: gRPC-Server#3

docs.body:
## Quick start (Python)

Connect a device, or start a project that produces frames, before running the streaming loop (see [Getting Started](Getting-Started.md)). Download `serialstudio.proto` as in the grpcurl quick start, then install the packages and generate the stubs:

```bash
pip install grpcio grpcio-tools
python -m grpc_tools.protoc -I. --python_out=. --grpc_python_out=. serialstudio.proto
```

```python
import grpc
import serialstudio_pb2 as pb
import serialstudio_pb2_grpc as rpc

channel = grpc.insecure_channel('localhost:8888')
stub = rpc.SerialStudioAPIStub(channel)

resp = stub.ExecuteCommand(pb.CommandRequest(id="1", command="io.getStatus"))
print(resp.result)
docs.title: gRPC-Server#4

docs.body:
# Each message is a FrameBatch
for batch in stub.StreamFrames(pb.StreamRequest()):
    for frame in batch.frames:
        print(frame.timestamp_ms, frame.frame)
```

## Service definition

The service is `SerialStudioAPI` in package `serialstudio`, defined in [`doc/grpc/serialstudio.proto`](https://github.com/Serial-Studio/Serial-Studio/blob/master/doc/grpc/serialstudio.proto).
docs.title: gRPC-Server#5

docs.body:
| RPC               | Description |
|-------------------|-------------|
| `ExecuteCommand`  | Execute a single API command and get the result. |
| `ExecuteBatch`    | Execute multiple commands in one request. |
| `StreamFrames`    | Server-streaming RPC that pushes parsed frames in real time. |
| `StreamRawData`   | Server-streaming RPC that pushes raw bytes from the device. Each message is a `RawBatch` whose `packets` hold `data` (bytes) and `timestamp_ms` (steady clock, as for `FrameData`). |
| `WriteRawData`    | Send raw bytes to the connected device. |
| `ListCommands`    | List all available API commands. |
docs.title: gRPC-Server#6

docs.body:
**Limits**

| Limit | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Frames per `FrameBatch` | 4096 |
| Payload of one `WriteRawData` | 1 MiB |
| Server-side queue for frames and for raw data | 4096 entries each; when a queue is full, new entries are dropped |

## Generating client stubs

Download `doc/grpc/serialstudio.proto` from the Serial Studio repository, then generate stubs for your language. The Python command is in the [Python quick start](#quick-start-python):

```bash
# C++
```

## Frame streaming

`StreamFrames` in the gRPC server (free edition) gives each client its own stream. The TCP/JSON server instead broadcasts JSON lines to every connected client. The server queues frames only while at least one client is streaming, so a client that connects late misses earlier frames, and frames sent while your stream is down are not replayed.

## External connections

The gRPC server (free edition) has no external-access setting of its own. It follows **Allow External API Connections** in **Preferences → General → API & Plugins**:

| Allow External API Connections | TCP/JSON (7777)  | gRPC (8888)      |
|--------------------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Off (default)                  | `127.0.0.1:7777` | `127.0.0.1:8888` |
| On                             | `0.0.0.0:7777`   | `0.0.0.0:8888`   |

Turning the switch on asks "Allow External API Connections?" with Yes and No, defaulting to No. Changing it restarts the gRPC listener, which ends any open streams.
docs.title: gRPC-Server#10

docs.body:
> **Security note.** External connections expose the API to your network, and the channel is plaintext: there is no TLS, so the token crosses the network in the clear. Keep external access off when you do not need it, and use a trusted network or tunnel when you do.
>
> Non-loopback clients must send the access token in the `x-serial-studio-token` request metadata; copy it from the **API Access Token** field. Loopback clients (`127.0.0.1` / `::1`) are exempt. A missing or wrong token gets gRPC status `UNAUTHENTICATED` ("Authentication required").

The **API Access Token** field is read-only and active only while **Allow External API Connections** is on. The refresh button next to it generates a new token.

## Typed schema export

**Preferences → General → API & Plugins → Export Protobuf File → Export…** writes an auto-generated typed schema (package `serialstudio.typed`, service `SerialStudioTypedAPI`) with one request message and one RPC per registered command. Use it as machine-readable documentation of every command's parameters. The running server implements only the `SerialStudioAPI` service, so generate client stubs from `serialstudio.proto`, not from the typed file.

## Comparison with the TCP/JSON API

| Feature            | TCP/JSON (port 7777)        | gRPC (port 8888)               |
|--------------------|-----------------------------|--------------------------------|
| Encoding           | JSON text                   | Protobuf binary                |
| Code generation    | Manual parsing              | Auto-generated stubs           |
| Browser support    | No                          | Needs a grpc-web proxy         |
| Tooling            | `nc`, `curl`, any TCP client | gRPC tooling                  |
